notes.content:
Database & Distributed Data Systems

Last-Minute Revision Handbook

Partitioning • Sharding • Replication • Rebalancing • Indexes • Transactions • Consistency • Distributed Databases

The interview mindsetFor every database decision, ask four questions: (1) What is the access pattern? (2) What must be consistent? (3) What can fail? (4) How will the system scale and rebalance? Most good answers are trade-offs between latency, throughput, consistency, availability, and operational complexity.



1. Data Models: Relational vs Document vs Key-Value vs Graph

Relational databases model normalized tables and relationships; strong fit for structured transactional data and joins.

Document databases keep related aggregates together; good when application reads/writes whole documents and schema evolves frequently.

Key-value stores optimize simple exact-key access and horizontal partitioning.

Graph databases optimize multi-hop relationship traversal, where joins over edges are the primary access pattern.

Interview rule: choose the model from access patterns, not from fashion.

2. OLTP vs OLAP

OLTP: many small reads/writes, low latency, user-facing transactions, row-oriented storage is common.

OLAP: large scans/aggregations, fewer writes, columnar storage and compression are common.

Mixing heavy analytics with OLTP can create resource contention; CDC/ETL to a warehouse is a standard separation.

3. Row-Oriented vs Column-Oriented Storage

Row store keeps all columns of a row together; efficient for point reads/writes of whole records.

Column store keeps values of the same column together; efficient for scans over a subset of columns and highly compressible.

Columnar systems often use vectorized execution, predicate pushdown, and late materialization.

4. B-Trees vs LSM-Trees

B-Tree: in-place/page-oriented updates, good read latency, mature range scans, but random-write amplification.

LSM-Tree: writes append to memory/WAL, flush to sorted files, compact later; excellent sequential write throughput but incurs compaction/read amplification.

Interview rule: B-Tree for read-heavy general OLTP; LSM-style for write-heavy ingestion and horizontally distributed storage.

Dimension
	B-Tree
	LSM-Tree

Write path
	Update pages / WAL
	Memtable + WAL, flush SSTables

Read path
	Direct tree traversal
	Check memtable + multiple sorted levels/files

Write amplification
	Page splits / WAL
	Compaction can be high

Read amplification
	Usually low
	Can be multiple files; Bloom filters help

Space amplification
	Moderate
	Old versions exist until compaction

Best fit
	General OLTP
	Write-heavy / distributed stores



5. Why Replicate Data

High availability: another copy can serve after node failure.

Lower latency: place copies near users.

Higher read throughput: spread read traffic.

Durability: tolerate disk/node/site loss.

Cost: replication increases storage, write traffic, and coordination complexity.

6. Leader-Follower Replication

One leader accepts writes and sends a replication log to followers.

Followers apply writes in leader order and can serve reads depending consistency needs.

Failover promotes a follower to leader.

Main challenge: replication lag and ambiguous leader failure.



7. Synchronous vs Asynchronous Replication

Mode
	Benefit
	Cost / Risk

Synchronous
	Follower has confirmed write before ACK; lower RPO
	Higher write latency; follower outage can block writes

Asynchronous
	Low write latency; leader independent of follower delay
	Recent acknowledged writes may be lost on leader failure

Semi-sync
	Wait for one follower, others async
	Middle ground



Interview sentenceUse synchronous replication only where the durability/consistency requirement justifies the latency and availability cost. Many production systems use one synchronous replica plus additional asynchronous replicas.

8. Replication Lag Problems

Read-after-write: user writes then reads from lagging replica and sees old data.

Monotonic reads: user observes newer data, then later gets an older replica and appears to go backward in time.

Consistent prefix reads: related events can appear out of causal order on different replicas.

Mitigations: sticky/session routing, leader reads after writes, version tokens/LSNs, bounded staleness, or causal metadata.

9. Leader Failover

1. Detect leader unavailability using heartbeats/consensus/lease.

2. Choose the most up-to-date eligible follower.

3. Fence old leader so it cannot accept writes after partition recovery.

4. Promote new leader and update routing/metadata.

5. Resync old leader as follower.

Danger: split brain if two leaders accept writes.

Danger: asynchronous replication may lose acknowledged writes.

Danger: stale follower promotion can resurrect old state or violate ordering.

10. Multi-Leader Replication

Multiple regions/leaders accept writes independently and replicate to one another.

Useful for multi-datacenter writes or offline/disconnected clients.

Creates write conflicts that must be detected/resolved.

Conflict approaches: last-write-wins, application merge, CRDT-like merge, custom conflict resolution.

Use only when concurrent writes to same logical records are acceptable/mergeable.

11. Leaderless Replication / Quorums

Clients/coordinators write to multiple replicas directly.

For N replicas, often reason about W acknowledgements for writes and R replicas for reads.

If W + R > N, read/write quorums overlap in idealized conditions.

Read repair and anti-entropy repair converge stale replicas.

Dynamo-style systems use this model with tunable consistency.

Term
	Meaning

N
	Number of replicas

W
	Write acknowledgements required

R
	Read replicas consulted

W + R > N
	Potential overlapping quorum

Sloppy quorum
	Use healthy fallback nodes when intended replicas unavailable

Hinted handoff
	Temporary node stores writes for unavailable owner



Quorum caveatW + R > N is not a magic linearizability formula. Network partitions, concurrent writes, sloppy quorums, clock issues, and conflict resolution still matter.



12. Partitioning / Sharding: Why

One machine cannot hold unlimited data or traffic.

Partition data across nodes so storage and throughput scale horizontally.

Good partitioning spreads both data size and request load.

Bad partitioning creates hot shards even when total cluster capacity is large.

13. Partition by Key Range

Example: A-M on shard 1, N-Z on shard 2, or timestamp ranges.

Excellent for range scans and ordered access.

Risk: sequential keys/timestamps send all new writes to one hot range.

Needs dynamic range splitting/merging to stay balanced.

14. Hash Partitioning

Compute hash(partition_key) and map hash range/bucket to shard.

Usually distributes keys more evenly.

Excellent exact-key scalability.

Range scans across original key order become expensive because adjacent keys are scattered.



15. Choosing the Partition Key

Partition key should distribute traffic, not just bytes.

It should align with dominant lookup pattern so one request hits one/few shards.

Avoid low-cardinality keys such as country if one value dominates.

Avoid monotonically increasing key as the only shard key in hash-unaware range systems.

Composite keys can combine tenant_id + hash(entity_id) or tenant_id + time bucket.

16. Hot Keys and Hot Partitions

Hot key = one logical key receives disproportionate traffic.

Hashing cannot split a single hot key automatically if all traffic must reach one owner.

Mitigations: cache hot reads, replicate read ownership, salt/shard a logical key, split counters, isolate celebrity tenants, use hierarchical aggregation.

For write hot keys, correctness requirements determine whether writes can be spread and later merged.

Classic exampleA celebrity account or global counter can overload one shard even with perfect hash distribution. Partitioning solves many-key imbalance, not a single inherently hot item.



17. Secondary Indexes in a Sharded Database

Approach
	How it works
	Trade-off

Local / document-partitioned index
	Index entries stored on same shard as base records
	Writes cheap; query by secondary field fans out to all shards

Global / term-partitioned index
	Index partitioned by indexed term
	Fast targeted reads; writes become distributed and harder to keep consistent



18. Rebalancing

Needed when adding/removing nodes, data grows unevenly, or hot shards emerge.

Goal: move ownership without large downtime or overload.

Naive hash(key) % N remaps most keys whenever N changes — usually bad.

Prefer fixed partitions/virtual nodes or dynamic ranges.

19. Fixed Number of Partitions

Create many logical partitions up front, many more than physical nodes.

Assign partitions to nodes; adding a node moves some partitions.

Simple and predictable but initial partition count must be chosen well.

20. Dynamic Partitioning

Ranges split when too large/hot and merge when small.

Adapts naturally to data growth.

Needs metadata service and split/merge machinery.

Empty dataset may need pre-splitting to avoid one initial hotspot.

21. Virtual Nodes / Consistent Hashing

Hash ring has many virtual positions per physical node.

Each node owns multiple small ranges; adding/removing nodes moves only a subset.

Virtual nodes help smooth uneven ownership and heterogeneous capacity.

Production systems often use explicit token/range assignment rather than a simplistic textbook ring.



22. Rebalancing Best Practices

Move data gradually; throttle migration so foreground traffic wins.

Replicate/copy first, verify, then switch ownership, then delete old copy.

Use versioned partition maps/epochs so stale routers cannot write to old owners.

Avoid moving too many replicas of the same failure domain simultaneously.

Monitor bytes moved, queue depth, p99 latency, disk utilization, and replica lag.

23. ACID Refresher

Atomicity: transaction commits all or none.

Consistency: application/database invariants preserved if transaction logic is correct.

Isolation: concurrent transactions behave according to an isolation model.

Durability: committed data survives failures according to durability guarantees.

24. Read Committed

Prevents dirty reads and dirty writes.

Each statement may still see different committed versions.

Non-repeatable reads and write skew are still possible.

25. Snapshot Isolation / MVCC

Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot.

Readers do not block writers; writers create new versions.

Prevents many anomalies but can allow write skew when transactions update different rows based on shared predicate.

MVCC needs garbage collection/vacuum of old versions.

26. Serializable Isolation

Strongest common transaction isolation: result equivalent to some serial order.

Can be implemented with strict two-phase locking, serial execution, or Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI).

Higher coordination/conflict cost than weaker isolation.

Isolation
	Prevents
	Can still allow

Read Uncommitted
	Very little
	Dirty reads/writes, anomalies

Read Committed
	Dirty reads/writes
	Non-repeatable read, lost update (depending DB), write skew

Snapshot Isolation
	Inconsistent reads; often lost update via checks
	Write skew / predicate anomalies

Serializable
	All serialization anomalies
	Performance/abort trade-offs



27. Lost Update

Two transactions read same value, calculate new value, both write; one overwrites the other.

Mitigate with atomic UPDATE expressions, compare-and-set/version columns, explicit locks, or serializable transactions.

Counters should use atomic increments rather than read-modify-write in application code.

28. Write Skew

Two transactions read overlapping data but update different rows, together violating an invariant.

Classic pattern: each checks that at least one resource remains available, then independently removes a different resource.

Snapshot isolation may allow it because there is no direct write-write conflict.

Need serializable isolation, predicate locks, materialized constraint/lock row, or application-level coordination.

29. Two-Phase Locking vs MVCC vs SSI

Approach
	Strength
	Trade-off

2PL
	Locks enforce serial order
	Blocking/deadlocks

MVCC/Snapshot
	Fast reads, fewer blocks
	Write skew possible

SSI
	Serializable with optimistic detection
	Abort/retry under conflicts



30. Distributed Transactions

One logical transaction spans multiple shards/services.

Hard because participants can fail independently and network messages can be lost/duplicated.

Options: 2PC, consensus-backed transaction protocols, sagas/compensation, or redesign to keep invariant local to one partition.

31. Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Phase 1 prepare: participants durably promise they can commit.

Phase 2 commit/abort: coordinator decides and informs participants.

Provides atomic commit but can block when coordinator is unavailable depending implementation.

Prepared transactions hold locks/resources and should be kept short.



32. Sagas

Break a cross-service workflow into local transactions.

On failure, execute compensating actions for prior steps.

Improves availability and autonomy but does not provide strict isolation/atomic rollback.

Best when business operations are naturally compensatable.

33. Linearizability

Each operation appears to occur atomically at one point between request and response.

After a write completes, later reads must observe it (subject to object semantics).

Useful for locks, unique constraints, leader election, account balances/invariants.

Costs coordination and becomes difficult under partitions/latency.

34. Sequential vs Causal vs Eventual Consistency

Sequential: one global order consistent with each client program order, but not necessarily real-time order.

Causal: causally related operations observed in causal order; concurrent independent operations may differ in order.

Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop, but no strong ordering guarantee.

Many social feeds/counters tolerate eventual; identity/locks/payments often need stronger semantics.

35. CAP Theorem - Correct Use

Under a network partition, a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee both availability for every request and linearizable consistency.

CAP is about behavior during partition, not a permanent three-way menu.

Latency and consistency trade-offs in normal operation are often better discussed using PACELC.

36. PACELC

If Partition: choose Availability or Consistency; Else: choose Latency or Consistency.

Useful to discuss geographically distributed databases where stronger consistency adds cross-region RTT even without failure.

Interview heuristicUse strong consistency only for data whose invariant truly requires it. Keep user-facing derived views, search indexes, analytics, feeds, and caches eventually consistent when possible.



37. Consensus: What Problem It Solves

Allows nodes to agree on an ordered log/value despite failures.

Used for leader election, replicated metadata, membership, and strongly consistent state machines.

Raft/Paxos-style systems require a majority quorum for progress.

Consensus does not make every data operation cheap; use it where coordination is needed.

38. Quorum and Majority

In a 3-node consensus group, majority = 2; tolerates 1 failure.

In a 5-node group, majority = 3; tolerates 2 failures.

Adding replicas improves fault tolerance/read locality but makes consensus messages more expensive.

Even-sized groups often add cost without increasing failure tolerance compared with the next lower odd size.

39. Shared-Nothing Distributed Database

Each node owns CPU, memory, disk, and a subset of partitions.

Replication provides durability/HA.

Router/coordinator uses partition map to send requests to owners.

No shared disk bottleneck; operational complexity moves into routing, rebalancing and distributed query/transaction logic.

40. Metadata / Placement Service

Tracks which shard/range/replica lives on which node.

Changes must be versioned/strongly consistent.

Clients/routers cache metadata and refresh on stale-routing errors.

Use epochs/generations to fence old owners.

41. Read Path in a Sharded Replicated DB

Router hashes/ranges the partition key.

Locate replica set.

Choose leader or local replica depending consistency level.

Read from cache/memtable/index/storage.

Return value plus version if needed.

42. Write Path in a Sharded Replicated DB

Route to shard leader/coordinator.

Append to WAL / replicated log.

Replicate to quorum/followers.

Apply to memtable/page structures.

ACK according to durability policy.

Flush/compact asynchronously if LSM-based.

43. Primary vs Secondary Index

Primary/clustered index determines or closely follows physical row organization.

Secondary index maps alternate key to row/primary key.

Every additional index speeds some reads but slows writes and consumes storage.

Interview rule: index only fields used by important access patterns.

44. Composite Indexes

Index (A,B,C) can efficiently serve prefixes beginning with A, then B, etc.

Column order should match filtering/selectivity/order-by patterns.

An index on (tenant_id, created_at) is common for tenant-scoped timelines.

45. Covering Index

Includes all columns needed by query so engine need not fetch base row.

Can dramatically reduce random I/O.

Costs more index storage/write amplification.

46. Bloom Filters

Probabilistic structure says definitely-not-present or maybe-present.

No false negatives; false positives possible.

LSM stores use Bloom filters to avoid checking SSTables that definitely do not contain a key.

47. Write-Ahead Log (WAL)

Persist intent/change sequentially before updating in-memory/page state.

After crash, replay WAL to recover committed changes.

Group commit batches fsync cost across transactions.

WAL also feeds replication/CDC in many systems.

48. Checkpoints and Snapshots

Periodically persist a consistent database state so recovery need not replay the entire log.

Consensus systems snapshot replicated logs after a point.

Snapshots must coordinate with WAL/log position for correct restore.

49. LSM Compaction

Merges sorted files, removes overwritten/deleted versions, and maintains level/size structure.

Size-tiered compaction favors write throughput but may use more space/read files.

Leveled compaction lowers read/space amplification but can increase write amplification.

Compaction must be throttled so background work does not destroy foreground latency.

50. Change Data Capture (CDC)

Read committed changes from WAL/binlog and publish them downstream.

Used for search indexing, caches, analytics, data warehouse, event-driven integration.

Need ordering, offset/checkpoint, schema evolution, replay and idempotent consumers.

CDC is often better than dual-writing DB + message broker in application code.

51. Dual-Write Problem

Application writes DB then message broker (or reverse). A crash between writes causes inconsistency.

Use transactional outbox: write business row + outbox row in one DB transaction, then relay outbox asynchronously.

Or use CDC from the DB log.

52. Failure Modes You Should Always Mention

Node crash.

Disk failure / corruption.

Network partition.

Slow node / GC pause.

Replica lag.

Leader split brain.

Hot partition.

Rebalancing overload.

Clock skew.

Partial write / timeout ambiguity.

53. Timeout Ambiguity

Client sends write, times out, but server may have committed it.

Retrying without idempotency can duplicate effects.

Use idempotency keys, unique constraints, transaction IDs, or read-back reconciliation.

54. Clock Problems

Wall clocks can jump or drift; NTP helps but does not make clocks perfectly synchronized.

Avoid using client timestamps to determine write order for strong correctness.

Use logical clocks, sequence numbers, consensus log positions, or hybrid logical clocks where appropriate.

55. Key Balancing Checklist

Estimate key cardinality and traffic distribution, not just average load.

Use hashing or sufficiently granular ranges/virtual partitions.

Monitor per-shard QPS, bytes, CPU, latency and queue depth.

Split/move hot ranges independently.

Isolate extremely large tenants.

Use caching/replication for hot reads and logical subsharding for mergeable hot writes.

56. Salting a Hot Key

Instead of counter:post123, write counter:post123:0..N-1.

Reads aggregate N sub-counters.

Great for commutative/mergeable values such as counters.

Not suitable when every operation must serialize on one canonical value.

57. Time-Series Hotspot Pattern

Range partition on timestamp alone makes current time range hot.

Use hash(device_id/tenant_id) + time bucket.

Queries for one device stay targeted; global time queries fan out by bucket/shard.

Choose bucket size from retention and query windows.

58. When to Use What: Partitioning

Need
	Prefer
	Why

Exact key lookup at huge scale
	Hash partitioning
	Even distribution

Ordered range scan
	Range partitioning
	Adjacent keys colocated

Tenant isolation + scale
	tenant_id + subshard
	Keep tenant locality while spreading large tenants

Time-series ingest
	entity hash + time bucket
	Avoid current-time hotspot

Hot counter
	Salt/subshard logical key
	Spread writes then aggregate



59. When to Use What: Replication

Requirement
	Pattern

Simple HA + strong primary writes
	Leader-follower

Multi-region local writes and conflict-tolerant domain
	Multi-leader

Tunable availability/eventual consistency
	Leaderless quorum

Strong ordered metadata/locks
	Consensus group

Analytics/read scaling
	Async read replicas



60. When to Use What: Consistency

Data
	Typical consistency

Payments/balance/unique username
	Strong / serializable or conditional writes

Distributed lock/leader metadata
	Linearizable

User feed
	Eventual / causal-ish

Like/view counts
	Eventual / approximate

Search index
	Eventual via CDC

Session read-after-login
	Read-your-writes/session consistency



61. Interview Pattern: Start from the Query

List top read/write queries first.

Choose partition key that localizes dominant operations.

Decide what must be strongly consistent.

Choose replication based on RPO/RTO and region needs.

Add caches/secondary indexes only after the base access path is clear.

62. Interview Pattern: Say the Trade-Off Out Loud

"Hashing gives balance but hurts range scans."

"Async replication improves latency/availability but permits stale reads and possible failover data loss."

"Fanout/global secondary index speeds reads but makes writes distributed."

"Serializable isolation protects invariants but may increase coordination/aborts."

"More replicas improve durability/read locality but increase write cost."

63. Interview Pattern: Avoid Premature Sharding

A single relational database with good indexes and replicas often handles more than candidates assume.

Shard only after one-node storage/write/throughput or availability constraints justify it.

Sharding makes joins, transactions, unique constraints, migrations and operations harder.



64. Last-Minute One-Page Mental Model

Question
	Think about

How do I store it?
	Row/document/KV/graph; B-tree vs LSM

How do I find it?
	Primary/composite/secondary/covering indexes

How do I scale it?
	Partition key, hash vs range, shard count

How do I survive failure?
	Replication, quorum, failover, WAL

How fresh must reads be?
	Leader read, replica read, session/causal/eventual

What if a shard is hot?
	Cache, split, salt, isolate, replicate

What if nodes change?
	Rebalancing, virtual nodes/range split, epochs

What about concurrency?
	Isolation level, MVCC, locks, CAS

What about cross-shard atomicity?
	Avoid if possible; 2PC/consensus/saga if required

How do downstream systems sync?
	CDC / transactional outbox

What happens after timeout?
	Idempotency + ambiguous-result handling

What should I measure?
	p99 latency, replica lag, shard skew, compaction, disk, queue depth



65. Interview Questions 

1. Why is hash partitioning good?

It spreads keys evenly and scales exact-key access, but sacrifices natural range locality.

2. Why can a cluster still have a hotspot after hashing?

A single hot key cannot be split by ordinary hashing.

3. Why is modulo sharding dangerous?

Changing node count remaps most keys unless using fixed logical partitions/consistent assignment.

4. How do you rebalance safely?

Copy gradually, verify, atomically switch ownership with a version/epoch, then remove old copy.

5. Why use virtual nodes?

They create many small movable ownership units and smooth capacity differences.

6. What causes stale reads?

Asynchronous replica lag.

7. How do you guarantee read-after-write?

Read from leader, sticky route to caught-up replica, or use version/LSN token.

8. What is quorum replication?

Require subsets of replicas for reads/writes; overlap can improve freshness/durability.

9. Why is W+R>N not enough for linearizability?

Concurrent writes, sloppy quorum, failures and conflict semantics can still violate it.

10. What is write skew?

Transactions update different rows based on a shared predicate and together violate an invariant.

11. How to prevent lost updates?

Atomic operations, CAS/version checks, locks, or serializable isolation.

12. Why is 2PC expensive?

Cross-node coordination, prepare logging, held locks/resources, and failure blocking.

13. Why use CDC?

Reliable ordered propagation of committed DB changes without unsafe application dual writes.

14. B-tree or LSM?

B-tree for strong general read/update behavior; LSM for high sequential write throughput at compaction cost.

15. What is compaction?

Background merging of immutable sorted files, removing obsolete versions/tombstones.

16. What is a Bloom filter?

Space-efficient probabilistic membership check used to skip unnecessary reads.

17. Why can adding replicas hurt?

More write/coordination cost and more replica management.

18. What is linearizability for?

When operations must respect real-time single-copy semantics, e.g. locks/unique ownership.

19. When should you shard?

When one node can no longer meet storage/write/availability needs, not simply because the system is "large".

20. Best final DB interview sentence?

Partition for scale, replicate for availability, choose consistency per invariant, and design explicitly for skew and failure.

66. Final Revision Checklist

• Data models: relational/document/KV/graph.
	• ACID, MVCC, snapshot isolation, serializable.

• OLTP vs OLAP; row vs column storage.
	• Lost update, write skew, CAS/locks.

• B-tree vs LSM; WAL, SSTables, compaction, Bloom filters.
	• 2PC vs saga; keep invariants local when possible.

• Leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless replication.
	• Linearizable, causal, eventual; CAP/PACELC.

• Sync vs async replication; lag and failover.
	• Consensus and majority quorum.

• Hash vs range partitioning; partition key selection.
	• CDC and transactional outbox.

• Hot keys, salting, tenant isolation.
	• Idempotency and timeout ambiguity.

• Fixed partitions, dynamic ranges, virtual nodes, rebalancing.
	• Clock skew and logical ordering.

• Local vs global secondary indexes.
	• Observability: p99, replica lag, shard skew, compaction, disk, queue depth.

notes.title: Design a URL Shortener — Complete System Design Interview Guide
notes.description: Design a URL Shortener — Complete System Design Interview Guide The core problem is simple; the interview depth comes from scale, uniqueness, caching, reliabili
notes.content:
Design a URL Shortener — Complete System Design Interview Guide



The core problem is simple; the interview depth comes from scale, uniqueness, caching, reliability, and product follow-ups.

1. Problem Statement

Design a service similar to TinyURL or Bitly that accepts a long URL and returns a compact URL. Visiting the compact URL should redirect the user to the original destination.

Example input: https://www.example.com/articles/system-design?id=12345

Example output: https://sho.rt/aZ91kLm

Redirect: GET /aZ91kLm -> HTTP redirect to the original URL.

What the interviewer is testingRequirement clarification, estimation, unique ID/key generation, database choice, caching, partitioning, redirect semantics, consistency, availability, and how you handle real-world follow-ups such as expiration, custom aliases, analytics, abuse, and multi-region deployment.

2. Clarifying Questions to Ask First

What are the core features: create + redirect only, or are custom aliases, expiration, deletion, analytics, etc. required?

What scale should we design for: new links/month and redirects/month?

Are users global? Do we need multi-region?

Are short links immutable, or can destinations change?

Should the same long URL always produce the same short URL?

Do links expire?

Do we need authentication/ownership?

Do we need exact or approximate analytics?

Interview-ready answerI would first lock the core scope as create + redirect. I’ll design for a read-heavy service and treat aliases, expiry, analytics, editing and other product features as follow-ups.

3. Functional and Non-Functional Requirements



Core requirements stay small; follow-ups are layered on after the primary read/write paths are correct.

Core Functional Requirements

Create a unique short code for a supplied long URL.

Resolve a short code to its long URL and return an HTTP redirect.

Return a predictable response for invalid, expired, disabled, or blocked codes.



Non-Functional Requirements

Very low redirect latency; a useful interview target is p95 around 100 ms service-side, with cache hits much lower.

High availability because links embedded across the web must keep working.

Durable mappings: once acknowledged, a normal link should not disappear.

Horizontal read scalability and hot-link protection.

Security/abuse controls appropriate for an open redirect service.

Likely Follow-up Requirements

Potential follow-ups include custom aliases, expiration/deletion, analytics, editable destinations, private links, and branded domains.

4. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Estimation

Assume the following interview workload. The exact numbers are less important than showing how they affect the design:



A realistic baseline makes the read-heavy nature of the system obvious.

Dimension
	Assumption
	Calculation
	Approx Result

New links
	100M/month
	100M / 30 / 86,400
	~39 writes/s average

Peak writes
	3× average
	39 × 3
	~120 writes/s

Redirects
	10B/month
	10B / 30 / 86,400
	~3,858 reads/s average

Peak redirects
	3× average
	3,858 × 3
	~11.6K reads/s

Read:write
	10B : 100M
	100 : 1
	Strongly read-heavy

Mapping storage
	1 KB/link
	100M × 1 KB
	~100 GB/month

1 year storage
	12 months
	100 GB × 12
	~1.2 TB raw

5 years
	~6B links
	6B × 1 KB
	~6 TB raw

Architecture implicationAt this scale, write QPS is modest. The hard path is redirect latency, high availability, hot keys, and maintaining a huge durable key-value mapping over time.

5. Short-Code Length and Base62

A common alphabet is Base62: digits + lowercase letters + uppercase letters. It avoids URL-reserved punctuation and packs many values into a short string.



Seven Base62 characters provide about 3.52 trillion possible codes.

6 chars: 62^6 ≈ 56.8 billion codes.

7 chars: 62^7 ≈ 3.52 trillion codes.

8 chars: 62^8 ≈ 218 trillion codes.

At 100M new links/month, a 7-character namespace is extremely large if codes are managed without collisions.

Interview pointCode-space capacity and collision probability are different questions. A large namespace does not remove collision handling if codes are chosen randomly.

6. API Design

Operation
	API
	Input
	Result

Create
	POST /v1/links
	longUrl, optional alias/expiry/redirectType
	201 + shortUrl/code

Redirect
	GET /{code}
	short code
	301/302/307/308 + Location

Get metadata
	GET /v1/links/{code}
	authenticated owner
	link metadata

Disable/delete
	DELETE /v1/links/{code}
	owner/admin
	204 / status change

Create Request Example

Request body{ "longUrl": "https://example.com/a/b", "customAlias": null, "expiresAt": null, "redirectType": 302 }

Support an Idempotency-Key header or request token for safe client retries.

Validate scheme; usually allow only http/https for normal product use.

Return 409 Conflict if requested custom alias is already taken.

Return 429 for rate-limited callers.



7. High-Level Design



The redirect path is cache-first; link creation writes durable mapping and obtains a unique key.

Primary components:

Edge / WAF / rate limiter: abuse protection and traffic entry.

Load balancer: distributes traffic to stateless services.

Shorten service: validates URL, handles idempotency/custom alias, reserves key, persists mapping.

Redirect service: resolves code, checks cache/database, returns redirect.

Key Generation Service: supplies unique short codes in the final scaled design.

Distributed cache: hot code-to-URL mappings.

Mapping store: durable source of truth.

Event stream + analytics pipeline: click events and non-critical side effects.

8. Link Creation / Write Path



Create is a low-QPS path compared with redirects, so correctness matters more than shaving every millisecond.

Validate authentication/tier, URL syntax, scheme, length, custom alias, expiration, and rate limit.

Check the idempotency key. If this create request already succeeded, return the existing result.

If custom alias: atomically reserve that alias with a conditional insert.

Else: get a unique code from the local KGS batch / key generator.

Persist the URL mapping durably with a uniqueness condition on short_code.

Optionally warm the distributed cache.

Return a short URL to the caller.

Publish non-critical events such as audit/analytics asynchronously.

9. Redirect / Read Path



The common-case redirect should avoid the database entirely.

1.  Parse and validate the short code format.

2.  Check a fast safety blocklist if blocked links must stop immediately.

3.  Check L1 local cache.

4.  On a miss, check the shared L2 distributed cache.

5.  On miss, read mapping store by primary key short_code.

6.  If missing/expired/disabled, return 404 or 410 and optionally negative-cache briefly.

7.  If active, populate caches with TTL bounded by expires_at.

8.  Emit click event asynchronously.

9.  Return redirect response with Location header.

Latency goalThe steady-state hot-link path is: edge/LB -> redirect service -> memory/distributed cache -> redirect. Database should see only cache misses and colder links.

10. Key Generation — The Main Deep Dive



There is no single mandatory algorithm; compare guarantees and operational complexity.

11. Option A — Global Counter + Base62

Generate monotonically increasing integer ID.

Encode integer in Base62 for compact code.

Uniqueness is simple if one authoritative counter/sequence allocates IDs.

Pros

No collisions by construction.

Shortest possible representation for the number of records.

Easy to explain and implement at modest scale.

Cons

Central counter/sequence can become a coordination dependency.

Sequential codes are enumerable/predictable; attackers can crawl links.

Multi-region generation needs range allocation or distributed ID scheme.

Interview-ready answerA sequence + Base62 is the simplest correct design for moderate scale. At large distributed scale I would allocate ID ranges per generator or switch to a KGS/random namespace if predictability is undesirable.

12. Option B — Hash the Long URL

Hash normalized long URL (e.g. cryptographic hash) and takes a prefix.

Check whether the prefix already exists. If collision with a different long URL, extend/re-hash/salt and retry.

Advantages

Deterministic mapping can deduplicate identical URLs.

No central sequence required.

Problems

Fixed short prefixes create collision probability; collision handling is mandatory.

Same long URL may need different links for different users, campaigns, expirations, redirect types, or analytics.

URL normalization is hard: fragments, tracking parameters, encoding, case rules, trailing slash semantics.

ImportantDo not claim “MD5/SHA has no collisions.” A shortener uses a truncated prefix, so collisions are much more likely than full-hash cryptographic collisions.

13. Option C — Random Base62 + Conditional Insert

Generate a random 7-8 character code.

Attempt atomic insert with short_code as unique key.

If conflict, generate another code and retry.

Easy to distribute because app instances generate locally.

Collision Reality

With 8 characters, namespace is ~218 trillion; at 100M existing/new items, conflicts are uncommon but not impossible.

As occupancy increases, retries become more frequent.

Database uniqueness is still the final authority.

Interview-ready answerRandom codes are attractive because generation is decentralized and non-sequential. I still rely on a conditional/unique insert and bounded retry for correctness.

14. Option D — Distributed ID Generator

Generate globally unique numeric IDs using time + worker ID + sequence bits, or allocate disjoint ranges per generator.

Encode numeric ID to Base62.

Removes a single DB sequence bottleneck.

Trade-offs

Time-based IDs can leak creation time/order.

Full 64-bit IDs can require longer Base62 strings than a 7-character fixed code.

Worker-ID allocation and clock behavior need care.

15. Option E — Pre-Generated Key Generation Service (Recommended Scaled Design)



KGS moves uniqueness work out of the user request and lets app servers reserve codes in batches.

One strong interview design is to pre-generate a pool of random unique 7-character codes ahead of demand. Shorten-service instances lease batches (for example 10,000 codes) and serve creates from memory.

Why It Works

Fixed short length and non-sequential codes.

Create path avoids collision checks in the normal case.

KGS calls happen per batch, not per user request.

Local batch lets create service survive a temporary KGS outage.

Correctness Rules

A key can move from AVAILABLE -> LEASED/USED exactly once.

Allocation transactions must be atomic.

If an app crashes with unused leased keys, wasting them is acceptable and safer than unsafe reuse.

Maintain low-watermark alerts and refill pool asynchronously.

Practical noteYou do not pre-generate all 3.5 trillion 7-character codes. Maintain a sufficiently large pool ahead of expected demand and continuously refill it.

Interview-ready answerFor a fixed-length public short code, I would use a KGS that leases unique random Base62 codes to app servers in batches. The mapping database still enforces unique short_code as a final invariant.

16. Which Key Strategy Should You Choose in the Interview?

Strategy
	Uniqueness
	Code Length
	Distributed
	Best Comment

Counter + Base62
	By sequence
	Very compact
	Needs range/sequence coordination
	Best simple answer

Hash prefix
	Needs collision check
	Fixed
	Yes
	Dedupe semantics are tricky

Random code
	Unique insert + retry
	Fixed
	Yes
	Simple decentralized

Distributed ID
	By ID algorithm
	Usually longer
	Yes
	Operationally robust

KGS
	Pool guarantees
	Fixed/short
	Yes via batch lease
	Best fixed-short-code deep dive



17. Database / Data Model



Keep the redirect lookup model simple: short_code is the primary key.

Core Record

short_code — primary key / unique.

long_url — destination.

owner_id — nullable for anonymous users; required for management features.

created_at, expires_at.

status — ACTIVE, DISABLED, BLOCKED, EXPIRED/TOMBSTONE as needed.

redirect_type — typically 302 by default.

url_hash — optional for idempotency/dedupe workflows.

Why Not Store Click Count on the Same Row?

Do not store/update per-click counters synchronously on this row; analytics is handled asynchronously.

18. SQL vs NoSQL for the Mapping Store



Area
	SQL
	Key-Value / NoSQL

Access pattern
	PK lookup works well
	PK lookup is the natural model

Transactions
	Strong and flexible
	Usually limited but enough for conditional key insert

Write scale
	Can scale very far; sharding adds work
	Often built for horizontal partitioning

Queries
	Flexible admin/report queries
	Model known access patterns

Operational simplicity
	Relational DB can be enough initially
	Managed KV can simplify very large scale

Recommended answerRedirects are simple short_code → long_url lookups, so a distributed key-value store fits well at scale. For modest write QPS, a relational database with a unique index is a simpler starting choice.



19. Partitioning / Sharding



Hash partitioning by short code gives good distribution for the dominant point lookup.

Partition key: short_code.

Use hash-based partitioning so sequential generation does not create one hot newest range.

A managed KV store can hide partition routing; otherwise use consistent hashing/directory service.

Cross-shard queries are rare on redirect path, which makes this data model ideal for partitioning.

Rebalancing

Adding/removing database nodes moves partitions/ranges.

Consistent hashing/virtual nodes reduce and smooth movement in self-managed systems.

Replicate mapping data across multiple failure domains/AZs.

Use synchronous or quorum durability within a region if losing acknowledged links is unacceptable.

Use asynchronous cross-region replication when lower write latency is preferred and short lag is acceptable.

Backups remain necessary; replication is not backup.

Immutable-data advantageMost URL mappings are immutable. Immutable key-value data is easy to cache and replicate because conflict resolution is rare. Editable links make consistency and invalidation much harder.

22. Caching Design

Goal: keep the redirect path fast and prevent the database from handling repeated lookups for popular links.

Cache Layers

L1 cache: small in-process cache on each redirect instance for extremely hot mappings.

L2 cache: shared distributed cache such as Redis for the broader hot working set.

L1 protects L2 from hot-key traffic; L2 protects the database from repeated reads.





L1 local cache protects L2 from extreme hot keys; L2 shared cache protects the database.

Cache Policy

Key: short_code

Value: long_url + status + expires_at + redirect_type

Use cache-aside:

TTL should not outlive the link: effectiveTTL = min(cacheTTL, expiresAt - now).

Immutable links can use longer TTLs.

Editable/disabled links need cache invalidation, shorter TTLs, or versioning.

Negative Caching

Negative caching means caching the fact that a key does not exist, instead of caching only successful results.

Imagine a bot sends 100,000 requests for the same invalid short code xyz123.Without negative caching, every request can eventually reach the database:

When the first request discovers that xyz123 doesn't exist, we temporarily cache that information with short TTLs (30 s)

Cache invalid code lookups for a short TTL (e.g. seconds/minutes) to prevent bots from repeatedly hitting DB with random codes.

Do not negative-cache too long if a code might legitimately be created soon afterward.

Ans.) update/invalidate cache on creation : Once the database insert succeeds, the create path should remove or overwrite any negative cache entry.

24. Viral Link / Hot-Key Handling

A single viral short link can overload one cache node even when overall system traffic is manageable.



Why sharding alone does not solve it

Suppose:  hash(abc123) → Cache Shard B

If abc123 receives 500K QPS, all reads still go to the same shard.

So:

Sharding solves aggregate capacity problems; replication helps with single hot-key problems.







A single hot link can be a bigger problem than aggregate traffic.

Mitigations: 

L1 in-process cache on every redirect instance for very hot mappings.

Replicate the hot mapping across cache shards or use a cache system with read replication.

Use CDN/edge redirect caching when product/analytics requirements allow.

Request coalescing/single-flight on misses.

Never synchronously increment a global click counter per redirect.

Autoscale redirect instances and cache read capacity.



Request coalescing:When many requests miss the same cache key at the same time, only one request fetches the value from the database. The other requests wait for and reuse that result. This prevents many identical DB reads.

Single-flight:Single-flight is a common way to implement request coalescing within one application instance. For a given key, one request becomes the leader and the others wait for its result.

With multiple application servers, each server may independently run its own single-flight, so you can still get roughly one DB request per server. If stronger cross-server coordination is needed, use a shared lock or distributed coordination mechanism.

Cache stampede:A cache stampede happens when many requests simultaneously miss the same expired or evicted hot key and all try to fetch it from the database. Request coalescing/single-flight helps prevent this.

Cache stampede = the problem

Request coalescing = the solution idea

Single-flight = one common implementation of request coalescing

25. HTTP Redirect Status: 301 vs 302 vs 307/308



Redirect status is a product and analytics decision, not just HTTP trivia.

301 Permanent

Clients/intermediaries may cache the redirect aggressively.

Reduces future load on shortener.

But the service may stop seeing every click, and changing destination becomes less reliable because clients can retain old redirect.

302 Temporary

Common interview default for URL shorteners when tracking and control matter.

Requests continue to reach the service, improving click visibility and allowing destination changes.

Higher ongoing service load.

307 / 308

307 temporary and 308 permanent preserve HTTP method/body semantics.

Most public short-link redirects are GETs, so 301/302 discussion is usually enough unless interviewer asks.

Default to 302 for tracking and control; use 301 for immutable links when stronger browser/CDN caching is preferred.

Same key + materially different request should be rejected as misuse.

33. Timeouts, Retries, and Circuit Breakers

Every network call has a timeout.

Retry only transient failures; use exponential backoff + jitter.

Create retries must be idempotent.

Redirect DB/cache retries should be tightly bounded because latency matters.

When cache is down, unbounded fallback to DB can cause a cascading outage. Apply circuit breaking/load shedding.



A transient failure is a temporary failure where retrying the same operation after a short delay may succeed.

Cache invalidation means removing or updating a cached value when the underlying source of truth changes, so users don't receive stale data.

Common approach: Cache-Aside:

Update request -> Update Database -> Invalidate Redis -> Success

Where does the circuit breaker come in?

The circuit breaker monitors calls to a dependency—in this case, we can use one around Redis and another protection policy around DB fallback.

A circuit breaker typically has three states:



CLOSED

   │ failures exceed threshold

  ▼

OPEN

  │ after cooldown

  ▼

HALF-OPEN

  │

  ├── success → CLOSE

  └── failure → OPEN



Protect the DB fallback:

Suppose the DB can safely absorb only an additional 10K QPS during cache failure.

Don't allow all 100K requests through, You might return: 503 Service Unavailable

This sounds bad, but In distributed systems, partial controlled failure is often better than total uncontrolled failure.

You can add more protections: DB circuit breaker, concurrency limits, rate limits, request queues with strict bounds, DB read replicas, and local L1 cache.



Circuit breaker: Stop repeatedly calling an unhealthy dependency.

Load shedding: Reject excess requests to protect the overall system



34. Multi-Region Design



Reads are easy to distribute globally; globally unique writes are the interesting part.

Redirects

Route users to the nearest healthy region using global DNS/anycast/edge routing.

Maintain regional caches.

Replicate mapping data across regions; immutable links tolerate asynchronous lag well after creation.

Creates

Simplest: choose one write/home region and replicate globally.

More available: allow regional creation if key spaces are disjoint or KGS allocates globally unique ranges/batches.

Read-After-Create Across Regions

Warm origin region cache and return there initially, or replicate synchronously enough for the product SLA.

Could include region/home information in create response/session routing if necessary.



A practical design is usually:

After creating the mapping, populate the local cache and prefer the creator’s write region for immediate reads. Other regions can receive the mapping asynchronously. If a remote region misses a newly created code, it can fall back to the authoritative region before returning 404.



Read-after-create across regions = making sure a newly created short URL does not temporarily return 404 because another region has not replicated it yet.

Interview-ready answerUse active-active regions for redirects. Keep link creation simpler with either one primary write region or coordinated key generation. Custom aliases need global uniqueness, so fully active-active writes are harder.

Q1. How will you generate short codes without collisions at scale?

Interview-ready answerStart by separating encoding from ID generation. A Base62 encoder only converts an ID into a compact URL-safe string; uniqueness comes from the underlying ID. For a distributed system, a Snowflake-style 64-bit generator is a strong choice: timestamp + worker identity + sequence produce unique IDs independently on many servers. Base62-encode the generated ID. Alternatives are random Base62 strings with collision checks, or a central counter for a simpler system. Avoid assuming that truncating a hash makes collisions impossible.

Q2. If you use random/hash-based codes and a collision occurs, what do you do?

Q26. How do you expire billions of short URLs?

Interview-ready answerStore expiresAt and index it. Enforce expiry on every redirect read, so correctness never depends on cleanup. A background worker scans the expiry index in bounded batches and tombstones/deletes expired rows. Redis TTL can mirror expiry. Avoid full-table daily scans because they become increasingly expensive.



Topics covered

TTL at data layer

Indexed expiry

Batch cleanup

Read-time validation

Background workers

Q27. What if the expiration cleanup worker is down for hours?

Interview-ready answerNothing incorrect should happen. The row may remain physically present, but the redirect handler compares expiresAt with current time and returns an expired/not-found response. Cleanup is storage maintenance, not the mechanism that defines whether the link is valid.



Topics covered

Separation of correctness and cleanup

Read-time expiry

Failure tolerance

Q28. Two users request the same custom alias at the same time. How do you decide who wins?

Interview-ready answerPut a unique constraint on alias/shortCode and attempt an atomic insert. Exactly one transaction succeeds; the other receives a uniqueness conflict and returns “alias already taken.” A Redis lock is optional optimization/coordination, but the database uniqueness constraint should remain the correctness guarantee.



Topics covered

Custom aliases

Uniqueness constraints

Atomicity

Concurrent writes

Q29. How do you rate limit the create API across many servers?

Interview-ready answerKeep rate-limit state in a shared low-latency store such as Redis. Use an atomic token-bucket or sliding-window algorithm keyed by user/API key/IP/tenant. Every create consumes capacity; requests beyond the policy receive HTTP 429. Token bucket permits controlled bursts while maintaining a long-term rate.



Topics covered

Distributed rate limiting

Token bucket

Sliding window

Atomic counters

HTTP 429

Q30. What capacity calculations should you be ready to do?

Interview-ready answerEstimate writes per second from monthly creates, reads per second from the read/write ratio, storage from mappings × bytes per row × retention, cache size from the hot working set, and network bandwidth from average request/response size. For example, 100 million creates/month is roughly 39 writes/s on average (100,000,000 / 2,592,000 seconds). If redirects are 100× writes, average redirect QPS is roughly 3,900; then apply a peak factor rather than designing only for averages.



Topics covered

Back-of-the-envelope estimation

QPS

Peak factor

Storage estimation

Cache working set

Bandwidth

Part VIII — Final interview walkthrough

A concise 10–15 minute answer structure

Clarify scope: create + redirect; ask whether aliases, expiry, analytics, deletion, and auth are required.

Establish scale/read-heavy nature and latency/availability goals.

Define POST /urls and GET /{shortCode}.

Choose shortCode generation: Snowflake 64-bit ID → Base62; discuss clock rollback and predictability.

Design mapping schema keyed/indexed by shortCode.

Draw create path and redirect path.

Add Redis cache-aside; discuss hot keys, stampede, avalanche, penetration.

Shard by hash(shortCode); evolve to consistent hashing + virtual nodes.

Replicate shards; discuss failover and replication lag/read-after-write.

Add multi-region routing and primary fallback on local miss.

Cover failures: Redis outage, DB shard outage, Kafka outage.

Finish with idempotency, deletion/invalidation, expiry, analytics, rate limiting, and abuse controls.

Final architecture decisions

Decision
	Recommended interview choice

Identifier
	Snowflake-style distributed ID → Base62

Primary lookup
	shortCode

Cache
	Redis cache-aside + local hot-key cache

Database
	Sharded durable KV/relational store; hash(shortCode)

Shard growth
	Consistent hashing + virtual nodes

Availability
	Per-shard replication + failover

Consistency
	Eventual replicas + cache warm / primary fallback for fresh reads

Multi-region
	Geo routing + regional cache/replicas + authoritative fallback

Analytics
	Async Kafka/queue

Expiration
	expiresAt read-time enforcement + indexed batch cleanup

Rate limit
	Distributed token bucket/sliding window in Redis



44. Final URL Shortener Cheat Sheet

Topic
	Remember This

Core
	Create + Redirect

Scale
	100M creates/mo; 10B redirects/mo; ~100:1 read/write

Code
	Base62; 7 chars ≈ 3.52T

Simple key
	Counter + Base62

Scaled key
	KGS or random + atomic unique insert

PK
	short_code

DB
	KV at scale; SQL is fine initially

Partition
	Hash short_code

Cache
	L1 + distributed L2; cache-aside

Negative cache
	Briefly cache invalid codes

Stampede
	Single-flight + TTL jitter

Hot link
	L1/edge/replicated cache; async clicks

Redirect
	302 for control/tracking; 301 for permanent caching

Consistency
	Strong uniqueness; eventual immutable reads

Replication
	Multi-AZ; cross-region async for reads

Analytics
	Async stream; separate OLAP

Expiry
	Serve inactive immediately; cleanup later

Custom alias
	Atomic conditional reservation

Security
	Rate limit + anti-phishing + fast disable

Multi-region
	Active-active reads; coordinated writes

Observability
	Redirect SLO, cache hit, DB, KGS pool, analytics lag
