notes.content:
Design Pastebin - Complete System Design Interview Guide





The core problem is simple; the depth comes from scale, lifecycle, security, and storage choices.

1. Problem Statement and Interview Framing

Design a Pastebin-like service where a user submits a block of text and receives a short URL. Anyone with permission to access that URL can retrieve the stored text. The baseline system is read-heavy, but the interview becomes interesting when the interviewer adds expiration, privacy, custom aliases, large pastes, search, analytics, or viral traffic.

Core operation 1: create a paste.

Core operation 2: retrieve a paste using a short identifier.

Core operation 3: expire or delete a paste.

Optional: user accounts, private pastes, custom aliases, syntax highlighting, search, analytics, edit/version history.



Interview scope disciplineDo not begin with search, moderation pipelines, multi-region active-active, and version history unless they are requested. First build a correct create/read system, then evolve it as follow-ups arrive.



2. Functional Requirements





Requirement
	Baseline Decision
	Follow-Up Variation

Create paste
	Text body -> generated pasteId
	Custom alias / idempotency / user account

Read paste
	GET by pasteId
	Raw vs rendered / authenticated private read

Expiration
	Optional expiresAt
	One-time paste / legal retention

Visibility
	Public or unlisted baseline
	Private ACL

Delete
	Owner can delete
	Soft delete / restore / audit

Edit
	Usually immutable baseline
	Versioned mutable pastes

Search
	Out of core scope
	Public-only async search index



Recommended baselineMake pastes immutable after creation. Immutability makes CDN caching, cache invalidation, replication, analytics, and viral traffic handling much simpler. Add versioned edits only if the interviewer explicitly asks.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

Property
	Target / Expectation
	Architectural Consequence

Read latency
	Low p95/p99; most reads under a few hundred ms
	Cache + optional CDN

Read availability
	High; viral links should survive spikes
	Stateless APIs, replicas, cache, CDN

Write durability
	Created paste should not disappear
	Durable metadata + body before success

Read-after-create
	Creator should immediately open returned URL
	Primary/session read or cache warm

Consistency
	Eventual reads acceptable for public replicas
	Strong uniqueness/delete semantics where needed

Security
	Untrusted user content
	Escaping, rate limits, moderation, access control

Cost
	Text can accumulate for years
	Object storage, TTL, lifecycle policies



Key design priorityPastebin is usually read-heavy and mostly immutable. That strongly favors cache/CDN, simple point-key lookup, append-oriented writes, and asynchronous side effects.



4. Capacity Estimation





Assume the following round numbers for the design discussion:

10 million new pastes per day.

100 million paste reads per day.

Average paste size = 10 KB; maximum paste size = 1 MB.

Peak traffic = approximately 5x average.

Average paste metadata = roughly 500 bytes.

Calculations:

Dimension
	Calculation
	Approximate Result

Average write QPS
	10M / 86,400
	~116 writes/sec

Peak write QPS
	116 x 5
	~600 writes/sec

Average read QPS
	100M / 86,400
	~1,160 reads/sec

Peak read QPS
	1,160 x 5
	~6,000 reads/sec

Body storage/day
	10M x 10 KB
	~100 GB/day

Body storage/year
	100 GB x 365
	~36.5 TB/year raw

Metadata/day
	10M x 500 B
	~5 GB/day





Why these numbers matterThe write QPS is not extreme, but long-term body storage is large and reads dominate writes. That makes cheap blob/object storage plus aggressive caching more valuable than designing a complicated write pipeline.



5. Paste ID Length and Code Space







Using digits + lowercase + uppercase gives 62 possible symbols per character.

Length
	Code Space
	Interview Interpretation

5
	62^5 ~ 916M
	Too small at large scale

6
	62^6 ~ 56.8B
	Possible sequentially; random collisions become relevant earlier

7
	62^7 ~ 3.52T
	Comfortable large code space

8
	62^8 ~ 218T
	Very large but URL becomes slightly longer



Sequential numeric IDs encoded in Base62 do not collide.

Random Base62 strings require a unique constraint and collision retry.

If unlisted URLs rely on secrecy, predictable sequential codes are weaker because enumeration becomes easy.



Recommended defaultUse 7-character Base62 paste IDs for the interview assumption. If IDs are random, enforce uniqueness atomically in the metadata store. If IDs come from a KGS or sequence, collision checking is unnecessary.



6. API Design

Operation
	Example
	Notes

Create
	POST /v1/pastes
	Body, expiry, visibility, language, optional customAlias

Read rendered
	GET /p/{pasteId}
	HTML page that safely renders escaped content

Read raw
	GET /raw/{pasteId}
	Serve text/plain, never execute paste contents

Delete
	DELETE /v1/pastes/{pasteId}
	Owner/auth required where applicable

Update optional
	PUT /v1/pastes/{pasteId}
	Prefer versioning if edits are required



Create Request

Example logical fields: content, expiresInSeconds/expiresAt, visibility, language, customAlias, idempotencyKey.

Create Response

Return pasteId, URL, createdAt, expiresAt, and possibly version. HTTP 201 Created is appropriate.

Error Semantics

400: invalid size/TTL/alias.

401/403: private paste or unauthorized mutation.

404: unknown paste.

409: requested custom alias already exists.

410 Gone: useful if you want to distinguish expired/deleted from never existing.

413: paste body too large.

429: create/read rate limit exceeded.



IdempotencyIf clients may retry POST after a timeout, accept an idempotency key for authenticated users. Store the idempotency key -> pasteId mapping for a bounded period so the same logical create does not create multiple pastes.



7. Data Model





The dominant access pattern is pasteId -> metadata/body.



Field
	Purpose

pasteId
	Primary lookup key; generated or custom alias

ownerId
	Nullable for anonymous paste

contentRef
	Object key or inline body reference

createdAt
	Creation timestamp

expiresAt
	Optional TTL / lifecycle boundary

visibility
	PUBLIC / UNLISTED / PRIVATE

language
	Syntax-highlighting hint

sizeBytes
	Validation / billing / diagnostics

status
	ACTIVE / DELETED / BLOCKED / EXPIRED

version
	Useful if edit/versioning is added



Make pasteId the partition/primary key for fast point lookups.

Avoid secondary indexes unless a real query requires them.

For authenticated user's 'my pastes' page, add an ownerId + createdAt access path/index or a separate user-paste index.

Do not place full-text search burden on the primary metadata database.

8. High-Level Architecture





The synchronous path is small; auxiliary work is asynchronous.



Clients access through CDN/edge, WAF, and load balancing.

Paste API service remains stateless.

Cache serves hot metadata/body.

Metadata store maps pasteId to contentRef + lifecycle/access fields.

Object store keeps large/long-lived body data.

KGS or distributed ID generation supplies unique IDs.

An event stream carries create/delete and view events from the right source: CDN edge events for public CDN-served views and API events for private/direct reads; search/moderation consume their own events.



Simple-first interview approachAt small scale, one SQL database can store pasteId and body together. The production-scale design separates metadata and bodies only after storage size, row size, or cost makes that worthwhile.



9. Create Paste - Detailed Write Path





Return success only after the durable mapping and body exist.

Rule (object-first): Generate candidate ID → store body under a unique no-overwrite object key → atomically claim URL ID in metadata → return URL.

Authenticate & Rate Limit: Verify the user (if required) and limit creation requests.

Validate Input: Check content format, size, TTL, visibility, and custom alias.

Generate Candidate ID: Use KGS, random ID, UUID, or sequence. A candidate is not authoritative until its URL key is committed.

Store Body Safely: Upload to a unique immutable object key (for example, uploads/<UUID>), not an unreserved pastes/<candidateId> key. Prevent overwrites with conditional creation where available.

Commit Metadata: Atomically insert the candidate ID/alias in the authoritative shared URL namespace and point it to the verified object key. Only committed ACTIVE records are readable.

Warm Cache: Optionally cache the paste after the database commit.

Return URL: Return the short URL only after both storage operations succeed.

Async Tasks: Trigger moderation, analytics, indexing, and expiry processing.

Cross-Store Failure Handling

Object Storage Fails: Abort creation; don't save metadata.

Metadata Insert Fails: If the candidate conflicts, keep the uploaded body at its independent object key and retry with a new generated ID. If creation is abandoned, garbage-collect the unreferenced object.

ID Collision: Never overwrite an existing object named for the colliding ID. Generate a fresh candidate and retry the atomic metadata insert (bounded attempts).

Client Timeout After Success: Use an idempotency key to prevent duplicate pastes.

Cache Failure: Don't fail the request; cache is optional.

Async Event Failure: Use a transactional outbox or reliable retry mechanism.

Alternative for large/pre-signed uploads: Atomically reserve the URL ID in metadata with status=PENDING; issue a scoped upload URL for a unique object key; verify the uploaded body; then transition PENDING → ACTIVE. PENDING records must not be readable. Clean up abandoned sessions.



Correctness priority

Rule: An unused object is acceptable, but a broken paste URL is not.

Case 1: Object stored, but DB fails (Acceptable)

- Body is successfully stored in object storage.

- Metadata insertion fails.

- The object becomes orphaned (stored but not referenced).

- A background cleanup job can delete it later.

Case 2: DB succeeds, but object storage fails (Not Acceptable)

- Metadata is saved in the database.

- Body upload fails.

- Users receive a paste URL pointing to missing content.

- This results in a broken link.



Interview Key Point: Prefer temporary storage waste over broken user-facing links. Always ensure the body exists before committing metadata and returning success.



Concurrency and Atomic Publication (Additional Detail)

Concurrent requests must never publish the same /p/{slug} twice or replace an existing object body. Separate an uncommitted candidate ID from the authoritative URL reservation.

Atomic claim: Use a unique constraint/conditional put on the normalized slug in the authoritative metadata store. For random IDs, retry collisions with a new candidate; for a custom alias, return HTTP 409.

Safe object key: An object-first upload uses a unique, no-overwrite storage key independent of an unreserved slug. A rejected metadata insert leaves only an orphan object, never a corrupted existing paste.

Alternative state transition: Reserve slug + idempotency record atomically as PENDING, upload and verify the body, then conditionally transition PENDING → ACTIVE. Reads must not expose PENDING records.

Concurrent retries: Scope idempotency keys to a user/client, store a payload fingerprint, and return the same paste for matching retries. Reject the same key with different content.

Recovery: Expire abandoned PENDING sessions and garbage-collect unreferenced objects. Use conditional transitions so late or duplicate finalization cannot publish a different body.

Interview trade-off: Object-first makes metadata visibility simple but requires safe staging/orphan cleanup; PENDING reservations simplify uniqueness and upload sessions but add state transitions and recovery work.



10. Read Paste - Detailed Read Path





Rule: CDN → L1 Cache → L2 Cache → Database → Object Storage → Response.

Check CDN: Serve public, immutable pastes directly from the CDN if cached. Otherwise, forward the request to the API.

Check L1 Cache: Look for the paste in the application's local in-memory cache.

Check L2 Cache: If L1 misses, check the distributed cache (e.g., Redis).

Fetch Metadata: On a cache miss, query the database using pasteId.

Validate Access: Check whether the paste exists, is active, has not expired, and the user has permission to access it.

Fetch Body: Retrieve the content from the database (if stored inline) or object storage (e.g., S3).

Update Cache: Cache the metadata and/or body with an appropriate TTL, never exceeding the paste's remaining lifetime.

Return Content: Return safely rendered HTML or raw text/plain to prevent XSS.

Async Analytics: Emit a nonblocking read event without slowing down the response.

Negative Caching

Negative caching means temporarily caching failed lookups to avoid repeated database queries.

Nonexistent Paste: Cache 404 results briefly (e.g., 30–60 seconds) to reduce database load.

Expired/Deleted Paste: Cache the unavailable status, potentially for longer if deletion is permanent.

Recently Created Paste: Avoid long negative TTLs because they could temporarily hide new pastes.

Unauthorized Requests: Do not cache user-specific 403 responses under a globally shared key.

Failure Handling

CDN/L1/L2 Cache Miss: Fall back to the next cache or database.

Cache Unavailable: Query the database directly, using rate limits to prevent overload.

Database Unavailable: Return an error if no valid cached copy can safely serve the request.

Object Storage Unavailable: Return a temporary server error; don't return incomplete content.

Analytics Failure: Don't block the read response.

Expired/Deleted Paste: Return 404 or 410, depending on API semantics.

Interview Key Point: Optimize reads using CDN and multi-level caching, but prioritize correct access control, expiry checks, and safe content rendering. Use negative caching to protect the database from repeated invalid requests.

11. Paste ID Generation - Decision Overview





There is no single required method; explain the trade-off.

Approach
	Advantages
	Disadvantages
	Good Interview Use

DB sequence + Base62
	Simple, unique, compact
	Predictable; central allocator bottleneck
	Small/medium system

Random Base62
	Distributed, opaque
	Collision check/retry; entropy quality
	Simple scalable baseline

KGS
	Unique and fast create path
	Extra service/state/lease design
	Large interview-scale system

Snowflake-style + Base62
	Distributed uniqueness
	Longer code, exposes structure
	Multi-region/high write scale



12. Sequential ID + Base62

Generate an integer using an auto-increment sequence.

Encode integer in Base62.

Uniqueness is guaranteed by the sequence.

Easy to implement and easy to explain.

Weaknesses

Central sequence can become an availability/throughput dependency.

Codes are enumerable; attackers can crawl adjacent IDs.

Sequence leaks approximate volume/order.

Mitigations

Allocate ID blocks to application servers.

Permute/obfuscate the numeric ID before Base62 encoding if enumeration is undesirable.



When to chooseFor a 3-YOE interview answer, this is acceptable if you explicitly mention predictability and central-allocation limits. You can evolve it to KGS or a distributed ID generator as scale grows.



13. Random Base62 Codes and Collisions





The authoritative URL-key unique constraint prevents collisions; object storage must also prevent overwriting existing bodies.



Generate a cryptographically strong random 7-character code.

Claim the candidate ID atomically in the shared URL namespace. If using object-first writes, store the body under a separate unique object key before this insert.

If the candidate conflicts, generate a new ID and retry the unique insert; never overwrite content stored under a conflicting pasteId.

As the code space fills, collisions rise; keep occupancy low by using a sufficiently large code space.

Why Not 'Check Then Insert'?

Two servers can check the same code concurrently, both see it absent, then both try to insert.

Uniqueness must be enforced atomically by the database/allocator, not by a non-atomic pre-check.



Security benefitRandom IDs make unlisted URLs difficult to enumerate. That is useful, but an unlisted URL is still not an authorization mechanism for genuinely private data.



14. Key Generation Service (KGS)





Lease key blocks so Paste API does not call KGS on every request.



KGS pre-generates unique Base62 keys and leases disjoint blocks to paste-service instances. These keys are unique within the generated pool; if aliases share the same URL path, the final namespace must also be protected from alias collisions.

KGS Data State

UNUSED keys.

LEASED keys assigned to an app instance/block.

USED keys - optional tracking; often a key never returns to the pool.

Lease Behavior

Lease 1,000 or 10,000 keys at once, not one key per request.

If app instance crashes, unused leased keys can be permanently abandoned. Wasting keys is safe because the key space is huge.

Never reissue an uncertain key just to save space; duplicate paste IDs are much worse.

KGS Availability

Paste servers continue creating from local leased blocks during a short KGS outage.

Alert before local pools run low.

Replicate KGS metadata or pre-partition key blocks by region.



Why KGS is interview-worthyIt removes the uniqueness check from the hot create path and keeps IDs short and opaque. The trade-off is a new stateful service that must safely allocate non-overlapping key ranges.



15. Custom Aliases

A user may request /p/my-resume instead of a generated code. If both use /p/{slug}, they must share one URL-key namespace.

Normalize case policy deliberately: case-sensitive or canonical lowercase.

Restrict allowed characters and length.

Reserve system paths such as /api, /admin, /raw, /login.

Enforce one authoritative unique constraint on the normalized /p/{slug} value for BOTH generated IDs and custom aliases. A generated-ID conflict retries; a requested-alias conflict returns 409.

Rate-limit alias probing to prevent namespace scanning.

For global multi-region writes, claim the shared URL key through one owning region/partition or a globally consistent uniqueness service; never trust an async replica to decide availability.



ImportantSame URL Path: Generated IDs and custom aliases using /p/{slug} must be unique across both.

Normalize: Apply consistent rules (e.g., lowercase) before saving.

Atomic Insert: Reserve the slug in the primary database to prevent duplicates.

Conflict: Return 409 if a custom alias already exists.

Separate Paths: Use separate namespaces only if routes are different.

Avoid Replicas: Never check slug availability using a stale read replica.



16. Database Choice

The primary access pattern is simple: pasteId -> metadata. That works well with either a relational database or a distributed key-value/document store.

Requirement
	SQL
	Distributed KV / NoSQL

Primary key lookup
	Excellent
	Excellent

Transactions/constraints
	Strong and familiar
	Product-dependent

Horizontal partitioning
	Possible, may require more planning
	Often built in

Schema flexibility
	Structured
	Often flexible

Ad-hoc queries
	Strong
	Usually weaker/secondary

Write scale needed here
	Easily sufficient at moderate scale
	Useful at very large scale



Recommended interview answerStart with SQL if the scale is moderate because the data model is simple and transactions/constraints are useful. At very large scale, a partitioned key-value store keyed by pasteId is natural because almost every read is a point lookup.



17. Storing Paste Bodies: Database vs Object Storage





Separate metadata from large bodies when storage volume or row size makes it worthwhile.

Inline Body in Database

One durable write and one lookup.

Simpler deletion/transaction semantics.

Good when max paste size is small and storage is modest.

Body in Object Storage

Cheap, durable, virtually unlimited blob storage.

Metadata rows stay small and cache-friendly.

Object lifecycle rules help expiration/archival.

Adds an extra network lookup and cross-store consistency.

Hybrid Policy

Store tiny bodies inline, large bodies in object storage.

This saves a network hop for common small pastes but complicates code paths.



Preferred large-scale designMetadata DB + object storage is a strong production-scale answer. The metadata row is the authoritative lifecycle/access record; the body object is immutable content.

18. Partitioning / Sharding





Hash partitioning fits the dominant exact-ID lookup.

Partition metadata by hash(pasteId).

Random/KGS-generated IDs already distribute well.

Point reads/writes hit one shard.

Avoid partitioning by createdAt; recent traffic would create a hot partition.

Avoid ownerId as the primary partition key if anonymous pastes dominate or individual users can be extremely hot.

Rebalancing

Consistent hashing/token ranges reduce movement when nodes are added.

Managed distributed databases may handle partition splitting automatically.

Secondary Access Paths

Owner history should use a separate ownerId-based index/table.

Search should use a dedicated search system, not scatter-gather across all shards.



When to Scale the Metadata Database (Additional Detail)

Do not shard only because the system sounds large. At the stated estimate of 10M creates/day, writes average ~116 QPS; however 500 B of metadata per paste adds ~5 GB/day (~1.8 TB/year raw before indexes, retention and replicas).

Start simple: Use one well-indexed SQL primary, read replicas if needed, and a UNIQUE/PRIMARY KEY on the authoritative slug. Measure CPU, IOPS, index size, storage growth, p95 latency and replication lag.

Scale reads first: Cache hot pastes and use read replicas when read load is the bottleneck. Replicas improve read capacity but do not solve primary write throughput or storage growth.

Manage data growth: Enforce expiresAt, run background cleanup, and consider time-based retention/archival. Keep large bodies outside metadata rows when their size makes SQL storage expensive.

Partition when justified: Hash partition by pasteId/slug when the single-primary write, storage, index or operational ceiling is reached. Preserve an authoritative global alias reservation mechanism.

Rebalancing cost: Partitioning adds routing, migrations, cross-shard operations and hot-key concerns; it should follow evidence of a real bottleneck.

Decision rule: Optimize the bottleneck you can measure: cache/replicas for reads, object storage + expiry for bytes, partitioning for one-node metadata limits.





Interview-ready answerThe core lookup is by pasteId, so I hash-partition on pasteId. That gives even distribution and single-partition reads. I create separate derived indexes for owner history or search instead of turning the primary key into a compromise.

19. Replication and Consistency





Replication improves availability, but replica lag matters immediately after create/delete.



Replicate metadata across nodes/AZs for availability.

Replicate object bodies using the object store's durability/replication mechanisms.

Public immutable reads can tolerate eventual replica consistency.

Creation must guarantee unique pasteId before success.

Deletion/private ACL changes need careful cache invalidation and may require stronger read consistency.





Read-After-Create  (Consistency)

Goal: After creating a paste, the user should be able to read it immediately, even if database replicas haven't caught up.

Problem:

User creates a paste, and metadata is saved in the primary database.

Read replicas may take time to receive the new data (replication lag).

If the next read goes to a stale replica, it may return 404 Not Found, even though the paste exists.

Strategies

Primary Commit + Cache Warm-Up

Save metadata in the primary database.

Warm the cache with the newly created paste.

Return the paste URL after successful commit (and cache warm-up if required).

Subsequent reads can access the cached data immediately.

Read From Primary

Route the creating user's reads to the primary database for a short period after creation.

Avoid stale replicas until replication catches up.

Trade-off: Increased primary database load.

Session Token / Version

Return a commit version or consistency token after creation.

On the next read, verify whether the replica has reached that version.

If the replica is outdated, wait briefly or fall back to the primary database.

Cache warming is the process of loading frequently accessed data into a cache before users request it, so that their requests can be served faster.

Interview Key Point: Use cache warming for fast reads, or primary reads/version tokens when stronger read-after-create consistency is required.

Read-After-Delete (Consistency)

Goal: Once a paste is deleted, users should no longer be able to access it, even if cached copies or object data still exist.

Correct Deletion Steps

Mark Metadata as DELETED

Update the database record to status = DELETED.

This is a logical deletion (soft delete).

The metadata becomes the source of truth for whether the paste is accessible.

Invalidate Caches

Remove the paste from L1 (local cache), L2 (Redis), and CDN.

Prevent subsequent reads from using stale cached content.

Use cache invalidation events to update multiple application instances.

Delete Object Asynchronously

Schedule physical deletion of the paste body from object storage.

Optionally retain it for a limited recovery window if retention policies allow.

Background workers permanently remove the object later.z

Important Failure Cases

Database Update Fails: Do not report successful deletion.

Cache Invalidation Fails: Stale cached copies may remain accessible; retry invalidation and use status/version checks.

CDN Purge Delayed: Old content might still be served until the purge completes.

Object Deletion Fails: Retry asynchronously using a queue or dead-letter queue.

Important Consistency Consideration

Marking metadata as DELETED does not automatically stop a CDN or cache from serving an old copy. For strict read-after-delete guarantees, cached responses must be revalidated or otherwise prevented from being served after deletion.

Interview Key Points:

Read-After-Create: Avoid stale replicas using cache warming, primary reads, or consistency tokens.

Read-After-Delete: Soft-delete first, invalidate caches, then physically remove the object asynchronously.

Trade-off: Strong consistency requires additional coordination and may increase latency or reduce availability.

20. Caching Strategy





Use multiple cache layers only when each has a clear role.

Cache-Aside

Check L1, then L2.

On miss, load metadata/body from source of truth.

Populate cache with TTL bounded by paste expiry.

Cache Key

paste:{pasteId}:v{version}

If rendered output depends on language/theme, keep body cache separate from rendered-page cache.

TTL

Immutable public paste: longer TTL.

Expiring paste: TTL <= remaining lifetime.

Private paste: short/shared-cache policy or no shared body cache depending on security model.

Negative 404: short TTL.

Stampede Protection

Single-flight/request coalescing so one backend fetch fills the cache.

TTL jitter to avoid mass expiry at one instant.

Serve stale-while-revalidate only if lifecycle/access rules permit.



Cache Invalidation Races (Additional Detail)

Deleting a paste and purging caches is not enough if a concurrent request can repopulate a deleted value.

Example race: Reader A misses cache and fetches ACTIVE metadata. Writer B commits DELETED and invalidates L1/L2/CDN. Reader A then fills the cache from its stale result.

Version fence: Include a record version/generation with cached entries. Before repopulating after a slow fetch, confirm the authoritative status/version has not changed, or use an equivalent coordinated cache-write guard.

Tombstone: Cache a short-lived DELETED marker (with its version) and reject older repopulation attempts. Deletion events should invalidate L1 caches on every app node and purge CDN copies.

Expiry and privacy: A cache hit must still obey expiresAt; private/ACL-sensitive reads cannot depend on globally reusable stale responses. Stale-while-revalidate is for content whose visibility rules permit it.

Strict revocation: A CDN purge is not instantaneous. If immediate takedown is required, use revalidation/access checks or a caching policy that does not permit a stale public response.

Trade-off: Short TTL and revalidation improve freshness but reduce cache hit ratio and increase read latency/origin load.





Cache sizing intuitionCache the working set: recent and popular pastes. A tiny fraction of keys often produces most reads, especially after a link goes viral.

21. CDN Strategy





The CDN is ideal for public immutable content, not for every visibility mode.



CDN Cache: Cache public, unchanging pastes for faster access.

Cache TTL: Set cache duration based on paste expiry.

Private Pastes: Never store in public caches.

Unlisted Pastes: Can be cached, but consider privacy risks.

Delete/Takedown: Clear CDN cache or use short TTLs.



CDN Cache Key

Cache Key: Usually host + path + version/format.

Avoid Unnecessary Headers/Cookies: They create extra cache entries and reduce cache hits.

Consistency: Same content should use the same cache key.

Origin Shield / Mid-Tier Cache

Purpose: A shared cache between CDN edges and the origin server.

Viral Content: Prevents multiple CDN edges from hitting the origin simultaneously.

Benefit: Reduces origin load and improves performance.

Request Coalescing: Combines multiple requests for the same missing content into one origin request.

Key Point: CDN caches speed up reads, while Origin Shield protects the backend from sudden traffic spikes.

Why CDN mattersPaste bodies are immutable and globally shareable, which is a near-perfect CDN workload. The CDN can absorb a viral paste without scaling the database or object store proportionally.



Example: Caching a Paste in CDN

Suppose a user creates a public paste: https://paste.com/abc123

1. First Request (CDN Cache Miss)

CDN doesn't have abc123.

API fetches the paste from S3.

API returns the content with:



Cache-Control: public, max-age=3600

Content-Type: text/plain



CDN stores the response for 1 hour.

2. Second Request (CDN Cache Hit)

CDN already has abc123.

No API, database, or S3 call is needed.

Response is faster.

3. What Does CDN Store?

Count CDN hits correctly: For public pages, emit/view-log one event at the CDN edge for each delivered read (cache hit or miss). For private/direct API reads, emit at the API. Do not count the origin fetch on a public CDN miss a second time; use request IDs/deduplication if both paths can emit.

Cache Key
	Cached Value

paste.com/abc123
	Paste content + relevant HTTP response headers

22. Viral / Hot Paste Handling





CDN Caching: Serve public viral pastes from CDN instead of hitting the backend.

Cache Replication: Replicate hot entries across cache nodes to distribute traffic.

L1 Cache: Store popular pastes in each application instance's local memory.

Request Coalescing: Combine multiple cache misses for the same key into one backend request.

Async View Counters: Update view counts asynchronously instead of writing to the DB on every read.

Concurrency Limits: Limit simultaneous backend requests to prevent overload.

Circuit Breaker: Temporarily stop requests to failing storage services.

TTL Jitter: Randomize cache expiration times to avoid simultaneous cache misses.

Cache Pre-Warming: Load popular pastes into cache before heavy traffic.

Stale-While-Revalidate: Serve cached content while refreshing it in the background, only when safe.

Important: Use longer cache TTLs for immutable public pastes. For mutable or deleted pastes, use cache invalidation or shorter TTLs.

Interview follow-upIf one paste gets 1 million reads/sec, sharding the database does not solve the hot-key problem because every request still targets the same logical key. Replication, CDN, and caching solve it.

23. Expiration and Cleanup





Serving correctness and physical cleanup do not need to happen at exactly the same moment.

Read-Time Expiration

Metadata contains expiresAt.

During Read: Check status = ACTIVE and expiresAt > NOW().

If Expired: Return 404 or 410, even if the status is still ACTIVE.

Background Worker: Periodically find expired pastes and delete their data or optionally mark them EXPIRED.

Cache: Ensure cached content is never served beyond expiresAt.

Background Cleanup

Database TTL: Automatically deletes expired metadata, but deletion may be delayed.

Sweeper Worker: Periodically scans expired records using an expiry index and marks or deletes them.

Object Lifecycle Policy: Automatically removes expired paste bodies from S3 after the configured retention period.

Why Lazy Expiration + Background Is Better

Lazy Expiration: Check expiresAt during reads and reject expired pastes immediately.

Background Cleanup: Delete expired data asynchronously to free storage.

Scalability: No need to schedule a separate timer for every paste.

Reliability: Even if cleanup fails or is delayed, expired pastes remain inaccessible.

Deletion semanticsExpiration is a logical state first and a storage cleanup event second. Use read-time expiration for correctness and background cleanup for storage management.

24. Public, Unlisted, and Private Pastes





Unlisted is not the same as private.

1. Public Paste

Access: Anyone can view.

Discoverability: Can appear in search results and listings.

CDN: Can be publicly cached.

Security: Requires abuse detection and moderation.

2. Unlisted Paste

Access: Anyone with the URL can view.

Discoverability: Hidden from search and public listings.

Security: Use a long, unpredictable URL as a secret.

Limitation: Anyone who gets the URL can access it, so it's not fully private.

3. Private Paste

Access: Only the owner or authorized users.

Authentication: Login required.

Authorization: Check owner/ACL before returning content.

CDN: Avoid public caching; use private caching only with proper access controls.

Security ruleAlways check authorization before returning private paste content.

Random URL: Makes links difficult to guess but doesn't guarantee privacy.

Authorization: Ensures only permitted users can access private content.

Key Point: A secret URL is not a replacement for authentication and authorization.

25. Delete, Edit, and Versioning

Delete Paste

Authorize: Verify the user is the owner or admin.

Soft Delete: Set status = DELETED in the database.

Invalidate Cache: Remove the paste from L1, L2, and CDN caches.

Async Cleanup: Delete the body from object storage after the retention period.

Response: Return success for deletion; future reads return 404 or 410.

Edit Paste (Optional)

Recommended: Keep pastes immutable by default. If editing is required:

Versioning: Create a new version for each edit (pasteId + version).

Current Version: Store currentVersion in metadata to identify the latest content.

Optimistic Locking: Use expectedVersion to prevent concurrent edits from overwriting each other.

Versioned Cache: Use pasteId:version as the cache key to avoid serving incorrect content.

Async Updates: Update search indexes and analytics in the background.



abc123:v1 → Original Content

abc123:v2 → Updated Content



Metadata → currentVersion = 2



Why versioning is BetterIn-Place Updates: Changing existing content makes cache invalidation difficult and may serve stale data.

Immutable Versions: Every edit creates a new version without modifying old content.

Metadata Pointer: currentVersion identifies the latest version.

Easy Caching: Each version has a unique cache key, avoiding content conflicts.

26. Syntax Highlighting & Content Security

Language Hint: Store an optional language type (java, python, json, plain) for syntax highlighting.

Syntax Highlighting: Apply highlighting in the frontend or rendering layer without changing the original code.

Raw Content: Always return raw paste content as text/plain.

HTML Escaping: Escape pasted content before rendering it as HTML to prevent XSS attacks.

Content Security Policy (CSP): Restrict script execution to prevent malicious code from running.

XSS interview point Keep original paste content unchanged, apply syntax highlighting separately, and prevent XSS by safely rendering user-provided content.

27. Search and Indexing Follow-Up

Search is optional for Pastebin. If required, use a dedicated search engine (e.g., Elasticsearch).

Public Only: Index only PUBLIC pastes, never private or unlisted.

Async Indexing: After paste creation, publish an event to a queue.

Search Indexer: Fetch paste content and store searchable text in an inverted index.

Delete/Expiry: Remove expired or deleted pastes from the search index using deletion events (tombstones).

Eventual Consistency: Search results may take time to reflect new or deleted pastes.

Access Control: Recheck visibility, status, and expiry before returning paste content.

Why Not Search the Primary DB?

Primary DB: Optimized for fast pasteId lookups.

Search Engine: Optimized for full-text search, tokenization, and ranking.



Use asynchronous indexing for public pastes. Accept eventual consistency in search results, but never compromise private content access or deletion enforcement.

28. Analytics







Async View Events: Public reads served by CDN generate edge logs/events; private/direct API reads generate API events. Neither view path waits for analytics.

Avoid DB Updates: Don't increment view counts on every read; it creates a hot write key.

Batch Processing: Feed both edge and API events into Kafka/queue; workers deduplicate as needed and aggregate total views, uniques, and trends.

Unique Visitors: Use approximate counting (e.g., HyperLogLog) when exact counts aren't required.

Analytics Storage: Store long-term analytics in an OLAP database or data warehouse, not the primary DB.

CDN accounting: If only the Paste API emits PasteViewed, CDN cache hits are invisible and reported totals undercount public views. Define whether the metric counts all delivered edge responses or only origin reads; edge log delivery may be delayed or approximate.

Delivery Semantics

At-Least-Once: Events may be delivered multiple times, causing duplicate counts.

Deduplication: Assign event/request IDs and avoid double counting public CDN misses (edge event plus origin fetch). Remove duplicate deliveries when accuracy matters.

Approximate Analytics: Small counting errors may be acceptable.

Failure Handling: Analytics failures should never block paste reads.

Design separationKeep the read path fast and analytics asynchronous. Use event streaming for aggregation instead of updating the database on every read.

29. Security, Abuse, and Moderation





Abuse controls are essential because anonymous text hosting is easy to weaponize.

1. Creation Controls

Rate Limiting: Limit paste creation per IP, user, or token.

CAPTCHA: Challenge suspicious users or bots.

Size Limits: Restrict maximum paste and request size.

Reserved Aliases: Block names like admin, login, or api.

2. Content Safety

Malware Detection: Scan for malicious links and phishing content.

Moderation: Scan content asynchronously; reject known dangerous content immediately.

Report/Takedown: Allow users to report and admins to remove harmful pastes.

3. Rendering Security

HTML Escaping: Prevent XSS attacks when displaying pasted content.

Strict CSP: Restrict script execution.

Raw Endpoint: Use text/plain and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

4. Enumeration & Scraping

Random IDs: Use long, unpredictable IDs for unlisted pastes.

Rate Limiting: Block excessive requests for nonexistent pastes.

Negative Caching: Cache invalid IDs briefly to reduce database load.

SSRF noteUnlike a URL shortener, Pastebin normally does not need to fetch arbitrary URLs submitted by users. SSRF becomes relevant only if you later add link previews or server-side URL fetching.

30. Compression

Text Compression: Compress large text pastes to reduce storage usage.

Storage vs CPU: Saves storage and bandwidth but increases CPU usage.

Small Pastes: Avoid compression when overhead exceeds savings.

HTTP Compression: Use CDN/reverse proxy with Gzip or Brotli for faster responses.

Compression Bombs: Limit decompressed size and CPU usage to prevent resource exhaustion.

Recommended Policy: Compress medium/large pastes, skip very small ones, and enforce safe decompression limits.

Simple policyCompression reduces storage and bandwidth costs but adds CPU overhead. Use it selectively based on paste size.

Which Algorithm? Gzip/Brotli for HTTP and Zstd for object storage.



Ways to Compress Data in Pastebin (Optional)

There are 4 common compression techniques for a Pastebin system.

1. Gzip

Popular compression algorithm for text.

Good compression ratio with moderate CPU usage.

Suitable for storing paste bodies and HTTP responses.

2. Brotli

Often compresses text better than Gzip.

Commonly used by CDNs and web servers.

Higher compression levels can consume more CPU.

3. Zstandard (Zstd)

Fast compression and decompression.

Good balance between speed and compression ratio.

Recommended for compressing stored paste bodies.

4. LZ4

Extremely fast compression and decompression.

Lower compression ratio than Gzip/Zstd in many cases.

Useful when low latency matters more than storage savings.

31. Very Large Paste Follow-Up



If the interviewer changes the maximum paste from 1 MB to hundreds of MB:

Avoid App Servers: Don't route large uploads through application servers to reduce server load.

Pre-Signed URL: Backend generates a temporary, secure upload URL for object storage (e.g., S3).

Direct Upload: Client uploads content directly to S3 using the pre-signed URL.

Verify & Finalize: Backend verifies the uploaded object before saving metadata and making the paste accessible.

Multipart Upload: Split very large files into smaller parts for reliable, parallel uploads.

Async Scanning: Scan uploaded content for malware or abuse before making it public.



Important: If scanning is required before publication, keep the paste in PENDING status until scanning succeeds. Clean up abandoned uploads asynchronously.

Architecture shift

Small Pastes: Store text directly in the database or object storage.

Large Pastes: Store content in S3 and only metadata in the database.

Control Plane (Paste API): Handles authentication, upload URLs, validation, and metadata.

Data Plane (S3): Handles actual file uploads, downloads, and storage.

Benefit: Reduces application server load and improves scalability.

32. Multi-Region Design





Global reads are easy; global writes and uniqueness need an ownership model.

Goal: Serve users globally with low latency, high availability, and reliable disaster recovery.

Read Path

Step-by-Step

Geo DNS / Traffic Manager: Routes the request to a nearby healthy region or edge.

CDN: Serves cached public immutable pastes immediately.

Regional API: Handles cache misses, private pastes, and requests requiring authorization.

Regional Cache: Checks L1 and Redis before accessing storage.

Regional Storage: Reads metadata and paste body from local replicas.

Replication: Metadata and objects are replicated from the write region to other regions.





Important Follow-Up: What if the user creates a paste in India and reads it immediately from the US?

Problem: The US replica might not have received the new paste yet.

Solutions:

Home-region fallback: Read from India if the US replica hasn't caught up.

Session routing: Temporarily direct the creator's reads to the write region.

Consistency token: Check whether the US replica has applied the required version before reading.

Trade-off: Local replicas reduce latency, but asynchronous replication introduces stale reads.



Generated ID Strategy Across Regions

Every paste needs a globally unique ID.

Even if several regions create pastes simultaneously, IDs must never conflict.



Strategy A: KGS (Key Generation Service)

KGS generates unique IDs and allocates separate batches to different regions.



India (Batch - A)

US (Batch - B)

Canada (Batch  - C)

Strategy B: Distributed ID (Snowflake)

Strategy C: Random IDs



Custom Alias Problem

Two regions can simultaneously try to claim /my-alias.Both regions check their local database.

Alias Available local db of both regions.

Both create the same alias before replication completes.

Problem: Two users now claim the same URL.

Solution 1: Single Home Region (Recommended)

Route every /p/{slug} reservation (generated or custom) to its authoritative home writer/partition; a globally consistent database is another option.



One atomic uniqueness constraint must cover both generated IDs and user aliases using the same path. Exactly one request can claim /p/my-alias; the other receives 409.

Benefits:

Simple implementation.

Strong alias uniqueness.

No multi-region write conflicts.

Trade-off:

Users far from the home region experience higher write latency.

Home-region failure can temporarily stop alias creation.



Solution 2: Globally Consistent Database

Use a database capable of globally coordinated uniqueness checks.

Benefit: Multiple regions can accept coordinated writes while preserving global uniqueness.

Trade-off: More complexity, higher infrastructure cost, and cross-region coordination latency.

Interview Key Point: Global custom alias uniqueness requires a single authoritative decision and a shared URL namespace with generated IDs when both use /p/{slug}.

Failure Recovery Steps

Health Monitoring: Detect region failure through health checks.

Traffic Failover: Route new requests to the US or Europe.

Read Replicas: Serve existing pastes using replicated metadata and objects.

Write Failover: If the failed region owned writes, promote or switch to another authorized writer.

Recovery: Synchronize data and caches when the original region returns.

If the paste was not replicated before the failure, the US region might not contain it.

A successful write in India does not automatically mean the data is already safe in every region.

RPO vs RTO



Concept

	Example

RPO (Recovery Point Objective)
	Maximum acceptable data loss

	Maximum acceptable recovery time

RPO = 0: Means no acknowledged writes may be lost during the failures covered by the design. This requires sufficiently strong durability coordination.

RTO = 2 minutes: Means the target is to restore service within two minutes.

Important Points

Graceful Degradation: Keep essential features working even when optional components fail.

Circuit Breaker: Stop repeated calls to failing services.

Bounded Retries: Retry temporary failures without overloading dependencies.

Failover: Switch to healthy replicas when the primary fails.

Monitoring: Detect failures quickly and trigger alerts.

Retry Policy & Failure Handling

Timeouts: Set maximum wait times for database and object storage calls.

Exponential Backoff: Increase delays between retries (e.g., 100ms → 200ms → 400ms).

Idempotency: Use idempotency keys to prevent duplicate paste creation during retries.

Bounded Retries: Limit retry attempts (e.g., 2–3) to prevent retry storms.

Fail Fast: Stop waiting when a dependency exceeds the API's latency budget.

Jitter: Add random delays to prevent multiple clients from retrying simultaneously.



Failure design principle

Core Services: Paste creation and reading depend on required metadata and content storage.

Optional Services: Analytics and search failures should not block paste reads.

Moderation: Run asynchronously where allowed; block publication if mandatory safety checks are incomplete.

39. Interviewer Follow-Ups and How to Respond

Follow-up: How do you guarantee the generated paste ID is unique?

Answer: Use a unique conditional insert for random IDs or uniquely allocated KGS/sequence IDs. If custom aliases share /p/{slug}, the final authoritative URL-key registry must prevent overlap between generated and user-chosen values. Do not use a separate check-then-insert.

Follow-up: What if a paste becomes viral?

Answer: Use CDN for public immutable pastes, L1/L2 caching, request coalescing, and origin protection. Sharding alone does not solve one hot logical key.

Follow-up: How do you expire millions of pastes?

Answer: Check expiresAt on every read for correctness, then clean metadata/body asynchronously with TTL/sweeper/object lifecycle rules. Do not create one timer process per paste.

Follow-up: What if users can edit pastes?

Answer: Use immutable versions with a small metadata pointer to currentVersion. This preserves cacheability and supports optimistic concurrency.

Follow-up: How do private pastes change the design?

Answer: Add authentication/ACL checks before serving, do not expose them through public CDN caches, and ensure search/analytics pipelines do not leak private content.

Follow-up: How do you support custom aliases?

Answer: Treat generated IDs and custom aliases as claims on the same normalized /p/{slug} namespace. Use an authoritative unique insert, reserve system routes, and return 409 on custom alias conflicts. In multi-region deployments route reservations to one owner or use globally coordinated uniqueness; never rely on local async replicas.

Follow-up: How do you count views?

Answer: Emit read events asynchronously and aggregate them. Never update one metadata row synchronously on every read.

Follow-up: How do you support full-text search?

Answer: Create an async public-only search index. Keep the primary paste database optimized for pasteId point lookups.

Follow-up: What if the maximum paste size is 500 MB?

Answer: Switch to direct object-storage uploads using pre-signed URLs/multipart upload. The API becomes a control plane and does not proxy the entire blob.

Follow-up: How do you prevent XSS?

Answer: Treat paste body as untrusted text: escape rendered output, use strict CSP, and serve raw content as text/plain.

Follow-up: What if the cache is lost?

Answer: Correctness remains because cache is not source of truth. Fall back to storage with rate limiting/request coalescing to avoid a thundering herd.

Follow-up: How do you handle a regional outage?

Answer: Use replicated metadata/object storage and DNS/edge failover. Decide RPO/RTO and whether cross-region writes are synchronous or asynchronous.

40. Detailed Interview Questions with Answers

1. Why is Pastebin primarily a read-heavy system, and how does that influence the architecture?

Answer: Once a paste is created, it may be read many times while the write happens only once. In our example the read:write ratio is about 10:1, and viral pastes can make the skew much higher. Therefore I optimize the architecture for cheap repeated reads: CDN for public immutable content, L1/L2 caches, point-key metadata lookup, and object storage for durable bodies. I avoid synchronous per-read writes such as updating a view counter in the main row because that would turn a read-heavy system into a hot-write workload.

2. How would you generate short paste IDs, and which approach would you choose?

Answer: There are several valid approaches. A database sequence plus Base62 is simplest and guarantees uniqueness but is predictable and introduces a central allocator. Random Base62 codes are decentralized and hard to enumerate, but the metadata store must atomically reject collisions. At larger scale I prefer a Key Generation Service that pre-generates unique 7-character keys and leases blocks to application instances; the create path then consumes a local key without a database collision check. I would choose the simplest method that meets the scale and secrecy requirements and explicitly discuss how I would evolve it.

3. Why use Base62 and how do you choose the code length?

Answer: Base62 uses digits, lowercase letters, and uppercase letters, giving 62 choices per character. Seven characters provide about 3.5 trillion possible values, which is far larger than the number of pastes in our assumed workload. The code length is a capacity and security decision: too short risks exhaustion/collisions, while unnecessarily long codes reduce usability. If codes are random, I also care about birthday-style collision probability and keep the occupied fraction of the namespace very low.

4. Why can't the service simply generate a random code, check whether it exists, and then insert it?

Answer: A separate 'check then insert' has a race condition. Two application servers can generate the same code, both query before either inserts, both observe that the key is absent, and then both try to claim it. The storage layer must provide an atomic uniqueness primitive such as a unique primary key or conditional put. If the insert conflicts, one request generates a new code and retries.

5. What is the purpose of a Key Generation Service, and how do you make it scalable?

Answer: KGS moves ID uniqueness work out of the paste-create hot path. It maintains a pool of unique keys and leases blocks of keys to paste-service instances, so an instance can create many pastes using only local memory. The KGS should allocate blocks atomically, replicate its allocator state, and maintain a large safety buffer. If a paste-service instance dies, I would rather waste its unused leased keys than risk reissuing them, because the key namespace is huge and duplicate IDs are a correctness failure.

6. Would you store the paste body in the database or in object storage?

Answer: For a small system, storing the body inline with metadata in SQL is the cleanest design because one transaction creates the paste and one lookup reads it. At larger scale, body storage grows much faster than metadata and bodies can be large, so I prefer a small metadata row plus an immutable object in object storage. That keeps database rows/indexes compact and uses a storage system optimized for durable blobs. The cost is an extra lookup and cross-store lifecycle management, so I would not split them prematurely.

7. How do you order the object-store and metadata writes so partial failures are safe?

Answer: For object-first writes, upload to a unique, no-overwrite staging/object key independent of the uncommitted candidate pasteId; then atomically insert ACTIVE metadata linking the claimed ID to that key. On collision, retry the ID without overwriting the existing body. An orphan object is cleanable, but visible metadata must never reference a missing body. For direct pre-signed uploads, reserve PENDING metadata first and publish only after verifying the object.

8. What database would you choose for the metadata store?

Answer: The dominant access pattern is an exact lookup by pasteId, so both SQL and distributed key-value databases fit. I would start with a relational database for moderate scale because it provides simple uniqueness constraints, transactions, and operational familiarity. At very large scale, a partitioned key-value store keyed by pasteId is natural because queries are simple and easy to distribute. The decision should be based on the required write scale, multi-region model, operational expertise, and consistency guarantees rather than the label SQL versus NoSQL.

9. How would you partition the metadata database?

Answer: I would hash-partition by pasteId. The IDs are high-cardinality and, if generated randomly or by a well-distributed allocator, spread traffic evenly. Each normal read or write touches one partition, which is exactly what we want. I would not partition by creation time because recent writes could create a hot shard, and I would create separate derived indexes for owner history or search rather than compromise the primary partition key.

10. How do you guarantee read-after-create if replicas are asynchronous?

Answer: After a successful create, an asynchronous read replica may not have the new metadata yet. I can solve this by reading from the primary for the creator's session, by warming the distributed cache after the authoritative commit, or by attaching a version/session token and refusing a replica that is behind. I do not need global strong consistency for every public read; I only need the user-visible guarantee that the URL I just returned works immediately.

11. How would you design the cache?

Answer: I would use cache-aside. Each API instance can have a small L1 in-process cache for the hottest entries and a shared L2 distributed cache for the broader working set. Cache keys should include pasteId and version if edits exist, and the TTL must never outlive the paste expiration time. On a miss the service loads metadata/body from durable storage and fills the cache. I would also use request coalescing and TTL jitter to protect the origin from stampedes.

12. Why is a CDN especially effective for Pastebin?

Answer: Public immutable pastes are highly cacheable and can become viral. A CDN serves content from edge locations close to users and absorbs huge spikes without sending each request to the application, cache cluster, or database. It also reduces global latency and origin egress pressure. However, private content must not enter a public reusable cache, and deletion/takedown semantics require either bounded TTLs or explicit purge/invalidation.

13. How do you handle one paste that suddenly receives millions of requests per second?

Answer: This is a hot-key problem, not a normal average-QPS problem. I would serve the paste from CDN, keep it in L1 caches across many API instances, replicate the shared cache entry where possible, and coalesce any origin miss so only one request fetches the body. I would not synchronously update a single view counter for every request because that creates another hot key. The origin should also have concurrency limits and circuit breakers so a CDN/cache failure cannot take down storage.

14. How should paste expiration work at large scale?

Answer: The read path should always check expiresAt and refuse to serve expired content. Physical deletion can be asynchronous: a sweeper or database TTL mechanism removes metadata later, and object-storage lifecycle rules delete the body. This avoids running one timer for every paste and keeps correctness independent from cleanup timing. Cache TTLs must be capped at the remaining paste lifetime so stale expired content is not served.

15. What is the difference between an unlisted paste and a private paste?

Answer: An unlisted paste is discoverability-based security: it is not listed/searchable, but anyone who knows the random URL can access it. A private paste has an actual authorization rule, such as owner-only or an ACL, and the service must authenticate and authorize every read. Random high-entropy IDs are useful for unlisted content but should never be presented as equivalent to access control. I would also keep private content out of public CDN caches and public search indexes.

16. How would you implement delete so a stale cache does not keep serving the paste?

Answer: I would first update the authoritative metadata state to DELETED, then invalidate or purge L1/L2/CDN entries, and finally delete the body asynchronously according to retention policy. Reads check metadata status or use cache entries with bounded TTLs, so deletion eventually reaches all layers. If takedown must be near-instant, the CDN needs an explicit purge mechanism and caches should not use very long immutable TTLs without purge support. For regulated content, I would define and monitor a deletion-propagation SLO.

17. What changes if pastes can be edited?

Answer: I would avoid in-place mutation of the body and instead create immutable versions. A small metadata record points to currentVersion, and each body is stored under pasteId/version. Updates use optimistic concurrency such as expectedVersion to prevent lost writes. This design keeps old bodies cacheable, provides history/rollback, and makes CDN/cache invalidation easier because a versioned URL never changes.

18. How would you add full-text search?

Answer: I would not put search queries on the primary paste metadata database. PasteCreated and PasteDeleted events feed an asynchronous indexer that writes only PUBLIC pastes into a dedicated search engine/inverted index. Search results can be eventually consistent because they are a discovery feature, but when a user opens a result the Paste API still rechecks current status and authorization. This prevents a stale search document from bypassing a recent deletion or privacy change.

19. How would you collect view counts and analytics without hurting read latency?

Answer: Keep reads independent of analytics. Count public reads at the CDN edge (hits and misses) because API-only events miss CDN hits; count private/direct API reads at the API. Send those events to Kafka/queue, deduplicate deliveries and prevent double counting on edge misses, then aggregate view counts and trends in an OLAP store. Never increment the primary paste row synchronously. If analytics is unavailable, reads still succeed; telemetry may be delayed or dropped per policy.



20. What are the main security risks in a Pastebin-like service?

Answer: The biggest application risk is untrusted content. Rendered views must HTML-escape paste contents, raw responses should be text/plain, and a strict Content Security Policy reduces script execution risk. Anonymous creation also attracts spam, phishing, malware indicators, scraping, and denial-of-service traffic, so I need rate limits, size limits, WAF rules, abuse reporting, and moderation workflows. Private pastes additionally need real authentication/authorization and careful logging that never dumps sensitive bodies.

21. How would you handle very large pastes or files?

Answer: Once paste sizes reach hundreds of megabytes, routing the entire payload through stateless API servers becomes inefficient. I would create an upload session, return a pre-signed object-storage URL, let the client upload directly, and then finalize metadata only after verifying the object. Multipart upload supports large bodies, and asynchronous scanning can run before public publication. The API becomes a control plane rather than a bulk-data proxy.

22. How does the design change for multi-region active-active writes?

Answer: Global reads are relatively easy because public content can be CDN-cached and metadata/object data can be replicated. Writes are harder because paste IDs and custom aliases must remain unique. Generated IDs can use disjoint KGS blocks per region or a region/worker-aware distributed ID, while custom alias creation may need a globally consistent coordinator or a single owning region. I would only choose fully active-active writes if the write-latency requirement justifies the extra conflict and consistency complexity.

23. What happens if the cache cluster goes down?

Answer: The cache is an optimization, so correctness should not depend on it. Requests fall back to metadata and object storage, but that can suddenly multiply origin load, so I would use request coalescing, rate limits, circuit breakers, and gradual cache warm-up. Capacity planning should assume at least a partial cache-loss scenario. The service may temporarily run at reduced throughput, but it should not return incorrect content.

24. What happens if the KGS is unavailable?

Answer: Paste-service instances should already hold leased blocks of unused IDs in memory or local durable state. They continue creating pastes from that reserve while the KGS is repaired. Monitoring alerts when local pools fall below a safe threshold. If all key pools are exhausted, new creates may fail while reads remain fully available; I prefer that to generating unsafe duplicate IDs.

25. Why not store the view counter, search text, body, owner history, and everything else in one database row?

Answer: Those features have different access and scaling patterns. The primary metadata row is optimized for pasteId point lookup and lifecycle checks, object storage is optimized for large immutable bodies, search uses an inverted index, and analytics uses append/aggregate workloads. Forcing all of them into one store couples unrelated traffic and makes viral reads or analytics writes contend with the critical create/read path. Separation is justified when the scale appears; a small V1 can still start with one database.

26. How do you prevent enumeration attacks against unlisted pastes?

Answer: Use high-entropy random IDs rather than sequential codes, keep the code space much larger than the number of active pastes, rate-limit clients that generate many 404s, and short-term negative-cache nonexistent IDs. However, I would clearly state that this only makes guessing difficult. If disclosure would be harmful, the paste should be PRIVATE and require authentication/authorization rather than relying on an unguessable URL.

27. How would you make paste creation idempotent?

Answer: For authenticated or API clients, accept an idempotency key with the create request. Store idempotencyKey -> pasteId together with a request fingerprint for a bounded period. If the client retries after a timeout, return the original paste instead of creating a duplicate; if the same idempotency key is reused with a different payload, reject it. This is especially important when the server committed the paste but the response was lost.

28. What would you monitor first in production?

Answer: I would start with user-facing read and write success rate, p95/p99 latency, and SLO burn. Then I would monitor cache/CDN hit ratio, metadata and object-store errors/latency, KGS key-pool depth, expiry/delete propagation, and asynchronous backlog. Logs/traces should identify whether slow reads came from cache misses, metadata, or object storage. I would avoid logging full paste contents, especially for private content.

29. How would you explain the final design in one sentence?

Answer: It is a read-optimized immutable-content service: stateless APIs create a globally unique short pasteId, store small lifecycle metadata in a point-key database and the body in durable blob storage, then serve public reads through CDN/L1/L2 caches while asynchronous streams handle analytics, moderation, search, and cleanup. The architecture keeps the critical create/read path small and separates lifecycle/security correctness from optional derived features.

30. What is the most important trade-off in this problem?

Answer: The most important design theme is simplicity versus read-scale optimization. A single relational database can solve the basic problem correctly, but at large scale we introduce object storage, caches, CDN, KGS, and async pipelines because the workload is immutable, read-heavy, and potentially viral. Each extra component should be justified by a bottleneck or requirement; otherwise it only increases operational complexity.

41. Final Pastebin Interview Cheat Sheet

Topic
	Recommended Baseline

Core model
	Immutable paste; create + read + optional expiry/delete

Scale assumption
	10M creates/day; 100M reads/day; 10 KB avg body

Paste ID
	7-char Base62

ID generation
	Random+conditional insert or KGS at scale

Primary key
	pasteId

Body storage
	Inline DB initially; object store at scale

Metadata DB
	SQL initially or partitioned KV at large scale

Partition key
	hash(pasteId)

Cache
	Cache-aside L1 + shared L2

CDN
	Public immutable pastes

Expiration
	Read-time check + background cleanup

Private paste
	Auth + ACL; no public cache

Analytics
	Async events; no per-read primary-row update

Search
	Async public-only index

Hot paste
	CDN + replicated cache + request coalescing

Multi-region
	Local reads; explicit global ID/alias ownership

Security
	escape HTML, text/plain raw, rate limits, moderation

Delete
	mark deleted -> invalidate -> async body cleanup





42. Review Quiz - Actual Design Problem

Question
	Answer

1. Why is pasteId a good partition key?
	Because the dominant access pattern is exact lookup by pasteId, and high-cardinality generated IDs distribute traffic evenly.

2. Why is object-first then metadata a safer cross-store write order?
	An orphan body can be garbage-collected, but visible metadata pointing to a missing body creates a broken paste.

3. Why is KGS useful?
	It guarantees short unique IDs outside the hot create path and lets app servers consume leased keys locally.

4. Why should cache TTL never exceed paste expiry?
	Otherwise an expired paste could still be served from cache after its logical lifetime ended.

5. Why does sharding not solve a viral paste?
	All reads still target one logical key; CDN/cache replication is the correct hot-key solution.

6. Why is unlisted not private?
	Anyone with the URL can read an unlisted paste; private content requires authorization.

7. Why should analytics be asynchronous?
	Synchronous view-counter writes add latency and create a hot write key on viral content.

8. What is the safest baseline for edits?
	Use immutable versions and a metadata pointer to currentVersion.

9. What should happen if KGS is briefly unavailable?
	Paste servers continue from leased local key blocks; reads are unaffected.

10. What are the first three things to say in the interview?
	Clarify immutable create/read/expiry requirements, estimate read/write/storage scale, then define APIs/data before drawing the architecture.
