notes.content:
Design PastebinSystem Design Revision Guide

SDE 2 • Concise companion to the complete 42-section HLD guide

INTERVIEW RULE  Start with a correct, simple create/read service. Add advanced components only when justified by scale, availability, cost, or product requirements.



How to use this guide

•  First pass: Read the 14 topic pages in order and understand the default decisions.

•  Second pass: Explain the write path, read path, failure paths, and consistency trade-offs aloud.

•  Final review: Use the checklist and ten interview questions on the last page.

The mental model

Client → Edge/CDN → Stateless Paste API → Cache → Metadata DB                                      └────────→ Object StorePasteCreated / PasteViewed / PasteDeleted → Async Workers



What matters most

High priority
	Follow-up priority
	Optional

Write/read correctness, IDs
	Hot keys, alias uniqueness
	Syntax highlighting

Cache/CDN & expiration
	Delete consistency, multi-region
	Compression internals

Storage/DB scaling
	Failure handling & DR
	Full-text ranking details



Use the detailed guide for implementation specifics and the original diagrams. This short guide is intentionally a quick revision companion.



01  Scope and Requirements

FRAME THE INTERVIEW BEFORE DRAWING BOXES

Core product

•  Create: User submits text; service returns a paste URL.

•  Read: Resolve the paste ID and serve raw text or safely rendered content.

•  Lifecycle: Optional expiration and owner deletion; keep pastes immutable by default.

•  Visibility: PUBLIC, UNLISTED, PRIVATE; optional custom aliases and accounts.

Non-functional requirements

Need
	What it changes

Low p95/p99 read latency
	Caches and optional CDN

Durable writes
	Persist body and authoritative mapping before success

Read-after-create
	Primary/session reads or cache warming

High availability
	Stateless replicas + metadata failover

Security
	Authorization, escaped rendering, rate limits

Cost control
	Object lifecycle, expiry, caching



Clarifying questions

•  Size: Typical paste size and hard maximum?

•  Volume: Creates/read per day, peak factor, viral traffic?

•  Consistency: Immediate read after create? Immediate delete/takedown?

•  Product: Private/unlisted? Edits? Search/analytics? Retention policy?

INTERVIEW RULE  Do not begin with multi-region writes, sharding, KGS, or full-text search unless a requirement or bottleneck calls for them.





02  Estimation and API

QUANTIFY ONLY WHAT AFFECTS THE DESIGN

Document assumptions

Input
	Derived quantity

10M pastes/day
	~116 creates/sec; ~600/sec at 5× peak

100M reads/day
	~1,160 reads/sec; ~6,000/sec peak

10 KB mean body
	~100 GB body/day; ~36.5 TB/year raw

500 B metadata/paste
	~5 GB metadata/day; ~1.8 TB/year raw

Read : write
	~10 : 1 average



These are planning assumptions, not measured production targets. TTL, compression, replication, and index overhead change retained bytes.

Basic endpoints

Endpoint
	Meaning

POST /v1/pastes
	Create paste; 201 on durable creation

GET /p/{slug}
	Escaped rendered paste

GET /raw/{slug}
	Raw text/plain

DELETE /v1/pastes/{slug}
	Authorize owner/admin and mark deleted

PUT /v1/pastes/{slug}
	Optional versioned edit



Important HTTP responses

•  400/413: Invalid request or body too large.

•  401/403: Authentication/authorization failure.

•  404/410: Missing or intentionally gone/expired, per product semantics.

•  409: Alias already claimed. 429: Rate limit.

INTERVIEW RULE  An estimate earns its place if it affects DB shape, cache/CDN need, object storage, cost, or reliability decisions.





03  Data Model and Storage

KEEP METADATA SMALL; BODIES IMMUTABLE WHERE PRACTICAL

Authoritative metadata

Field
	Purpose

slug / pasteId
	Unique URL lookup key

ownerId / visibility
	Ownership and access control

contentRef
	Inline body or immutable object key

createdAt / expiresAt
	Lifecycle checks

status
	PENDING / ACTIVE / DELETED / BLOCKED

sizeBytes / language
	Limits and display hint

version / currentVersion
	Optional immutable edit versions



Storage options

•  Inline SQL: Simpler transaction/lookup for small pastes and modest scale.

•  Metadata DB + object store: Scales bytes cost-effectively; introduces a second durable write and read.

•  Hybrid: Keep tiny pastes inline and large bodies in S3; extra branching complexity.

Recommended evolution

V1: SQL row {slug, metadata, body}V2: SQL/KV metadata {slug → objectKey} + durable object bodyV3: Cache/CDN and partitioning only when justified



INTERVIEW RULE  A visible ACTIVE mapping must always reference a verified, durable body. A temporary orphan object is easier to clean than a broken paste URL.





04  IDs and Custom Aliases

UNIQUENESS COMES FROM AN ATOMIC AUTHORITY

Option
	Benefit
	Cost / caveat

Sequence + Base62
	Simple, collision-free
	Enumerable, central sequence

Random Base62
	Opaque, decentralized
	Conditional insert + retry

KGS batches
	Fast short ID leasing
	Stateful allocator + recovery

Snowflake + Base62
	Distributed generation
	Worker/clock correctness



Seven-character code space

62⁷ ≈ 3.52 trillion values. A 7-character random ID is a convenient interview baseline, but it is not a strong security secret at large occupancy. Use longer high-entropy tokens for unlisted links when guessing resistance matters.

Collision / alias decision

Generated candidate OR requested alias              ↓Shared authoritative /p/{slug} unique reservation        ↙                         ↘  Insert wins                Insert conflicts  201 Created              random: retry / alias: 409



•  Same path, same namespace: Generated IDs and user aliases must not claim the same slug.

•  Never check-then-insert: A pre-check is racy across app instances/regions.

•  Multi-region: Reserve through one home writer/partition owner or a globally coordinated database.

INTERVIEW RULE  KGS uniqueness inside its own generated pool does not automatically prevent collisions with user-chosen aliases.





05  Write Path and Concurrency

CORRECTNESS COMES BEFORE PUBLICATION

Baseline write flow

Authenticate + validate + rate limit               ↓Generate candidate ID + safe unique object key               ↓Durably store body → atomic ACTIVE metadata insert               ↓Return URL → optional cache warm / async events



•  Safe object key: Do not upload to a path that could overwrite an existing paste before the slug is reserved.

•  ID collision: Unique DB reservation rejects it; retry a fresh generated ID. Requested alias conflict returns 409.

•  Object succeeds / DB fails: Orphaned object; delete asynchronously or via GC.

•  Object fails: Do not publish the paste or return success.

Alternative for pre-signed or large uploads

Atomic reservation: status=PENDING, unique slug        ↓  Issue scoped pre-signed upload URLUpload + verify object size/hash/identity        ↓  Conditional PENDING → ACTIVEPublish URL; GC abandoned PENDING uploads



Retries and concurrency

•  Idempotency key: Scope to user/client, bind to request fingerprint, and return the same paste on matching retries.

•  Conditional state change: Only the expected PENDING/version can transition to ACTIVE; a late finalize cannot overwrite another body.

INTERVIEW RULE  Publishing ACTIVE is the visibility boundary. Ensure all bytes exist before it, and never let concurrent requests silently overwrite an object or slug.





06  Read Path and CDN

FAST PATH WITH EXPIRY AND ACCESS CHECKS

Step by step

Public immutable: Client → CDN hit → response                        CDN miss ↓              Paste API → L1 → Redis L2                        miss ↓             Metadata DB → body/S3                        ↓               Validate + cache + return



•  Metadata checks: ACTIVE status, expiresAt, visibility and authorization before returning sensitive content.

•  Cache TTL: min(defaultTTL, expiresAt-now). A cached response must never extend logical expiry.

•  Raw response: Content-Type: text/plain + nosniff; rendered HTML must escape paste text.

•  Negative caching: Cache nonexistent IDs briefly. Do not share user-specific 403 responses publicly.

CDN policy

•  Public immutable: Cache at edge with a bounded TTL; invalidate if product supports takedown.

•  Unlisted: URL is a bearer secret, and edge/cache-key leakage is a risk; decide policy deliberately.

•  Private: Do not place in public CDN cache; authorize each relevant access path.

Analytics gotcha

On a CDN hit, the Paste API is not called. Count public delivered views using CDN edge logs/events; use API events for private or direct reads. Avoid counting an origin fetch as an extra public view.

INTERVIEW RULE  CDN for latency; metadata for lifecycle/access correctness; edge events for public view accounting.





07  Database and Scaling Decisions

SCALE THE BOTTLENECK, NOT THE BUZZWORD

SQL vs distributed KV

Start with SQL when…
	Consider distributed KV when…

Constraints, transactional insert, owner queries matter
	Very large partitioned point-key metadata workload

Moderate primary QPS fits one server
	One-node metadata write/storage ceiling is real

You want simpler operations
	You accept rebalancing / consistency complexity



Why pasteId is a good partition key

•  Dominant lookup: Exact slug → metadata/body.

•  Hash partitioning: Distributes many different generated IDs evenly; each normal read hits one shard.

•  Do not partition by createdAt alone: New writes can overload the newest partition.

•  Owner history: Use a separate ownerId + createdAt index/table, not the primary partition key.

Scaling order

Measure CPU / IOPS / p99 / storage / replica lag       ↓Cache hot reads + read replicas if reads are the limit       ↓Expire/archive data + move large bodies out of SQL       ↓Hash-partition metadata when primary limits are reached



In the assumed workload, ~116 average write QPS does not alone demand sharding, but billions of retained metadata records may eventually create storage and index limits.

INTERVIEW RULE  Read replicas do not increase the primary writer’s capacity; sharding does not solve a single hot key.





08  Cache Design, Hot Keys, Races

KEEP THE FAST PATH CORRECT UNDER CONCURRENCY

Cache architecture

•  L1 in-process: Serves the hottest keys from each application node.

•  L2 (Redis): Shared distributed cache for the larger hot working set.

•  CDN: Global public immutable reads; an origin shield can coalesce multi-edge misses.

•  Cache-aside: On miss, fetch durable data, fill cache with bounded TTL.

Hot paste (1M reads/sec)

•  Prioritize: CDN → L1/L2 → hot entry replicas → request coalescing → read replicas.

•  Origin protection: Concurrency limit, bounded fallback, circuit breakers and load shedding.

•  Avoid hot writes: Never synchronously increment one metadata view counter per read.

•  Optional extras: Pre-warm viral items; TTL jitter; stale-while-revalidate only when safe.

Critical invalidation race

Reader A: cache miss → fetch old ACTIVEWriter B: status=DELETED → purge cachesReader A: late cache fill → stale resurrection!



•  Prevent: Version/generation fencing or tombstones block an older fill; revalidate status/version when needed.

•  All layers: Propagate invalidation to L1, L2 and CDN; strict takedown may require stronger read revalidation.

INTERVIEW RULE  Cache hit ratio helps performance, but no cache layer should violate expiry, privacy, deletion or content-version rules.





09  Expiry, Delete, Edits, Visibility

LOGICAL CORRECTNESS NOW; PHYSICAL CLEANUP LATER

Expiration

•  Read time: Require status=ACTIVE and (expiresAt absent or now < expiresAt). Reject expired reads even if the cleanup worker is late.

•  Background: TTL-index/sweeper removes expired metadata; object lifecycle removes old bodies.

•  No per-paste timer: Async cleanup is cheaper and can lag without violating read-time expiry.

Deletion

Authorize owner/admin → metadata DELETED        ↓Invalidate L1/L2/CDN; guard against stale repopulation        ↓Async object deletion after approved retention



•  404 vs 410: Choose by API semantics. Deleted/expired content must not be served.

•  Immediate revocation: Requires more than a best-effort CDN purge.

Visibility model

Visibility
	Read rule
	Cache policy

PUBLIC
	Everyone
	CDN may cache

UNLISTED
	Anyone with hard-to-guess URL
	Treat token as secret; decide carefully

PRIVATE
	Authenticate + owner/ACL
	Never reuse public CDN response



Editing (optional)

Prefer immutable body versions and a small currentVersion metadata pointer. Conditional expectedVersion avoids lost updates. Include version in cache key and invalidate the unversioned latest URL.



10  Failure Handling and Retries

PROTECT THE CORE PATH FROM CASCADING FAULTS

Failure
	Expected behaviour / guardrail

L1/L2 cache down
	Bounded DB fallback, circuit breaker, concurrency limit

Metadata primary down
	Existing safe cached reads may work; failover before writes

Object storage down
	Valid cached bodies may serve; cold reads fail cleanly

KGS down
	Use pre-leased IDs until local pool exhausted

CDN down
	Fallback to origin with rate limits and capacity checks

Event stream down
	Reads keep working; retry/buffer optional telemetry

One app down
	LB health checks remove unhealthy node



Retry strategy

•  Timeouts: Choose a short per-dependency deadline within the end-to-end API budget.

•  Backoff + jitter: 100ms → 200ms → 400ms with randomness; do not synchronize retries.

•  Bounded retries: Two or three attempts only when the operation is retry-safe and the deadline permits.

•  Idempotency: A timed-out create may already have committed; blind POST retries can duplicate pastes.

•  Fail fast/load shed: Protect metadata/object storage when dependencies or fallback paths are overloaded.

Correctness vs optional subsystems

Search and analytics should not block paste reads. When moderation is legally/policy required before publication, keep a new paste PENDING until checks complete; do not bypass safety just because the event stream is down.

INTERVIEW RULE  Graceful degradation means partial functionality without returning incorrect content.





11  Multi-Region and Disaster Recovery

KEEP GLOBAL READS EASY AND UNIQUENESS AUTHORITATIVE

Read side

•  CDN: Global public reads near users.

•  Regional API/cache: Private or cache-miss requests reach a healthy region.

•  Regional replicas: Replicate metadata and body objects; do not serve a metadata pointer when its body is missing.

Write and ID ownership

•  Baseline: Single home write region; regional replicas for reads.

•  KGS: Lease disjoint ID blocks; Snowflake needs globally distinct region/worker assignment; random IDs need global authoritative claims.

•  Custom alias: All /p/{slug} reservations must share a consistent uniqueness authority across generated IDs and user aliases.

Replica lag and read-after-create

Create in India → primary commitsRead from US replica (not caught up) → false 404?Use home-region primary / session stickiness / version token



Region fails

Concept
	Meaning

RPO
	How much acknowledged data loss can be tolerated?

RTO
	How long until service recovers?

Async cross-region writes
	Lower latency but replication lag/data loss risk

Sync cross-region writes
	Stronger durability; higher latency/availability cost



INTERVIEW RULE  Active-active reads plus one authoritative write owner are usually a better first answer than complex multi-region concurrent writes.





12  Optional Pipelines and Large Uploads

SEPARATE DIFFERENT WORKLOADS FROM PASTE READS

Analytics

CDN edge public view  ──┐                         ├→ Queue → Aggregator/dedupe → OLAPAPI private/direct view ──┘



•  Avoid synchronous view counters: One viral paste creates a hot write key.

•  At-least-once events: Duplicate deliveries require dedupe if accuracy matters; approximate counts may tolerate small errors.

Search

•  Index PUBLIC pastes only using async workers and an inverted-index search engine.

•  On delete/expire: Send a removal/tombstone event; recheck access and expiry on opening a search hit.

Large direct upload

Client → API: upload session + pasteID / scoped URLClient → S3: direct upload (multipart for huge bodies)Client → API: finalize; verify object, size, integrityAPI: commit ACTIVE only after required scanning



Compression / security

•  Compression: Gzip/Brotli for HTTP; Zstd is an option for stored text; skip tiny bodies if overhead dominates.

•  Decompression safety: Enforce expanded size and CPU limits.

•  Rendering safety: Escape pasted HTML; strict CSP; raw text/plain + nosniff; rate-limit abuse.

INTERVIEW RULE  Analytics/search derive data asynchronously. Moderation can also be async, but publication must wait if required by policy.





13  Cost, Observability, Evolution

OPERATIONAL CHOICES FOLLOW USER-FACING REQUIREMENTS

Cost drivers

Cost
	First optimization

Object storage size
	Expiry/retention + optional compression

Origin read I/O
	Cache hot working set + CDN public traffic

Cross-region traffic
	Replica only where justified

Analytics writes
	Stream/batch aggregate; avoid per-read DB writes

Metadata storage/indexes
	Retention, archiving; shard at real limits



What to measure

•  QPS and latency: Create/read throughput plus p50, p95 and p99.

•  User-visible failures: Valid read and create success, 5xx rates, deletion/takedown propagation.

•  Dependencies: L1/L2/CDN hit ratios, object/DB latency and errors, KGS key pool.

•  Async pipelines: Backlog/lag for moderation, search, analytics and expiry cleanup.

•  Logs/traces: Trace cache → DB → object fallback; do not log full private paste contents.

Example targets (illustrative)

99.99% successful valid public reads; p95 regional cached read under 100ms; 99.9% supported paste creation success; explicitly specified takedown window.

Evolution: an interview-friendly sequence

SQL + one app → stateless replicas/LB → cache       → object storage → CDN → partition if needed       → KGS/async pipelines → multi-region DR



INTERVIEW RULE  These are possible evolution stages, NOT a mandatory implementation order. Each component needs an identifiable trigger and trade-off.





14  Interview-Ready Cheat Sheet

EXPLAIN THE WHY, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE THE COST

Decision
	Default answer

Baseline
	Immutable pastes; simple SQL if modest scale

Unique slug
	Random+atomic insert; KGS at justified scale

Write path
	Verified body + authoritative ACTIVE mapping

Read path
	CDN public; L1/L2; metadata/object fallback

Metadata DB
	Point lookup by slug; hash partition when needed

Hot key
	CDN, local/shared cache, coalescing, origin limits

Expiry/delete
	Read-time checks; soft delete; async cleanup

Privacy
	Unlisted secret URL ≠ private authorization

Analytics
	CDN edge public views + API private/direct events

DR
	Regional reads, explicit write ownership/RPO/RTO



Answer trade-offs in five steps

1. Requirement → 2. Choice → 3. Benefit → 4. Cost → 5. When you would choose differently.

Five high-value prompts

•  Why is pasteId a natural partition key, but insufficient for a hot paste?

•  What prevents two concurrent creates or aliases claiming the same URL?

•  What if DB and S3 partially succeed? Why use PENDING?

•  What if cache invalidation races with an in-flight cache fill?

•  How will public view counts include CDN cache hits?

INTERVIEW RULE  Be ready to draw the write path and read path, explain two failures, and defend the major trade-offs without reading your notes.

notes.content:
Design an API Rate Limiter



Interview phase
	Study in this guide
	Why it comes now

1. Clarify
	Sections 1–3
	Define what “100 requests per minute” actually means.

2. Simple solution
	Sections 4–6
	Demonstrate allow/deny with one server; select an algorithm.

3. Correct shared design
	Sections 7–13
	Explain token math, Redis ownership and safe concurrency.

4. Scale + survive failures
	Sections 14–23
	Add layered rules, sharding, hot-key protection and failover.

5. Advanced follow-ups
	Sections 24–29
	Multi-region, rule changes, tests and interview drills.





INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

The baseline is a regional gateway + Token Bucket + one authoritative Redis state owner per bucket. Everything more advanced must be justified by a new requirement.























Contents — jump to a section

SDE-2 Quick Interview Summary

1. Understand the Problem

2. Clarifying Questions Before Drawing Anything

3. Requirements and Non-Functional Goals

4. First Build a Tiny Rate Limiter

5. Where Should Enforcement Live?

6. Compare the Five Classic Algorithms

7. Token Bucket — Explain It from Zero

8. Scale the First Solution: Multiple Gateways

9. High-Level Design — the Regional Baseline

10. Complete Request Flow: Allow, Deny, Unknown

11. Data Model: Rules, Keys and Bucket State

12. Concurrency Correctness — The Two Gateway Race

13. Time, Fractional Tokens and Safe TTL

14. Hierarchical Limits and the Partial-Charge Problem

15. Weighted Requests, Concurrency and Billing Quotas

16. HTTP 429, Retry Headers and Client Behavior

17. Scaling: Shard Independent Buckets

18. Hot Keys, Tenant Isolation and Quota Leasing

19. Failure Handling: Keep the Rate Limiter Reliable

20. Rule Configuration: Control Plane vs Data Plane

21. Security, Identity and DDoS Boundaries

22. Multi-Region: Exactness vs Latency

23. Performance and Cost Optimization

24. Observability, Monitoring and SLOs

25. Testing the Guarantees

26. Common Follow-Ups: Add Only When Asked

27. Interview Time Plan — 45 Minutes

28. Interviewer Questions — Ready to Say Aloud

29. Final Revision Sheet and Checklist



SDE-2 Quick Interview Summary

Core requirements: Define the subject, quota semantics, burst allowance, scope, and behavior when requests exceed the limit.

Baseline design: Client → CDN/WAF → Gateway (authentication + local policy snapshot) → Redis primary (atomic token check) → Backend API.

Algorithm choice: Use Token Bucket when sustained traffic and short bursts are required; Fixed Window for calendar quotas; Sliding Log for exact rolling windows.

Redis correctness: Store balance and last effective time per canonical rule/subject key; refill, decide, consume, and update TTL atomically on one owner.

Failures: A Redis timeout is an unknown outcome. Choose fail-open, fail-closed, or conservative local fallback per rule; avoid blind consume retries.

Scale: Partition independent bucket keys across Redis shards. One hot tenant remains hot; isolate it or use bounded central quota grants if necessary.

Response: On quota exhaustion return HTTP 429 with an optional Retry-After estimate. Use 503 for relevant dependency failure when the endpoint cannot proceed.

Interview scope: Explain this baseline first. Only add multi-region leasing, reservations, exact billing, or fencing when the requirement warrants the complexity.





1. Understand the Problem

A rate limiter decides whether a caller may START a request at the present time. It protects the application from too much traffic from one user, IP address, API key, or tenant. If requests exceed a chosen allowance, the server rejects or delays the excess.

Business example
	Policy
	Reason

Social posting
	2 posts per user / second
	Avoid spam and sudden bursts.

Account creation
	10 new accounts per IP / day
	Slow abuse from one origin.

Reward claims
	5 claims per device / week
	Protect incentives.

Paid partner API
	100 requests per API key / minute
	Control external cost.

Login attempts
	5 per account / 10 min
	Help slow guessing attacks.



Three motivations:

protect backend capacity and availability

reduce expensive downstream work and API costs

enforce predictable fairness and product usage policies. This does not replace network-level DDoS protection.

What the interviewer wants

Start with a working simple answer. Then explain exactly what is counted, why your chosen algorithm fits, how multiple gateway instances share state, how a concurrent decision remains correct, what you return on rejection, and what happens when Redis or a region fails.

2. Clarifying Questions Before Drawing Anything

Ask the interviewer
	Why it changes the design
	Our baseline assumption

Client-side or server-side enforcement?
	Clients can be bypassed.
	Server-side middleware at API gateway.

Who is limited?
	Determines key and identity trust.
	API key or authenticated user; IP for coarse abuse.

What does 100/min mean?
	Fixed calendar window vs rolling vs refill.
	Sustained rate plus controlled burst.

What happens to excess traffic?
	429 vs delayed queueing.
	Return 429 for synchronous APIs.

One region or global quota?
	Changes latency and coordination.
	One region first; global as follow-up.

Exact accounting or approximate safety?
	Changes storage/durability choices.
	Atomic per key while its owner is healthy.

What if state store is down?
	Security vs availability decision.
	Endpoint-specific fallback.

Do long requests need protection?
	Rate is not equal to concurrency.
	Add separate concurrency limit if needed.





INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Say your assumptions out loud. “I will start with one region, a server-side limiter, token bucket for sustained rate and bursts, and 429 for excess calls.”

3. Requirements and Non-Functional Goals

Functional requirements

Rate Limits: Limit requests by user, IP, API key, tenant, or endpoint.

Flexible Limits: Set requests per second, burst allowance, or daily/monthly quotas.

Early Rejection: Block excess requests before they reach the backend.

HTTP 429: Return an error with a suggested retry time.

Dynamic Rules: Update limits without restarting servers; allow approved exceptions.

Different Limits: Set separate limits for login, posting, exports, and partner APIs.

Non-functional requirements

Low latency: rate-limiter decision should take a tiny fraction of request time (example regional p99 target below 5 ms).

Concurrency correctness: two gateways cannot consume the same final token on one healthy authoritative owner.

Availability: a limiter outage should not automatically take every protected API offline.

Horizontal scale: one million decisions/sec and many active limiter keys should be feasible by sharding.

Memory efficiency: inactive counters and buckets expire safely.

Observability: see 429 spikes, hot keys, slow Redis, policy rollout lag and fallback decisions.

Scope boundary: Rate limiting controls arrival rate. It does not guarantee overall concurrency, network DDoS defense, or billing-grade monthly accounting. These may be separate systems.

Six terms you will hear throughout this interview

Term
	Simple meaning

Identity / subject
	The user, IP, tenant or API key whose allowance is counted.

Rule / policy
	A configured limit such as 20 requests/sec for one route.

Bucket / counter
	The small changing state that records current allowed traffic.

Gateway
	A server that receives requests before application services and applies shared rules.

Redis
	A fast in-memory store; here it holds authoritative per-key counters.

Shard
	One member of several store nodes that owns part of the key space.

TTL
	Time-to-live: when unused state may be deleted safely.



4. First Build a Tiny Rate Limiter

Imagine one API server and one client. The rule is 2 requests per second. A simple middleware counts recent accepted calls and blocks any request above the allowance. This is enough to explain behavior before mentioning Redis, sharding or multiple regions.



Figure 1. Simplest server-side limiter: first two requests pass; third gets 429.

1.  The client sends request #1; middleware checks its counter and forwards the request.

2.  Request #2 arrives in the permitted period; it also passes.

3.  Request #3 arrives before allowance recovers; middleware rejects it with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests.

What is wrong with keeping all state in process memory? If requests go to multiple app/gateway instances, each has its own allowance. Ten instances with independent “2/sec” counters can admit roughly 20/sec. Crashes also reset limits. We solve this only when the system becomes distributed.

5. Where Should Enforcement Live?

Location
	Benefit
	Limit

Client SDK
	Reduces unnecessary client calls.
	Client can forge or skip it; not security enforcement.

Application service
	Knows actual domain work.
	Bad traffic already reached the service.

Middleware / API gateway
	Shared rule point before backend work; can authenticate.
	Adds a latency/failure dependency.

CDN / WAF edge
	Stops obvious bots and abuse before origin.
	Exact global identity-based limits can be harder.

Recommended combination
	Edge coarse + gateway quotas + service concurrency.
	Each extra layer needs a clear purpose.



Baseline: Apply API rate limits at the existing API Gateway.

Gateway middleware (recommended): Easy to add if a gateway already exists. No extra service needed.

Custom limiter library: Avoids extra network calls but must be implemented in every gateway language.

Dedicated limiter service: Centralizes rate-limiting rules but adds an extra network call and complexity.

Best choice: Use gateway middleware for simplicity and lower latency.

6. Compare the Five Classic Algorithms

Choose according to the required meaning of time windows, bursts, state size and request behavior. Token Bucket is our default only because the assumed API needs a steady rate plus short bursts.

Algorithm
	Intuition
	Good for
	Trade-off

Fixed Window
	Count requests in calendar periods.
	Simple daily quotas.
	Boundary allows two full periods close together.

Sliding Window Log
	Store individual accepted timestamps.
	Exact recent-window rules at low volume.
	Memory proportional to accepted traffic.

Sliding Window Counter
	Combine current and fraction of last window.
	Smooth approximate policy.
	Assumes uniform arrivals in previous window.

Token Bucket
	Earn tokens at rate r, save up to capacity C.
	Ordinary APIs; bursts and weighted work.
	Choose rate/capacity and keep updates atomic.

Leaky Bucket
	Bounded queue empties at steady rate.
	Worker shaping.
	Queues increase waiting time; need limits.



6.1 Fixed Window: the boundary problem

A policy of 100 requests per calendar minute can allow 100 requests at 12:00:59.9 and another 100 at 12:01:00.1. That is 200 requests in 0.2 seconds even though each calendar minute respects its count. Use fixed windows when calendar-period semantics are the actual requirement.

When
	Counter
	Result

12:00:59.9
	100 / minute ending 12:01
	100 allowed

12:01:00.1
	100 / new minute
	Another 100 allowed

Rolling 0.2 seconds
	200 accepted requests
	Burst across boundary



6.2 Sliding Window Log: exact but heavy

Keep a timestamp for each accepted request in a rolling interval, usually with a Redis sorted set. Before checking a new request, prune expired entries; then count and add only if allowance remains. Store unique event IDs, not just timestamp as the set member, so simultaneous requests do not overwrite each other.

Example: two accepted requests at 1:00:01 and 1:00:30; a third at 1:00:50 is denied under 2/minute. At 1:01:40 the two old timestamps are outside the window and new work can proceed. Some implementations count or retain rejected attempts too; that is a different policy and can consume more memory under attack.

6.3 Sliding Window Counter: approximate rolling count

Keep just the previous and current window counts. Estimated usage = current count + previous count × (remaining overlap fraction). This smooths fixed-window resets without storing every request timestamp.

W = 60s, current window age = 20sPrevious count = 90, current count = 30Previous overlap = (60 - 20) / 60 = 2/3Estimated rolling count = 30 + 90 × 2/3 = 90

The number is approximate because previous requests might have arrived mostly at the beginning or end of their window. Do not promise exact rolling enforcement from this formula.

6.3.1 Why Approximation Is Acceptable

A sliding window counter is useful for high-traffic systems where slight differences from strict rate limits are acceptable.

It reduces memory usage and improves performance while maintaining reasonable accuracy.

Key consideration: Occasionally allowing a few extra requests may be acceptable, depending on business requirements.

6.4 Leaky Bucket: stable output

Requests enter a fixed-size queue and are processed at a constant rate. If the queue is full, new requests are rejected.

It smooths sudden traffic spikes but increases waiting time. For example, with 100 requests queued and a processing rate of 10 requests/sec, the last request may wait around 10 seconds.

Best for: Background jobs and traffic shaping, not low-latency APIs.



Hard and soft limiting

Hard Limiting: Enforces the defined rate bound under the chosen window semantics and healthy-state assumptions. Useful for login and brute-force protection.

Soft Limiting: Allows slightly more requests than the limit in some situations. Best for high-traffic APIs where performance matters more than perfect accuracy.





INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Token Bucket: Best for handling controlled bursts.

Sliding Window Log: Best for accurate rate limiting.

Fixed Window: Best for daily/monthly quotas.

Leaky Bucket: Best for processing requests at a steady rate.





7. Token Bucket — Explain It from Zero

A token is permission to start a request. The bucket holds at most C tokens and earns r tokens per second. A request costing k tokens passes only if the balance after refill is at least k. For a simple read API k = 1. For an expensive export k may be 10.

Term
	Meaning
	Example

Capacity C
	Largest saved allowance; maximum initial burst
	C = 10 tokens

Refill rate r
	Tokens earned per second
	r = 2 tokens/sec

Request cost k
	Token units charged to this rule
	k = 3 per export

Saved balance B
	Unused permission after last request
	B = 1 token

Last update time
	Where we last accounted for refill
	time = t0



A new bucket often starts full, giving its caller immediate burst credit. Tokens must stop accumulating once C is reached. Refilling does not require a background timer for every user: calculate earned credit when the next request arrives. This is called lazy refill.



elapsed = max(0, now - last_update)

available = min(C, B + r * elapsed)

if available >= k: ALLOW, new_balance = available - k

else: DENY, new_balance = available

retry_wait = max(0, (k - available) / r)   # on DENY, r > 0

Figure 2. Token Bucket worked denial: 2.5 available tokens cannot fund a 3-token request.

Worked timeline — compute it yourself

Time
	Tokens after refill
	Decision
	Saved balance

0.00 s
	10
	Allow cost 3
	7

0.00 s
	7
	Allow cost 3
	4

0.00 s
	4
	Allow cost 3
	1

0.00 s
	1
	Deny
	1

0.75 s
	1 + 2 × .75 = 2.5
	Deny
	2.5

1.00 s
	2.5 + 2 × .25 = 3
	Allow cost 3
	0

6.00 s
	min(10, 0 + 2 × 5) = 10
	Allow cost 3
	7



At 0.75 seconds, the bucket needs 0.5 more tokens. With a refill rate of 2 tokens/sec, the request can retry after 0.25 seconds. Since HTTP Retry-After uses whole seconds, round it up to 1 second.

However, retrying does not guarantee success because other requests may consume the tokens first.

Important points:

Full refill time: Capacity ÷ Refill Rate = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 seconds.

Request cost > Bucket capacity: The request can never succeed, even after waiting.

Precision: Keep fractional tokens and convert milliseconds to seconds correctly.

8. Scale the First Solution: Multiple Gateways

When an application runs on multiple API Gateways, each gateway should not maintain its own rate-limit counter.

For example, suppose a user is allowed 100 requests/minute, and we have 3 gateways. If each gateway maintains its own counter, the user could make up to 300 requests/minute, bypassing the intended limit.

Solution: Centralized Rate Limiting Using Redis

Use Redis as a shared store so all gateways check and update the same rate-limit counter.







Figure 3. Multiple gateways check and consume the same bucket through its authoritative Redis owner.

How It Works

A request reaches any API Gateway.

The gateway identifies the user and generates a unique key, such as rate_limit:user123:login.

The gateway checks the user's available tokens in Redis.

Redis atomically checks and updates the token count, preventing multiple gateways from consuming the same token.

If tokens are available, the request proceeds. Otherwise, return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests).

Why Redis?

Redis is fast, stores data in memory, and supports atomic operations. This makes it suitable for rate limiting across multiple gateways.

Redis is the shared source of truth for rate-limit counters, but replication and failover can still cause temporary inconsistencies.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Use a shared Redis-backed rate limiter instead of independent gateway counters. This ensures all gateways enforce the same limit, regardless of which gateway handles the request.

9. High-Level Design — the Regional Baseline

The rate limiter should be fast, scalable, and independent of unnecessary database calls.





Figure 4. Production-oriented regional architecture. Rule updates and telemetry are outside the per-request critical path.

CDN/WAF: Blocks obvious malicious traffic before reaching the application.

API Gateway: Authenticates the user and reads rate-limit rules from its local cache.

Redis: Atomically checks and updates the user's available tokens.

Backend API: Processes the request only if Redis allows it.

Background Operations

Rule Publisher: Updates rate-limit policies across gateways without requiring database lookups for every request.

Metrics/Analytics: Collects rate-limiting statistics asynchronously without slowing down requests.





INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Keep the request path simple: Gateway → Redis → Backend API. Do not add the control-plane database or analytics queue to each request. Both are important operational systems, but the hot path should use cached policy and one bounded state decision.

9.1 Complete Example — From HTTP Request to Redis

Request: An authenticated user123 sends GET /v1/search to Gateway A.

Policy: ruleId=search_user, version=v1842, capacity=40 tokens, refillRate=20 tokens/sec, cost=1.

Key: Gateway builds rl:search_user:v1842:user123 using the trusted user identity and normalized route template.

Atomic decision: Redis refills from the last effective timestamp, checks that tokens ≥ 1, deducts 1 on ALLOW, and saves balance + timestamp + safe TTL in one script.

Allow: If balance becomes 17, Gateway A forwards the request to the protected API and records nonblocking metrics.

Deny: If balance is below 1, Redis returns DENY and an estimated wait; the gateway returns 429 and does not invoke the backend.

Unknown: If the Redis response times out, the gateway cannot assume no tokens were consumed; it follows the configured endpoint fallback without blindly retrying.

Implementation detail: A bucket can be stored as a Redis hash with fields balance and lastEffectiveTime, plus a key TTL. Use one atomic script for reads, writes and expiry.

10. Complete Request Flow: Allow, Deny, Unknown



Figure 5. An allowed request reaches the API; exhausted allowance gets 429; a state-store timeout uses the configured fallback.

Allow Path (Request Accepted)

Validate: Perform basic validation and security checks.

Identify User: Authenticate the user and identify the API endpoint.

Load Rules: Get applicable rate-limit rules from the gateway's local cache.

Generate Key: Create a unique rate-limit key based on user, API, and policy.

Check Redis: Atomically refill, check, and consume tokens in Redis.

Forward Request: If all required limits pass, send the request to the backend service.

Record Metrics: Log the decision asynchronously without increasing request latency.

Deny Path (Rate Limit Exceeded)

Reject Request: If insufficient tokens are available, do not forward the request.

Return HTTP 429: Inform the client that the rate limit has been exceeded. Optionally include Retry-After.

Record Metrics: Track rate-limit rejections separately from system failures.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Allow: Client → Gateway → Redis (Token Check) → Backend API

Deny: Client → Gateway → Redis (Insufficient Tokens) → HTTP 429

The goal is to reject excess requests early, protect backend services, and keep rate-limiting decisions fast.

One important detail: When multiple rate-limit rules apply, ensure the system doesn't accidentally consume tokens from some buckets before rejecting on another. Prefer a joint atomic check when keys are colocated. Otherwise, clearly define partial charging or a deduplicated reservation protocol; blind refunds are unsafe.

Unknown path

If Redis times out, we don't know whether the tokens were consumed. Redis might have updated the counter, but the response was lost.

How to handle it:

Fail Closed: Reject the request. Best for security-sensitive APIs like login.

Local Fallback: Temporarily use a conservative local rate limit.

Avoid Blind Retries: Retrying may consume tokens twice.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

A Redis timeout does not mean the request was denied or tokens were untouched. Follow a predefined failure policy based on the API's importance.

11. Data Model: Rules, Keys and Bucket State

Rule field
	Example
	Why needed

ruleId, version
	search_user, v1842
	Identify policy and safe updates.

scope / selector
	user + GET /v1/search
	Which requests use the rule.

algorithm
	TOKEN_BUCKET
	How decisions work.

refillRate, capacity
	20/s, 40 tokens
	Sustained rate and burst.

cost
	1 or 10 tokens
	Weighted request units.

identity source
	authenticated user
	Cannot trust raw client-supplied subject.

failurePolicy
	FAIL_OPEN / FAIL_CLOSED
	Behavior during state outage.

region scope
	regional / global
	Meaning of quota.

charging mode
	attempt / admitted
	Whether earlier successful checks may remain charged.



Per-bucket field
	Description

balance
	Remaining tokens; preserve fractions or fixed-point units.

lastEffectiveTime
	Timestamp through which refill credit was accounted.

ruleVersion
	If stable keys survive policy updates.

TTL
	Remove inactive bucket without minting extra tokens.



Example canonical key:rl:search_user:v1842:user_9Avoid raw API secrets in Redis keys. Hash/HMAC sensitive identifiers.

A globally shared counter, a per-user counter and an endpoint counter represent different rules/keys. Normalize paths to route templates: raw /users/123 and /users/456 usually share the same route rule, not a different rule per user ID in the path.

Concrete rule configuration

A simple configuration can say: the login API allows at most 5 attempts in one minute per account. The original chapter shows rule descriptors in files, loaded through workers and caches. In a larger production design, an audited rule DB plus versioned publisher can take the same role.

rule: login_attemptsscope: account + POST /v1/loginalgorithm: SLIDING_WINDOW_LOGlimit: 5 accepted or attempted events / 60sfailure_policy: FAIL_CLOSED

12. Concurrency Correctness — The Two Gateway Race

Suppose one token remains. Gateway A reads 1; Gateway B reads 1 before A writes. If both perform GET, compute and SET over separate network calls, both may return ALLOW and write 0. Two requests passed despite only one remaining token.



Figure 6. The correct implementation serializes the complete read/refill/consume/update transition on one owner.

Atomic Rate Limiting in Redis

When multiple gateways access the same Redis counter, checking and consuming tokens must happen atomically to prevent race conditions.

For example, if only 1 token remains and two gateways check simultaneously, both might allow the request unless the operation is atomic.

Solution: Redis Lua Script

Use a Redis Lua script to perform all operations together:

Read: Get the current token balance.

Refill: Add tokens based on elapsed time, up to the bucket capacity.

Check: Verify whether enough tokens are available.

Consume: If sufficient, deduct tokens and allow the request. Otherwise, reject it.

Save: Update the token balance, timestamp, and expiry in Redis.





















ATOMIC_OPERATION(key):

    state = Redis.get(key)

    refill_tokens(state)

    if state.tokens >= request_cost:

        state.tokens -= request_cost

        decision = ALLOW

    else:

        decision = DENY



    Redis.save(key, state, TTL)

    return decision





Why Atomicity Matters: Redis executes the Lua script without interleaving other commands, so two gateways cannot consume the same available token on the same primary.

Important: Atomic execution does not automatically guarantee exactly-once retries, safe failover, or atomicity across different Redis Cluster slots.

Why Not Just Use Redis INCR and EXPIRE?

For a fixed-window limiter:

INCR increases the request counter.

EXPIRE sets when the counter resets.

If these commands execute separately, a failure between them could leave a counter without an expiry.

Solution: Execute them together using a Redis Lua script or an appropriate transaction.

For a sliding window log, Redis Sorted Sets can store request timestamps, but removing expired entries, counting, and adding the new request should also be atomic.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Use Redis Lua scripts to make rate-limit decisions atomic. This prevents race conditions between multiple gateways while keeping the operation fast.

Remember: Atomicity on one Redis primary is not the same as guaranteed correctness during failover.



13. Time, Fractional Tokens and Safe TTL

Accurate time calculations and proper token storage are important to prevent incorrect rate limiting.



1. Time Calculation

Always use consistent time units.

For example, if the refill rate is 2 tokens/sec and elapsed time is in milliseconds:

New Tokens = (Elapsed Milliseconds / 1000) × 2



2. Fractional Tokens

Store fractional tokens (e.g., 2.5 instead of 2) to avoid losing tokens during small refills.



3. Trusted Time

Use Redis/server time instead of client timestamps to prevent manipulation. Handle backward clock changes safely.



4. Safe TTL (Expiration)

Redis should not delete a bucket before it has had enough time to refill completely.

Formula:

Time to Full = (Capacity − Current Tokens) / Refill Rate

A safe TTL is at least Capacity / Refill Rate, plus a small margin.



5. State Eviction

If Redis deletes a bucket early and recreates it with full tokens, users can bypass rate limits.

Example:

Bucket capacity: 100 tokens

Refill rate: 1 token/sec

Bucket status: becomes empty

After 10 seconds, the bucket should have only 10 tokens.

But if Redis deletes the bucket and recreates it as full, the user gets 100 tokens, exceeding the intended limit.

Solution: For strict rate limits, prevent premature eviction and use conservative recovery when state is lost.

 

14. Hierarchical Limits and the Partial-Charge Problem

Multiple Rate-Limit Rules

A single API request may need to satisfy multiple rate limits:

Global Limit: Protects the entire system.

Tenant Limit: Limits requests from an organization.

User Limit: Limits requests from an individual user.

Route Limit: Limits requests to a specific API endpoint.

Example: A request is allowed only if all four limits have available capacity.

Important: Custom rules can override specific quotas, but mandatory security limits must always apply.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Use AND logic for mandatory rate limits. If even one limit fails, reject the request with HTTP 429.



Figure 7. Sequential charging can spend the tenant token before a later user rule denies the request.

Policy
	How it works
	Trade-off

Sequential consume
	Check and deduct tokens one bucket at a time.
	Simple, but tokens may be deducted even if a later rule rejects.

Attempt charging
	Charge tokens even for requests rejected by another rule.
	Prevents abuse but may penalize valid users.

Joint atomic consume
	Check all buckets and deduct tokens together in one atomic operation.
	Accurate, but requires keys on the same Redis shard and may create hotspots.

Cross-shard reservation
	Reserve tokens across shards, then confirm or cancel.
	More complex; useful when strict consistency is required.



Prefer Joint Atomic Consume when multiple rate limits must pass together and their keys can be colocated.

For simpler systems, Sequential Consume may be acceptable if partial token deductions are allowed.

Race Conditions with Multiple Rate Limits

When a request must satisfy multiple rate limits, checking all buckets before consuming tokens is not safe.

Another request might consume tokens between the check and deduction, causing incorrect rate limiting.

Solution:

Same Redis shard: Use a single atomic Lua script to check and consume tokens across all buckets.

Different Redis shards: Atomicity is harder. Use a carefully designed reservation mechanism or accept controlled approximation.

Avoid Blind Refunds: Refunding tokens without tracking previous deductions can accidentally add extra tokens, especially during retries.



Checking and consuming tokens must be atomic. Separate checks and deductions can cause race conditions, while unsafe refunds can incorrectly increase available tokens.



15. Weighted Requests, Concurrency and Billing Quotas

1. Weighted Rate Limiting

Not all API requests consume the same resources. Assign different token costs based on how expensive an operation is.

For example:

GET /health → 1 token

POST /export → 10 tokens

Example:

Bucket capacity: 40 tokens

Refill rate: 20 tokens/sec

Export cost: 10 tokens

This allows 4 exports immediately and 2 exports/sec continuously.

Important: The server determines request costs, not the client. If a request costs more than the bucket capacity, it can never be allowed.



2. Rate Limiting vs Concurrency Limiting

Rate Limiting: Controls how many requests can start per second.

Concurrency Limiting: Controls how many requests can run simultaneously.

Example: If 20 requests start every second and each takes 60 seconds on average, approximately 1,200 requests could be running simultaneously.

Solution: Use a Token Bucket for rate limiting and a Semaphore for concurrency limiting.

For long-running tasks, concurrency permits also need safe release and crash handling.



3. Billing-Grade Quotas

Rate limiting and billing quotas serve different purposes.

Rate Limiting: Protects APIs from excessive traffic. Redis is usually sufficient.

Billing Quotas: Tracks exact usage for paid plans, such as 10,000 API credits/month.

For billing, use a durable database with idempotent transactions to prevent incorrect charges or duplicate deductions.







INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Use Token Bucket to control request frequency, Semaphore to control simultaneous requests, and a durable database/ledger to track paid API credits accurately.



16. HTTP 429, Retry Headers and Client Behavior

When a user exceeds the API rate limit, return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests).





HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests

Retry-After: 2

Content-Type: application/json

{

  "error": "rate_limit_exceeded",

  "message": "Please retry later"

}



Here, Retry-After: 2 suggests the client wait 2 seconds before retrying.

Important Points

HTTP 429: Rate limit exceeded.

HTTP 503: Rate-limiting service unavailable, if the API cannot safely process the request.

Retry-After: Suggests when to retry but does not guarantee success.

Exponential Backoff: Clients should increase waiting time after repeated failures, with random jitter to avoid simultaneous retries.

Idempotency Key: Prevents duplicate business operations when retrying requests such as payments.

Caching: Avoid caching 429 responses as reusable responses for other requests.

Queueing: Queue excess requests only if the API supports delayed processing.

Client-Side Optimization: Cache reusable responses and limit outgoing requests to reduce unnecessary API calls. However, the server must always enforce the actual rate limit.

17. Scaling: Shard Independent Buckets

When a single Redis primary cannot handle all rate-limit requests, distribute buckets across multiple Redis shards.

Each rate-limit bucket should belong to one Redis shard to ensure atomic updates.





Figure 8. Shards distribute different keys, but a single hot logical tenant still overwhelms its owner.

Planning input
	Illustrative value

Peak API traffic
	1,000,000 requests/sec

Mean rule checks
	2 per request

Total bucket transitions
	2,000,000/sec

Measured safe shard throughput
	100,000 transitions/sec

Raw primaries required
	20

At 2/3 planned utilization

Active buckets
	20 million

Estimated state cost

These are illustrative estimates. Actual capacity depends on Redis hardware, scripts, replication, and traffic distribution.

Important Considerations

1. Consistent Routing: All requests for the same bucket must go to the same Redis shard to prevent race conditions.

2. Hot Keys: Sharding distributes different buckets, but one heavily used bucket can still overload its shard.

For example, if a single tenant generates 300,000 operations/sec, adding more shards won't solve that tenant's hotspot.

3. Redis Cluster Hash Slots: Multiple keys can be updated atomically using Lua only when they belong to the same Redis hash slot.

4. Avoid Poor Shard Keys: Sharding only by ruleId can put all users under one rule on the same shard. Prefer a combination such as (ruleId, subjectId) for better distribution.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Shard Redis by a stable rate-limit key to distribute load while keeping each bucket's updates atomic.Remember: More shards improve overall throughput but do not automatically solve hot-key problems.

18. Hot Keys, Tenant Isolation and Quota Leasing

A hot key occurs when a single tenant, API key, or rate-limit rule receives too many requests, overloading its Redis shard.

Problem: Adding more Redis shards won't solve this because all requests for the same bucket must reach the same shard.

Solutions

1. Dedicated Resources: Move high-traffic tenants to dedicated Redis shards to prevent them from affecting other users.

2. Split Buckets: Divide a large quota into smaller independent buckets when the rate-limit policy allows it.

3. Quota Leasing: Instead of checking Redis for every request, allocate a limited number of tokens to gateway groups in advance.

Example: Quota Leasing

Suppose a tenant is allowed 10,000 requests/minute.

Rather than making 10,000 Redis checks:

A central Redis allocator reserves 1,000 tokens for Gateway A.

It reserves 1,000 tokens for Gateway B.

Both gateways consume their allocated tokens locally.

When tokens run low, they request additional allocations.

This reduces Redis traffic and improves latency.

Trade-offs

Unused Tokens: Reserved tokens may remain unused, reducing available quota.

Policy Changes: Previously allocated tokens may still be spent after the limit is reduced unless grants are revoked or fenced.

Complexity: Requires tracking allocated tokens, expiration, and preventing duplicate grants.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Use dedicated shards for hot tenants and quota leasing for extremely high-traffic buckets.

Quota leasing reduces Redis operations while keeping allocations centrally controlled. However, it introduces complexity around unused tokens, failures, and policy changes.

19. Failure Handling: Keep the Rate Limiter Reliable

If Redis fails or becomes slow, the rate limiter should not unnecessarily bring down the entire application.

Solution: Define a fallback strategy based on the API's security and availability requirements.





Figure 9. Redis timeouts trigger endpoint-specific failure policies, not a blanket decision for every API.

Failure mode
	Fallback
	Suitable example

Fail open
	Allow requests even if Redis is unavailable.
	Low-risk public APIs

Fail closed
	Reject requests when rate limiting cannot be verified.
	Login, OTP, sensitive APIs

Emergency local bucket
	Apply temporary per-gateway rate limits.
	General APIs during short outages

Conservative static cap
	Apply a predefined emergency rate limit.
	High-load or dependency failures



Important Considerations

1. Local Limits Can Multiply

If 20 gateways each allow 10 requests/sec during a Redis outage, the system may allow 200 requests/sec overall.

2. Prevent Redis Overload

Use short timeouts, circuit breakers, limited concurrent calls, and randomized retries to avoid overwhelming Redis during recovery.

3. Redis Timeout

A timed-out operation might have already consumed tokens. Blind retries could deduct tokens twice.

For safe retries, use a unique request/decision ID and store the result atomically.

4. Redis Failover

If Redis fails before replicating recent token deductions, those deductions may be lost, allowing extra requests.

Lua scripts guarantee atomic execution on the primary, not durability across failovers.

INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Choose fail-open or fail-closed behavior based on the API's risk. Use conservative local limits for temporary outages and circuit breakers to protect Redis.For strict rate limits, also account for duplicate deductions during retries and lost state during failover.

20. Rule Configuration: Control Plane vs Data Plane



Separate rate-limit rule management from real-time request processing to keep the system fast and reliable.



Figure 10. Audited rule changes propagate to local gateway snapshots; the request path never queries the configuration DB.

Control plane
	Data plane

Creates, updates, and deletes rate-limit rules.
	Applies rules to incoming requests.

Stores rules in a database with audit history.
	Uses locally cached rules for fast access.

Validates and publishes rule updates.
	Checks and consumes tokens atomically in Redis.

Handles policy versions and rollbacks.
	Continues using cached rules if the configuration DB fails.

Important: The API Gateway should never query the configuration database for every request.

Handling Policy Changes

Suppose a user's rate limit changes from 100 requests/sec to 20 requests/sec.

Simply updating the rule may leave extra tokens in the existing bucket, allowing more requests than intended.

Solution:

Version Rules: Track each policy version.

Reset Bucket: Create a new bucket for the updated policy with a defined initial balance.

Migrate Balance: Atomically adjust the existing token balance to match the new policy.

Rule Priority and Overrides

More specific rules can override general rules.

For example, a tenant-specific route limit may override the tenant's default route limit.

However, mandatory security limits must still apply, even when custom overrides exist.

Additional Considerations

Canary Rollouts: Test new policies on limited traffic before full deployment.

Rollback: Quickly restore previous rules if problems occur.

Monitoring: Track the policy version and snapshot age used by each gateway.

Fallback: Continue using the last-known-good rules if the configuration service fails.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Control Plane manages rate-limit policies; Data Plane enforces them. Keep policy rules cached in gateways, use Redis for atomic decisions, and propagate updates asynchronously without slowing down API requests.

21. Security, Identity and DDoS Boundaries

A rate limiter must correctly identify users and prevent attackers from bypassing limits.

Important Considerations

1. User Identification

Prefer authenticated user IDs or API keys for rate limiting. Otherwise, attackers may change identities to get fresh rate-limit buckets.

2. IP-Based Rate Limiting

For anonymous users, use IP addresses or device signals.

However, multiple users may share one IP (NAT), and attackers can rotate IPs to bypass limits.

3. Trusted Headers

Trust X-Forwarded-For only when provided through trusted proxies. Attackers can spoof untrusted headers to bypass IP-based limits.

4. Route Normalization

Use route templates like /users/{id} instead of unique URLs such as /users/123 to avoid creating excessive Redis keys.

5. Protect Sensitive APIs

Apply stricter combined account, IP, and device limits to login, OTP, signup, and password-reset endpoints.

6. DDoS Protection

Use CDN/WAF and network-level protection for large-scale DDoS attacks. API Gateway rate limiting alone cannot prevent network overload.

7. Secure Rule Management

Restrict access to rate-limit configuration APIs, audit policy changes, and never log raw API keys or authentication tokens.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Use trusted identities, normalize rate-limit keys, and apply stricter limits to sensitive APIs.

Rate limiting protects application resources, while CDN/WAF handles large-scale DDoS protection.



22. Multi-Region: Exactness vs Latency

This is a follow-up, not the baseline. 

When an application runs across multiple regions (US, Europe, Asia), users may share the same global rate limit.

Challenge: How do we enforce a global quota without increasing latency?

For example, a tenant has a global limit of 1,000 requests/sec. Requests from all regions must collectively respect this limit.





Figure 11. Strict global coordinator versus reserved regional grants: choose based on the real quota guarantee.

Multi-Region Strategies



Strategy
	How It Works
	Trade-off

Global Redis Authority
	All regions check one central rate-limit authority.
	More accurate global enforcement, but higher network latency.

Independent Regional Limits
	Each region maintains its own quota.
	Fast, but the combined traffic may exceed the intended global limit.

Static Quota Split
	Divide the global quota among regions.

Example: Dynamic Quota Leasing

Suppose the global quota is 10,000 requests/minute.

A central allocator distributes tokens:

US region → 4,000 tokens

Europe → 3,000 tokens

Asia → 3,000 tokens

Each region processes requests locally using its allocated tokens.

When a region needs more tokens, it requests additional quota from the central allocator, which must ensure that total allocated quota stays within the global budget.

Benefit: Lower latency without checking the global authority for every request.

Trade-off: Unused tokens may remain reserved, and policy changes or failures require careful handling.

Handling Policy Changes

Suppose a global quota is reduced while regions still hold previously allocated tokens.

If 40 gateway pools each hold 100 old tokens:

Maximum Remaining Old Tokens = 40 × 100 = 4,000

Up to 4,000 previously granted tokens may still be spent unless those grants are revoked or invalidated.

This is a simplified bound, not a general overshoot guarantee.



INTERVIEW KEY POINT:

Choose multi-region rate limiting based on the accuracy and latency requirements.

Strict global limits: Use a globally coordinated authority or carefully managed quota reservations.

Low-latency global APIs: Use regional quota leasing.

Approximate limits: Use independent regional counters with asynchronous synchronization.





23. Performance and Cost Optimization

The goal is to reduce latency, Redis operations, and infrastructure costs while maintaining reliable rate limiting.

Optimization Strategies

1. Cache Rules Locally: Store rate-limit policies in gateway memory instead of querying the database for every request.

2. Optimize Redis Calls: Use atomic Lua scripts, connection pooling, pipelining, and short timeouts to reduce latency. Remember that pipelining does not guarantee atomicity across keys.

3. Manage Memory: Safely expire inactive buckets to reduce Redis memory usage without accidentally resetting active limits.

4. Reduce Unnecessary Checks: Avoid applying redundant rate-limit rules to every request.

5. Monitor Hot Keys: Track heavily used tenants, rules, and Redis shards to identify bottlenecks.

6. Edge Protection: Use CDN/WAF to block malicious traffic before it reaches expensive backend services.

7. Regional Limits: For global applications, use local or approximate regional limits when strict global coordination adds too much latency.

28. Interviewer Questions — Ready to Say Aloud

Why Token Bucket?

The requirement is a sustained request rate with a controlled short burst. Token Bucket expresses that with a refill rate and capacity, supports request costs, and keeps constant state per active subject.

Why not a local counter in every gateway?

Each gateway gives another independent allowance; load balancing multiplies the effective limit. I use one shared owner or deliberately divided reserved quotas.

What must be atomic?

Load, calculate refill, check cost, consume, save timestamp and expiry. A separate GET and SET race even though both individual Redis commands are atomic.

Is Redis Lua enough for global exactness?

No. It serializes decisions on one executing owner. It does not by itself solve cross-slot transactions, replication-loss failover or globally coordinated multi-region rules.

What if Redis times out?

Outcome is unknown: it may have consumed and lost the reply. I apply this rule’s outage policy; exact replay needs an atomic saved decision ID/result.

What if the user bucket denies after tenant allows?

Sequential charging can spend the tenant token. I state that as attempt/conservative charging, or colocate related buckets for joint check-and-consume when admitted-only semantics are required.

How do you handle a global hot key?

One key remains serialized on one owner despite normal sharding. I can isolate it, or reserve regional/gateway token grants if the required quota semantics allow delegation.

What happens on Redis failover?

An asynchronous promoted replica may miss recent consumption, restoring permission. I explicitly state the tolerance or use stronger recovery measures for strict rules.

Why separate rate and concurrency limits?

Rate bounds starts over time, but 60-second tasks can still pile up. Concurrency permits bound in-flight resource usage.

How do clients recover from a 429?

Honor Retry-After when supplied, add jitter/backoff, bound attempts, and use business request idempotency for non-idempotent retries.

Why not one global limiter DB?

Global per-request coordination adds WAN round trips and a partition dependency. Regional grants reduce latency at the cost of utilization and precisely bounded failure/policy-change semantics.

How do you know the limiter is working?

Track user-visible error/denial patterns, decision p99, Redis health, key skew, config-version lag and rule-specific fallback; test with controlled clocks and parallel histories.

29.1 A Few More Interview Questions Worth Practicing

Why not a normal SQL table for every API hit?

Every request would add a durable write with index/lock cost to a latency-sensitive path. In-memory atomic counters are faster for protective quotas; use durable storage separately for paid credits.

What if two requests arrive at exactly the same timestamp?

An atomic owner decides their order. For a sliding log, store a unique member per request as well as the timestamp score so one request cannot overwrite another.

How do you choose bucket capacity?

Capacity is the maximum saved burst. Size it from backend headroom and desired behavior, not only the refill rate. Large capacity may allow a burst the service cannot survive.

What is rate limiting at edge versus gateway?

Edge limits block coarse IP/device abuse before origin. Gateway limits can use authenticated user, tenant, method and route context for business policies.

Is a per-user rate limit equal to a per-IP rate limit?

No. A shared NAT IP can group legitimate users, and users may change addresses. Prefer authenticated identity for product limits and IP for coarse abuse.

Why are all Redis reads not safe from replicas?

A lagging replica can show previously available tokens already consumed on the primary. The authoritative consume must happen at the owning primary.

What does a hot key look like in metrics?

One exact tenant/rule key has very high transitions/sec, causing a shard latency spike even when most shards are lightly loaded.

Can fixed window counter count rejected attempts?

Yes, by incrementing before comparing, but that is a different contract from tracking only accepted requests. Declare which one is enforced.

Why not retry the same Redis consume immediately?

A timeout may have committed and lost its reply. A second consume can double-charge without an atomic decision-id/result cache.

How are rule changes pushed out?

Store audited versions, publish snapshots, keep last-known-good locally, canary changes, and define the migration for existing token balance.

How can multiple regions enforce one exact quota?

Use coordinated ownership or safely pre-reserved disjoint budget grants. Independent fully provisioned regional buckets do not equal one global quota.

Can hard limits survive any Redis failover?

Not automatically. Lost replicated deductions can mint credit; define failover tolerance or use stronger durability/recovery for truly strict policies.

Appendix A. Advanced Option: GCRA

Generic Cell Rate Algorithm (GCRA) is an alternative representation of the same general rate+burst idea. Instead of storing token balance, it maintains a theoretical arrival time (TAT). This is an advanced follow-up, not necessary to explain the baseline.



I = 1 / refill_rate

Candidate allowed if now >= TAT - burst_tolerance

On allow: TAT = max(now, TAT) + cost * I

On deny: retry_time ~= (TAT - tolerance) - now

Benefit: one timestamp-like state and a compact atomic decision. Trade-off: less intuitive than Token Bucket and the precise burst tolerance must be defined correctly.

Appendix B. Redis Implementation Notes

Pseudocode below describes the logic to place in a short Redis Lua script, Redis Function, or equivalent atomic per-key operation; it is not a production-ready script. In real code choose fixed-point numeric representation, safe now/time handling, TTL installation, trusted request IDs, error paths, and script performance limits.



function check(key, now, C, r, cost):

  B, last = redis.read(key) or (C, now)

  effectiveNow = max(now, last)

  available = min(C, B + r * (effectiveNow - last))

  allowed = (available >= cost)

  newBalance = available - cost if allowed else available

  redis.atomic_write(key, newBalance, effectiveNow, safeTTL)

  return allowed, newBalance, retryEstimate

WATCH/MULTI/EXEC alternative: watch key, read current state, calculate prospective update, transactionally write if the watched value remains unchanged, and retry conflicts within a bounded deadline. Contended hot keys cause extra round trips; Lua avoids client-side CAS retries but each script must stay fast.

Appendix B.1 Java / Spring Boot Gateway Implementation Sketch

Filter: In a Spring Cloud Gateway filter (or equivalent middleware), authenticate the request, normalize its method and route, and fetch the compiled policy from local memory.

Key generation: Construct an HMAC-safe Redis key from ruleId, version, and trusted subjectId. Never use raw bearer tokens as key components.

Redis access: Call a preloaded Lua script/Redis Function through a pooled Redis client. Pass trusted capacity, refill rate, request cost and a controlled time source.

Result handling: ALLOW forwards downstream; DENY returns HTTP 429 and optional Retry-After; TIMEOUT triggers the rule-specific failure policy.

Metrics: Emit bounded-cardinality counters and latency histograms asynchronously; do not put a relational write in the request path.

Implementation note: A per-instance ConcurrentHashMap is suitable only for a single-instance prototype or an explicitly conservative emergency fallback, not a globally shared quota.

Appendix B.2 Quick Calculation Drill

Question: A bucket has capacity 30, refill 6 tokens/sec, and request cost 3. How many requests can pass immediately from full, and what is the long-term sustained request rate?

Answer: 10 requests immediately; 2 requests/sec sustained. Full refill from empty needs 30/6 = 5 seconds.
