notes.description: Design DynamoDB / Distributed Key-Value Store Advanced System Design Interview Guide Problem 31 | Partitioning, Replication, Quorums, Versioning, Repair & Failu
notes.content:
Design DynamoDB / Distributed Key-Value Store

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 31 | Partitioning, Replication, Quorums, Versioning, Repair & Failure Recovery

GoalDesign a horizontally scalable, highly available key-value database inspired by Dynamo-style systems. Cover partitioning, consistent hashing, virtual nodes, replication, tunable consistency, quorum reads/writes, conflict resolution, sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, Merkle-tree anti-entropy, compaction, membership, rebalancing, hot partitions, durability, and multi-region trade-offs.



Interview focusThe important discussion is the trade-off between availability, consistency, latency and operational complexity. Do not stop at 'use consistent hashing.' Explain exactly where replicas live, what happens during failures, how reads reconcile versions, and how replicas repair after recovery.



1. Functional Requirements

PUT(key,value), GET(key), DELETE(key).

Optional conditional/versioned writes.

Configurable replication factor.

Horizontal node addition/removal without full reshuffle.

Survive node and rack/AZ failures.

Optional TTL and batch APIs.

Expose tunable read/write consistency.

2. Non-Functional Requirements

Very high availability and predictable low latency.

Linear horizontal scale with data/traffic.

Durable acknowledged writes under stated consistency level.

No single metadata/data bottleneck.

Automatic failure detection, repair and rebalancing.

Support very large keyspace and uneven workloads.

Clear consistency semantics during partitions.

3. API Contract

PUT(key,value, consistency, request_id, expected_version?)

GET(key, consistency) -> value + version/context

DELETE is normally represented as a tombstone, not immediate physical removal.

Consistency levels can map to ONE, QUORUM, ALL or explicit R/W counts.

request_id makes retried writes idempotent where operation semantics require it.

4. Capacity Estimation

Assume billions of keys and petabytes of data.

Reads/writes may reach millions of operations/sec globally.

Average values may be KB-scale, but enforce maximum item size.

Replication factor N=3 is a common interview assumption.

Metadata per key/version also matters at large scale.

Network replication and repair traffic must be budgeted separately from client QPS.

5. High-Level Architecture



6. Partitioning the Keyspace

Hash each key into a large fixed hash space.

A partition/token range is the unit of ownership; a physical node owns many ranges.

Hashing distributes arbitrary application keys more uniformly than lexical partitioning.

The routing layer maps key hash -> partition -> replica set.

Partition boundaries should be small enough to move independently during scaling.

7. Consistent Hashing

Arrange hash space as a logical ring.

Hash keys and node tokens onto the same ring.

A key belongs to the first token clockwise, with additional clockwise distinct nodes forming replicas.

Adding/removing a token moves only neighboring ranges instead of rehashing the entire dataset.

Basic one-token-per-node hashing still suffers from imbalance; virtual nodes improve it.



8. Virtual Nodes (Vnodes)

Without vnodes
	With vnodes

One/few large ranges per server
	Many small token ranges per server

Harder to balance capacity
	Assign more/fewer tokens by capacity

Node loss transfers huge contiguous range
	Recovery spreads ranges across peers

Skew more likely
	Statistical balancing improves

Rebalance coarse
	Fine-grained movement



Key pointConsistent hashing limits movement; virtual nodes make movement and load distribution operationally practical. They are related concepts, not substitutes.



9. Replication

Replication factor N defines how many independent replicas hold each partition.

Choose replicas across distinct physical failure domains—hosts, racks and preferably AZs.

The preference list is the ordered set of eligible replica nodes for a key/range.

Replica placement must avoid counting two vnodes on the same physical node as two fault-independent copies.

Replication provides durability/availability; it does not by itself define read consistency.

10. Coordinator

Any front-end/storage node can act as coordinator, or clients can route directly with topology awareness.

Coordinator hashes the key, obtains preference list, sends read/write to replicas, waits for required acknowledgements, reconciles versions, and returns.

Coordinator is not the permanent owner of the key and should be stateless/retriable.

Avoid one central coordinator service that becomes a throughput/availability bottleneck.

11. Quorum Model

Symbol
	Meaning

N
	Number of replicas

W
	Write acknowledgements required

R
	Read responses required



If R + W > N, read and write quorums overlap under ideal replica-set assumptions.

Example N=3, W=2, R=2 gives a common quorum configuration.

W=1/R=1 minimizes latency/raises availability but allows stale reads.

W=3/R=1 makes writes less available but reads cheap.

Quorum math alone does not automatically guarantee strict linearizability in a Dynamo-style system with sloppy quorum, concurrent versions and failures.

Interview nuanceDo not say 'R + W > N means strong consistency' without qualifications. It ensures overlap for the intended replica set, but linearizability also needs ordering/version semantics and careful handling of failures, sloppy replicas and concurrent writes.



12. Write Path

Client sends PUT with key/value and requested consistency.

Coordinator hashes key and finds N preferred replicas.

Assign/accept version metadata according to chosen versioning model.

Send write concurrently to replicas.

Replica appends to durable WAL/commit log, updates memtable/in-memory state, then ACKs according to durability contract.

Coordinator returns success after W valid ACKs.

Remaining replicas continue asynchronously if necessary.

Background repair eventually heals missing replicas.

13. Read Path

Coordinator locates preference list.

Issue reads to enough replicas for requested R, often with speculative extra request for tail latency.

Collect value versions/tombstones.

Select dominating/newest version if ordering is known; preserve concurrent siblings if versions conflict.

Return resolved value/context to client.

Optionally perform read repair by sending resolved/current versions to stale replicas.

14. Versioning and Concurrent Writes

A timestamp alone is dangerous because clocks skew and two clients may write concurrently.

Dynamo-style designs can carry vector clocks/version vectors to represent causality.

If version V2 descends from V1, V2 supersedes V1.

If neither version dominates the other, they are concurrent siblings.

Resolution may be application-level merge, deterministic last-writer policy, CRDT, or server-defined rule.

The interview answer should state the conflict semantics explicitly.

15. Vector Clock Example

Version
	Clock
	Meaning

V1
	{A:1}
	A writes

V2
	{A:2}
	A updates V1

V3
	{A:1,B:1}
	B updates from V1 concurrently with A's V2

Compare V2 vs V3
	Neither dominates
	Concurrent siblings



A vector X dominates Y if every component in X >= Y and at least one is greater.

Vector metadata can grow with many writers; practical systems prune/compact metadata or use alternative version schemes.

Vector clocks establish causality, not wall-clock recency.

16. Read Repair

A quorum read may discover replica A has V5 while replica C has V4.

Return the appropriate current/resolved version to client.

Asynchronously write V5/resolution to stale replica C.

Read repair fixes keys that are actively read.

It is insufficient for cold data; anti-entropy repair handles the full keyspace.

17. Sloppy Quorum

During failures, one or more preferred replicas may be unavailable.

To preserve write availability, coordinator may write temporarily to healthy fallback nodes outside the normal preference list.

Still obtain W acknowledgements from reachable nodes, but this is a 'sloppy' quorum.

The temporary node stores a hint identifying the intended replica.

When intended replica returns, hinted handoff transfers the data.

This improves availability but weakens the simple quorum-overlap story.

18. Hinted Handoff



Hints need expiry and bounded storage; a long outage cannot fill disks indefinitely.

Handoff is best-effort repair, not the only repair mechanism.

If hinted node also fails, other replicas/anti-entropy still protect according to replication and durability assumptions.

19. Anti-Entropy Repair

Replicas periodically compare partition contents to find divergent keys without transferring every value.

Merkle trees hash ranges hierarchically; equal subtree hashes prove those ranges match.

If root/subtree differs, recursively descend only into mismatching ranges.

Exchange actual key/version data for mismatched leaves and reconcile.

Repair is bandwidth/IO intensive; schedule/rate-limit it so foreground latency remains healthy.



20. Storage Engine

A common write-optimized design uses WAL + memtable + immutable SSTables (LSM-tree family).

Write: append WAL, update memtable; flush memtable to sorted immutable table when threshold reached.

Reads consult memtable plus SSTables, accelerated by Bloom filters/indexes/caches.

Compaction merges SSTables, removes superseded versions and eventually purges safe tombstones.

LSM trades write efficiency for read amplification and compaction IO.

21. Tombstones and Deletes

Immediate physical deletion is unsafe because an offline replica may later resurrect an old value.

Write a tombstone version and replicate it like a normal write.

Tombstone must remain long enough for all replicas/repair guarantees to observe it.

After a configured grace period plus successful repair assumptions, compaction can physically remove old value and tombstone.

Long outages beyond tombstone grace can cause resurrection unless repair/retention policy prevents it.

22. Bloom Filters

Bloom filters cheaply answer 'definitely not present' or 'possibly present' for an SSTable.

They reduce unnecessary disk reads for missing keys.

False positives are allowed; false negatives are not.

Size/hash count trade memory for false-positive probability.

They optimize storage reads but do not replace indexes or version reconciliation.

23. Compaction

Type
	Trade-off

Size-tiered
	Good write throughput; more overlapping tables/read amplification

Leveled
	Better bounded reads; more write amplification

Time-window
	Useful for TTL/time-series-like expiration patterns



Compaction consumes disk bandwidth and CPU; throttle it to protect foreground latency.

Compaction also removes overwritten versions and expired tombstones when safe.

Disk-space headroom is mandatory because compaction temporarily needs additional space.

24. Membership and Gossip

Nodes need a shared view of membership, token ownership and liveness.

Gossip can disseminate membership/state incrementally without one central broadcaster.

Failure detector uses heartbeat/phi-style suspicion; suspicion is not proof of permanent failure.

Ring/topology changes need epochs/generations so stale nodes cannot rejoin with old ownership.

Separate 'node is unreachable' from 'node is administratively removed/replaced'.

25. Failure Detection

Timeout too short causes false positives during GC/network jitter; too long delays failover.

Accrual detectors estimate suspicion from heartbeat arrival history.

Client/coordinator can route around suspected nodes while repair later restores them.

Network partition may make two sides see different liveness; version/conflict semantics must tolerate this.

A node recovering from outage should not instantly absorb full traffic before catch-up.

26. Node Failure Walkthrough

Replica B becomes unreachable.

Coordinators mark/suspect B and continue with A/C if requested consistency can be met.

For high-availability writes, fallback D may accept hinted writes for B.

B recovers and is fenced/validated with current generation.

Hinted handoff sends missed versions to B.

Anti-entropy compares B's ranges against peers to catch anything hints missed.

Only after catch-up should B receive normal full traffic.

27. Adding a Node

Assign the new node a set of vnode/token ranges chosen to improve balance.

Existing owners stream corresponding partition data to it.

During movement, routing metadata identifies source/target and migration epoch.

Dual-read/write or forwarding rules prevent lost updates during streaming.

After target catches up, atomically publish new ownership epoch.

Throttle streaming so rebalance does not destroy foreground p99 latency.

28. Removing/Replacing a Node

Planned removal streams its ranges to new owners before ownership changes.

Unexpected permanent failure promotes/creates replacement replicas from surviving copies.

Re-replication must restore N distinct failure-domain copies.

Avoid mass simultaneous repair after large outage; rate-limit and prioritize under-replicated data.

Decommission metadata must prevent the removed node from reappearing as a stale owner.

29. Hot Keys and Hot Partitions

Hashing balances key count, not request frequency.

One celebrity key can overload all N replicas for that key.

Mitigations: read-through cache, request coalescing, more read replicas, application key sharding, CDN where applicable.

A hot partition may require splitting ranges/vnodes or moving them to higher-capacity nodes.

Write-hot single key cannot be arbitrarily sharded without changing consistency/application semantics.

30. Adaptive / Capacity-Aware Placement

Heterogeneous nodes should own token counts proportional to capacity.

Track disk, CPU, IOPS, network and p99 latency, not just bytes.

Move small vnode ranges rather than entire server-sized partitions.

Placement should respect racks/AZs and avoid correlated replica failure.

Automated balancing needs movement budgets/hysteresis to avoid endless churn.

31. Stronger Consistency Option

Dynamo-style quorum/version reconciliation favors availability and eventual consistency.

If a table/key requires linearizable conditional writes, use a leader/consensus group per partition or a dedicated transaction protocol.

Consensus serializes writes and provides a clear committed order but sacrifices availability when quorum cannot be reached.

A production service may expose both eventually consistent and strongly consistent operations using different internal paths.

State the chosen semantics instead of mixing AP and CP claims.

32. CAP and PACELC

During a network partition, a system cannot simultaneously guarantee availability for every request and strong consistency across partitioned replicas.

Dynamo-inspired systems commonly choose availability with eventual/conflict-resolved consistency for the base path.

PACELC adds the normal-operation trade-off: Else (no partition), choose between latency and consistency.

Tunable quorum lets applications move along that trade-off but does not erase it.

33. Multi-Datacenter / Multi-Region

Model
	Benefits
	Costs

Single-region N replicas
	Low latency, simpler
	Region failure risk

Async cross-region replication
	Fast local writes
	RPO > 0 / conflict handling

Multi-region quorum
	Stronger durability/consistency
	WAN write latency

Active-active eventual
	High regional availability
	Concurrent conflict resolution



Place replicas according to explicit regional failure goals.

Do not casually count three replicas in one AZ as regional durability.

Conflict/version metadata must survive cross-region replication.

Repair bandwidth across WAN should be controlled.

34. Read Tail Latency

A quorum request can be dominated by the slowest required replica.

Send requests in parallel and return after R/W threshold.

Hedged/speculative read to another replica after a short delay can reduce p99.

Track per-replica health/latency and prefer healthy nodes while preserving consistency rules.

Do not let unlimited hedging amplify overload.

35. Backpressure and Overload

Bound coordinator queues and per-node in-flight requests.

Reject/throttle before memory exhaustion.

Prioritize foreground reads/writes over repair/rebalance/compaction where necessary.

Admission control can be per tenant/partition to isolate noisy neighbors.

Expose retry-after/backoff signals; clients use exponential backoff with jitter.

Repair and hinted-handoff replay must be rate-limited after outages.

36. Durability Semantics

Define whether replica ACK occurs after WAL fsync, OS page cache, or memory only.

W=2 is meaningful only if the two ACKs satisfy the promised durability boundary.

Battery-backed/storage-controller assumptions must be explicit in high-stakes systems.

Periodic snapshots/SSTables do not replace the WAL for recent acknowledged writes.

Disk corruption requires checksums plus healthy replica repair.

37. Checksums and Corruption

Store block/record checksums to detect bit rot or torn/corrupt data.

A corrupt replica should not return a value merely because it is reachable.

Read from another replica and repair the damaged copy.

Scrubbing jobs proactively verify cold data.

Merkle anti-entropy detects logical divergence; checksums detect physical corruption.

38. TTL and Expiration

Store expiration metadata with the version.

Expired value behaves as logically deleted even before compaction physically removes bytes.

Replicate expiration/tombstone semantics so old replicas cannot resurrect data.

Background compaction reclaims expired values.

Avoid synchronized expiration storms with bucketing/jitter/capacity planning.

39. Secondary Indexes?

A pure key-value store is optimized for primary-key access.

Global secondary indexes introduce additional partitioning, write fan-out and consistency questions.

Index update can be synchronous with base write for stronger semantics or async via change stream for availability/latency.

Query fan-out across all partitions is expensive; design indexes around known access patterns.

For the core interview problem, keep primary-key semantics first and discuss indexes as an extension.

40. Transactions?

Single-key conditional update can use version/CAS or partition leader.

Multi-key transaction across partitions requires coordinator, locks/2PC or consensus-backed transaction protocol.

This adds latency and failure states; do not add it unless requirements demand it.

Many Dynamo-style workloads instead model data so atomicity boundary is one item/partition.

Idempotency remains necessary even with transactions because client responses can be lost.

41. Observability

Metric
	Why

p50/p95/p99 GET/PUT
	User latency

Read/write timeout rate
	Availability

Replica lag/divergence
	Consistency health

Hint backlog/age
	Recovery health

Repair backlog
	Anti-entropy health

Compaction debt
	Storage health

Disk utilization
	Capacity

Hot partitions/keys
	Skew

Rebalance bytes/rate
	Operational impact

Tombstone density
	Read/space cost

Quorum failures
	Replica/failure-domain health



42. Failure Scenarios

Scenario
	Expected behavior

One replica down, N3 W2
	Write can succeed on remaining preferred replicas

Two replicas down, W2
	Fail or use sloppy quorum if policy allows

Coordinator dies after replicas write
	Client retries; version/request semantics avoid harmful duplication

Network partition
	Each side follows configured availability/consistency policy

Node returns stale
	Hinted handoff + repair

Cold key inconsistent
	Anti-entropy eventually repairs

Delete replica was offline
	Tombstone prevents resurrection if retained/repaired safely

Disk corruption
	Checksum detect, fetch healthy replica

Rebalance during writes
	Migration epoch/forwarding/dual path preserves updates

Repair storm
	Rate-limit/background priority



43. Common Interview Mistakes

Stopping at consistent hashing and replication.

Saying R+W>N automatically guarantees linearizability.

Ignoring concurrent write conflicts.

No tombstone strategy, causing deleted data resurrection.

No cold-data repair beyond read repair.

Treating hinted handoff as permanent replication.

Counting vnodes on same server as independent replicas.

No failure-domain-aware placement.

No migration semantics while adding nodes.

No hot-key plan.

Ignoring compaction/repair traffic and disk headroom.

Claiming exactly-once network delivery.

44. Final Production Architecture

Hash keys into a partition/token space; physical nodes own many virtual-node ranges.

Each partition has N replicas placed across independent failure domains.

A stateless coordinator routes parallel reads/writes and waits for configured R/W responses.

Writes append to durable WAL + memtable and later flush to SSTables; compaction reclaims old versions/tombstones.

Version metadata detects causality/concurrent siblings; application/server policy resolves conflicts.

Sloppy quorum plus hinted handoff maintains availability during temporary failures.

Read repair fixes hot keys; Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs the entire keyspace.

Gossip/failure detection maintains decentralized topology knowledge.

Rebalancing streams small vnode ranges with versioned ownership and throttling.

For stronger semantics, use consensus/leadered partitions rather than pretending eventual quorum is linearizable.

One-sentence architecturePartition the hash space into many virtual-node ranges, replicate each range across N failure-independent nodes, route operations through stateless coordinators with tunable R/W quorums, persist via WAL+LSM storage, track versions for conflict resolution, and recover using sloppy quorum, hinted handoff, read repair and Merkle-tree anti-entropy.



45. Detailed Interviewer Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Why consistent hashing?

Detailed answer: It minimizes key movement when nodes join/leave and decentralizes ownership across a hash space.

Follow-up: Why virtual nodes?

Detailed answer: They give each physical server many small ranges, improving balance, capacity weighting and recovery parallelism.

Follow-up: How choose replication factor?

Detailed answer: From durability/availability and failure-domain goals. N=3 is common for interviews, but placement across racks/AZs matters as much as N.

Follow-up: Does R+W>N guarantee strong consistency?

Detailed answer: It guarantees overlap of intended quorums under assumptions, not full linearizability by itself. Sloppy quorums, concurrent versions and ordering semantics complicate the guarantee.

Follow-up: What happens with W=1?

Detailed answer: Lowest write latency/high availability, but acknowledged data may exist on only one replica initially and reads can be stale depending R/routing.

Follow-up: What is a sloppy quorum?

Detailed answer: When preferred replicas are unavailable, fallback healthy nodes temporarily count toward the acknowledgement threshold to preserve availability.

Follow-up: What is hinted handoff?

Detailed answer: Fallback replica stores data plus a hint for the intended owner, then transfers it when that owner recovers.

Follow-up: Why still need anti-entropy?

Detailed answer: Hints can expire/fail and cold inconsistent keys may never be read. Anti-entropy systematically compares full ranges.

Follow-up: Why Merkle trees?

Detailed answer: They identify mismatching subranges using hashes so replicas avoid transferring all data just to find differences.

Follow-up: Read repair vs anti-entropy?

Detailed answer: Read repair fixes divergence discovered by foreground reads; anti-entropy scans/compares ranges independent of access.

Follow-up: Why tombstones?

Detailed answer: A delete must replicate as a version so an offline stale replica cannot resurrect the old value.

Follow-up: When can a tombstone be removed?

Detailed answer: Only after a grace/repair policy makes it safe to assume replicas have observed the delete; otherwise resurrection is possible.

Follow-up: Why not wall-clock timestamps only?

Detailed answer: Clock skew and concurrent writers can misorder causality. Use explicit version/causal metadata or accept clearly defined LWW semantics.

Follow-up: What is a vector clock?

Detailed answer: A per-writer/version counter map representing causal history; incomparable vectors indicate concurrent versions.

Follow-up: What if vector clocks grow forever?

Detailed answer: Prune/compact metadata, bound writer identities, or use a different versioning scheme; this is a real operational cost.

Follow-up: How do you add a node safely?

Detailed answer: Assign vnode ranges, stream existing data, keep migration epoch/forwarding for concurrent writes, catch up, then publish new ownership.

Follow-up: What if a node fails during rebalance?

Detailed answer: Ownership epochs and surviving replicas define authoritative data; pause/recompute movement and restore replication before continuing.

Follow-up: How handle hot keys?

Detailed answer: Cache/coalesce reads, add read replicas where semantics allow, or application-shard the key; hashing alone cannot distribute one key's writes.

Follow-up: How do you provide linearizable conditional writes?

Detailed answer: Use a leader/consensus group for the partition or a stronger dedicated path; eventual quorum reconciliation is insufficient.

Follow-up: Give the one-minute design.

Detailed answer: Hash keys into a ring/token space split into many vnodes. Each range is replicated to N nodes across failure domains. Any coordinator maps a key to its preference list, sends requests in parallel and waits for configured W or R. Replicas durably append writes to WAL/memtable and later SSTables. Version metadata identifies stale versus concurrent values; reads reconcile and perform read repair. During outages, sloppy quorum writes to fallback nodes with hints, then hinted handoff restores intended replicas. Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs cold divergence, gossip tracks membership, and versioned/throttled range streaming handles rebalancing. For linearizable operations I would switch that partition to consensus rather than overclaim quorum consistency.

46. Additional Detailed Q&A

1. What is a preference list?

Detailed answer: Ordered physical nodes eligible to store replicas for a key/range.

2. What is a token?

Detailed answer: A point/boundary in the hash space used to define range ownership.

3. What is a vnode?

Detailed answer: A small logical token range assigned to a physical node.

4. What is quorum failure?

Detailed answer: Fewer than required R/W valid responses arrive before deadline.

5. Can coordinator cache ring metadata?

Detailed answer: Yes; metadata is versioned and refreshed on topology changes.

6. What if client sends request to wrong node?

Detailed answer: Node can coordinate/forward using current topology or redirect a topology-aware client.

7. What is read amplification?

Detailed answer: One logical read touches multiple SSTables/replicas/blocks.

8. What is write amplification?

Detailed answer: One logical write is rewritten multiple times during compaction/replication.

9. What is compaction debt?

Detailed answer: Accumulated SSTables/work waiting to be compacted, threatening reads/disk space.

10. Why disk headroom?

Detailed answer: Compaction/rebalance need temporary duplicate bytes and full disks can destabilize nodes.

11. Can repair overwrite newer data?

Detailed answer: No; repair exchanges version metadata and only applies dominating/resolved versions.

12. What if replicas return siblings?

Detailed answer: Return siblings/context for application merge or apply deterministic configured resolver.

13. What is a tombstone storm?

Detailed answer: Large volumes of deletes/expirations increase read/compaction overhead.

14. Why rate-limit repair?

Detailed answer: Recovery traffic can otherwise overload disks/network and cause a second outage.

15. What is a failure domain?

Detailed answer: Infrastructure sharing correlated failure risk, such as host, rack, AZ or region.

16. How detect bit rot?

Detailed answer: Checksums/scrubbing; retrieve healthy replica and repair.

17. Can Bloom filters say a key exists?

Detailed answer: Only 'possibly'; a positive may be false. A negative is definitive for that table.

18. Why not store everything in memory?

Detailed answer: Cost, capacity and durability; memory is cache/memtable, disk/SSD holds durable dataset.

19. How support TTL?

Detailed answer: Replicated expiration metadata plus logical expiration and later compaction.

20. Most important invariant?

Detailed answer: Acknowledged data obeys the stated durability/consistency contract, and replicas can deterministically reconcile/repair after failures.

47. Scenario Deep Dives

N=3, W=2. One preferred replica is down during a write.

If strict preferred quorum is required, the other two preferred replicas can still satisfy W=2. If two preferred replicas are unavailable and sloppy quorum is enabled, fallback nodes may temporarily accept hinted copies; otherwise the write fails.

Coordinator returns success, then crashes.

Coordinator state is not authoritative. The W replica acknowledgements already establish the promised write durability. A retry reads/writes using version/idempotency semantics and must not depend on the original coordinator process.

Two clients write different values during a partition.

Both sides may accept writes under an AP configuration. Their version vectors can be incomparable, producing siblings. After healing, read/repair surfaces both or invokes the configured merge/LWW/CRDT resolver.

A node is offline longer than tombstone grace.

This is dangerous: it may retain a pre-delete value after peers physically purge the tombstone. Operational policy must ensure repair/rebuild before grace expiry or retain tombstones long enough; otherwise deleted data can resurrect.

A new node joins during peak traffic.

Assign a bounded set of vnodes, stream them gradually from current replicas, throttle bandwidth/IO, preserve concurrent writes with migration epochs/forwarding, and shift client traffic only after target catch-up.

48. Advanced Drill: Quorum Examples

N/R/W
	Behavior

3/1/1
	Fast/high availability; stale reads likely

3/2/2
	Overlapping majority-style quorums; common balanced choice

3/1/3
	All replicas must ACK writes; cheap reads, poor write availability

5/3/3
	More fault tolerance/storage; larger quorum latency

3/2/1
	Fast writes, read quorum can reconcile replicas



Latency depends on the R-th/W-th fastest valid replica, not average replica latency.

Sloppy quorum may use fallback nodes, so reason about actual replica intersection rather than only arithmetic.

Consistency levels can be per request/table if product exposes tunability.

49. Advanced Drill: Rebalance Timeline

Topology service selects vnode range P to move A -> D.

Publish migration epoch E where A remains source and D is target.

Stream snapshot of P from A/other healthy replica to D.

Concurrent writes to P are forwarded/dual-recorded or replayed from a change log.

D catches up to a known sequence/version frontier.

Validate replica count/checksums.

Publish epoch E+1 making D authoritative owner and removing A from preference list for P.

Garbage-collect A's old copy only after safety delay.

50. Advanced Drill: Storage Read

Check memtable/row cache.

Consult Bloom filters to skip SSTables that definitely lack the key.

Search candidate SSTable indexes/blocks newest-first or by LSM strategy.

Collect versions/tombstone visible for key.

Resolve local latest version.

Coordinator combines results across R replicas and reconciles causal versions.

Optionally issue asynchronous read repair.

51. Advanced Drill: Repair Safety

Repair compares version metadata, never blindly copies one replica over another.

Concurrent siblings must be preserved until resolution policy chooses a merged value.

Repair range boundaries/topology epoch must be stable during comparison or explicitly versioned.

Throttle by bytes/sec and outstanding compaction pressure.

Prioritize under-replicated ranges before cosmetic divergence.

Record repair frontier/time so operators can prove tombstone safety assumptions.

52. Advanced Drill: Security and Multi-Tenancy

Authenticate requests and authorize table/key namespace access.

Encrypt in transit and at rest; manage per-tenant/customer keys where required.

Apply per-tenant quotas to storage, QPS and repair impact.

Prevent noisy tenant hot partitions from exhausting shared coordinators.

Audit administrative topology/data operations.

Backups/snapshots need the same access controls and encryption as live data.

53. 45-Minute Interview Flow

Time
	Coverage

0-5 min
	Requirements, API, consistency contract

5-10 min
	HLD + hash partitioning

10-15 min
	Consistent hashing + vnodes + placement

15-21 min
	Replication + N/R/W quorum

21-27 min
	Write/read paths + version conflicts

27-32 min
	Sloppy quorum + hinted handoff

32-36 min
	Read repair + Merkle anti-entropy

36-40 min
	LSM/WAL/tombstones/compaction

40-43 min
	Membership, failure, rebalance, hot keys

43-45 min
	CAP/strong option + final summary



54. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

30-second answerI would hash keys into many virtual-node ranges and replicate each range to N physical nodes across independent failure domains. Any stateless coordinator maps the key to its preference list, sends operations in parallel, and returns after the requested R or W responses. Replicas durably append to WAL and an LSM-style store. Version metadata distinguishes stale from concurrent values, so quorum reads can reconcile and perform read repair. During temporary failures, sloppy quorum can write to fallback nodes with hints; hinted handoff later restores intended replicas, while Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs cold divergence. Gossip/failure detection manages membership, and versioned, throttled vnode streaming handles rebalancing. If the requirement is linearizability, I would use a consensus-backed partition rather than claiming ordinary Dynamo quorum provides it.



55. Final Interview Checklist

API and explicit consistency/durability contract.

Hash partitioning and consistent hashing.

Virtual nodes and capacity-aware placement.

Replication factor and failure-domain awareness.

Coordinator and N/R/W quorum mechanics.

Write/read path.

Version vectors/concurrent siblings.

Read repair.

Sloppy quorum and hinted handoff.

Merkle-tree anti-entropy.

WAL, memtable, SSTables and Bloom filters.

Tombstones and safe deletion.

Compaction and disk headroom.

Membership/gossip/failure detection.

Node join/remove and migration epochs.

Hot keys/partitions.

CAP/PACELC and stronger consensus option.

Multi-region trade-offs.

Backpressure, repair storms and observability.

20 detailed follow-ups, 20 additional Q&As, scenarios, quorum/rebalance/storage/repair drills and colorful diagrams.

notes.title: Design Dropbox/ Google Drive
notes.description: Design Dropbox/ Google Drive Cloud Storage, File Sync, Chunking, Conflicts and Sharing How to study this design Metadata: Stores file details, names, and curren
notes.content:
Design Dropbox/ Google Drive

 Cloud Storage, File Sync, Chunking, Conflicts and Sharing



How to study this design

Metadata: Stores file details, names, and current versions.

Immutable Chunks: File chunks cannot be changed once stored.

Efficient Uploads: Upload only new or missing chunks.

Version Control: A new version becomes visible only after the metadata is committed.

Synchronization: Clients use an ordered change log to stay updated.

Conflict Handling: Detect changes using the original version and preserve both edits.









Dropbox is simultaneously a storage problem, synchronization problem, metadata problem, and conflict-resolution problem.

1. Problem Statement and Interview Scope

Design a Dropbox/Google Drive-like service that stores files in the cloud and keeps a user's files synchronized across desktop, mobile, and web clients. Users should be able to upload/download, organize folders, edit files offline, restore versions, and share content.

The difficult part is not merely storing blobs; it is keeping many devices consistent without wasting bandwidth.

Metadata operations are small but correctness-sensitive.

Blob transfers are huge but mostly immutable and can be optimized independently.

Offline clients create true distributed-write conflicts.



Recommended baselineAssume desktop sync is the primary deep dive. Support file/folder create, update, rename/move, delete, version history, and sharing. Files may be large, devices may go offline, and sync should be near-real-time when online.

2. Functional Requirements







Follow-Up
	Feature
	Baseline Behavior

Direct blob upload / multipart
	Upload
	Resumable; large files supported

CDN for shared downloads
	Download
	Resume/range/chunk-based

Near-real-time hint + delta log
	Sync
	Changes propagate to all devices

Very large shared folders
	Folders
	Create/list/move/rename/delete

Retention policy / restore
	Versioning
	Retain old file revisions

Conflicted copy / merge
	Offline edits
	Sync on reconnect

Permission inheritance/revocation
	Sharing
	Users/folders + links

Restore window / hard delete
	Delete
	Trash/tombstone before GC



Out of scope unless askedCollaborative Google-Docs-style character-by-character editing is a different CRDT/OT problem. A Dropbox-like filesystem usually treats arbitrary files as opaque bytes and resolves concurrent offline edits at file/revision granularity.

3. Non-Functional Requirements

Property
	Expectation
	Design Consequence

Durability
	Extremely high; user files must not disappear
	Replicated durable blob storage

Availability
	Uploads/downloads should survive node failure
	Stateless services + replicated storage

Bandwidth efficiency
	Do not resend whole large files
	Chunking + dedup/delta sync

Sync latency
	Seconds when online
	Push hint + ordered change log

Offline support
	Hours/days disconnected
	Local DB + queued changes + conflict detection

Metadata correctness
	No duplicate names/lost revisions
	Strong/serialized namespace writes

Security
	Private user content
	Auth, ACL, encryption, audit

Cost
	Huge long-term storage
	Dedup, lifecycle, cold tiers, compression where useful



4. Capacity Estimation





Use rough scale to justify chunking and metadata/blob separation.



Total Users: 100 million registered users.

Daily Active Users: 10 million.

Devices: Average 3 devices per active user (~30M devices).

Daily File Changes: 5 files per user → 50 million file revisions/day.

Average File Size: 4 MB, but some files can be GBs or TBs.

Daily Storage Growth: ~200 TB/day before deduplication.

Metadata Traffic: Higher than file changes due to listing, renaming, sharing, and synchronization.

Key Point: Google Drive/DropBox needs to handle massive file storage, frequent synchronization, and high metadata traffic



ImportantThe storage-growth number is intentionally large enough to force object/blob storage. The exact number is less important than recognizing that metadata is tiny compared with file content and must scale independently.

5. Why the Client Sync Engine Matters





The client participates in hashing, retry, local state, and conflict detection.



File Watcher

Uses OS filesystem notifications to detect create/modify/delete/rename.

Filesystem notifications can be lossy; periodically reconcile with a local snapshot.

Local Metadata Database

Stores fileId/path, last synced revision, local mtime/size/hash, sync state, and server cursor.

Allows the client to restart without rescanning every remote file.

Transfer Manager

Limits concurrency.

Retries chunks independently.

Persists upload session so restart resumes.

Sync Worker

Long-polls/push-wakes for remote changes.

Pulls ordered deltas from server cursor.

Applies changes while avoiding feedback loops back into watcher.



Interview maturity signalMany candidates draw only server boxes. For Dropbox, explain what the desktop client stores and how it recovers after restart/offline periods. That is central to a realistic sync design.



6. High-Level Architecture





Metadata and file bytes take different paths.



Metadata Service manages namespace, revisions, ACLs, current pointers, and transactional updates.

Blob/Chunk Storage stores immutable file chunks.

Chunk Index maps content hashes to storage locations and reference information.

Sync Service exposes change cursors and notification channels.

Change Log/Event Stream records ordered metadata changes.

Clients upload/download large bytes directly to transfer/blob infrastructure rather than through metadata servers.



Core splitTreat metadata as the control plane and file bytes as the data plane. Control-plane requests need correctness and low size; data-plane transfers need throughput, resumability, and cheap storage.



7. Metadata Model





Stable file IDs survive rename/move; revisions are immutable.



Entity
	Key Fields
	Purpose

FileEntry
	fileId, parentFolderId, name, currentRevision, owner/ACL, status
	Current namespace object

FileRevision
	revisionId, fileId, baseRevision, chunk list, size, timestamp
	Immutable version

Chunk
	chunkId/hash, size, storageRef, checksum, refs
	Immutable content block

Folder
	folderId, parentFolderId, name, ACL/version
	Directory namespace

ChangeEvent
	cursor/seq, resourceId, operation, revision
	Client delta sync



Use stable fileId instead of path as the identity.

Rename changes name; move changes parentFolderId; neither changes fileId.

currentRevision points to one immutable FileRevision.

A revision contains an ordered list of chunkIds.



Why stable IDs matterIf path were the identity, renaming a parent folder would conceptually rename millions of child paths. Stable IDs let the namespace update only the moved node while paths are resolved from parent relationships or indexed views.



8. Folder Namespace and Path Operations





Represent folders as parent-child relationships.



Create/Rename/Move

Within one parent folder, enforce name uniqueness if product semantics require it.

Rename is a metadata transaction on the entry.

Move updates parentFolderId and should validate no directory cycle is introduced.

List Folder

Index children by parentFolderId + normalizedName.

Paginate large folders.

Use an opaque pagination cursor so concurrent changes do not require offset scanning.

Very Large Shared Folder

Partition children/listing data if one folder has millions of entries.

Cache directory pages cautiously because permission/rename/delete changes require invalidation.



Atomic namespace operationsMetadata operations such as 'rename file if target name does not already exist' are correctness-sensitive. Use a transaction/conditional write rather than eventually consistent check-then-write.



9. Chunking Files





Chunking is the foundation of resumable transfer and delta sync.



Example fixed size: 4 MiB per chunk; exact size is a design choice.

Client computes a strong hash for each chunk.

Chunks can upload/download in parallel.

Failed transfer retries only the missing chunk.

A changed file can reuse unchanged chunks from the previous revision.

Chunk Size Trade-Off

Smaller Chunks
	Larger Chunks

Better delta granularity
	Lower metadata overhead

More hashes/requests/manifest entries
	Better sequential transfer efficiency

More dedup opportunities
	Fewer round trips

Higher CPU and index overhead
	More bytes resent for small edits





Practical answerChoose a few MiB as a simple baseline, then adapt by file size/workload. Tiny files may be stored as one chunk; huge files can use larger chunks to keep manifests manageable.



10. Fixed-Size vs Content-Defined Chunking





Content-defined chunking can preserve reuse when bytes are inserted/removed.



Fixed-Size

Simple and fast.

Excellent for random range access.

Insertion near the start shifts later boundaries, making many hashes change even if content mostly stayed the same.

Content-Defined Chunking (CDC)

Rolling hash/Rabin fingerprint finds boundaries based on content.

After insertion, boundaries often realign, preserving many unchanged chunks.

More CPU and implementation complexity.



Interview choiceFor a straightforward Dropbox design, fixed-size chunks are enough. Mention CDC/rsync-style rolling hashes as an optimization for workloads where small insertions into very large files would otherwise resend too much data.



11. Content-Addressed Storage





A strong chunk hash can identify immutable content.



Compute SHA-256 (or another strong content hash) for each chunk.

Use chunkId as the logical identity.

Blob key can be derived from chunkId.

Verify uploaded bytes match claimed hash before accepting.

Store an independent checksum/integrity metadata if desired.



Hash collision stanceCryptographic collisions are astronomically unlikely, but correctness-sensitive systems can still verify chunk length/hash and treat a conflicting same-hash/different-content observation as a severe integrity event.



12. Deduplication





Chunk dedup avoids storing identical blocks more than once.



Upload-Time Dedup

Client sends chunk hashes/manifest.

Server returns which chunkIds are missing.

Client uploads only missing chunks.

Within-User vs Cross-User Dedup

Within-user dedup is simpler from a privacy perspective.

Cross-user dedup saves more storage but can leak whether content already exists if the API reveals too much.

Security Side Channel

If an attacker can ask 'does hash X exist globally?' they may infer another user stores known content.

Mitigate by making dedup result opaque or limiting dedup to tenant/user scope.

Encryption Trade-Off

Server-side encryption preserves server-visible plaintext hashes for dedup.

True client-side end-to-end encryption makes cross-user dedup difficult because ciphertext differs per key.



Interview answerI would start with within-account or server-side dedup. I would not casually expose global chunk existence to clients because storage optimization can create a confidentiality side channel.



13. Resumable Upload Protocol





Chunks are durable before the metadata revision becomes visible.



Step-by-Step

1. Client scans/chunks file and computes ordered chunk hashes.

2. Client calls BeginUpload(fileId/baseRevision, manifest summary).

3. Server returns uploadSessionId and list of missing chunkIds, or pre-signed chunk upload URLs.

4. Client uploads missing chunks in parallel with retries.

5. Client calls CommitUpload(sessionId, full ordered manifest, expectedBaseRevision).

6. Metadata service verifies required chunks exist and expectedBaseRevision still matches.

7. In one metadata transaction, create new revision, update currentRevision, and append change-log event.

8. Return committed revision to client.

Why Commit Last?

Uploaded but uncommitted chunks are invisible and safe to garbage-collect later.

Metadata never points to missing chunks.

Retrying Begin/Commit can be made idempotent using uploadSessionId.



Visibility pointThe metadata commit is the moment a new version exists. Chunk uploads are preparation; they do not change what other devices see until CommitUpload succeeds.



14. Direct Upload: Control Plane vs Data Plane





Avoid routing GB-scale bytes through metadata/API servers.



Metadata API authenticates user and starts an upload session.

It issues short-lived upload tokens or pre-signed URLs scoped to specific chunk IDs.

Client uploads chunks directly to blob storage/transfer tier.

Server validates hashes/size, then metadata commit references them.



BenefitApplication servers stay small and horizontally scalable because they coordinate transfers instead of proxying every byte. This reduces network cost, memory pressure, and blast radius.



15. Download Flow





Authorize metadata first; then serve immutable chunks efficiently.



1. Client requests fileId/current revision or a specific historical revision.

2. Metadata API authenticates user/share link and checks ACL.

3. Return revision manifest containing ordered chunk IDs and short-lived signed download URLs/tokens.

4. Client compares manifest against locally cached chunks and downloads only missing ones.

5. Download chunks in parallel with range/resume support.

6. Verify hash/checksum and reassemble file locally.

CDN

Immutable chunks are CDN-friendly when authorization is implemented with signed URLs/cookies.

Hot shared downloads benefit from edge caching.

Private blobs should not become publicly addressable just because the underlying chunk hash is known.



ImportantThe manifest is permission-sensitive metadata. The chunk data is immutable, but access to it still needs scoped authorization or signed URLs.



16. File Versioning





Each edit creates a new immutable revision that reuses unchanged chunks.



FileEntry.currentRevision points to latest revision.

Revision stores baseRevision and ordered chunks.

Unchanged chunks are shared between revisions.

Version history retention can be time-based or plan-based.

Restore creates a new latest revision referencing the old version's chunks; it does not rewrite history.



Why immutable revisionsThey simplify rollback, conflict detection, auditing, caching, and dedup. The mutable part is only the small pointer to which revision is current.



17. Change Log and Sync Cursor





A client should not list every file after each change.



Maintain an ordered per-user/account/namespace change feed:

Every committed metadata mutation appends a ChangeEvent.

Client remembers last cursor.

GET /changes?cursor=1050 returns events after 1050 plus a new cursor.

Paginate very large deltas.

Cursor is opaque and monotonic within its scope.

Events

FILE_CREATED / REVISION_COMMITTED.

RENAMED / MOVED.

DELETED / RESTORED.

SHARE_PERMISSION_CHANGED.

Ordering Scope

A single global sequence across all users is unnecessary and hard to scale.

Partition/order by account, namespace, or ownership shard so each client gets deterministic order for relevant changes.



Source of truthThe change log is the authoritative mechanism for catching up. Real-time notifications only tell a client that it should query the change log.



18. Push Notifications / Long Polling





Never depend on push delivery for correctness.



Online client opens long-poll/WebSocket/push channel.

Server sends a lightweight 'changes available' hint.

Client calls delta API using its durable cursor.

If notification is lost, periodic poll or reconnect still retrieves all changes.

Why Not Push Full Changes?

Clients may be offline.

Push delivery can duplicate or reorder messages.

A change may be too large.

The ordered change log already provides retryable/paginated state transfer.



Simple modelPush answers WHEN to sync. The change log answers WHAT to sync.



19. Notification Storms





Large shared folders and reconnect events can generate huge fan-out.



Coalesce repeated updates into one 'changes available' hint.

Do not emit one push notification per file mutation.

Add random reconnect jitter after outage.

Rate-limit delta requests and paginate large catch-ups.

Prioritize active clients and allow background clients to catch up gradually.

For extremely large shared folders, partition subscriber fan-out and use per-member cursors.



Failure scenarioAfter a 30-minute notification outage, millions of clients may reconnect at once. Design the notification layer and metadata read path for thundering-herd recovery, not only normal steady state.



20. Offline Editing and Conflict Detection





Use revision ancestry, not wall-clock last-write-wins.



Each client edits a file based on a known base revision.

Device A edits base revision 10 while offline.

Device B commits revision 11 from the same base.

When A reconnects, it tries CommitUpload(expectedBase=10).

Server sees currentRevision=11, so A is not a simple successor; it is a concurrent branch.

Conflict Resolution Options

Strategy
	Benefit
	Problem

Last Write Wins
	Simple
	Can silently destroy user work

Conflicted Copy
	Never loses either file version
	User must resolve manually

Auto-merge text
	Good UX for mergeable formats
	Format-specific and can be wrong

CRDT / OT
	Fine-grained collaborative editing
	Not suitable for arbitrary binary files





Recommended baselineFor arbitrary files, preserve both revisions and create a conflicted copy such as 'report (Alice's conflicted copy).docx'. Never silently overwrite one offline edit with another.



21. Conflict Edge Cases

Rename vs edit: preserve edit under the file's stable ID; apply/resolve namespace rename separately.

Delete vs edit: a client editing a file that another device deleted may restore as a conflicted/new file rather than resurrect silently.

Move vs move: resolve based on versioned namespace operation; preserve one move or ask user/admin policy.

Folder delete with child updates: tombstone generation/version prevents stale device from recreating old hierarchy unknowingly.

Case-only rename can conflict on case-insensitive filesystems.

Different OS filename rules require canonicalization and local name mangling.



Cross-platform syncWindows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android have different path, case, reserved-name, and filesystem semantics. A production sync client needs a canonical server namespace plus platform-specific local translation.



22. Delete, Trash, Tombstones, and Garbage Collection





Delete from namespace first; reclaim bytes only when safely unreferenced.



Deleting a file creates a tombstone/change event so offline clients learn that it was removed.

Keep trash/restore history for a retention window.

Old revisions may continue referencing chunks.

Shared files or dedup may reference the same chunk from other owners/revisions.

Garbage Collection Safety

A chunk can be physically deleted only after it has zero live/retained references.

Use delayed GC/safety age so in-flight commits cannot race with deletion.

Reference count alone can be corrupted by crash/race; periodic mark-and-sweep or reconciliation is safer as a repair mechanism.



Do not immediately delete a blobA file deletion is a metadata event. Blob deletion is a later storage-management event because other revisions/users may still reference the same chunk.



23. Sharing Files and Folders





Authorization belongs in metadata, not inside chunk objects.



Direct User Sharing

ACL entries: principalId -> role (owner/editor/viewer).

Folder ACL may be inherited by descendants.

Permission changes append change events so sync clients update UI/state.

Share Links

High-entropy token maps to resourceId and permission.

Optional expiry, password, download-only, domain restriction.

Token must be revocable.

Large Shared Folder

Do not copy every file's ACL for every user on each change.

Use inheritance/group membership or computed authorization with caching.

Permission revocation must invalidate signed URLs/cache tokens quickly.



Security boundaryKnowing a chunk hash or fileId should never be sufficient for access. Every manifest/download authorization derives from the current resource ACL/share-link state.



24. Metadata Consistency

The system needs stronger consistency for metadata than for immutable blob replication.

File name uniqueness within a folder.

Compare-and-swap on currentRevision.

Move/rename/delete ordering.

ACL updates and revocation.

Change-log order for a namespace/account.

Optimistic Concurrency

Commit new revision with condition currentRevision == expectedBaseRevision.

If condition fails, return conflict.

This prevents lost updates without locking a file for the entire offline edit duration.

Blob Consistency

Immutable chunks can be replicated asynchronously after durable creation.

Metadata should not expose a revision until its required chunks meet durability policy.



Consistency answerUse strong conditional metadata writes for namespace/revision correctness. Use immutable content and asynchronous replication for bulk bytes once the commit's durability threshold is satisfied.



25. Metadata Database and Partitioning

Metadata needs transactional conditional updates and scalable point/range queries.

Partition users/accounts by userId/accountId or a stable namespace shard.

Within an account, index folder children by parentFolderId.

FileEntry lookup by fileId should be direct.

Change log is partitioned consistently with the account/namespace owner.

SQL vs Distributed KV

Relational DB is attractive for namespace constraints and transactions at moderate scale.

At huge scale, use a distributed metadata store that supports conditional writes/transactions within a partition.

Avoid cross-shard transactions by co-locating an account or folder subtree when feasible.

Hot Metadata Partitions

Very large shared folder can concentrate metadata traffic.

Shard its child listings or split collaboration/activity concerns from core namespace state.



Partitioning goalKeep operations that must be atomic in the same metadata partition whenever possible. That is often more important than perfectly uniform load.



26. Blob Storage and Durability

Chunks are immutable; blob storage is optimized for append/write-once and high durability.

Replicate across multiple disks/nodes/AZs or use erasure coding.

Verify integrity on write and periodically scrub stored checksums.

Cold historical versions can move to lower-cost storage tiers.

Do not rely on one cache/CDN copy as durable storage.

Replication vs Erasure Coding

Replication
	Erasure Coding

Simple reads/repair
	Better storage efficiency

More storage overhead
	More CPU/network during reconstruction

Good for hot/new data
	Good for cold/large durable data





TieringA practical service may keep newly uploaded/hot chunks replicated for fast access and later encode colder data more efficiently.



27. Checksums and Corruption Detection

Client computes strong chunk hash.

Server validates bytes against expected hash.

Storage maintains checksum/scrub metadata.

Download client verifies chunk integrity.

If one replica is corrupt, repair from another healthy replica/erasure fragment.



End-to-end integrityChecking only at the disk layer misses corruption elsewhere in the path. An end-to-end content hash lets the client and server agree on exactly which bytes a chunk represents.



28. Security and Encryption

In Transit

TLS for API and chunk transfer.

Short-lived scoped upload/download tokens.

At Rest

Encrypt chunks using managed/server-side keys or envelope encryption.

Encrypt metadata containing names/ACLs as appropriate.

Client-Side / End-to-End Encryption Trade-Off

Strong privacy: server cannot inspect plaintext.

But server-side search, malware scanning, previews, and cross-user dedup become difficult/impossible.

Key recovery/sharing UX becomes much more complex.

Malware / Abuse

Scan shared/public downloads when policy requires.

Quarantine suspicious uploads before external sharing.



Dedup vs privacyGlobal plaintext-content dedup and true end-to-end encryption pull in opposite directions. State that trade-off instead of claiming you can maximize both simultaneously.



29. Quotas and Accounting

Quota is usually logical user-visible bytes, not raw physical deduplicated bytes.

Otherwise two users uploading the same data could consume different quota depending on who uploaded first.

Track logical file sizes per account in metadata/accounting service.

Physical storage savings from dedup are an internal optimization.

Reserve quota before large upload commit to avoid overrun races.



Why logical quotaProduct billing/accounting should be stable and understandable. Dedup implementation details should not leak into whether a user's 1 GB file 'counts' against quota.



30. Multi-Region Design





Global blob distribution is easier than globally writable metadata.



Assign each account/namespace a home metadata region for strong writes.

Replicate metadata to a failover region.

Replicate chunks/object data across regions according to durability and locality policy.

Serve downloads from nearest replica/CDN.

On regional failover, promote metadata owner with fencing/epoch to avoid split-brain writes.

Active-Active?

Possible with globally consistent database or carefully partitioned ownership.

More expensive and complex for rename/move/conflict semantics.



Recommended baselineUse single-writer/home-region metadata per account with multi-region blob replication. It provides a clean correctness model and is usually sufficient unless write latency in every geography is a hard requirement.



31. Failure Modes





Keep optional components out of the critical correctness path.



Failure
	Behavior

Metadata service instance
	LB retries another stateless instance

Metadata DB leader
	Failover; pause writes rather than risk split brain

Blob upload interrupted
	Resume missing chunks using upload session

Chunk upload completed but no commit
	Invisible orphan; GC later

Push service down
	Clients continue delta polling / long-poll fallback

Client crashes mid-sync
	Local DB/cursor makes operation resumable

Region down
	Fail over metadata owner; serve replicated blobs

Chunk index/dedup unavailable
	Disable new dedup optimization if safe; correctness first





Failure priorityWhen uncertain, preserve file correctness and durability even if sync becomes slower. Users tolerate delayed sync much better than corrupted or silently lost files.



32. Idempotency and Retry Safety

BeginUpload(uploadId) is idempotent.

PUT chunk by content hash is naturally idempotent: same hash means same expected bytes.

CommitUpload(sessionId, expectedBaseRevision) is idempotent and conditional.

Delete/rename operations carry operationId or expected namespace version where needed.

Push notifications may duplicate; client delta cursor prevents duplicate state application.



Key ideaA sync system lives on unreliable networks. Every operation that can be retried after timeout must either be idempotent or carry enough state to detect duplicate execution.



33. Handling Small Files

Chunking millions of tiny files into separate object requests creates overhead.

Small files can be stored inline in metadata or packed into larger storage segments.

Threshold policy: e.g. <= 64 KB inline, larger files chunked.

But inline data makes metadata DB backups/replication heavier.



Trade-offOptimize for the workload. Dropbox-style systems need both tiny text/config files and huge media files, so a hybrid small-file policy can reduce request overhead without forcing all content into the metadata database.



34. Large Files and Parallel Transfer

Upload/download chunks concurrently, but cap concurrency so one client does not saturate network/CPU.

Persist per-chunk completion state.

Use adaptive concurrency based on observed bandwidth/latency.

Multipart/object upload APIs are natural for large chunks/files.

Prioritize foreground user-requested downloads over background sync.

Pause sync on metered/mobile networks according to client settings.



User experienceA good sync client is a bandwidth scheduler. It should be efficient without making the user's video call or active download unusable.



35. Hot Shared Files and CDN

A public/shared link to a popular file can become a read hotspot.

Serve immutable revision/chunks through CDN using signed links where required.

Cache by chunk hash/revision because content never changes.

Permission revocation invalidates future signed URL issuance; use short-lived tokens for fast revocation.

Do not put mutable 'latest file' URLs into long-lived CDN cache without versioning.



Versioned URLsServe /file/{fileId}/revision/{revId} or signed chunk URLs rather than caching an ambiguous 'latest' response forever. Immutable identifiers make CDN behavior safe.



36. Observability and SLOs

Upload success rate and time-to-commit.

Download success rate and throughput.

Sync convergence latency: server commit -> other online device applied.

Conflict rate.

Example SLOs

99.9% metadata availability.

99% online sync notifications within several seconds.

Upload commit should recover cleanly from transient network loss.



Best metricFor sync, measure convergence: how long from one device's committed revision until another healthy online device observes and applies it. Component latency alone does not measure the user experience.

39. Final Production Architecture





The final design after each component is justified by a requirement.



Critical synchronous path:

Client detects local file change.

Chunks/hash manifest are prepared locally.

Missing chunks upload to durable blob storage.

Metadata service atomically commits new revision using expected base revision.

Change log records the mutation.

Propagation path:

Notification layer wakes other devices.

Devices pull ordered deltas from their cursors.

They download only missing chunks and update local metadata.

Background path:

GC reclaims unreferenced chunks after safety/retention windows.

Audit/analytics collect noncritical events.

Storage scrubbing verifies checksums and repairs corrupt replicas.
