notes.description: DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX Complete Video Streaming System Design Interview Handbook Upload -> Processing -> HLS/DASH -> CDN -> Playback -> Discovery -> Reliabili
notes.content:
DESIGN YOUTUBE / NETFLIX

Complete Video Streaming System Design Interview Handbook

Upload -> Processing -> HLS/DASH -> CDN -> Playback -> Discovery -> Reliability



Study strategyIn an interview, spend most of your depth on transcoding, adaptive streaming, CDN/origin behavior, hot-video spikes, and playback quality.





A modern video platform is a media pipeline plus a global delivery network.





01  Problem Framing

Understand what YouTube and Netflix share and where their product assumptions differ.

Design a large-scale video platform where creators or content providers upload video, the platform processes it into streamable formats, and viewers play it globally with low startup latency and minimal buffering.

YouTube emphasis: user-generated upload, moderation, enormous catalog, search and recommendations.

Netflix emphasis: controlled catalog, entitlement, DRM, regional rights, playback quality.

The shared core is video ingest, transcoding, segmented packaging, origin storage, CDN delivery, playback sessions, and QoE analytics.





The streaming core is reusable; ingestion and rights/discovery differ.





02  Requirements





Separate functional behavior from playback-quality goals.



Area
	Baseline Decision
	Likely Follow-Up

Upload
	Resumable creator/source upload
	Huge files, mobile upload, quotas

Processing
	Multiple resolutions/bitrates
	Multiple codecs, subtitles, thumbnails

Playback
	VOD with seek/resume
	DRM, regional entitlement, offline download

Discovery
	Metadata + search
	Recommendations, trending

Engagement
	Optional likes/comments/views
	Anti-fraud counts

Availability
	Playback prioritized over ancillary systems
	Multi-CDN, region failover





Recommended interview scopeBuild VOD first. Live streaming is a different latency/ingest problem and should be treated as a follow-up unless explicitly requested.



03  Non-Functional Requirements

Playback startup should feel fast; time-to-first-frame is a critical user metric.

Rebuffering should be rare; adaptive bitrate should prefer continuity over maximum resolution.

Video source and published assets must be highly durable.

Playback should remain available even if search, comments, or analytics are degraded.

Media bandwidth is the dominant cost, so CDN hit ratio and codec efficiency matter.

The system must absorb viral premieres without melting origin storage.



04  Capacity Estimation





The exact numbers are assumptions; the architectural conclusion is that media bytes dominate.



Assume 2M uploads/day, average 500 MB source -> ~1 PB/day raw ingest before transcodes.

Assume 1B playback starts/day -> ~11.6K average play-start requests/sec before peaks.

A 20-minute video at 3 Mbps transfers roughly 450 MB; higher qualities multiply egress.

The system therefore needs petabyte-scale storage and multi-terabit global delivery capacity.



Scale takeawayMetadata QPS is manageable compared with media throughput. Do not route large media through ordinary application servers; use object storage, worker fleets, and CDN.



05  Video Lifecycle and State Machine





The READY transition is the publication boundary.



State
	Meaning
	Viewer Behavior

UPLOADING
	Source bytes not finalized
	Not playable

PROCESSING
	Transcoding/packaging underway
	Show processing

READY
	Required renditions/manifests available
	Playable

FAILED
	Processing failed permanently/needs retry
	Creator action/support

BLOCKED
	Moderation/rights restriction
	Not served

DELETED
	Logically removed
	Do not play; clean assets later





06  High-Level Architecture





The modern design has a control plane and a media data plane.



Metadata/API tier owns video records, visibility, publication state, rights, and upload sessions.

Object storage holds immutable source and generated assets.

Processing orchestrator places independent jobs onto queues/streams.

Worker fleets transcode/package thumbnails/subtitles without blocking API requests.

Playback service issues manifest URLs/tokens; CDN serves the media bytes.

Search/recommendations/analytics consume metadata and playback events asynchronously.



07  API Surface

Operation
	Example
	Important Semantics

Begin upload
	POST /videos/upload-sessions
	quota, expected size, idempotency

Upload parts
	PUT signed object URLs
	multipart/resume/checksum

Finalize upload
	POST /upload-sessions/{id}/complete
	source becomes immutable

Get video
	GET /videos/{videoId}
	metadata/status

Playback
	POST /videos/{id}/playback
	authorization + manifest/token

Search
	GET /search?q=...
	eventually consistent index

Delete
	DELETE /videos/{id}
	logical delete first





08  Metadata Model





Keep media references and policy state small and queryable.



Video: videoId, owner/channel, title, description, createdAt, duration, status, visibility.

Asset/Rendition: codec, resolution, bitrate, manifest/object references, processing state.

Playback Policy: region rights, age restrictions, subscription tier, DRM requirements.

Do not store video bytes in the relational/document metadata database.



09  Resumable Upload





Application servers coordinate; object storage receives the data.



BeginUpload authenticates creator and creates uploadSessionId.

Return short-lived pre-signed URLs or an upload token scoped to the session.

Client uploads directly to origin/object storage.

Finalize only after all parts exist and checksums match.

Source object becomes immutable once the session commits.



Why direct uploadA 20 GB video should not pass through a fleet designed for 10 KB JSON requests. Direct object upload lowers cost and avoids memory/network bottlenecks in the API tier.



10  Multipart Upload and Resume





Failure restarts a part, not the entire video.



Client stores uploadSessionId and completed part numbers/ETags.

Parts can upload concurrently with a bounded concurrency limit.

Retries are idempotent per part number/session.

On reconnect, ask server/object store which parts already exist.

Abandoned incomplete sessions expire and their temporary parts are garbage-collected.



11  Processing Pipeline





Asynchronous staged processing isolates expensive CPU/GPU work.



Probe source format and validate duration/container/codecs.

Transcode into required codec/resolution/bitrate variants.

Package variants into HLS/DASH segments and manifests.

Generate thumbnails/storyboards, extract captions, and run policy/moderation checks.

Each job records state so a failed rendition can retry without repeating completed work.



Job orchestrationTreat processing as a DAG/state machine, not one giant worker. It improves retries, parallelism, observability, and the ability to add new renditions later.



12  Transcoding and Encoding Ladder





The encoding ladder gives the player choices.



Generate several resolutions/bitrates rather than one giant file.

Bitrate should depend on content complexity, not only resolution.

Avoid producing expensive 4K/AV1 variants for source content/users that do not justify it.

For long-tail uploads, delayed/on-demand high-end encodes can reduce compute/storage cost.



13  Codec Trade-Off





Codec choice is bandwidth-versus-compute-versus-device compatibility.



H.264 has broad device support and fast hardware decoding.

AV1/HEVC-class codecs can reduce egress for the same quality, especially at scale.

New codecs cost more CPU/GPU time to encode and may require dual catalogs during migration.

The platform can choose codec per device capability and content popularity.



14  HLS / DASH: Manifests and Segments





Playback fetches a manifest and then many small immutable media segments.



Master manifest lists available variants.

Each variant playlist references time-aligned segments.

Segment durations are commonly a few seconds; shorter segments improve responsiveness but increase request overhead.

Segments are immutable and ideal CDN objects.

Seeking maps playback time to segment ranges rather than random reads inside one monolithic file.



15  Adaptive Bitrate Streaming





The client chooses quality continuously rather than the server hard-coding it.



Player estimates recent network throughput.

Player observes buffer occupancy and recent rebuffer events.

It chooses the next segment representation conservatively.

Quality should rise gradually and fall quickly enough to avoid stalls.

ABR can incorporate device resolution, codec support, data-saver mode, and battery/CPU constraints.



QoE priorityA stable 720p stream is usually a better experience than oscillating 1080p with repeated buffering. ABR optimizes overall quality of experience, not maximum pixels.



16  Playback Path





The API authorizes playback; the CDN carries the heavy traffic.



1. Viewer opens a video page; metadata is served from API/cache.

2. Player requests a playback session/manifest URL.

3. Playback service checks READY status, visibility, entitlement/region/DRM policy.

4. Return master manifest URL plus short-lived playback token if required.

5. Player requests manifest/segments from nearest CDN edge.

6. CDN HIT serves immediately; MISS goes to origin shield/origin.

7. Player emits QoE events asynchronously.



17  CDN and Origin Shield





The origin should not see one request per viewer.



CDN caches immutable segments close to users.

Origin shield/mid-tier cache coalesces simultaneous misses from many edges.

Use long cache TTLs/versioned object names because segment content never changes.

Serve manifests with shorter TTL if publication/rights can change; media segments themselves remain immutable.

Multi-CDN may improve resilience, cost leverage, and geography coverage at very large scale.



18  Hot vs Cold Videos





One cache policy is inefficient for both a viral premiere and a never-watched upload.



Hot videos: pre-warm edges, keep early segments resident, possibly replicate across CDN providers.

Cold videos: leave at origin; cache on demand; use cheaper storage tiers where playback SLO allows.

Popularity predictors can promote/demote objects between tiers.

The first few segments are disproportionately valuable because every playback requests them.



19  Viral Premiere / Thundering Herd





Synchronized viewers create a special burst shape.



Pre-warm manifests and first segments before a scheduled premiere.

Origin shield/request coalescing prevents every edge miss from reaching storage.

Reserve CDN/origin capacity and use multi-CDN failover for massive launches.

Gracefully reduce top quality variants before allowing widespread rebuffering if capacity is constrained.



20  Storage Strategy

Source master: highest durability, retained per product policy.

Published renditions: immutable generated assets; can be recreated from source if necessary, but regeneration may be expensive.

Long-tail/cold assets can move to colder object tiers.

Thumbnails/manifests are tiny and widely cached.

Use lifecycle/retention rules for failed/abandoned uploads and obsolete rendition versions.



Source vs derived assetsThe source upload is usually the strongest recovery asset. Transcoded renditions are derived, but deleting them casually may create huge recompute cost; choose retention based on economics.



21  Metadata Database and Partitioning

Primary video lookup by videoId should be direct and highly cached.

Partition metadata by videoId or stable ownership shard.

Creator/channel listing requires a secondary author/channel index.

Use transactions/conditional writes for status transitions such as PROCESSING -> READY and delete/visibility changes.

View counters/search/recommendation features should not overload the metadata row.



22  Search





Search is a separate indexing workload.



Index title, description, tags, channel, captions/transcript, language, and policy metadata.

Use an inverted index for lexical retrieval; vector/semantic retrieval can be added for modern search.

Metadata events update the index asynchronously.

Opening a search result rechecks current visibility/rights because the index may lag.



23  Recommendations

Candidate sources: subscriptions, similar videos, collaborative behavior, trending, channel affinity.

Retrieve a few hundred/thousand candidates, score/rank, then apply diversity/safety/business rules.

Use watch-time/completion/skip signals rather than only clicks.

Cold-start new videos can use metadata/content embeddings and controlled exploration.



Interview boundaryUnless this is specifically an ML system-design interview, keep recommendation details at candidate retrieval -> scoring -> filtering. Spend the HLD depth on streaming infrastructure.



24  Views, Watch Time, and Playback Analytics





High-volume telemetry should not update the video row synchronously.



Player emits play-start, segment-download, bitrate-switch, buffer, error, heartbeat/progress, and finish events.

Event stream buffers traffic and supports replay.

Streaming analytics produces real-time QoE dashboards and approximate live counts.

Warehouse/OLAP computes durable views, watch time, creator analytics, experimentation, recommendations.

Fraud/anti-bot logic validates view counts separately from raw playback events.



25  DRM, Entitlement, and Regional Rights





Licensed streaming adds a control decision before encrypted media playback.



Entitlement service checks subscription/account tier.

Rights policy checks user region and content availability window.

License service issues short-lived decryption/license material to approved devices.

Segments stay encrypted in CDN/object storage.

Keys/licenses should not be embedded permanently in manifests.



26  Security and Abuse

Authenticate upload/finalize/delete operations.

Use short-lived scoped pre-signed upload/download tokens.

Validate MIME/container/codec rather than trusting filename extensions.

Rate-limit upload sessions and metadata mutations.

Scan uploaded media for malware and policy violations where applicable.

Protect private/unlisted content with authorization; an opaque videoId alone is not sufficient for private access.



27  Content Moderation and Copyright

Run asynchronous visual/audio/text classifiers after ingest; high-risk checks may gate publication.

Maintain moderation state in authoritative metadata.

Fingerprinting can detect known copyrighted/reuploaded media.

If a video is blocked, playback service must deny new sessions even if old CDN objects still physically exist.

Purge/expire manifests/tokens as required for urgent takedown.



28  Consistency Model

Data
	Recommended Consistency

Video upload/finalize/status
	Strong/conditional state transitions

Playback authorization/rights
	Current enough to enforce policy

Search index
	Eventual

Recommendations
	Eventual

View counts
	Eventual / approximate in real time

CDN segments
	Immutable; consistency trivial by versioned key





Key ideaStrong consistency belongs around user intent, publication state, deletion, and entitlement. Search, recommendations, counters, and analytics can lag.



29  Multi-Region Design





Global playback is naturally edge-first; metadata writes still need ownership/failover rules.



Upload/metadata writes can use a home region per creator/video or a globally consistent metadata service.

Source/transcoded media replicate across origin regions according to durability/locality policy.

Playback metadata/cache replicas serve viewers locally.

CDN handles most segment delivery, so origin regions see only misses.

Failover must preserve video state machine and avoid two orchestrators publishing conflicting asset versions.



30  Failure Modes and Recovery





Different layers fail independently and should degrade differently.



Failure
	Expected Behavior
	Recovery

One transcode worker
	Only that job/rendition retries
	Queue retry, idempotent output key

Processing backlog
	Publishing delayed
	Autoscale, priority queues

One CDN POP
	Route to another POP/CDN
	DNS/anycast/provider failover

Origin shield
	Edges miss to alternate shield/origin
	Capacity guardrails

Metadata writer
	Uploads/changes pause or fail over
	Leader/DB failover

Search/recommendation
	Playback remains available
	Catch up asynchronously





Failure priorityPlayback of already-published videos should survive failures in upload processing, search, recommendations, comments, and analytics.



31  Idempotency and Retry Safety

BeginUpload uses client idempotency key to avoid duplicate video records.

Part upload is idempotent by session + part number/object key.

Processing job output path includes videoId + assetVersion + rendition so retries overwrite/confirm the same logical result safely.

State transitions use expected previous state/version.

Analytics events may be at-least-once; downstream aggregates deduplicate where exactness matters.



32  Observability and QoE SLOs

For a streaming platform, backend availability is not enough; measure what the player experiences.

Time to first frame / startup latency.

Rebuffer ratio and rebuffer events per hour.

Average delivered bitrate / quality switches.

Playback fatal error rate.

CDN edge hit ratio and origin egress.

Transcoding queue wait + processing duration per rendition.

Upload completion/retry rate.

Manifest/segment p95/p99 latency by ISP/region/device.



Best product metricA request can return HTTP 200 and still be a terrible stream. Playback QoE metrics such as startup time and rebuffer ratio should be first-class SLOs.



33  Cost Drivers and Optimization

Cost Driver
	Optimization

CDN egress
	Better codecs, CDN price routing, regional peering

Transcoding compute
	Popularity-aware/on-demand renditions, hardware encoders

Origin storage
	Cold tiers, lifecycle, deduplicate identical assets where safe

Multi-region replication
	Replicate based on durability + locality

Search/ML
	Async batching and tiered inference

Viral launch
	Pre-warm CDN; origin shield





Streaming economicsAt scale, a 10-20% bitrate reduction can save more money than many backend optimizations because every watched minute crosses the delivery network.



34  YouTube-Specific Product Follow-Ups

Subscriptions: maintain channel->subscribers and user->subscriptions; notify/feed asynchronously.

Comments: separate comment service, paginated/threaded store, moderation/ranking.

Likes: idempotent user-video relation + asynchronous aggregate counters.

Creator analytics: warehouse from playback/engagement events, not synchronous metadata updates.

Unlisted/private videos: playback API authorizes every session; CDN uses signed tokens/URLs as needed.



35  Netflix-Specific Product Follow-Ups

Regional licensing windows and subscription entitlement are part of playback authorization.

Multiple audio tracks, subtitles, accessibility tracks, and device certification matter.

Offline download uses encrypted device-bound assets and expiring licenses.

Catalog may be much smaller than YouTube but each title receives extremely high watch volume and sophisticated encoding.

Playback quality and DRM are typically deeper interview areas than creator upload moderation.



36  Architecture Evolution

Stage
	Design
	Trigger

V1
	Metadata API + one object store + one encoded file
	Small launch

V2
	Async transcode workers + several renditions
	Device/network diversity

V3
	HLS/DASH + CDN
	Playback scale

V4
	Origin shield + multi-region origin
	Viral/global traffic

V5
	Search + analytics streams
	Discovery/operations

V6
	Popularity-aware encoding/storage
	Cost scale

V7
	DRM/multi-CDN/recommendations
	Mature global product





37  Final Production Architecture





The final system isolates media transport from control-plane correctness.



Upload/processing path:

Creator -> Upload API -> direct multipart source upload -> finalize.

Event/job stream -> transcode/package workers -> immutable segments/manifests -> origin storage.

Metadata transitions to READY only after required assets are valid.

Playback path:

Viewer -> Playback API authorization -> master manifest.

Player -> CDN edge -> origin shield -> origin only on misses.

ABR chooses each next segment quality.

Derived path:

Metadata/playback events -> search, recommendations, analytics, creator dashboards, moderation.



38  How to Present This in a 45-60 Minute Interview

Time
	Coverage

0-5 min
	Clarify YouTube vs Netflix, upload + VOD + playback requirements

5-10 min
	Scale: ingest bytes, watch time, egress

10-18 min
	HLD + metadata/data-plane separation

18-28 min
	Resumable upload + processing/transcoding pipeline

28-38 min
	HLS/DASH + ABR + CDN/origin shield

38-46 min
	Metadata/storage/search/analytics

46-53 min
	DRM/security/multi-region/failures

53-60 min
	Interviewer-selected deep dive + final summary





Do not memorize every paragraphMemorize this flow: resumable source upload -> durable source -> async transcode ladder -> HLS/DASH segments/manifests -> origin storage -> CDN -> player ABR -> QoE analytics. Then remember the two big interview truths: media bytes bypass normal APIs, and already-published playback should survive failures in noncritical subsystems.



39  Interviewer Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Why not stream the original uploaded file directly?

Answer: The original may use unsupported codecs/resolution/bitrate and is usually one large object. Transcoding creates device-compatible representations; segment packaging enables CDN caching, seeking and adaptive bitrate.

Follow-up: Why split video into segments?

Answer: Segments let the player switch quality between boundaries, retry a small piece, seek efficiently, and cache immutable objects independently at CDN edges.

Follow-up: How do you avoid reuploading a 20 GB file after Wi-Fi fails?

Answer: Use multipart resumable upload with a durable session and per-part checksums/acknowledgements. On reconnect, query completed parts and send only missing ones.

Follow-up: What happens if one transcode job fails?

Answer: Retry that rendition idempotently. Keep processing stages/jobs independent so one failed 4K encode does not repeat thumbnails or block all other videos.

Follow-up: How does adaptive bitrate choose quality?

Answer: Use recent throughput, buffer level, screen/device capabilities and previous rebuffer history. The goal is high stable quality with minimal stalls, not simply the highest resolution.

Follow-up: How do you handle a viral premiere?

Answer: Pre-warm CDN, cache first segments widely, use an origin shield/request coalescing, reserve capacity and optionally route across multiple CDNs.

Follow-up: What if CDN misses increase suddenly?

Answer: Protect origin with mid-tier shield and concurrency/rate limits; investigate cache-key/TTL changes. Prefer graceful quality reduction over origin collapse.

Follow-up: How do deletes/takedowns work if segments are cached?

Answer: Make playback authorization/metadata immediately deny new sessions, purge manifests/tokens/edge objects for urgent cases, and clean immutable segment objects asynchronously.

Follow-up: How do you support multiple codecs?

Answer: Maintain separate rendition sets/manifests and let playback select based on device support. Encode expensive next-gen codecs only where bandwidth savings justify compute/storage.

Follow-up: Why not update view count on every segment/play request?

Answer: It would create hot synchronous writes. Emit playback events to a stream and aggregate validated views/watch time asynchronously.

Follow-up: How does Netflix differ most from YouTube?

Answer: Netflix has controlled ingest and heavier entitlement/DRM/rights logic, while YouTube has user-generated upload, moderation and huge long-tail discovery. Streaming/CDN mechanics are largely shared.

Follow-up: How does multi-region change the design?

Answer: Serve playback locally via CDN/replicated origin and keep explicit ownership/failover for metadata/upload state. Replicate media asynchronously according to durability/locality policy.





40  Detailed Interview Questions with Answers

1. What is the hardest part of a YouTube/Netflix system design?

Answer: The hardest engineering cost is moving and serving enormous media bytes reliably and cheaply while maintaining good playback quality. Metadata CRUD is comparatively small. The design must therefore separate a control plane for video records, rights and sessions from a data plane built around object storage, processing workers, immutable segments and CDN. The key interview deep dives are resumable ingest, transcoding/packaging, adaptive bitrate, CDN/origin behavior, viral spikes and QoE.

2. Why should video upload bypass ordinary application servers?

Answer: Large uploads may be many gigabytes. If every byte travels through stateless API servers, those servers become expensive network proxies and need huge connection/memory budgets. Instead, the API authenticates the creator and creates an upload session, then issues short-lived scoped URLs/tokens so the client sends parts directly to object storage. The API later finalizes the session and starts processing. This cleanly separates control traffic from bulk data transfer.

3. How do you make a huge upload resumable?

Answer: Split the source into independently uploadable parts and persist an uploadSessionId plus expected file metadata. Each part has a stable part number and checksum. The client records completed parts locally; the object store/server also records them. After a disconnect, the client lists completed parts and uploads only the missing ones. Completing the multipart upload atomically creates the source object. Incomplete sessions expire and temporary parts are garbage-collected.

4. When should the platform acknowledge an upload as complete?

Answer: There are two milestones. First, source upload completion means the original source object is durably stored and verified. Second, publication/READY means required processed assets and manifests exist. The creator can receive an upload-success response after the source commit while the UI shows PROCESSING. Normal viewers should only be routed to published/READY assets unless the product deliberately supports progressive/partial publication.

5. Why is video processing asynchronous?

Answer: Transcoding can take seconds to hours and consumes expensive CPU/GPU resources. Running it inside the upload HTTP request would time out, waste server resources and make retries dangerous. An asynchronous job/state-machine pipeline lets workers scale independently, retry failed stages, prioritize jobs, run several renditions in parallel and preserve a durable processing state. It also isolates a bad video or slow encoder from unrelated uploads.

6. What stages would you put in the processing pipeline?

Answer: A practical pipeline probes/validates the source, extracts technical metadata, runs security/moderation checks, transcodes required codec/resolution/bitrate variants, packages them into HLS/DASH segments, creates manifests, generates thumbnails/storyboards, handles subtitles/captions, and updates metadata to READY. Each stage should be idempotent with versioned output keys so retries do not create conflicting assets.

7. Why generate multiple resolutions and bitrates?

Answer: Viewers have different bandwidth, screens, devices and network changes during playback. One 4K file would waste bandwidth for mobile users and fail on slow connections. Multiple representations let the player select a suitable bitrate and switch between them as conditions change. This improves startup speed and reduces buffering. It also lets the platform choose codecs/quality based on device capability and data-saver policy.

8. How do you choose an encoding ladder?

Answer: Start with a small ladder such as 240p/480p/720p/1080p at progressively higher bitrates, then tune based on codec, content complexity and observed devices. Sports/action may need more bitrate than a static lecture at the same resolution. I would not encode every upload into every possible format: popularity-aware encoding can delay or skip expensive 4K/AV1 variants for long-tail videos until demand justifies them.

9. H.264 vs AV1/HEVC - how do you decide?

Answer: H.264 has excellent compatibility and hardware support but needs more bits for comparable quality. Newer codecs can reduce CDN bandwidth substantially but cost more to encode and may not play on all clients or have licensing constraints. A mature platform often stores multiple codec families and chooses per device. For popular content, bandwidth savings may easily justify extra encoding compute; for cold content, simpler encoding may be cheaper overall.

10. What do HLS and DASH solve?

Answer: They package a video as short time-aligned segments plus manifests describing available representations. The player fetches the master manifest, chooses a representation and downloads segments over ordinary HTTP/CDN. This enables seeking, retries, CDN caching and adaptive bitrate switching between segment boundaries. The platform no longer needs a custom continuous video socket for VOD; standard HTTP delivery becomes highly scalable.

11. How does adaptive bitrate streaming work?

Answer: The player continuously estimates sustainable throughput and tracks its playback buffer. Before requesting the next segment, it selects a representation whose bitrate should arrive before the buffer runs out, also considering device resolution, codec support and recent rebuffer history. Good ABR algorithms avoid rapid quality oscillation and prioritize uninterrupted playback. When bandwidth drops, the player quickly chooses a lower bitrate rather than waiting for a high-quality segment that causes a stall.

12. Why is the CDN so important?

Answer: Video egress dwarfs API traffic. Without a CDN, every segment request would traverse to central object storage, causing huge latency, bandwidth cost and origin overload. CDN edges cache immutable segments close to users and absorb repeated demand. Since popular videos account for a large portion of traffic, hit ratio can be extremely valuable. The origin should serve only misses, protected by an origin shield/mid-tier cache.

13. What is an origin shield and why use it?

Answer: When many edge POPs miss the same new segment, they can all request it from origin simultaneously. An origin shield is a regional mid-tier cache that collapses those requests: only one/few requests reach object storage, then the shield serves the edges. This is especially valuable during premieres or sudden viral spikes and reduces origin bandwidth/connection pressure.

14. How do you handle a viral premiere with millions of simultaneous viewers?

Answer: Pre-warm the master manifest and first segments at major edges before launch, use an origin shield/request coalescing, reserve CDN capacity, monitor per-region startup/rebuffer metrics and optionally use multiple CDN providers. First segments deserve special attention because every viewer requests them together. If capacity is constrained, reducing maximum quality is safer than letting widespread buffering occur.

15. What should be cached and for how long?

Answer: Versioned media segments are immutable, so they can use very long CDN TTLs. Manifests may use shorter TTLs if rights/publication state or available renditions can change, although versioned manifests can also be immutable. Metadata pages/API responses use normal application caching. Playback authorization/entitlement should not be hidden behind an unsafe public cache. Cache keys should include asset/version/codec/rendition so objects never mutate in place.

16. How do hot and cold videos differ operationally?

Answer: Hot videos should be present at many CDN edges, may be pre-warmed and can justify expensive efficient codecs because egress dominates cost. Cold long-tail videos may remain only in origin/cold storage and populate edge caches on demand. The platform can use popularity predictions and recent access to tier assets. Applying the same replication/cache/encoding policy to every video wastes enormous storage and compute.

17. How would you model video metadata?

Answer: Use a compact Video record with videoId, owner/channel, title/description, visibility, duration, status and publication fields. Separate Asset/Rendition records describe codec, resolution, bitrate and manifest/object references. A PlaybackPolicy or related records can capture region rights, age restrictions and DRM/entitlement. This keeps the database queryable while all large media bytes remain in object storage.

18. What database would you choose for metadata?

Answer: The metadata workload is relatively small compared with media, and it benefits from conditional state transitions and secondary queries by owner/channel. SQL is a strong starting choice; a sharded/distributed relational or document/KV system can be used at huge scale. The important design is direct videoId lookup, an owner/channel index and safe transitions such as PROCESSING to READY or ACTIVE to DELETED. I would not choose a database based on video file size because files are not stored there.

19. How does video search work?

Answer: Search consumes metadata/READY events asynchronously and builds an inverted index over title, description, tags, captions/transcript, channel and language; modern systems may add vector/semantic retrieval. The search index can lag the metadata store. When a user opens a result, the playback/metadata API rechecks visibility and rights so a stale search document cannot bypass deletion or privacy.

20. How would recommendations fit without turning this into an ML interview?

Answer: Keep it layered: candidate retrieval from subscriptions, similar videos, user history, trending and collaborative signals; then rank a few hundred/thousand candidates using freshness, predicted watch time/engagement and diversity/safety/business constraints. The streaming architecture is independent: recommendations produce video IDs, while playback still uses the same metadata/CDN pipeline. Unless asked, do not dive into model architecture.

21. How do you count views correctly at massive scale?

Answer: Do not increment a single video row for every playback. Players emit start/progress/finish events into a durable stream. Streaming/batch jobs validate sessions, remove obvious duplicates/bots, apply business rules such as minimum watch time and aggregate views/watch time. A real-time counter can be approximate; durable creator analytics can reconcile later from the event log/warehouse.

22. Which playback analytics matter most?

Answer: Time to first frame, rebuffer ratio, rebuffer events per hour, fatal playback error rate, delivered bitrate/resolution, quality-switch frequency and CDN/segment latency by region/ISP/device are core QoE metrics. Watch time and completion matter for product/recommendation, but a streaming team first needs to know whether playback actually starts quickly and continues smoothly.

23. How do DRM and entitlement fit?

Answer: Before issuing a playback session, the service checks that the account is entitled, the title is allowed in the user's region/time window and the device is acceptable. Media segments remain encrypted at rest/in CDN. A license service issues short-lived decryption/license material to the approved client. This protects keys from being permanently embedded in manifests and lets rights changes stop new playback even though encrypted segments are widely cached.

24. How do you delete or block a video that is already cached worldwide?

Answer: First change authoritative metadata/status so playback API denies new sessions immediately. Invalidate API/metadata caches. For urgent takedowns, purge the manifest/segments at CDN or use short-lived signed playback tokens/manifests so stale edge objects cannot be requested by unauthorized clients. Physical deletion from origin/CDN can happen asynchronously after the logical policy is enforced.

25. What happens if a transcoding worker crashes mid-job?

Answer: Jobs are idempotent and persisted in a queue/state machine, so another worker retries the failed rendition. Output object names include videoId, assetVersion, codec and rendition, letting a retry safely detect/replace the same logical output. Completed independent renditions do not need to rerun. The video stays PROCESSING until the required asset set passes validation.

26. What happens if the CDN fails?

Answer: A single POP failure should route users to another POP. A provider-wide regional issue can use multi-CDN or alternate routing for a mature platform. CDN misses can fall back through origin shield/origin, but origin must have capacity guardrails so a CDN outage does not create an uncontrolled thundering herd. Playback may temporarily reduce maximum quality to preserve continuity.

27. What if origin storage becomes slow?

Answer: Edge hits continue normally. Misses will suffer, so the shield should coalesce requests and apply bounded concurrency/backpressure. Popular assets should already have high edge residency. For critical titles, multiple origin replicas/regions reduce risk. The goal is to prevent one origin incident from evicting or bypassing the cached data plane that still works.

28. How would multi-region deployment work?

Answer: Upload/metadata writes have explicit ownership or a globally consistent metadata layer. Source and published assets replicate to durable origin regions. Playback APIs and metadata caches run regionally, while CDN serves most bytes locally. Processing jobs can run where the source/compute is available and publish versioned assets globally. Failover must ensure only one logical publication state/version is authoritative.

29. Why are media segments easy to make eventually consistent?

Answer: They are immutable and versioned. Once a segment object exists, it never changes; a new processing version gets a new key/manifest. Therefore replication can be asynchronous without worrying that two replicas will serve conflicting mutable contents for the same key. The harder consistency problem is the small metadata pointer that decides which asset version is published/authorized.

30. How do you handle subtitles and multiple audio tracks?

Answer: Treat them as timed media assets associated with the same video/version. Processing extracts/generates/transcodes tracks, and the manifest advertises available subtitle/audio alternatives. They are small compared with video and cache well. The playback client selects based on user language/accessibility preferences. Rights/moderation may apply independently to tracks.

31. How would offline downloads work for Netflix-like content?

Answer: The client downloads encrypted segments/manifests to device storage using a controlled workflow. A device-bound DRM license with expiry/offline policy authorizes decryption for a limited period. The app tracks download state and refreshes/invalidates licenses when online. Raw unencrypted files should not be exposed as normal downloadable objects. This is a product/security extension to the same segmented asset model.

32. How do you optimize cost at very large scale?

Answer: Focus on the big multipliers: egress bitrate, transcoding compute, replication and storage. Use more efficient codecs for popular titles, popularity-aware encoding ladders, object lifecycle/cold tiers for long-tail assets, hardware encoders, CDN price/performance routing and regional origin placement. Even a modest bitrate reduction across billions of watched minutes can dwarf savings from optimizing metadata servers.

33. What should be strongly consistent and what can be eventual?

Answer: Strong/conditional consistency is useful for upload-finalization state, publication/deletion, visibility and entitlement/rights because these are user intent/security boundaries. Search, recommendations, view counts, creator analytics and most discovery indexes can be eventually consistent. Media segment objects are immutable/versioned, so their replication can be asynchronous once durability requirements are met.

34. What would you monitor first in production?

Answer: I would monitor playback QoE first: startup time, rebuffer ratio, fatal error rate and delivered bitrate segmented by ISP/region/device. Then CDN hit ratio/origin egress, manifest/segment latency, processing queue wait and job failure rates, upload completion, metadata/playback API errors and multi-region replication health. For a streaming service, HTTP success alone does not prove users had a successful watch experience.

35. Give the complete design in 30 seconds.

Answer: Creators upload source videos directly to durable object storage using resumable multipart sessions. Finalization publishes an asynchronous processing DAG that transcodes multiple codec/bitrate variants, packages HLS/DASH segments, generates manifests/thumbnails and marks the video READY. Playback API checks status, privacy/entitlement/DRM and returns a manifest; the player fetches immutable segments from CDN and uses adaptive bitrate based on bandwidth/buffer. Origin shield protects storage from misses and viral launches. Search, recommendations, moderation and analytics consume metadata/playback events asynchronously, while metadata and publication state remain authoritative.





41  Final Interview Cheat Sheet

Topic
	Recommended Baseline

Core split
	Control plane metadata vs media data plane

Upload
	Direct resumable multipart to object storage

Publication
	Source durable first; READY after required assets

Processing
	Async DAG/state machine

Encoding
	Multiple bitrate/resolution representations

Packaging
	HLS/DASH manifest + immutable segments

Playback
	Playback API auth -> CDN manifest/segments

ABR
	Client chooses next segment quality

CDN
	Edge -> origin shield -> origin

Hot video
	Pre-warm/cache/multi-CDN as needed

Cold video
	Origin/cold tier; on-demand edge fill

Metadata
	Small DB records, not video bytes

Search
	Async inverted/semantic index

Analytics
	Playback events -> stream -> QoE/warehouse

DRM
	Entitlement/license + encrypted segments

Delete
	Authoritative deny first; purge/cleanup later

Multi-region
	Local playback; explicit metadata write ownership

Best SLOs
	Startup time + rebuffer ratio + fatal error rate





30-second final answerCreators upload source videos directly to durable object storage using resumable multipart sessions. After finalize, an asynchronous processing pipeline validates, transcodes multiple codec/bitrate variants, packages HLS/DASH segments and manifests, and marks the video READY. Playback API checks visibility/entitlement and returns a manifest; viewers fetch immutable segments from CDN, with an origin shield protecting storage and ABR choosing quality based on bandwidth and buffer. Search, recommendations, moderation and analytics are asynchronous derived systems; metadata/publication/rights remain authoritative.



42  Review Quiz - Actual Design Problem

Question
	Answer

1. Why not stream the original upload?
	It may be too large/unsupported and cannot adapt bitrate; transcode + segment it.

2. What is the publication boundary?
	Metadata becomes READY only after required durable processed assets/manifests exist.

3. Why use multipart upload?
	Resume/retry only missing parts instead of restarting multi-GB uploads.

4. Why are HLS/DASH segments CDN-friendly?
	They are small immutable HTTP objects with stable versioned keys.

5. What does ABR optimize?
	Smooth playback and quality under changing bandwidth/buffer constraints.

6. Why use an origin shield?
	Collapse many edge misses so origin does not receive a thundering herd.

7. What should happen during a viral premiere?
	Pre-warm edges/first segments, reserve capacity, shield/coalesce misses, possibly multi-CDN.

8. Why not update view counts synchronously?
	It creates a hot write path; aggregate validated playback events asynchronously.

9. What data needs stronger consistency?
	Publication/delete/visibility/entitlement state, not search or view counters.

10. What are the best streaming SLOs?
	Startup latency, rebuffer ratio, fatal error rate and delivered quality.
