notes.content:
Design YouTube / User-Generated Video Platform

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 23 | Uploads, Transcoding, Streaming, Viral Scale, Counters, Search & Recommendations

GoalDesign a global user-generated video platform where creators upload videos and viewers discover, stream, like, comment, subscribe, and receive recommendations. The system must handle huge media objects, asynchronous processing, CDN delivery, viral traffic, very high event volume, mutable social metadata, abuse/moderation, and global availability.



1. Why YouTube Is Different from Netflix

Dimension
	Netflix-like VOD
	YouTube-like UGC

Content producers
	Controlled studio/catalog pipeline
	Millions of independent creators

Uploads
	Curated ingestion
	Continuous unpredictable uploads

Catalog
	Large but controlled
	Enormous long-tail corpus

Quality
	Known masters
	Arbitrary codecs/resolutions/quality

Social state
	Limited
	Likes, comments, subscriptions, views

Virality
	Planned releases
	Unexpected viral spikes

Moderation
	Catalog review
	Continuous automated + human moderation

Discovery
	Recommendations important
	Search/recommendations are core



Interview framingDo not design YouTube as only a video CDN. The hard parts are creator upload reliability, asynchronous media processing, global playback, viral fan-out, counters/social interactions, discovery, moderation, and separating strong metadata correctness from eventually consistent analytics.



2. Functional Requirements

Area
	Requirements

Upload
	Resumable large-video upload, status, thumbnail

Processing
	Validate, transcode, segment, generate manifests

Playback
	Adaptive streaming, seek, captions

Metadata
	Title, description, tags, visibility

Social
	Views, likes, comments, subscriptions

Discovery
	Search, trending, home/recommendations

Creator
	Publish/unpublish/delete, analytics

Safety
	Moderation, copyright/abuse workflow

Notifications
	Notify subscribers selectively



3. Non-Functional Requirements

Very high playback availability and low startup latency.

Uploads must survive flaky mobile networks and multi-GB files.

Processing is asynchronous; publish readiness may take seconds/minutes.

Playback bytes should come from CDN, not application servers.

Viral videos must scale without hot-origin collapse.

View/like counters may be eventually consistent; ownership/visibility changes need stronger semantics.

Global system with regional failures and graceful degradation.

Media durability is critical; raw originals must not be lost.

4. Scope and Clarifying Questions

Focus on on-demand uploaded video; live streaming is a detailed extension.

Support public/unlisted/private visibility.

Assume adaptive bitrate streaming with HLS/DASH-like manifests.

Search by title/description/tags/transcript; recommendations are architectural, not model-training deep dive.

Comments and subscriptions are included.

Monetization/ads are optional extensions.

Copyright and moderation are system-design flows, not legal-policy analysis.

5. Capacity Estimation

Dimension
	Illustrative scale
	Implication

Daily viewers
	500M+
	Global edge delivery

Peak playback QPS
	Millions of segment requests/s
	CDN-centric architecture

Uploads/day
	Millions
	Massive async pipeline

Average upload
	Hundreds of MB
	Resumable multipart upload

Stored renditions
	Several per video
	Storage amplification

View events
	Billions/day
	Streaming counters/analytics

Comments/likes
	Very high write volume
	Partitioned social stores

Catalog
	Billions of videos
	Search/index partitioning



Capacity lessonApplication QPS is not the dominant bandwidth problem. Video segment delivery is orders of magnitude larger, so the architecture must push bytes to CDN/object storage and keep metadata services off the media data path.



6. Core APIs

API
	Purpose

POST /videos/uploads
	Create upload session

PUT /uploads/{id}/parts/{n}
	Upload chunk/part

POST /uploads/{id}/complete
	Finalize upload

PATCH /videos/{id}
	Edit metadata/visibility

GET /videos/{id}
	Video metadata/playback info

POST /videos/{id}/views
	Record view event

PUT /videos/{id}/like
	Like/unlike

POST /videos/{id}/comments
	Create comment

GET /search?q=...
	Search

GET /feed/home
	Recommendations/home feed

POST /channels/{id}/subscribe
	Subscribe



7. Data Model

Entity
	Key fields

Video
	video_id, owner_id, title, description, visibility, state, duration, created_at

UploadSession
	upload_id, owner, parts, checksum, status

MediaAsset
	video_id, original_uri, rendition, codec, bitrate, dimensions, manifest

Channel
	channel_id, owner, profile, counters

Subscription
	subscriber_id, channel_id, created_at

Like
	video_id, user_id, state

Comment
	comment_id, video_id, author, parent_id, text, state, created_at

ViewEvent
	video_id, viewer/session, timestamp, watch_ms, context

Counter
	entity_id, metric, approximate_value

ModerationState
	video_id, checks, restrictions, review state



8. High-Level Architecture



YouTube-style high-level architecture

9. Upload Architecture

The API server should authorize uploads but should not proxy multi-GB media through itself.

Client requests an upload session with filename, expected size/type, and metadata.

Upload service creates video_id/upload_id and returns signed multipart/object-storage upload URLs.

Client uploads chunks directly to nearby object storage.

Each part has checksum and idempotent part number.

Client can resume after network failure by querying completed parts.

Complete call validates all parts/checksum and atomically marks raw asset available.

An event starts validation/transcoding/moderation pipelines.

Video remains PROCESSING until minimum playable renditions and required checks are ready.

10. Resumable Multipart Uploads



Resumable direct-to-storage upload

Chunk size balances retry cost and request overhead.

Upload session has expiry and ownership checks.

Part completion is idempotent.

Storage validates checksums; final object can have whole-file checksum.

Client retries individual failed parts, not the entire video.

Regional upload endpoints reduce creator latency.

11. Upload State Machine

State
	Meaning

CREATED
	Metadata/session exists

UPLOADING
	Parts arriving

UPLOADED
	Original durably finalized

VALIDATING
	Container/codec/security checks

PROCESSING
	Transcoding, thumbnails, captions, checks

READY_PRIVATE
	Playable but not necessarily public

PUBLISHED
	Eligible for discovery/playback

RESTRICTED
	Moderation/copyright restriction

DELETED
	Tombstoned and removal workflow started



Correctness invariantNever expose a manifest that references renditions which are not durably available. Publish playback metadata only after the minimum playable asset set is committed.



12. Media Validation

Verify declared MIME/container against actual bytes.

Reject malformed/decompression-bomb-like media and unsafe payloads.

Extract duration, streams, codec, dimensions, frame rate, audio properties.

Check corruption and decodeability.

Normalize rotation/color metadata.

Enforce size/duration/account limits.

Create a canonical media-processing job from validated metadata.

13. Transcoding Pipeline



Distributed transcoding and packaging

Job planner chooses codec/resolution/bitrate ladder based on source.

Independent renditions can run in parallel.

Long videos can be split into GOP-aligned chunks for distributed encoding, then packaged.

Workers are stateless; job state lives durably.

Outputs go to immutable object keys.

Retries must be idempotent: same job/version writes deterministic or versioned outputs.

Manifest is generated only after required segments exist.

14. Adaptive Bitrate Ladder

Rendition
	Example use

144p/240p
	Very constrained mobile

360p/480p
	Low/medium bandwidth

720p
	HD mobile/web

1080p
	Full HD

1440p/2160p
	High-resolution sources/devices



The exact ladder should depend on source quality, codec, content complexity, and device ecosystem. Do not upscale a poor source just to fill every rung.

15. Segmentation and Manifests

Encode each rendition into small time-aligned segments.

Manifest lists available renditions and segment locations.

Segment boundaries align across renditions so the player can switch quality cleanly.

Shorter segments improve adaptation/seek responsiveness but increase request overhead.

Media segments are immutable and ideal for CDN caching.

Manifest can be short-lived/versioned if access policy or newly completed renditions change.

16. Playback Request Flow

Viewer opens video page; metadata service checks visibility/restrictions.

Playback service returns authorized manifest URL/token and video metadata.

Player fetches manifest from CDN/origin.

Player estimates bandwidth and selects initial rendition conservatively.

Segments are fetched from nearby CDN edge.

Player continuously adapts bitrate based on throughput and buffer.

Seek jumps to segment near requested timestamp.

QoE events such as startup time, stalls, bitrate changes, and errors are emitted asynchronously.

17. CDN and Origin Architecture



Playback through CDN hierarchy

CDN edges serve most segment bytes.

Regional origin shields reduce simultaneous origin misses.

Request coalescing prevents a viral segment from causing thousands of identical origin fetches.

Immutable segment URLs permit long TTLs.

Pre-warming may be used for scheduled high-interest content, but UGC virality is often unpredictable.

Multi-CDN can improve reach and resilience at extreme scale.

18. Viral Video Problem

A previously cold video can become globally viral in minutes. The design must avoid hot metadata keys, origin stampedes, counter contention, and recommendation/feed overload.

CDN caches absorb media bytes; request coalescing protects origin on first misses.

Replicate/cache video metadata aggressively.

Shard view events by random/time bucket rather than incrementing one row synchronously.

Serve approximate counters from aggregated shards.

Use queue-based fan-out for notifications; never synchronously notify millions of subscribers.

Autoscale comment reads/writes and cache top comments separately.

Trending/recommendation pipelines consume event streams asynchronously.

Key insightVirality is not just a bandwidth problem. It simultaneously stresses CDN cold misses, metadata, counters, comments, notifications, search freshness, and ranking pipelines.



19. View Counting

Playback emits view/watch events to an ingestion stream.

Validation filters obvious retries/bots/duplicate noise according to product semantics.

Partition events by video/time/hash.

Stream processors maintain near-real-time partial counts.

Persist aggregates in a scalable counter store and periodically compact.

Displayed count may lag slightly and be approximate.

Raw events feed creator analytics and recommendation features separately.

Do not do thisDo not execute UPDATE videos SET views=views+1 for every playback on a single primary row. A viral video turns that row into a global serialization point.



20. Likes and Dislikes

User-video reaction is keyed by (user_id, video_id) for idempotency.

Changing reaction updates state, not blindly adding another count.

Write durable user reaction first; emit delta event for aggregate counter.

Counter is eventually consistent and repairable from source-of-truth reactions/events.

Read path can return viewer's exact reaction plus approximate aggregate count.

Partition aggregate updates for hot videos.

21. Comments

Concern
	Design

Write
	Partition by video_id plus bucket for hot videos

Ordering
	created_at or ranked/top-comments views

Replies
	parent_comment_id / thread model

Pagination
	Cursor, not offset at huge scale

Moderation
	Async classifier + synchronous policy checks where required

Deletes
	Tombstone comment and update thread views

Hot reads
	Cache top comments and first page

Counts
	Async aggregated counter



22. Subscription Model

Store subscriber→channels for home/subscription feed reads.

Also store channel→subscriber partitions for notifications/fan-out where needed.

Celebrity channels create huge fan-out sets; partition heavily.

Subscription write is idempotent.

Do not materialize every upload into every subscriber inbox synchronously at upload time for massive channels unless using a hybrid strategy.

Home feed can use fan-out-on-read/hybrid recommendation generation.

23. Notifications for New Uploads

Video becomes eligible for notification after publish checks.

Notification event enters durable queue.

Audience service reads channel subscribers in partitions.

Apply notification preferences, rate limits, relevance, and dedupe.

Workers enqueue/send notifications asynchronously.

Checkpoint progress so retries do not resend uncontrollably.

For channels with enormous audiences, spread delivery over partitions/time and protect downstream push providers.

24. Search Indexing

Index title, description, tags, channel, language, transcript/captions, and selected engagement/quality features.

Publishing emits an index event; deletion/restriction emits a tombstone/update.

Search index is eventually consistent but moderation removals need fast suppression.

Shard index by document/video and replicate.

Ranking can combine text relevance, freshness, engagement, channel authority, personalization, and safety.

Autocomplete/trending queries are separate precomputed structures.

25. Recommendation Architecture



Two-stage recommendation system

Candidate generation retrieves hundreds/thousands from subscriptions, similar-content, collaborative signals, trending, and exploration.

Ranking scores a much smaller set with user/context/video features.

Post-ranking applies safety, dedupe, diversity, freshness, and creator/content constraints.

Feature pipelines consume watch, search, like, skip, and subscription events.

Fallback recommendations should work when ML services fail.

26. Trending

Consume view/engagement streams in time windows.

Use velocity and acceleration, not only lifetime views.

Normalize by geography/category and suppress abuse.

Compare recent activity to baseline so old mega-videos do not dominate forever.

Maintain top-K per region/category with streaming heaps/sketches.

Trending is eventually consistent and can tolerate seconds/minutes of lag.

27. Metadata Storage Strategy

Data
	Suggested pattern

Video/channel metadata
	Partitioned replicated KV/document/relational service

Upload sessions
	Strongly durable transactional store

Media bytes
	Object/blob storage

Likes/subscriptions
	Partitioned KV/relational by composite key

Comments
	Wide-column/document store partitioned by video

Counters
	Sharded counter/stream aggregates

Search
	Distributed inverted index

Events
	Durable log/stream

Analytics
	Data lake/warehouse



28. Consistency Model

Operation
	Consistency need
	Why

Upload finalize
	Strong/idempotent
	Do not lose/corrupt original

Visibility change
	Strong-ish authoritative metadata
	Private video must not leak

Playback counter
	Eventual
	Scale and availability

Like count
	Eventual aggregate
	Exact user reaction stored separately

Comment creation
	Read-your-write desirable
	User UX

Search indexing
	Eventual
	Derived index

Recommendation features
	Eventual
	Derived

Delete/restrict
	Fast suppression
	Safety/privacy



29. Deletion Workflow

Authoritative metadata marks video DELETED/UNAVAILABLE.

Playback authorization immediately refuses new manifest access.

Search/recommendation indexes receive high-priority tombstones.

CDN URLs/tokens are invalidated or become inaccessible; immutable cached bytes must not be newly authorized.

Comments/likes become hidden according to policy.

Async garbage collection removes renditions, thumbnails, originals after retention rules.

Analytics may retain allowed aggregates separately.

Deletion workflow is idempotent and auditable.

30. Moderation Pipeline

Run automated checks on upload metadata, frames/audio/transcript, spam, malware, and policy classifiers.

Some checks block publication; others can run after private processing.

Store moderation decision/version separately from media.

Human-review queue handles uncertain/high-impact cases.

Restrictions must propagate to playback, search, recommendations, comments, and notifications.

Reprocessing is possible when classifiers/policies change because originals/derived metadata are retained appropriately.

31. Copyright / Content Fingerprinting

Generate robust audio/video fingerprints during processing.

Compare against reference fingerprint index.

A match emits a claim/review workflow rather than modifying media pipeline directly.

Fingerprint lookup must tolerate transformations such as re-encoding/cropping within system capability.

Keep claim state separate from video asset state.

Playback/monetization/region restrictions consume resolved claim policy.

Fingerprint computation is asynchronous and horizontally scalable.

32. Captions and Transcripts

Accept creator-provided caption tracks.

Speech-to-text jobs can generate automatic captions asynchronously.

Store timed text separately from video segments.

Transcript feeds search indexing and accessibility.

Caption corrections create new track versions without retranscoding video.

Player fetches selected language track independently.

33. Thumbnail Generation

Extract candidate frames at multiple timestamps after validation/transcode.

Generate several sizes/aspect ratios.

Allow creator-selected/uploaded thumbnail subject to checks.

Store immutable thumbnail assets behind CDN.

Recommendation/search cards should never fetch frames from video at request time.

34. QoE Telemetry

Metric
	Meaning

Time to first frame
	Startup latency

Rebuffer ratio
	Playback stalls

Average bitrate/resolution
	Delivered quality

Bitrate switches
	ABR stability

Playback errors
	Reliability

Seek latency
	Random-access quality

CDN hit/miss
	Delivery efficiency

Watch duration
	Engagement/quality signal



35. Creator Analytics

Raw playback/engagement events enter durable stream/data lake.

Streaming jobs provide near-real-time approximate views/watch time.

Batch jobs reconcile authoritative daily analytics.

Dimensions include geography/device/source while respecting privacy thresholds.

Creator dashboard reads pre-aggregated cubes, never scans raw events interactively.

Late events are handled with watermarking/recomputation.

36. Hot Key Mitigation

Cache immutable/video metadata at edge/service layer.

Shard counters into N buckets and sum on read/cache aggregate.

Partition comments for extreme videos by time/hash bucket.

Replicate read-heavy metadata partitions.

Use request coalescing for cache misses.

Avoid channel subscriber list on one partition for celebrity channels.

Autoscale consumers by stream lag, not only CPU.

37. Failure Scenarios

Failure
	Behavior

Upload worker/API dies
	Client resumes parts using durable upload session

Transcode worker dies
	Lease expires; idempotent job retries

One rendition fails
	Retry it; publish lower ladder only if policy permits

CDN region fails
	Route to alternate edge/CDN/origin shield

Counter pipeline delayed
	Playback works; displayed count lags

Search indexing delayed
	Video playable by direct URL but discovery may lag

Recommendation service fails
	Fallback to subscriptions/trending

Comment store overloaded
	Playback unaffected; degrade comments

Moderation service slow
	Keep video private/processing if blocking check

Region outage
	Metadata failover; media still CDN/object replicated



38. Multi-Region Architecture

Uploads terminate near creators and write to durable regional object storage with replication.

Metadata has an authoritative partition/home or globally coordinated strategy for ownership/visibility writes.

Media renditions replicate/origin from multiple regions and distribute through CDN.

Playback authorization and metadata reads are active-active regionally.

Event streams replicate into analytics/search/recommendation pipelines.

Transcoding can run where compute/storage economics permit; outputs are immutable.

Deletion/restriction events receive priority global propagation.

Avoid synchronous cross-region calls in the playback segment path.

39. Live Streaming Extension

VOD
	Live

Entire file exists before publish
	Media arrives continuously

Offline transcode possible
	Real-time encoding required

Long CDN TTL for segments
	Segments become available over time

Manifest mostly stable
	Manifest continually advances

Retry processing freely
	Strict latency deadline

Views on static asset
	Concurrent session scale + chat



Ingest live stream into regional media servers.

Encode multiple bitrates in real time.

Produce short segments/chunks and update live manifest.

Push/pull segments through CDN with low-latency configuration.

Archive live segments to create VOD after stream.

Live chat is a separate high-fan-out messaging system.

40. Security

Signed upload URLs are scoped by object key, part, expiry, and creator.

Validate ownership on finalize/edit/delete.

Private/unlisted playback uses authorization and short-lived playback tokens.

Never trust uploaded MIME/metadata.

Scan malformed media and isolate codecs/transcoders in sandboxed workers.

Rate-limit comments/likes/uploads and detect automation abuse.

Secrets and object-store credentials never go to untrusted clients.

41. Observability

Metric
	Why

Upload success/resume rate
	Creator reliability

Upload finalize latency
	Ingestion health

Transcode queue age
	Processing backlog

Per-rendition failure rate
	Codec pipeline

Publish latency
	Creator UX

Playback startup p95/p99
	Viewer QoE

Rebuffer ratio
	Delivery quality

CDN hit rate/origin egress
	Cost + performance

Counter stream lag
	Freshness

Search index lag
	Discovery freshness

Moderation backlog
	Safety operations

Delete propagation latency
	Critical control path



42. End-to-End Upload Example

Creator requests upload session and receives video_id plus signed multipart URLs.

Client uploads 200 chunks directly to object storage, retrying only failed chunks.

Finalize verifies all part checksums and creates immutable original asset.

Upload-complete event starts validation, moderation, thumbnail, caption, and transcode jobs.

Planner creates 360p/720p/1080p jobs based on source.

Workers encode and package aligned segments into immutable rendition keys.

Manifest builder verifies required segments and publishes playback asset version.

Metadata moves video to READY_PRIVATE.

Creator changes visibility to PUBLIC after required checks.

Search/recommendation index events fire; subscriber notification workflow begins.

CDN fills segments on viewer demand; viral growth does not touch transcoders.

43. End-to-End Playback Example

Viewer opens video page.

Metadata service returns title/channel/social state and verifies availability.

Playback authorization returns signed manifest access.

Player fetches manifest and initial low/medium bitrate segments from CDN.

ABR increases quality as bandwidth/buffer confidence grows.

View event is emitted after product-defined qualification threshold.

Watch events stream to counters, recommendations, creator analytics, and trending.

Likes/comments write to their own services; playback is isolated from their failures.

If one CDN edge is unhealthy, traffic moves to another edge/provider.

Displayed view count may update seconds later without affecting playback.

44. Final Production Architecture

Direct resumable multipart uploads to object storage; application servers only control sessions/auth.

Durable event-driven processing validates originals and fans out independent transcode, thumbnail, caption, fingerprint, and moderation jobs.

Immutable segmented renditions and manifests are stored in object storage and served primarily from CDN with origin shielding/request coalescing.

Authoritative video metadata controls ownership, visibility, publish state, and deletion.

Views/likes/comments/subscriptions use separate partitioned services and asynchronous aggregate counters.

Search consumes publish/update/tombstone events into a distributed index.

Recommendations use candidate generation plus ranking over asynchronously produced features.

Viral scale is handled with CDN, caches, sharded counters, partitioned comments/subscribers, and asynchronous fan-out.

Global restrictions/deletions use high-priority propagation paths.

Playback remains available when analytics, comments, recommendations, or counters are degraded.

One-sentence architectureUpload originals directly and durably, asynchronously turn them into immutable adaptive-streaming assets, deliver those bytes through CDN, keep mutable metadata/social state in independently scalable services, and drive counters/search/recommendations from durable event streams so viral traffic never creates a single synchronous bottleneck.



45. Key Trade-offs

Decision
	Option A
	Option B
	Recommended reasoning

Upload
	Proxy via API
	Direct object upload
	Direct

Processing
	Synchronous
	Async jobs
	Async

Media
	Mutable files
	Immutable renditions
	Immutable

Counters
	Single row
	Sharded/event aggregates
	Sharded

Feed
	Push all
	Pull/hybrid
	Hybrid for celebrity scale

Search
	DB LIKE
	Inverted index
	Index

Playback
	Origin
	CDN
	CDN

Publish
	Wait all possible jobs
	Minimum required + progressive extras
	Policy dependent



46. Common Interview Mistakes

Sending video bytes through normal API servers.

Treating transcoding as one synchronous request.

No resumable upload design.

No upload/video processing state machine.

Storing only one video quality.

Serving media from application servers.

Incrementing a single view-count row per playback.

Ignoring viral cold-cache stampedes.

Coupling comments/recommendations to playback availability.

Not separating exact user reaction from approximate aggregate count.

Ignoring deletion/restriction propagation to CDN/search/recommendations.

No moderation/copyright architecture.

No idempotency for upload completion or transcode retries.

Designing recommendation ML but forgetting media pipeline fundamentals.

47. 45-Minute Interview Flow

Time
	Coverage

0-5 min
	Requirements, scale, UGC-specific challenges

5-10 min
	HLD and APIs/data model

10-16 min
	Resumable direct upload + state machine

16-23 min
	Transcoding, segmentation, manifests

23-28 min
	Playback, ABR, CDN, viral traffic

28-33 min
	Views/likes/comments/subscriptions

33-37 min
	Search/recommendations/trending

37-41 min
	Moderation, deletion, consistency

41-44 min
	Failures, multi-region, observability

44-45 min
	Trade-offs and summary



Memorize the flowUpload session -> direct multipart storage -> durable completion event -> validation/transcode/package -> immutable renditions/manifest -> publish metadata -> CDN playback. Everything else—views, likes, comments, search, recommendations, notifications, analytics—is decoupled through independent services and event streams.



48. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Detailed Answers

Follow-up: Why should the client upload directly to object storage instead of through the API service?

Detailed answer: Video files can be gigabytes. Proxying them through API servers doubles network transfer, consumes connections and memory, complicates retries, and makes autoscaling the control plane dependent on media bandwidth. The upload service should authenticate the creator, create an upload session, enforce quotas, and issue scoped signed multipart URLs. The client then sends bytes directly to durable storage. The API remains a lightweight control plane, while object storage is the data plane.

Follow-up: How do you make a 10 GB upload reliable on a bad mobile network?

Detailed answer: Use resumable multipart upload. Split the object into independently retryable parts, number them deterministically, and store part completion/checksum state in the upload session or object-store multipart protocol. The client can ask which parts already exist after reconnecting and resume only the missing ones. Finalization is idempotent and verifies all parts plus the expected object checksum before emitting the upload-complete event.

Follow-up: What happens if the client calls complete twice?

Detailed answer: Completion must be idempotent. The upload_id is the idempotency key. The service reads the durable state: if already finalized with the same part set/checksum, return the existing video result rather than creating another asset or duplicate jobs. Downstream processing events also carry a video/version identifier so consumers can deduplicate. Exactly-once delivery is not required if effects are idempotent.

Follow-up: How do you parallelize transcoding a long video?

Detailed answer: Parallelize by rendition and, for very long media, by time chunks aligned to codec GOP/keyframe boundaries. A planner probes the source and creates jobs such as 1080p chunks 0..N, 720p chunks 0..N, and so on. Workers encode independently to versioned temporary outputs. A packaging step verifies continuity, joins/references chunks, creates aligned segments, and publishes only when the rendition is complete. This reduces wall-clock processing time while keeping retries localized.

Follow-up: What if the 1080p transcode fails but 720p is ready?

Detailed answer: That is a product/policy decision encoded in the state machine. A useful design allows publication once a minimum required ladder is ready, while higher renditions continue processing. The manifest version initially exposes only complete renditions and is updated/versioned later when 1080p becomes available. Never expose references to incomplete segments. For premium/quality-sensitive workflows, publication can wait for all mandatory renditions.

Follow-up: How does adaptive bitrate streaming work?

Detailed answer: The manifest advertises multiple time-aligned renditions. The player measures recent throughput, buffer occupancy, device/network constraints, and playback stability. It requests the next segment from an appropriate bitrate. Because segment boundaries align, it can switch quality at a boundary without restarting playback. A conservative startup bitrate reduces time to first frame; quality rises as confidence grows. If throughput falls, the player lowers bitrate before the buffer empties.

Follow-up: How do you handle a video going viral before the CDN has it cached?

Detailed answer: Use regional origin shields and request coalescing. The first edge miss goes to a shield; concurrent requests for the same segment collapse behind one origin fetch rather than all reaching object storage. Once fetched, the immutable segment receives a long cache lifetime. Metadata is independently cached/replicated. View counts are sharded/event-based, and comments/subscriber fan-out are partitioned so the viral event does not simply move the hotspot from media to databases.

Follow-up: How would you count views accurately at massive scale?

Detailed answer: First define product semantics: a segment request is not necessarily a qualified view. The player emits watch events; ingestion validates session/video/timing and filters obvious duplicate/bot noise. Events are durably logged and partitioned. Stream processors compute near-real-time per-video partial counts, often across buckets, while batch jobs reconcile. The displayed number can be eventually consistent. Creator analytics can be more carefully reconciled from the event source.

Follow-up: Why are likes different from view counts?

Detailed answer: A like is user-specific mutable state and should be idempotent: a user either likes a video or does not. Store the exact reaction keyed by user_id+video_id. Then emit +1/-1 deltas to an eventually consistent aggregate. A view is an event stream with qualification/deduplication semantics and may have many events from one viewer. Keeping the exact per-user state separate from the aggregate prevents counter races.

Follow-up: How would comments scale for a video with 50 million comments?

Detailed answer: Do not store one unbounded partition if the database has partition-size/hotspot limits. Partition by video plus time/hash bucket, maintain indexes for newest/top/thread views, and use cursor pagination. Cache the first/top comment pages because most readers never traverse deeply. Comment count is an async aggregate. Replies carry parent IDs. Moderation/deletion uses tombstones. Playback remains independent if comments are degraded.

Follow-up: How do you notify 100 million subscribers of a creator?

Detailed answer: Never synchronously fan out during the publish transaction. Publish a durable notification event. Audience workers scan subscriber partitions, apply notification preferences/relevance/rate limits, and enqueue delivery in batches. Checkpoint progress and use idempotency keys. Spread delivery to protect push/email providers. In many products, only a subset receives immediate push while the upload appears in a subscription/home feed for everyone else.

Follow-up: Push or pull for the subscription feed?

Detailed answer: Use a hybrid. Fan-out-on-write works well for ordinary channels because subscriber sets are moderate and reads become cheap. For celebrity channels, writing one feed item into tens of millions of inboxes is expensive and creates spikes, so store the upload once and merge it at read time or through an asynchronous shared feed layer. Recommendations already require pull/ranking, making a hybrid natural.

Follow-up: How do you delete a video that is cached globally?

Detailed answer: First change authoritative metadata so new playback authorization fails immediately. Emit high-priority tombstones to search, recommendations, feeds, and moderation caches. If media URLs require short-lived signed authorization, cached bytes cannot be newly accessed without permission. Where necessary, issue CDN purge/invalidation. Async garbage collection later deletes renditions/originals according to retention rules. Logical unavailability must happen before physical deletion finishes.

Follow-up: How do you prevent a private video from leaking through CDN?

Detailed answer: The CDN should not be the authority for visibility. Playback begins with metadata/authorization that verifies the viewer and returns short-lived signed manifest/segment access or a protected CDN token. Cache keys and token validation must prevent unauthorized reuse. A visibility change revokes future authorization quickly. For highly sensitive private media, use stricter token lifetimes and purge strategy.

Follow-up: How do search and recommendations learn about a newly published video?

Detailed answer: The publish transaction writes authoritative video state and emits an outbox/event containing video_id and version. Search indexing consumes it to fetch/index title, description, transcript, tags, and visibility. Recommendation pipelines ingest metadata and early engagement features. These are derived systems and may lag slightly, but a restriction/deletion uses a high-priority suppression path so safety does not wait for normal eventual indexing.

Follow-up: How do you design recommendations without going too deep into ML?

Detailed answer: Describe the serving architecture. Candidate generators independently retrieve videos from subscriptions, similar content, collaborative behavior, trending, and exploration. Union/dedupe perhaps thousands of candidates. A ranking service scores a smaller set using user, video, context, and freshness features from an online feature store. Post-ranking applies safety and diversity. Events update offline/streaming features. If ML is unavailable, fall back to subscriptions/trending.

Follow-up: How do you handle moderation before and after publication?

Detailed answer: Some checks are blocking—for example malformed media, malware, or product-defined high-risk signals—so the video remains private/processing until they complete. Other classifiers can run asynchronously and update moderation state. Store decisions separately with model/policy versions. A restriction event propagates to playback authorization, search, recommendations, comments, and notifications. Human review handles uncertain cases. Idempotent reprocessing supports model upgrades.

Follow-up: What is the role of the event bus in this design?

Detailed answer: It decouples the authoritative upload/metadata path from many downstream consumers: transcoding, thumbnails, captions, moderation, fingerprinting, search, counters, analytics, recommendations, notifications, and creator analytics. Producers commit durable state and publish via an outbox/transactional pattern. Consumers process independently and retry. This prevents one slow subsystem from blocking video publication or playback.

Follow-up: How would multi-region upload and playback work?

Detailed answer: Creators upload to a nearby region/object endpoint for latency. The original is durably replicated according to policy. Transcoding can run near the object or in compute-efficient regions, producing immutable assets. Playback metadata/authorization is active-active or regionally replicated, while CDN serves media globally from edge caches. Cross-region synchronous calls are kept out of the segment path. Deletion/restriction events receive priority global replication.

Follow-up: What should still work if recommendations, comments, and analytics are all down?

Detailed answer: Core playback. The viewer should still be able to open an authorized video and stream it from CDN using metadata/playback services. Home feed can degrade to subscriptions/popular cached lists, comments can show unavailable, and counters can remain stale. Analytics events can buffer in the log. Designing these dependencies as optional around the playback core is a major availability principle.

49. Additional Detailed Interview Q&A

1. Why keep the original upload after transcoding?

Detailed answer: It allows future codec/bitrate improvements, new device formats, better thumbnails/captions, and reprocessing without asking the creator to re-upload. Originals live in cheaper durable storage and can follow lifecycle policies.

2. How do you avoid duplicate processing events?

Detailed answer: Every job has video_id, asset_version, job_type, and deterministic job ID. Workers record completion idempotently. Re-delivery sees the existing successful output and acknowledges instead of encoding again.

3. Why are media segments immutable?

Detailed answer: Immutability enables long CDN TTLs, simple cache correctness, safe replication, deterministic rollback, and no reader locking. New processing creates a new asset version rather than mutating bytes in place.

4. How do you support seeking?

Detailed answer: Segments are time-indexed and manifests map playback time to segment sequence. The player jumps to the nearest suitable keyframe/segment and resumes downloading from there.

5. What is origin shielding?

Detailed answer: A regional cache layer between many CDN edges and object origin. Multiple edge misses converge on the shield, which fetches one copy and protects the origin from fan-in.

6. What is request coalescing?

Detailed answer: If many requests miss the same cache key simultaneously, one request performs the upstream fetch while others wait for that result instead of all fetching independently.

7. How do you choose segment duration?

Detailed answer: Short segments improve startup, seek, and ABR reaction but increase HTTP/manifest overhead and reduce encoding efficiency. Longer segments do the opposite. Choose a few-second class duration based on latency/product needs.

8. How would you support 4K without exploding cost?

Detailed answer: Generate it only for sources/devices/content where justified, use efficient codecs, store immutable assets in tiered object storage, and rely on CDN. Encoding can be scheduled at lower priority because 4K is not required for initial publish.

9. How do you update title without retranscoding?

Detailed answer: Video metadata is separate from media assets. Update the authoritative metadata record, increment metadata version, and emit search/recommendation index update events. Renditions remain unchanged.

10. How do you make publish atomic across metadata and event emission?

Detailed answer: Use a transactional outbox: commit the authoritative video state and an outbox row in one transaction. A relay publishes the event and marks it sent. Consumers are idempotent.

11. What if search still shows a deleted video?

Detailed answer: The search result renderer/playback authority must recheck availability for sensitive transitions, and deletion sends a high-priority index tombstone. Search is derived; authoritative metadata wins.

12. How do you calculate trending without scanning all videos?

Detailed answer: Streaming processors maintain windowed counts/velocities by video and region, then local top-K structures are merged. Approximate sketches/heaps can bound memory.

13. How do you store billions of subscriptions?

Detailed answer: Composite-key partitions such as subscriber_id→channel IDs for reads, plus channel_id→subscriber partitions where fan-out is needed. Celebrity channel reverse lists are partitioned into many buckets.

14. How do you prevent duplicate notifications?

Detailed answer: Use a notification idempotency key such as upload_id+subscriber_id+notification_type, durable send state/checkpoints, and dedupe at enqueue/provider boundaries.

15. How do you handle late analytics events?

Detailed answer: Event time is stored separately from processing time. Stream windows use watermarks; late events update/retract aggregates within a policy window. Batch reconciliation fixes older totals.

16. How do you isolate transcoder security risk?

Detailed answer: Run untrusted media decoders in sandboxed, resource-limited workers with no broad network/storage credentials. Validate formats and cap CPU/memory/output sizes.

17. How do you support multiple codecs?

Detailed answer: The planner chooses codec ladders by source/device support. Manifest can expose compatible variants. Codec rollout is versioned and does not require changing the metadata API.

18. Why not store comments in the same video metadata row?

Detailed answer: Comments are unbounded, high-write, separately paginated/moderated data. Embedding them creates huge hot rows and couples unrelated scaling/failure domains.

19. What data should the home feed read synchronously?

Detailed answer: A precomputed/retrieved candidate set, compact online features, authoritative availability checks for final items, and cached metadata. It should not synchronously scan watch history or run huge joins.

20. Give the one-minute architecture summary.

Detailed answer: Creators upload multipart media directly to durable object storage. Completion emits events to a horizontally scalable processing DAG for validation, transcoding, packaging, thumbnails, captions, moderation, and fingerprinting. Immutable adaptive-streaming renditions are distributed through CDN. Authoritative metadata controls visibility and deletion. Views, likes, comments, subscriptions, search, recommendations, notifications, and analytics are separate partitioned services driven by durable events. Viral scale is absorbed by CDN, origin shields, caches, sharded counters, and asynchronous fan-out; noncritical systems can degrade without breaking playback.

50. Scenario-Based Deep Dives

A 2-hour video upload reaches 99% and the creator loses network.

The upload session remains durable. The client reconnects, lists completed multipart parts, uploads only missing parts, and finalizes using the same upload_id. No transcoding starts until final object validation succeeds.

A celebrity uploads and 30 million viewers arrive in five minutes.

Media bytes are absorbed by CDN with shield/coalescing on cold segments. Metadata is cached/replicated. View events go to sharded streams rather than one counter. Notifications are asynchronous and partitioned. Comments use hot-video partitions. Autoscaling follows CDN miss rate, queue lag, and service saturation.

A video is made private while millions are watching.

Authoritative metadata immediately stops issuing new playback authorization. Short-lived tokens bound continued access; stricter products can purge/revoke. Search/recommendations receive suppression events. Existing sessions follow product policy. Physical media remains until lifecycle cleanup.

Transcoding backlog grows to six hours.

Prioritize jobs: minimum publish renditions before 4K/secondary codecs; autoscale workers; separate queues by cost/SLA; apply admission/quotas; monitor queue age. Upload durability is unaffected because originals are already safe.

Recommendation service deploy is broken.

Route home feed to a previous model/service or deterministic fallback: subscriptions, recent popular/trending, and cached editorial lists. Direct video playback/search remain independent.

51. Review Quiz with Answers

1. Why direct-to-object upload?

Answer: Keep huge media bytes out of API servers.

2. Why multipart?

Answer: Resume individual chunks and localize retries.

3. What starts processing?

Answer: Durable upload-complete/finalized event.

4. Why immutable renditions?

Answer: CDN caching, rollback, replication, simple readers.

5. How is viral media handled?

Answer: CDN + shields + request coalescing.

6. How are viral view counts handled?

Answer: Event stream + sharded partial counters.

7. Exact like state vs like count?

Answer: Exact per-user reaction; eventual aggregate.

8. How does publish reach search?

Answer: Outbox/event to derived search index.

9. What must happen first on deletion?

Answer: Authoritative suppression/playback denial, then async cleanup.

10. Core design principle?

Answer: Separate media data plane from metadata/control/social/event planes.

52. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

30-second answerI would make upload and playback media paths object-storage/CDN centric. A creator gets a resumable multipart session and uploads directly to durable storage. Finalization emits an event to an asynchronous DAG that validates, transcodes multiple aligned bitrate renditions, packages immutable segments/manifests, and runs thumbnails, captions, moderation, and fingerprinting. Viewers obtain authorized playback metadata and fetch segments from CDN with origin shielding. Video metadata controls visibility; views, likes, comments, subscriptions, search, recommendations, notifications, and analytics are independently scalable services driven by durable event streams. Viral videos are handled with CDN caching, request coalescing, sharded counters, partitioned hot data, and async fan-out, while deletion/restriction has a fast global suppression path.



53. Final Interview Checklist

UGC-vs-Netflix differences explained.

Requirements, scale, APIs, and data model covered.

Direct resumable multipart upload covered.

State machine and idempotent finalization covered.

Validation/transcoding/packaging/ABR covered.

CDN, origin shield, request coalescing, viral traffic covered.

Views, likes, comments, subscriptions, notifications covered.

Search, recommendations, trending covered.

Moderation, fingerprinting, captions, thumbnails covered.

Deletion/private visibility and consistency covered.

Hot keys, multi-region, failures, security, observability covered.

Live-streaming extension covered.

20 detailed follow-ups, 20 detailed Q&As, scenarios, quiz, and interview flow included.
