09  Holds, expiry and the critical race



Figure 5 — Seat inventory state machine. Expiry is a conditional state transition.

Expiry implementation

Truth: store expires_at in DB and compare against database time during confirm and reassignment.

Fast cleanup: delay queue or scheduled worker receives hold_id + deadline and conditionally releases only matching HELD rows.

Safety net: periodic indexed sweeper finds overdue HELD rows; user requests can lazily reclaim expiry inside the same hold transaction.

Old expiry messages cannot touch a re-held or BOOKED seat because they check hold_id and state before update.

Use immutable hold generation / version to reject stale workers if a seat is held again after an expiry.

Confirm vs expiry at the exact deadline



Figure 6 — Both branches use the same DB lock/predicate, giving one legal winner.

Strict policy: confirmation requires the current hold owner, status HELD and DB_NOW < expires_at (or an explicit persisted, bounded payment grace deadline). Even if cleanup has not run, an expired hold does not get confirmed. If confirmation wins before expiry, expiry is a no-op. If expiry wins after deadline, confirmation fails and the payment branch compensates. State the equality-boundary policy; never depend on application-machine clocks.

Do not confuse a DB status with a live DB row lock

The five-minute “lock” is a persisted hold/lease state. A real SELECT ... FOR UPDATE lock exists only for the milliseconds-long transaction. Keeping the transaction open while users type card details is a major anti-pattern.

10  Payment, confirmation and exact-once business effect

Payment is the other correctness boundary. The provider cannot join our transaction. Persist a saga/state machine and assume requests, responses and webhooks can be lost, delayed, duplicated and reordered.

Chosen baseline: authorize → commit → capture



Figure 7 — Authorization separates seat confirmation from money capture; each edge needs durable retry/compensation.

1. At order creation, verify the hold still belongs to the user. Freeze server-calculated final price, taxes, fees, show and seat selection in the order.

2. Initiate provider authorization using a stable, server-persisted payment intent/idempotency reference. Store PAYMENT_PENDING and a durable attempt record first.

3. On verified authorization success, execute a short local transaction: revalidate hold/deadline; mark seats BOOKED; create booking/ticket entitlements; set order to BOOKED_CAPTURE_PENDING; add outbox row; commit.

4. Capture funds using the same provider reference; retry uncertain capture idempotently and reconcile until captured, reversed, or escalated. Issue usable tickets only when the paid + booked entitlement policy is satisfied.

5. If seat confirmation failed because the hold expired or another owner won, void the authorization; if charge was captured under a charge-first model, issue a tracked refund. Never allocate another owner’s seat.

Important trade-off you should explicitly discuss

Option
	Pros
	Unavoidable complexity

Charge then confirm
	Simple providers; common asynchronous webhook flow
	Charge may succeed without inventory; refund + pending UX

Authorize → confirm → capture (chosen)
	Usually avoids charges for failed holds
	Capture may fail AFTER inventory booked; needs recovery or deliberate cancellation policy

Confirm before payment
	Minimizes seat race
	Unpaid seats can be stranded without compensation



DO NOT CLAIM  “Once booking commits payment is guaranteed” is false. A separate payment capture may still fail or become UNKNOWN. Keep provisional paid/capture states, reconcile with PSP truth, and define compensation or manual resolution.



Order state machine

HELD → ORDER_CREATED → AUTH_PENDING → AUTHORIZEDAUTHORIZED → BOOKED_CAPTURE_PENDING → PAID_CONFIRMED → TICKET_READYAUTH_PENDING → UNKNOWN → (AUTHORIZED | FAILED) via PSP reconciliationEXPIRED / PAYMENT_FAILED → VOID_OR_REFUND_PENDING → CLOSEDBOOKED_CAPTURE_PENDING + capture failure → RETRY / escalation / governed reversal

Idempotency: scope + durable result

Hold: unique (user, hold-operation, key) plus request fingerprint; replay identical response; reject key reuse with changed seats.

Payment: use one stable provider merchant reference per attempt; client double-click cannot create a second charge.

Webhook: verify signature/timestamp; unique (provider, event_id); handle out-of-order callbacks by consulting current order/provider status.

Booking: enforce UNIQUE(order_id) and UNIQUE(hold_id) in confirmed booking rows; consumer retries reuse result.

Outbox: at-least-once publication is acceptable when downstream consumers deduplicate by event_id.

11  Cross-system boundaries, outbox and recovery

Exactly what commits atomically

For a show owned by shard K: one DB transaction commits seat_inventory HELD→BOOKED, booking/entitlement records, order transition, and outbox event. This gives a local atomic commit. Other stores (search index, email, analytics, PSP) are updated through explicit asynchronous workflows.

Transactional outbox

1. Inside the same local DB transaction that changes the booked inventory, insert event_id, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, committed_at into outbox.

2. An outbox publisher polls the table or uses CDC. It publishes into Kafka/a queue; it may repeat an event after a crash.

3. Each consumer applies idempotently, tracking event_id and, where needed, aggregate version. Ticket generation, emails and seat-map projections can retry safely.

4. Alert on outbox age and backlog. Avoid letting a notification outage block the booking transaction.

The separate-database trap

If your services use...
	Atomic guarantee you can honestly claim
	How to recover

Shared show-local DB
	Inventory + booking + outbox commit together
	HTTP retry loads committed result

Inventory DB + independent Order DB
	Cannot commit both with one local ACID TX
	Durable saga with intermediate ownership/pending states

Search index / Cassandra projection
	Eventual updates, never hard booking authority
	Rebuild and backfill from authoritative log

PSP external ledger
	Only provider knows final charge/capture truth
	Webhook + polling + financial reconciliation



Recovery loop for ambiguous state

A reconciler periodically selects orders in AUTH_UNKNOWN, BOOKED_CAPTURE_PENDING, PAID_BUT_UNCONFIRMED, REFUND_PENDING and unacknowledged callback states. It queries the payment provider using the original reference, compares canonical inventory/booking state, then executes an idempotent finish/void/refund action. Escalate aged mismatches; expose user-facing pending status instead of silently failing.

12  Scale hot events with admission control



Figure 8 — A waiting room controls HOW MANY reach inventory, not WHO owns a seat.

Virtual waiting room: safety, fairness, mechanics

1. Before the on-sale, clients enter a per-show waiting room; the edge serves low-cost static waiting assets and checks bot/device/account risk.

2. Assign signed queue/session claims. Define the fairness policy (FIFO, pre-sale tier, randomized prequeue) and communicate it. Protect tokens against replay, tampering, and cross-show use.

3. Admission controller reads DB p95/p99, active lock count, failures, payment throughput, remaining inventory, and circuit-breaker state; gradually grants short-lived tokens.

4. Booking API validates token, subject, show, expiry and purchase limits on every hold attempt. Rate-limit admitted users too; admission alone does not prevent retry storms.

5. As tickets sell out, stop admitting additional users or switch to a sold-out/waitlist screen; preserve accurate order status for users already in checkout.

Why “put Kafka in front of booking” is insufficient

Kafka is useful as a durable event stream but does not automatically deliver interactive queue fairness, wait position, admitted browser sessions or immediate UI feedback. For an HTTP flash-sale, use a purpose-built waiting-room/admission service. Queue/state storage may use Redis, DynamoDB or Kafka internally if its semantics are explicitly designed.

Hot partitions and protective controls

Shard by show_id to keep a multi-seat transaction local. A single celebrity show remains one hotspot even with many global shards.

Prefer adaptive admission and dedicated shard capacity before complex per-section splitting.

Bound transactions, concurrent connections, queued lock wait, deadlock retry attempts and upstream payment requests.

Use graceful 429/503 with Retry-After and order-status recovery; avoid retrying every conflict immediately.

Activate waiting room automatically on burst metrics, not only on anticipated “large” shows.

15  General admission and adjacent seating

General admission is a quantity, not an identity

For an unassigned section of 2,000 places, use an authoritative per-(show_id, section_id, price_tier) inventory aggregate with total, held, sold, and available. Preserve total = held + sold + available. A hold of 4 succeeds only if available >= 4 in the same atomic transaction that moves 4 units from available to held.

UPDATE ga_inventory SET available=available-:qty, held=held+:qty, version=version+1 WHERE show_id=:show AND section_id=:section AND available>=:qty;-- Require affected_rows = 1; insert GA hold atomically.

Adjacent seat group selection

Seat recommendation logic can suggest contiguous seats by scanning the versioned availability snapshot, but final hold remains one atomic multi-seat operation. If one seat conflicts, return an explicit conflict and optionally re-suggest a new nearby block—never silently commit an incomplete order.

Pricing

A dynamic price engine may propose the next price, but a valid order’s final quoted amount, fees, currency and policy are frozen server-side at the agreed checkout point. Store price version and quote expiry. When expired, force a fresh user-accepted quote rather than trusting client totals.

17  Multi-region ownership and failover



Figure 9 — Any region can serve browsing; a given show has one fenced inventory writer.

Design choice

Catalog reads can be active-active across regions, with caches and local search indexes.

For each show_id, one home region/leader has write authority at a time. Requests from elsewhere route to its booking endpoint.

Replicate committed inventory and booking state durably for disaster recovery; understand RPO/RTO trade-offs, do not claim zero-loss async failover.

Promoting a new leader requires fencing the old leader at the storage layer—e.g. epoch/term validated on every write.

If leadership cannot be established under partition, stop booking writes for affected shows. Zero oversell is more valuable than write availability.

Cross-region read-after-hold

After a successful hold, the response includes hold_id, expiry and owning region. Client checkout/status can be routed to the same home region or a strongly consistent read endpoint. A lagging nearby replica must not claim the seat is free for another purchase.

Tests that expose wrong designs

Concurrency: 1,000 clients request the same seat; assert exactly one HELD/BOOKED winner.

Multi-seat overlap: random seat sets arrive out of order; assert all-or-nothing and no deadlocks beyond bounded retries.

Time boundary: freeze DB clock around expires_at; run expiry and confirm concurrently and prove unique result.

Crash matrix: kill process after each commit/HTTP step; ensure retry recovers same state and no double capture.

Webhook chaos: reordered/duplicate webhook events; stable final payment/booking state.

Region split-brain: old writer resumes after promotion; storage fences it.

Search index lag: stale seat count and wrong event availability cannot authorize a hold.

Load: verify waiting room reduces DB concurrent work as arrival rate increases.

	Separate virtual waiting room with signed admission
	No queue for small predictable demand

Strong seat map?
	Eventual snapshot; authoritative hold validation
	Stronger reads only for specific premium UX

Two regions booking same show?
	One home leader with fencing
	Globally coordinated transactional infrastructure

Charge-first or authorization?
	Explicitly pick and defend compensation states
	Depends on provider capabilities and product SLAs



21  Live 45-minute interview script

0–5 minutes: take control of scope

“I will cover discovery, selecting multiple exact seats, a five-minute hold, checkout and electronic ticket confirmation. I will initially defer refunds, resale and recommendations. We need strong seat-ownership consistency, while search may be slightly stale. Is that the right scope?”

5–10 minutes: scale, API and entities

“Average QPS understates a flash sale, so I will design for one popular show receiving more buyers than its inventory. Key rows are show-seat availability, hold, order, payment and booking. API endpoints are search, seat snapshot, hold, start payment and get order status.”

10–17 minutes: draw baseline

“CDN and an optional search index serve catalog; the booking service sends seat ownership operations to a show-scoped SQL shard. Short local transactions create HELD rows; payment goes to an external PSP. Outbox emits ticket and read-model events after booking commits.”

17–28 minutes: deep dive correctness

“For seats A10 and A11, I acquire row locks in a deterministic order, verify both are free or expired, write one hold and the two HELD rows, and commit in milliseconds. If another user holds A11, the transaction rolls back, so no partial holds. Expiration is DB-time guarded, not a five-minute database lock.”

28–35 minutes: money and retries

“I persist order state and an idempotency key before calling the payment provider. Provider timeout becomes UNKNOWN. Under an authorize-confirm-capture policy, I convert the current hold and booking in one local transaction and then capture, using durable retries and compensation if capture is ambiguous. No cross-provider ACID is assumed.”

35–41 minutes: scaling

“I protect popular shows with a per-show virtual waiting room that controls issued admission tokens based on shard health. Seat map updates are cached snapshots plus versioned deltas; neither cache nor Elasticsearch can approve a booking.”

41–45 minutes: edge cases + finish

“On region partition, there is one fenced writer per show. On paid-but-not-confirmed, a reconciler voids/refunds or completes safely. The invariant is zero double-sold seats; the trade-off is sometimes temporary booking unavailability.”

22  Interviewer follow-ups: short, defendable answers

Question
	Answer

Why not keep a DB lock for five minutes?
	Row locks are for the short hold transaction. Five-minute ownership is persisted state + deadline.

Two users click A12 at same time?
	Single authoritative row transition serializes; exactly one hold commits.

A10+A11 request, A11 taken?
	Rollback full transaction; no partial reservation.

Expiry event arrives twice?
	Conditional compare on HELD, hold_id and deadline makes replay harmless.

What if a seat expires before the worker runs?
	DB predicate treats it as expired and allows safe lazy reclamation.

Payment timeout?
	Unknown, never blindly retry charge with new key; query PSP intent.

Money captured but seat gone?
	Do not double book; track and refund/void as policy allows.

Capture fails after booking committed?
	Retain provisional state; retry/reconcile, then compensate or escalate by policy.

Does Kafka guarantee fair queueing?
	No; admission service manages fairness and signed active sessions.

Can Redis alone prevent oversell?
	No, not under generic lease loss/failover; DB must reject invalid final transitions.

Why show_id shard?
	Most requested seat sets belong to one show; local multi-seat transaction.

One event saturates its shard?
	Admission, dedicated capacity, then controlled partition/serialized owner if measured.

How do customers get live updates?
	Snapshot + ordered SSE/WebSocket deltas and refetch on gap.

What if search says seat free?
	Search is advisory; POST /holds reads authoritative inventory.

Multi-region split brain?
	Fenced single writer per show; pause booking if no safe leader.

How to validate a copied QR?
	Atomic online entry status, replay-resistant tokens, offline reconciliation trade-off.



23  One-page revision sheet

The entire architecture in one diagram



Figure 10 — The five business transitions that must be defensible.

Five claims to memorize

Discovery/search may be eventually consistent; ONLY the inventory authority can allocate seats.

Short DB transaction + owner/deadline/version guarantees atomic multi-seat holds and prevents double sales.

Expiry is a predicate on database state/time; background workers improve cleanup, not correctness.

Payment is a durable saga: idempotent intent, unknown handling, revalidation, reconciliation, void/refund when needed.

Flash-sale waiting room protects finite inventory capacity; a fenced home writer preserves correctness during failover.

Must-draw on the whiteboard

API + edge → Search/Event + Seat-map projections → Booking Service → Inventory SQL show shard; external PSP; transactional outbox → async ticket/read-model consumers. Be explicit which arrows are synchronous and which are eventual.

30-second final answer

CLOSING PITCH  I would split Ticket Booking into a scalable, eventually consistent discovery plane and a strongly consistent show-scoped inventory plane. Users receive a short-lived atomic hold for the complete seat set. The checkout is an idempotent payment workflow, with a local booking transaction, outbox publication and reconciliation of unknown charges or expired holds. A virtual waiting room limits contention during hot on-sales. Each show has one fenced inventory writer, so the system never intentionally sacrifices seat ownership correctness for availability.



Quality checklist

□ Scope and assumptions clear   □ Correct per-show seat model   □ All-or-nothing holds   □ Race demonstrated   □ Expiry predicate   □ Payment compensation   □ One DB transaction boundary   □ Outbox   □ Hot-show admission   □ Cache is advisory   □ Region fencing   □ Failure matrix



Important reconciliation of conflicting teaching approaches

Alternative taught in sources
	What these notes deliberately choose
	Why

Redis TTL as the core temporary lock
	DB-authoritative HELD state; Redis optional
	Correctness persists across Redis restart/leader failover

Cassandra + Debezium + Elasticsearch as default
	SQL catalog baseline + supported outbox/CDC to index
	Avoid extra infrastructure without demonstrated scale

Kafka waiting queue as primary admission
	Signed session-based virtual waiting room
	Fair queueing and HTTP/browser admission are separate concerns

Charge-before-booking or authorize-first
	Explicit authorize→local confirm→capture policy
	Trade-off is documented; capture failures are not concealed

Independent booking and inventory DBs
	Single local commit boundary for core rights
	Prevents unjustified claim of distributed ACID



When discussing another valid architecture in an interview, do not call it “wrong” merely because it differs. State its guarantees, failure assumptions, synchronization mechanism and operational costs. The safer choice is the one whose invariants you can prove.

notes.title: Design Amazon Shopping Cart
notes.description: Design Amazon Shopping Cart Advanced System Design Interview Guide Problem 35 | Cart State, Multi-Device Consistency, Pricing, Inventory, Promotions & Checkout
notes.content:
Design Amazon Shopping Cart

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 35 | Cart State, Multi-Device Consistency, Pricing, Inventory, Promotions & Checkout

GoalDesign a highly available shopping cart service used across web and mobile. The cart must support anonymous and logged-in users, multi-device edits, quantity changes, save-for-later, item expiry, price refresh, promotion evaluation, cart merge at login, and a safe handoff into checkout without pretending the cart itself reserves inventory or locks price forever.



Core interview ideaA shopping cart looks simple until concurrent devices, anonymous sessions, stale prices, limited inventory, promotion rules, and checkout races appear. The cart should remain highly available and user-friendly, while checkout performs authoritative validation of price, inventory and payment.



1. Functional Requirements

Add item/SKU to cart.

Remove item.

Update quantity.

View cart across devices.

Support anonymous carts.

Merge anonymous cart after login.

Save item for later.

Apply coupon/promotion code.

Show current estimated price/tax/shipping.

Persist cart for days or weeks.

Start checkout from a consistent cart snapshot.

2. Non-Functional Requirements

Very high availability and low latency.

Cart writes should feel instant.

Multi-device edits should converge predictably.

No silent item loss on retries.

Cart can tolerate eventual consistency for some derived fields.

Checkout must revalidate price and inventory authoritatively.

Scale to hundreds of millions of users/carts.

Isolate cart service from catalog/inventory outages where possible.

3. Scope

Cart is not the order system.

Cart does not permanently reserve inventory.

Cart price is an estimate unless explicitly quoted.

Checkout creates a point-in-time snapshot and invokes downstream order/payment workflows.

Recommendations are out of core scope.

Seller marketplace complexity is represented through SKU/offer IDs.

4. Cart API

API
	Purpose

GET /cart
	Fetch active cart

POST /cart/items
	Add SKU/offer

PATCH /cart/items/{lineId}
	Change quantity/options

DELETE /cart/items/{lineId}
	Remove line

POST /cart/coupons
	Attach coupon

POST /cart/merge
	Merge guest into user cart

POST /cart/save-for-later
	Move line

POST /cart/checkout-snapshot
	Create checkout handoff



5. Data Model

Entity
	Important fields

Cart
	cart_id, owner/session_id, version, currency, updated_at, expires_at

CartLine
	line_id, sku/offer_id, quantity, selected options, added_at, line_version

CouponRef
	code, attached_at, validation_state

PriceView
	observed unit price, source version, refreshed_at

SavedItem
	sku/offer_id, metadata

CheckoutSnapshot
	snapshot_id, cart_version, immutable lines, expiry



6. Anonymous vs Logged-In Cart

Anonymous cart keyed by browser/app session token or anonymous cart ID.

Logged-in cart keyed by stable user/account ID.

Anonymous cart is persisted server-side if recovery across refresh/device transfer is desired.

Client may cache a local copy, but server cart is authoritative for cross-device behavior.

Login triggers an explicit merge policy rather than blindly replacing either cart.

7. High-Level Architecture



8. Why a KV / Document Store Fits

Primary access pattern is fetch/update one cart by cart_id or user_id.

Cart contents are naturally a bounded document/map of line items.

Horizontal partitioning by cart_id is straightforward.

Strong transactions across unrelated carts are unnecessary.

Conditional update/version compare is useful for concurrent writes.

Secondary analytics queries should consume events rather than scan cart storage.

9. Partitioning

Hash cart_id/user_id to a cart shard.

All lines for one cart live together to keep reads and updates local.

Cart documents have maximum line/item count to bound document size.

Very large B2B carts may require a different segmented model.

Replicate each partition for availability.

Do not partition individual normal cart lines across many shards unless scale forces it.

10. Add Item Flow

Authenticate user or validate guest cart token.

Resolve sku/offer identity; reject structurally invalid item.

Read current cart/version.

Apply add semantics: create line or increment existing compatible line.

Enforce per-line and total-line limits.

Persist with atomic version update.

Return cart quickly, using cached/last-known price metadata if necessary.

Refresh derived pricing/availability asynchronously or in parallel.

11. Line Identity

Two entries for the same SKU may still be different lines if seller, size, color, subscription option, gift configuration or fulfillment option differs.

Define a normalized line key from offer/SKU + option tuple.

Repeated Add may increment quantity of same normalized line.

Stable line_id helps clients issue idempotent updates.

Do not use mutable display name as identity.

12. Cart Versioning

Cart has monotonically increasing version.

Every mutation returns the new version.

Client may send expected_version for optimistic concurrency.

Server can reject stale replacement-style updates with conflict response.

Intent-style commands such as ADD quantity +1 can often be safely reapplied/merged.

Version enables checkout snapshot and event ordering.

13. Multi-Device Concurrency



14. Intent-Based vs Replacement Updates

Mutation
	Safer semantics

Add 1 item
	Delta/intention: +1

Remove line
	Delete by stable line_id

Set quantity to 3
	CAS/versioned replacement

Apply coupon
	Attach code idempotently

Move save-for-later
	Atomic line move

Replace whole cart
	Avoid except admin/import



Intent-based operations compose better under concurrency.

A stale 'set entire cart' from one device can erase newer edits from another.

Use idempotency IDs for retried commands when applying deltas.

15. Idempotency

Network retry after timeout must not double-increment quantity.

Mutation request can include operation_id/idempotency_key.

Store recent operation IDs per cart or in side dedupe store.

Return previous result for exact retry.

Idempotency TTL only needs to cover realistic client retry duration.

Checkout snapshot creation also needs idempotency.

16. Cart Merge at Login

Conflict
	Possible policy

Same line in both
	Sum quantities, capped by max

Different options
	Keep separate lines

Coupon guest vs user
	Re-evaluate promotion compatibility

Saved item duplicates
	Deduplicate

Unavailable SKU
	Keep but mark unavailable

Max cart size exceeded
	Prioritize recent/explicit or ask user



ImportantMerge should preserve user intent rather than choose 'guest wins' or 'account wins' wholesale. Merge line-by-line, then revalidate derived price, promotion and availability.



17. Merge Flow

Authenticate user and load account cart.

Load guest cart using signed guest token.

Lock/serialize merge for this user or use compare-and-swap retry loop.

Normalize line identities.

Apply merge policy line by line.

Attach/re-evaluate coupons.

Persist merged user cart as a new version.

Mark guest cart merged/tombstoned so retry is idempotent.

Return merged cart and asynchronously refresh price/inventory.

18. Price Semantics

Cart may display a recently observed price, but checkout must revalidate authoritative current price.

Store observed price + price version + observed_at for UX and change detection.

Do not silently charge a different price without policy/user confirmation.

Show 'price changed' on cart refresh if current catalog/pricing differs.

Dynamic shipping/tax depends on address and fulfillment context and may remain estimated until checkout.

19. Why Cart Should Not Lock Price Forever

Users can keep carts for weeks.

Catalog prices, promotions, seller offers and taxes change.

Locking price would create financial and inventory complexity.

Price guarantees, if offered, should be explicit short-lived quote objects.

Checkout creates/fetches a fresh authoritative quote.

20. Price Refresh Architecture

Cart service stores only lightweight observed price metadata.

Pricing service owns authoritative price calculation.

On GET cart, price service can batch price multiple lines.

Use cache keyed by offer/pricing context/version.

If pricing is temporarily down, return cart lines with last-known price and clear freshness status rather than making cart inaccessible.

Checkout must not proceed on stale price without validation.

21. Inventory Semantics

Core ruleAdding an item to cart does NOT normally reserve inventory. The cart can show an availability hint, but authoritative availability/reservation occurs later, typically during checkout/order creation.



Cart can retain currently unavailable items so the user can revisit.

Inventory service returns available/unavailable/low-stock hints.

Quantity in cart may exceed current stock; checkout adjusts or rejects.

Flash-sale products may use short reservation earlier, but that is a separate inventory-reservation workflow.

22. Inventory Race

User adds last unit to cart.

Another user also adds same SKU.

Both carts remain valid because no reservation occurred.

User A begins checkout; inventory service atomically reserves/decrements stock.

User B checkout then sees out-of-stock or reduced quantity.

Cart is updated with user-visible resolution.

23. Promotion / Coupon Evaluation

Promotions can depend on cart subtotal, SKU categories, seller, user eligibility, time, coupon, quantity and payment method.

Keep promotion rule authoring in a separate control plane.

Compile active rules into efficient evaluator state.

Cart GET may show estimated promotion savings.

Checkout re-evaluates using authoritative cart snapshot and current policy version.

Store applied promotion IDs and explanation for debugging/support.

24. Promotion Conflicts

Rule
	Example policy

Coupon + site discount
	Stack if allowed

Two coupons
	Mutually exclusive or choose best

BOGO + percentage
	Priority/stack matrix

Seller coupon + platform coupon
	Independent budget buckets

Expired coupon
	Remove/reject on refresh



25. Tax and Shipping Estimates

Tax may require delivery address, jurisdiction and product category.

Shipping depends on seller, fulfillment center, destination, speed and cart grouping.

Cart can display an estimate when enough context exists.

Checkout performs authoritative calculation.

Derived totals should include freshness/version metadata.

Do not persist a single 'grand total' as immutable cart truth.

26. Save for Later

Saved items are separate from active purchasable lines.

Moving between active and saved lists should be atomic within one cart document.

Saved items may have longer retention than active cart.

Prices/availability remain dynamic.

Saved list can be capped to prevent abuse/storage growth.

27. Cart TTL and Expiration

Guest carts may expire after days/weeks of inactivity.

Logged-in carts can live much longer.

Use expires_at and background TTL cleanup.

Do not synchronously delete large numbers of expired carts at exact midnight.

Expiry is storage cleanup; business policy may also archive or retain saved items.

Events generated at expiry should not trigger financial side effects.

28. Checkout Snapshot



29. Snapshot Semantics

Checkout requests a snapshot tied to cart version.

Snapshot contains exact lines/options/quantities and validated pricing context.

Inventory may be reserved during or immediately after snapshot depending checkout design.

Snapshot is immutable and short-lived.

Further cart edits create newer cart versions but do not mutate an in-progress checkout snapshot.

Retry with same checkout idempotency key returns same snapshot.

30. Why Snapshot Matters

Without it, user changing cart on another device while payment is running creates ambiguity.

Order needs a stable list of items and prices.

Payment amount must map to one immutable checkout view.

Inventory reservations need stable requested quantities.

Snapshot provides clean boundary between highly available cart and stricter checkout transaction workflow.

31. Cache Strategy

Data
	Caching

Cart document
	Short-lived cache / write-through or cache-aside

Catalog metadata
	Versioned cache

Price estimate
	Very short TTL / versioned

Inventory hint
	Very short TTL

Promotion rules
	Compiled in-memory snapshot

User cart ID mapping
	Longer-lived cache



Cart cache is not the sole source of truth unless backed by durable replicated KV semantics.

Cache invalidation is easier when each cart has version.

32. Event Stream

Emit CartItemAdded, QuantityChanged, ItemRemoved, CartMerged, CheckoutStarted.

Events support analytics, abandoned-cart messaging and recommendations.

Use transactional outbox or storage-native change stream so cart write and event publication cannot diverge silently.

Consumers are asynchronous and idempotent.

Do not put marketing consumers on the cart mutation critical path.

33. Abandoned Cart Notifications

Consumer tracks cart inactivity.

Wait configured period before reminder.

Recheck current cart/version and user preferences before sending.

Do not notify if cart became empty/checked out.

Rate-limit reminders and honor consent.

Notification failure never affects cart persistence.

34. Consistency Model

Area
	Recommended consistency

Single-cart mutation
	Strong per-key / conditional update

Cross-device read
	Read-your-writes where possible

Price estimate
	Eventual/freshness-tagged

Inventory hint
	Eventual

Promotion display
	Eventual but checkout authoritative

Checkout snapshot
	Strong against exact cart version

Analytics
	Eventual



35. Lost Update Example

Bad approachPhone reads cart quantity 1. Laptop reads quantity 1. Phone sets quantity 2. Laptop later writes stale full-cart document with quantity 1, erasing the phone update.



FixUse versioned conditional writes and intent-based operations. Laptop's stale replacement is rejected or rebased; ADD/REMOVE commands can merge according to defined semantics.



36. Retry Semantics

GET is naturally idempotent.

DELETE line is idempotent by line ID.

SET quantity to N is idempotent if same line/version semantics are clear.

ADD +1 requires operation ID to prevent double increment.

MERGE requires merge transaction/idempotency token.

Checkout snapshot creation requires idempotency.

37. Multi-Region Strategy

Users should normally have a home region for cart writes.

Route reads/writes for a cart to its home region to simplify ordering.

Replicate cart data asynchronously to secondary region for DR.

Global active-active cart writes require conflict resolution per line and are harder.

Mobile roaming can still route to home region; latency is often acceptable for cart operations.

Failover promotes secondary with an explicit RPO/fencing strategy.

38. Active-Active Option

If requirements demand local writes in multiple regions, model cart lines as mergeable records/CRDT-like state rather than one opaque document.

Addition/removal semantics need stable line IDs and tombstones/version vectors.

Quantity 'set' conflicts remain product-semantic choices.

Coupon/promotion state is harder to merge.

Most interviews should prefer single-writer home region unless active-active is explicitly required.

39. Failure Scenarios

Failure
	Expected behavior

Cart node crashes after write
	Replicated store retains committed cart

Response lost
	Retry idempotently

Price service unavailable
	Return cart with stale/unknown price marker

Inventory unavailable
	Return cart; checkout later validates

Promotion service unavailable
	Cart works, discount marked pending/unavailable

Merge retries
	Guest tombstone/idempotency prevents double sum

Cache stale
	Version mismatch refreshes from store

Region outage
	Failover per RPO policy

Checkout races with edit
	Immutable snapshot isolates checkout



40. Backpressure and Degradation

Cart CRUD is higher priority than analytics/recommendation events.

Bound enrichment calls to pricing/inventory with deadlines.

If enrichment misses deadline, return base cart plus freshness flags.

Rate-limit pathological clients repeatedly mutating carts.

Cap number of lines and mutation size.

Queue noncritical events rather than blocking cart writes.

41. Security

Guest cart IDs must be unguessable and signed/authorized.

Logged-in user can access only own cart unless explicit shared-cart feature exists.

Do not store payment credentials in cart.

Sanitize coupon/custom text fields.

Audit support/admin cart modifications.

Encrypt cart data at rest/in transit; treat cart contents as potentially sensitive behavioral data.

42. Observability

Metric
	Why

GET/PUT p95/p99
	UX

Mutation conflict rate
	Concurrency quality

Idempotency hit rate
	Retry behavior

Cart merge failures
	Login UX

Price refresh latency/failure
	Derived-data health

Inventory stale rate
	UX accuracy

Checkout snapshot conflict
	Handoff quality

Cart size distribution
	Capacity/abuse

Expired cart backlog
	Storage hygiene

Region replication lag
	DR health



43. Common Interview Mistakes

Treating cart as a simple browser cookie only.

Reserving inventory when every item is added to cart.

Assuming cart price is permanently locked.

Replacing whole cart on every device write.

No idempotency for ADD quantity.

No guest-to-user merge semantics.

No checkout snapshot boundary.

Calling pricing/inventory synchronously with no fallback on every cart mutation.

Making cart unavailable if promotions fail.

No TTL/cleanup strategy.

No per-cart version or conflict handling.

Mixing payment/order state into cart service.

44. Final Production Architecture

Partition carts by cart_id/user_id into a replicated low-latency KV/document store.

Model cart as versioned lines with stable line IDs and intent-based mutations.

Use operation IDs for retry-safe delta commands.

Anonymous and user carts are separate until an explicit idempotent line-by-line merge.

Catalog, price, inventory and promotions are enrichment services; cart remains usable if some are temporarily unavailable.

Observed price/availability are freshness-tagged hints, not permanent guarantees.

Cart does not normally reserve stock.

Checkout creates an immutable versioned snapshot and then authoritatively revalidates price/inventory.

Cart events flow asynchronously through outbox/change stream for analytics and reminders.

Home-region ownership simplifies multi-device ordering; secondary replication provides DR.

One-sentence architectureStore each cart as a versioned, partition-local document with stable line IDs and idempotent intent-based mutations; merge guest/user carts explicitly, treat price/inventory/promotion data as refreshable hints, and create an immutable checkout snapshot where authoritative price and stock validation begins.



45. Detailed Interviewer Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Does adding to cart reserve inventory?

Detailed answer: Normally no. Cart is user intent, not a stock lock. Reserve/decrement inventory during checkout/order creation unless the product explicitly needs temporary holds.

Follow-up: Why not lock price in cart?

Detailed answer: Carts may live for weeks while prices/promotions/taxes change. Keep observed price for UX and revalidate at checkout.

Follow-up: How do you support multiple devices?

Detailed answer: All devices use the same server-side user cart. Mutations are versioned; intent-based commands merge better than replacing the whole cart.

Follow-up: How do you prevent lost updates?

Detailed answer: Use cart version/compare-and-swap for replacement-style changes, plus stable operation IDs for delta commands.

Follow-up: What happens if two devices both add the same SKU?

Detailed answer: If normalized line identity matches, both idempotent ADD intents can increment quantity; the final quantity reflects both accepted operations, subject to max limits.

Follow-up: What if one device removes while another increments?

Detailed answer: Define ordering/version semantics. Stable line IDs and serialized per-cart mutations make the outcome deterministic; later command sees current state.

Follow-up: How do guest carts merge?

Detailed answer: Line-by-line: combine matching items, preserve distinct options, cap quantities, re-evaluate coupons, keep unavailable lines marked, then tombstone guest cart.

Follow-up: How do you make merge idempotent?

Detailed answer: Use merge transaction ID and mark guest cart as merged into user cart with resulting version; retry returns same result.

Follow-up: What store would you use?

Detailed answer: A replicated KV/document database partitioned by cart ID; access is overwhelmingly one-cart-at-a-time.

Follow-up: Should cart be strongly consistent?

Detailed answer: Per-cart mutation ordering should be strong enough to prevent lost updates. Derived price/inventory/promotion views can be eventual.

Follow-up: How do you handle stale price?

Detailed answer: Return last-known/observed price with freshness marker, then refresh. Checkout must obtain authoritative current price.

Follow-up: How do you handle out-of-stock item?

Detailed answer: Keep it visible but mark unavailable/reduced stock; checkout prevents purchase until valid.

Follow-up: Why checkout snapshot?

Detailed answer: It freezes exact lines/quantities for payment/order workflow while the live cart may continue changing on another device.

Follow-up: What if cart changes after checkout starts?

Detailed answer: The existing checkout snapshot remains immutable; new cart changes affect only future checkout attempts.

Follow-up: How do coupons work?

Detailed answer: Cart can attach/evaluate them for estimate, but checkout revalidates eligibility and stacking under the current rule version.

Follow-up: How would you support a flash sale?

Detailed answer: Use explicit short-lived inventory reservation/queue service at checkout or even before cart if product requires it; don't overload normal cart semantics.

Follow-up: How do you handle cart service dependency outages?

Detailed answer: Cart persistence is primary. Pricing/inventory/promo enrichment has short deadlines and degrades to stale/unknown fields.

Follow-up: How do you scale abandoned-cart reminders?

Detailed answer: Emit cart-change events, track inactivity asynchronously, recheck current state/preferences before notification.

Follow-up: How would you do multi-region?

Detailed answer: Prefer home-region writes plus async DR replication. Active-active requires mergeable line-level state and more complex conflict semantics.

Follow-up: Give the one-minute design.

Detailed answer: Use a server-side cart service backed by a replicated KV/document store partitioned by cart ID. Each cart has a version and stable line IDs; use intent-based operations plus idempotency keys to avoid retries/lost updates across devices. Guest and user carts merge line-by-line at login. Catalog, price, inventory and promotions enrich the cart but are not authoritative guarantees: price and stock are revalidated during checkout. Adding to cart does not reserve inventory. Checkout creates an immutable snapshot tied to cart version so payment/order processing is isolated from later cart edits. Events are published asynchronously for analytics/reminders, and a home-region write model simplifies consistency and DR.

46. Additional Detailed Q&A

1. What is cart version?

Detailed answer: Monotonic revision used for optimistic concurrency and checkout handoff.

2. What is line_id?

Detailed answer: Stable identity for one normalized cart entry.

3. Why operation_id?

Detailed answer: Prevents duplicate effects when mutation response is lost and retried.

4. Can cart be stored client-side?

Detailed answer: As a cache, yes; server-side state is needed for cross-device/account recovery.

5. What is a normalized line key?

Detailed answer: Offer/SKU plus option tuple defining merge compatibility.

6. Should unavailable items be removed automatically?

Detailed answer: Usually no; keep and mark them so user understands what changed.

7. Why batch price lookup?

Detailed answer: Avoid one pricing RPC per line.

8. How long should carts live?

Detailed answer: Product-specific; guest carts shorter, authenticated carts often weeks/months.

9. What is save-for-later?

Detailed answer: Non-purchasing list attached to the cart/account.

10. Why not calculate final tax in cart?

Detailed answer: Address/fulfillment can change; checkout has authoritative context.

11. What is a quote?

Detailed answer: Short-lived authoritative price/tax/shipping result with version/expiry.

12. Can quantity exceed stock?

Detailed answer: The cart may temporarily show it; checkout revalidates and adjusts/rejects.

13. Why outbox/change stream?

Detailed answer: Guarantees cart-change events are not silently lost after durable mutations.

14. What if coupon expires in cart?

Detailed answer: Mark invalid/remove estimate on refresh; checkout rejects if expired.

15. What is read-your-writes?

Detailed answer: A user sees their accepted mutation on subsequent reads.

16. Can we cache carts?

Detailed answer: Yes, but versioned durable store remains source of truth.

17. Why cap cart lines?

Detailed answer: Bound document size, abuse and worst-case enrichment/query costs.

18. Can users share carts?

Detailed answer: Possible extension; needs explicit ACL and collaborative merge semantics.

19. What is active-active challenge?

Detailed answer: Conflicting line quantity/removal/coupon state across regions.

20. Most important invariant?

Detailed answer: Checkout/order must use one immutable, validated interpretation of the user's cart intent.

47. Scenario Deep Dives

Phone adds 2 units while laptop sets quantity to 1 from an old version.

ADD uses an intent/idempotent operation and advances version. Laptop's stale SET with expected older version is rejected or returned as conflict; client refreshes and asks user/reapplies intentionally.

Guest cart has SKU A quantity 2; account cart has SKU A quantity 3.

Merge recognizes same normalized line and sums to 5 subject to per-line cap. The merge transaction is recorded so retry does not produce 7 or 8.

Pricing service is down during cart view.

Return the durable cart with last-known prices/freshness markers and indicate totals may be unavailable/stale. Do not make the cart inaccessible. Checkout waits for authoritative price validation.

Inventory drops from 5 to 1 while user has quantity 4 in cart.

Cart can show low-stock/unavailable update. At checkout inventory authority accepts at most available quantity or rejects according to policy; cart is updated with clear resolution.

User starts checkout from cart v40, then removes an item on another device.

Checkout continues using immutable snapshot of v40. The live cart becomes v41. If checkout succeeds, post-order cart cleanup removes purchased lines carefully using snapshot line IDs/version semantics rather than wiping newer unrelated changes.

48. Advanced Drill: Cart Mutation State Machine

Mutation state
	Meaning

RECEIVED
	Authenticated/validated command

DEDUP_CHECK
	Look for prior operation_id

LOAD_VERSION
	Read current cart/version

APPLY_INTENT
	Apply add/remove/set rule

COMMIT
	Conditional durable write

EVENT_PENDING
	Outbox/change event exists

ACKED
	Return new cart version



49. Advanced Drill: Merge Algorithm

Load guest G and user U.

Build map by normalized line key.

For each G line, if no U equivalent, add it.

If equivalent, combine quantity according to policy and caps.

Preserve distinct options/sellers as separate lines.

Merge saved-for-later with dedupe.

Attach candidate coupons but re-evaluate stacking/eligibility.

Write U' with expected U.version.

Record guest G -> merged(U, version) tombstone.

Retry conflict loop if U changed concurrently before commit.

50. Advanced Drill: Checkout Snapshot Correctness

Snapshot request contains cart_id + expected cart_version + idempotency key.

If version differs, return conflict/current cart so caller can refresh.

Batch authoritative catalog/price/inventory validation.

Create immutable snapshot with validated amounts and expiry.

Optionally reserve inventory under separate reservation IDs.

Persist snapshot before returning.

Later order creation references snapshot_id, not mutable cart contents.

51. Advanced Drill: Post-Purchase Cart Cleanup

Do not simply set cart empty after order because user may have added new items during checkout.

Snapshot records line IDs and quantities purchased.

After successful order, issue idempotent cleanup operation referencing snapshot/order ID.

Remove or decrement only purchased lines if they still correspond to snapshot semantics.

Preserve newer lines/options and concurrent edits.

Mark cleanup event so retry is safe.

52. Advanced Drill: Conflict Matrix

Concurrent operations
	Suggested behavior

ADD + ADD same line
	Both deltas apply once

SET qty + stale SET qty
	Version conflict

REMOVE + ADD same line
	Serialize; later intent defines state

Coupon attach + remove
	Idempotent set semantics

Merge + device mutation
	CAS/retry merge against newest user cart

Checkout snapshot + cart edit
	Snapshot immutable; cart continues



53. Advanced Drill: Capacity Estimate

Assume 300M monthly active shoppers and 100M active carts.

Average 8 lines/cart, ~0.5-1 KB metadata/line -> roughly hundreds of GB to low TB active logical cart data before replication/index overhead.

Peak reads can greatly exceed writes because cart icon/count and checkout pages fetch frequently.

Partitioning by cart ID spreads load naturally; hot-cart risk is small compared with hot catalog items.

Derived pricing/inventory calls can dominate backend QPS, so batch and cache them.

54. Advanced Drill: Cart Count Badge

Header cart-count needs very low latency.

Store item-count summary in cart document/cache.

Update count atomically with line mutation.

Client can optimistically update badge after accepted mutation.

Do not fetch full cart merely to render count.

Count usually means sum quantity or distinct lines; define product semantics.

55. Advanced Drill: Cart Event Ordering

Partition cart events by cart_id to preserve per-cart order.

Event includes cart_version.

Consumers ignore stale/replayed older versions where appropriate.

Analytics may process all events; stateful consumers checkpoint latest version.

Cross-cart global order is unnecessary.

Outbox publisher retries at least once; consumers are idempotent.

56. 45-Minute Interview Flow

Time
	Coverage

0-5 min
	Requirements and cart vs checkout boundary

5-10 min
	API, data model, HLD

10-15 min
	Storage/partitioning/versioning

15-21 min
	Multi-device concurrency + idempotency

21-26 min
	Guest merge

26-31 min
	Price/inventory/promotion semantics

31-35 min
	Checkout snapshot

35-39 min
	TTL/events/cache

39-42 min
	Multi-region/failures

42-45 min
	Scenarios/invariants/summary



57. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

30-second answerI would store each cart as a versioned document in a replicated KV store partitioned by cart ID. Use stable line IDs, intent-based mutations and idempotency keys so retries and multiple devices do not cause lost or duplicate updates. Guest and logged-in carts merge explicitly line-by-line at login. Catalog, price, inventory and promotion services enrich the cart, but price and stock are only hints until checkout; adding to cart normally does not reserve inventory. Checkout creates an immutable snapshot against an exact cart version and then performs authoritative price/inventory validation. Cart events publish asynchronously for analytics and reminders, while home-region writes simplify ordering and DR.



58. Final Interview Checklist

Cart vs order/checkout boundary.

Anonymous and logged-in carts.

Cart/line data model.

KV/document storage and partitioning.

Cart version and optimistic concurrency.

Intent-based mutation semantics.

Idempotency for retries.

Multi-device conflict handling.

Guest-to-user merge.

Observed price vs authoritative quote.

Inventory hint vs reservation.

Promotion/coupon re-evaluation.

Tax/shipping estimates.

Save-for-later and TTL.

Checkout snapshot.

Post-purchase cleanup.

Cache and event stream.

Multi-region strategy.

Failure/degradation behavior.

20 follow-ups, 20 Q&As, scenarios, merge/snapshot/conflict drills and diagrams.

59. Deep Dive: Guest-to-Account Merge Architecture



Merge is a transactional transformation of two user-intent sets, not a database UNION.

Use normalized line identity so the same offer/options can be combined while distinct seller/size/subscription choices remain separate.

The account cart is the durable destination. Guest cart becomes a tombstone pointing to the resulting account-cart version.

Compare-and-swap the account version so a device mutation that races with login is not lost.

Coupon state, price and availability are recomputed after structural merge.

If the account cart changed during merge, retry the merge against the newest version using the same merge transaction ID.

60. Deep Dive: Shared / Family Carts

A shared cart is not just a normal cart with more readers; it introduces collaborative write semantics and ACLs.

Model owner plus member roles such as viewer/editor/checkout-authorized.

Each mutation records actor ID and cart version for audit.

Use the same per-cart serialized/versioned write path so two family members cannot overwrite one another.

Optional activity feed can show who added/removed an item.

Checkout permission should be explicit because shared viewing does not imply authority to spend.

Shared carts can be separate objects instead of overloading a user's personal cart, which keeps merge and ownership semantics cleaner.

61. Deep Dive: Flash-Sale / Limited Inventory Mode

Normal carts do not reserve inventory, but flash-sale products may require a short hold to prevent a terrible checkout experience.

Create a separate reservation service with reservation_id, SKU, quantity, owner, expiry and state.

Reservation is time-bounded, for example 2-10 minutes, and does not turn the cart database into the inventory authority.

Cart line can reference the reservation token and countdown.

Checkout converts reservation to committed inventory consumption idempotently.

If the timer expires, reservation is released and the cart line remains but returns to ordinary unavailable/non-reserved state.

Do not silently extend reservations on every cart read; renewal policy must be deliberate to prevent stock hoarding.

62. Deep Dive: Coupon and Promotion Consistency

Coupon attachment to the cart and promotion calculation are separate concepts. Attaching code SAVE20 does not guarantee the code will still be valid at payment time.

Persist the coupon code and last evaluation result/version for UX.

Promotion engine evaluates eligibility using user, lines, quantities, seller, current time, and rule version.

If two coupons are mutually exclusive, the cart can choose best discount or require explicit user selection according to product policy.

Checkout re-evaluates every promotion from the immutable checkout snapshot.

Promotion budget exhaustion is analogous to inventory: a displayed promotion may become unavailable before checkout unless a short-lived benefit reservation exists.

Explain removed/changed discounts explicitly; silent total changes reduce trust.

63. Deep Dive: Price Quote Service

For higher assurance, introduce a short-lived quote object rather than treating cart totals as authoritative.

Quote fields: quote_id, cart/snapshot version, line prices, taxes, shipping, discounts, currency, expiration, pricing-rule version.

Quote creation batches authoritative reads from pricing/promotion/tax/fulfillment.

Checkout can accept only an unexpired quote whose snapshot matches the order request.

Quote expiration is expected; regenerate instead of extending indefinitely.

A quote simplifies payment amount correctness because the payment request references one immutable amount breakdown.

64. Deep Dive: Persistence Schema Options

Model
	Advantages
	Trade-offs

One document per cart
	Single-key read/write, simple versioning
	Document size limit, whole-document rewrites

Cart header + line rows
	Fine-grained updates, large carts
	Multi-row read/transaction complexity

Event-sourced cart
	Perfect history, flexible projections
	Operational complexity, replay cost

CRDT/mergeable lines
	Active-active regions
	Complex product semantics for set/remove/coupons

For an interview-scale consumer cart, a bounded document or header-plus-lines colocated in one partition are both defensible. Choose based on database limits and expected cart size.

65. Deep Dive: Event Sourcing as an Alternative

Instead of storing only current cart state, append events such as ItemAdded, QuantitySet, ItemRemoved and CouponAttached.

Current cart is a projection of events.

Benefits: auditability, replay and analytics.

Costs: event growth, projection recovery, schema evolution and duplicate-event handling.

Snapshot every N events to bound replay.

For a typical shopping cart interview, event sourcing is optional; a versioned KV document plus outbox is simpler and usually sufficient.

66. Deep Dive: Post-Order Cleanup Race

Order succeeds from snapshot S containing line A quantity 2 and line B quantity 1.

While payment was running, another device adds line C and increments A by one.

A naive 'clear cart' would delete C and the new A increment.

Cleanup uses snapshot/order ID and compares purchased line identities/quantities.

For additive quantity semantics, decrement only the quantity consumed by S when the current line still represents the same offer/options.

Preserve any newer line or excess quantity.

Cleanup itself is idempotent so payment/order retry cannot repeatedly decrement the cart.

67. Deep Dive: Cross-Region Failover

Cart home region writes version 90 and asynchronously replicates to DR region at version 89.

Home region fails before v90 arrives. Product must state whether one recent cart edit can be lost (RPO) or whether writes require synchronous cross-region replication.

Promote secondary under fencing/epoch so the old region cannot later accept independent writes.

Clients reconnect and read the promoted cart version.

When the old region returns, replicate from the new authority; do not merge two opaque full-cart histories blindly.

For stronger RPO, replicate the cart log synchronously or use a consensus-based global store, accepting WAN latency.

68. Deep Dive: Abuse and Resource Limits

Cap number of active lines, saved items, coupon codes and mutation rate.

Reject extremely large quantities beyond commerce policy.

Rate-limit automated cart churn that can pressure pricing/inventory dependencies.

Guest-cart creation needs bot controls to prevent storage exhaustion.

Expire abandoned guest carts aggressively relative to authenticated carts.

Per-tenant or marketplace-seller metadata should not allow unbounded custom payloads inside a cart line.

69. Deep Dive: Availability During Dependency Failure

Dependency
	Cart behavior
	Checkout behavior

Catalog
	Show cached name/image if safe
	Must validate purchasable offer

Pricing
	Show stale/unknown price
	Block until authoritative price

Inventory
	Show stale/unknown availability
	Block/reserve authoritatively

Promotions
	Show previous/pending discount
	Re-evaluate before payment

Tax
	Estimate unavailable
	Calculate before final total

Recommendations
	Ignore failure
	No effect

70. More Detailed Interview Follow-Ups

Follow-up: Would you store cart lines separately or as one document?

Detailed answer: For normal consumer carts, one bounded document gives a simple single-key transaction and read. If database document limits or B2B cart sizes are large, colocated line rows are better.

Follow-up: What if the same guest cart is logged into two different accounts?

Detailed answer: Guest merge must claim/tombstone the guest cart atomically. The first successful account merge owns it; the later attempt sees it already merged and follows explicit product policy instead of duplicating items.

Follow-up: How do you support a cart count without reading the cart?

Detailed answer: Persist a small count summary alongside the cart and update it atomically with mutations; cache the summary for header reads.

Follow-up: Can the cart return stale data?

Detailed answer: Derived data can be stale, but the structural cart should provide read-your-writes/per-cart version semantics. Mark price/inventory freshness explicitly.

Follow-up: How would you handle 10,000-line enterprise carts?

Detailed answer: Move from one document to partition-local line records, paginated reads, batch pricing, and perhaps a separate B2B cart service with different limits.

Follow-up: How do you prevent promotion service from becoming a latency bottleneck?

Detailed answer: Compile rules, batch-evaluate lines, cache rule versions, use deadlines, and let cart degrade without final discount while checkout remains authoritative.

Follow-up: Why not store calculated grand total in the cart?

Detailed answer: It becomes stale when quantity, price, tax, shipping, coupon or address changes. Store component observations/version; calculate derived total from current inputs.

Follow-up: What happens if a guest merge succeeds but the response is lost?

Detailed answer: Retry uses the merge transaction ID and guest tombstone to return the already-produced account cart version instead of merging quantities again.

Follow-up: How do you reconcile active cart after an order?

Detailed answer: Consume the successful checkout snapshot/order ID and perform an idempotent line-level decrement/removal, preserving newer concurrent changes.

Follow-up: When would you choose CRDTs?

Detailed answer: Only when true multi-region active-active cart writes are required and product semantics for add/remove/set/merge are explicitly defined. A home-region writer is simpler for most commerce systems.

71. Interview Whiteboard Plan

Draw client -> cart service -> partitioned KV/document store.

Add catalog, pricing, promotions and inventory as side enrichment services rather than cart ownership.

Write 'cart_version + operation_id' beside the mutation path.

Draw guest cart and user cart flowing into an explicit merge box.

Draw checkout snapshot as the hard boundary into order/payment/inventory reservation.

Show outbox/change stream to analytics/reminders.

Finish with home-region ownership and asynchronous DR replica.

72. Extended Correctness Invariants

Invariant
	Mechanism

Retry does not duplicate an additive mutation
	operation_id dedupe

A stale device cannot overwrite newer cart state
	expected version / intent commands

Guest merge happens once
	merge ID + guest tombstone

Cart price is never mistaken for permanent guarantee
	freshness metadata + checkout validation

Cart item does not imply reserved stock
	separate inventory authority

Checkout is stable despite later cart edits
	immutable snapshot

Successful order cleanup preserves newer cart changes
	snapshot-aware line cleanup

Dependency outage does not erase structural cart
	cart persistence independent from enrichment

notes.title: Design Amazon / Large-Scale E-commerce Platform
notes.description: Design Amazon / Large-Scale E-commerce Platform Advanced System Design Interview Guide Problem 24 | Catalog, Search, Cart, Inventory, Checkout, Orders, Payments
notes.content:
Design Amazon / Large-Scale E-commerce Platform

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 24 | Catalog, Search, Cart, Inventory, Checkout, Orders, Payments & Flash Sales

GoalDesign a global Amazon-style marketplace supporting product discovery, search, product detail pages, carts, inventory, checkout, payments, orders, shipment tracking, reviews, recommendations, sellers, promotions, and extreme events such as flash sales. The central challenge is combining read-heavy discovery with correctness-sensitive inventory, money, and order workflows.



Core interview principleDo not force one consistency model onto the whole system. Catalog/search/recommendations can be eventually consistent. Inventory reservation, payment state, order transitions, and idempotent checkout need much stronger correctness. The architecture should explicitly separate these worlds.



1. Functional Requirements

Area
	Requirements

Discovery
	Browse categories, search, filters, ranking

Product
	Product detail, variants, images, seller offers

Cart
	Add/remove/update quantity, persistent cart

Inventory
	Available stock, reservations, replenishment

Checkout
	Address, shipping, tax, promotions, final quote

Payment
	Authorize/capture/refund with external providers

Order
	Create, track, cancel, return

Marketplace
	Multiple sellers/offers per product

Social
	Ratings and reviews

Personalization
	Recommendations and recently viewed

Operations
	Flash sales, fraud controls, observability



2. Non-Functional Requirements

Product browsing/search should be highly available and low latency.

Checkout must be idempotent: retries cannot create duplicate orders or charges.

Do not oversell scarce inventory beyond defined business tolerance.

Money state must be auditable and reconcilable.

Search/index freshness can lag product source-of-truth by seconds/minutes.

A cart can tolerate eventual synchronization; an order cannot silently disappear.

Services should degrade independently: recommendations/reviews can fail without blocking checkout.

Global reads, regional writes, disaster recovery, and large traffic spikes are required.

3. Scope and Clarifying Questions

Physical goods first; digital goods are an extension.

Marketplace supports multiple sellers and fulfillment options.

Inventory is tracked per SKU and fulfillment location.

Payment provider is external; we design orchestration and state.

Search and recommendations are included architecturally.

Warehouse optimization is out of scope, but fulfillment handoff is covered.

Returns/refunds are included as post-order workflows.

4. Capacity Estimation

Dimension
	Illustrative scale
	Implication

Daily active users
	100M+
	Global read scale

Catalog
	100M+ products, far more SKUs/offers
	Partitioned source + indexes

Search requests
	Hundreds of thousands QPS peak
	Distributed search + cache

PDP reads
	Very high
	CDN/cache/read models

Cart writes
	Tens of thousands QPS
	Partition by user/cart

Orders/day
	Millions
	Durable workflow

Inventory updates
	High and bursty
	Atomic SKU/location operations

Flash-sale SKU
	Extreme single-key contention
	Special admission/reservation path



5. Core APIs

API
	Purpose

GET /search?q=...
	Search products

GET /products/{id}
	Product detail

GET /products/{id}/offers
	Seller offers

GET /carts/{id}
	Read cart

PUT /carts/{id}/items/{sku}
	Idempotent add/update item

POST /checkout/quotes
	Price/shipping/tax quote

POST /orders
	Place order with idempotency key

GET /orders/{id}
	Order status

POST /orders/{id}/cancel
	Cancel

POST /returns
	Start return

POST /reviews
	Create review



6. Core Data Model

Entity
	Important fields

Product
	product_id, title, brand, category, attributes, media

SKU
	sku_id, product_id, variant attributes

Offer
	offer_id, sku_id, seller_id, price, fulfillment, condition

Inventory
	sku_id, location_id, on_hand, reserved, version

Cart
	cart_id/user_id, item snapshots, version, updated_at

Reservation
	reservation_id, sku, qty, location, expires_at, state

Order
	order_id, user_id, totals, state, idempotency_key

OrderItem
	order_id, sku, offer, qty, price snapshot, fulfillment

Payment
	payment_id, order_id, provider_ref, amount, state

Shipment
	shipment_id, order_items, carrier, tracking, state

Review
	review_id, product_id, user_id, rating, text, state



7. High-Level Architecture



Amazon-style high-level architecture

8. Bounded Contexts / Service Boundaries

Service
	Owns
	Should not own

Catalog
	Product/SKU descriptive truth
	Stock or payment

Offer/Pricing
	Seller offer, current price rules
	Order history

Search
	Derived searchable documents
	Authoritative product state

Cart
	User intent before checkout
	Inventory guarantee

Inventory
	Stock and reservations
	Payment

Checkout
	Orchestration/quote
	Long-term order truth

Order
	Order lifecycle
	Card credentials

Payment
	Payment workflow/provider refs
	Catalog

Fulfillment
	Shipment lifecycle
	Checkout pricing

Review
	Ratings/reviews
	Order transaction



9. Catalog Modeling: Product, SKU, Offer

Critical distinctionProduct is the conceptual item, SKU is a purchasable variant, and Offer is a seller's commercial proposal for that SKU. A single phone model can have color/storage SKUs, and each SKU can have several seller offers with different price, condition, shipping promise, and fulfillment method.



Product attributes are category-specific and evolve over time.

SKU identity should be stable even if price changes.

Offer is mutable and can become inactive independently.

PDP read model denormalizes product, selected variants, buy-box-like offer summary, rating summary, and availability hints.

Do not make the search engine the catalog source of truth.

10. Catalog Write and Read Paths

Seller/internal system submits catalog mutation.

Catalog service validates schema/category rules and writes authoritative product/SKU version.

Outbox emits product-changed event.

Consumers update PDP read model, search document, recommendation features, cache invalidations, and analytics.

PDP service serves a denormalized cached representation and calls dynamic offer/inventory services only where freshness matters.

Why CQRS-like read models helpA product page joins many domains. Building that page from normalized source tables on every request creates latency and coupling. Maintain denormalized read models for stable descriptive data, then overlay dynamic price/availability using bounded calls or cached summaries.



11. Search Architecture



Product search and indexing

Inverted index for title, brand, category, attributes, seller text, synonyms.

Faceted index supports category, price range, brand, rating, delivery promise, availability.

Query understanding handles spelling, synonyms, units, category intent.

Candidate retrieval then ranking; exact availability may be checked late for top results.

Search documents are versioned derived state and can be rebuilt from catalog/events.

12. Search Ranking

Text relevance and field boosts.

Category/query intent match.

Price competitiveness and availability.

Delivery promise and fulfillment quality.

Rating/review quality with anti-abuse signals.

Sales/engagement/popularity and freshness.

Personalization and geography.

Business/sponsored constraints applied transparently in product logic.

Ranking features should not require dozens of synchronous calls. Precompute most features into the search document or online feature store; fetch only a small amount of dynamic state for top candidates.

13. Product Detail Page Read Path

Resolve product ID and fetch cached PDP read model.

Fetch/select current offers for requested SKU.

Fetch availability/delivery summary for viewer region.

Fetch rating summary and optionally first review page.

Fetch recommendations asynchronously or with strict timeout.

Return core page even if recommendations/reviews fail.

Data
	Freshness expectation

Title/images/specs
	Seconds/minutes acceptable

Price/offer
	Much fresher

Inventory message
	Fresh hint, not final reservation

Rating summary
	Eventual

Recommendations
	Eventual/optional

Checkout price
	Authoritative recomputation



14. Cart Semantics

Cart represents intent, not guaranteed stock or guaranteed price.

Partition primarily by user_id/cart_id.

Use item-level idempotent upsert rather than append-only duplicates.

Store selected SKU/offer and display snapshot, but revalidate at checkout.

Guest cart can be token/device keyed and merged after login.

Cross-device updates can use optimistic versioning; last-writer/item-wise merge is acceptable depending on UX.

Cart expiry is much longer than inventory reservation expiry.

15. Cart Merge and Conflict Handling

Scenario
	Possible behavior

Same SKU on two devices
	Merge quantities up to limits

Item removed on one device
	Use version/timestamp semantics

Guest logs in
	Merge guest and account cart

Price changed
	Show changed-price message at checkout

Offer disappeared
	Suggest alternate offer

SKU out of stock
	Keep item but mark unavailable

Quantity exceeds stock
	Adjust/ask user during checkout



16. Checkout Is a Workflow, Not One DB Transaction



Checkout / order saga

No distributed ACID transaction across inventory, order database, and external payment provider.

Use saga/orchestrated state machine with durable steps and compensations.

Every external call carries idempotency/reference keys.

Persist workflow state before/after side effects so recovery knows what happened.

Timeout is an unknown outcome, not automatically a failure. Query provider/reservation state before retrying.

17. Checkout Idempotency

InvariantThe same logical checkout retry must return the same order result and must not create a second order or second payment. Require a client-generated or server-issued idempotency key scoped to the shopper/checkout attempt.



Receive POST /orders with idempotency key.

Atomically create/read idempotency record.

If completed, return stored order response.

If in progress, return/recover same workflow rather than start another.

All downstream reservation/payment requests use deterministic operation IDs.

Store final response/status for safe retries.

18. Pricing and Quote Versioning

PDP price is informational; checkout recomputes authoritative price.

Quote contains line prices, promotions, shipping, tax, currency, and expiry/version.

Order stores immutable price snapshots for audit.

Promotion service should return deterministic decisions for a quote context.

If quote changes materially before order confirmation, product may require user acceptance.

Never reconstruct historical order total from today's catalog price.

19. Inventory Model

Field
	Meaning

on_hand
	Physical/accounted units at location

reserved
	Units held for active checkout/orders

available
	Typically on_hand - reserved - safety buffers

version
	Optimistic concurrency/fencing

reservation
	Temporary durable hold with expiry/state

allocation
	Location selected for fulfillment



Core invariantFor a strict-stock SKU/location, committed reservations must never exceed sellable stock. The exact implementation can use conditional atomic updates, row locks, compare-and-swap, or serialized partition processing.



20. Inventory Reservation Algorithm

Checkout asks inventory service to reserve SKU quantities with reservation_id.

Inventory service routes each SKU/location to authoritative partition.

Atomically check available >= requested quantity.

If yes, increment reserved and persist reservation with expiry in same correctness boundary.

Return reservation token/version.

On order success, convert reservation into committed allocation/decrement semantics.

On failure/expiry, release exactly once.

Background sweeper repairs expired holds; event reconciliation detects leaks.

21. Preventing Overselling

Approach
	Pros
	Cons

DB row lock/transaction
	Simple, strong
	Hot row bottleneck

Optimistic CAS/version
	High concurrency when conflicts low
	Retries under contention

Atomic conditional counter
	Efficient
	Needs authoritative single-key operation

Serialized partition/actor
	Natural ordering
	Partition hotspot

Preallocated stock buckets
	Scales flash sales
	More complexity/rebalancing



For normal SKUs, atomic conditional reservation per SKU/location is usually enough. For extreme flash sales, introduce admission control and stock-token/bucket techniques rather than letting millions of requests contend on one row.

22. Multi-Item Reservation

A cart can contain items owned by different inventory partitions. Avoid pretending they can be reserved in one global transaction.

Attempt reservations with one checkout workflow ID.

If all succeed, continue.

If any fails, release successful reservations idempotently.

Order workflow records every reservation outcome.

For partial-order products, split fulfillment/order groups explicitly; otherwise all-or-nothing at checkout.

Subtle failureIf the checkout service times out after asking inventory to reserve, it must query by reservation_id before issuing another reservation. A timeout means the result is unknown.



23. Reservation Expiry

Reservations need TTL so abandoned checkouts do not lock stock forever.

Expiry is persisted, not just an in-memory timer.

A delayed queue/timer wheel can trigger releases, plus a periodic sweeper as safety net.

Commit vs expiry race needs atomic state transition: ACTIVE -> COMMITTED or ACTIVE -> EXPIRED.

Payment latency must fit reservation TTL or reservation can be extended with fencing.

Do not use cache TTL alone as inventory truth.

24. Flash Sale Architecture



Flash-sale admission and inventory control

Cache product page aggressively; do not let refresh traffic hit origin.

Use waiting room/admission tokens before scarce-stock path.

Rate-limit per account/device/IP signals and detect bots.

Queue admitted purchase attempts to smooth burst.

Preallocate a bounded number of stock tokens across allocator partitions when appropriate.

A token is not a completed order; checkout/payment still uses idempotent workflow.

Return sold-out quickly when inventory budget is exhausted.

25. Payment State Machine

State
	Meaning

CREATED
	Payment intent exists

AUTHORIZING
	Provider request in progress

AUTHORIZED
	Funds reserved/approved

CAPTURING
	Capture requested

CAPTURED
	Money captured

FAILED
	Known failure

VOIDED
	Authorization released

REFUNDING
	Refund in progress

REFUNDED
	Refund completed

UNKNOWN
	Outcome must be reconciled



Payment ruleNever infer payment failure merely from an HTTP timeout. The provider may have charged successfully. Use a merchant operation/idempotency key and query/reconcile provider state.



26. Payment Integration

Create internal payment intent linked to order and amount snapshot.

Persist operation ID before provider call.

Call provider with idempotency key.

Persist returned provider reference/state.

Receive webhooks asynchronously; dedupe by provider event ID.

State machine accepts only legal transitions.

Reconciliation job queries provider for stale/UNKNOWN payments.

Capture timing depends on business flow; refunds are separate durable workflows.

27. Order State Machine

State
	Typical transition

PENDING
	Workflow created

RESERVED
	Inventory held

PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED
	Payment approved

CONFIRMED
	Customer order accepted

ALLOCATED
	Fulfillment location assigned

SHIPPED
	Carrier has shipment

DELIVERED
	Delivered

CANCEL_REQUESTED
	Cancellation workflow

CANCELLED
	Cancelled/compensated

RETURNED
	Return completed



Keep order state authoritative and append an audit/event history. Avoid arbitrary service writes to order rows; transitions should be validated by the order domain.

28. Order Creation and Outbox

Order DB transaction writes order/order-items and outbox event together.

Outbox relay publishes OrderConfirmed, OrderCancelled, etc.

Fulfillment, notifications, analytics, loyalty, and recommendation consumers are idempotent.

This avoids the dual-write problem where DB commit succeeds but event publish fails.

Event includes order_id, version, event_id, timestamp, and minimal immutable facts.

29. Fulfillment and Shipment

Order may split into fulfillment groups by seller/location/shipping speed.

Allocation chooses location based on stock, promise, cost, capacity, and constraints.

Fulfillment service sends pick/pack/ship tasks to warehouse/seller systems.

Carrier tracking updates are normalized into shipment state.

Order page aggregates shipment states into customer-friendly status.

Shipment failures do not mutate historical checkout price/payment facts.

30. Cancellation

Validate whether item/order is still cancellable.

Atomically mark cancellation requested with version.

Stop fulfillment if possible.
