notes.description: Design Google Maps / Navigation Platform Advanced System Design Interview Guide Problem 22 | Geospatial Search, Map Tiles, Routing, Traffic, ETA & Location Upda
notes.content:
Design Google Maps / Navigation Platform

Advanced System Design Interview Guide

Problem 22 | Geospatial Search, Map Tiles, Routing, Traffic, ETA & Location Updates

GoalDesign a Google Maps-style global mapping and navigation system. Users can browse maps, search places, request routes, receive turn-by-turn navigation, see live traffic, and share/update locations. The design must handle planetary-scale geospatial data, road graphs, enormous read traffic, frequent traffic updates, and low-latency routing.



1. Problem Statement

Build a global maps platform that serves visual map data and place information, finds nearby places, computes routes over a massive road network, estimates travel time using current and historical traffic, and supports navigation as conditions change.

2. What the Interviewer Is Testing

Geospatial indexing and map tiling.

Road-graph modeling and shortest-path routing.

Why plain Dijkstra is insufficient at continental scale.

Traffic ingestion and map matching.

ETA estimation and route re-ranking.

Static versus dynamic map data.

Caching at client/CDN/server layers.

Location updates, privacy, and high-write telemetry.

Multi-region serving and degraded navigation.

3. Clarifying Questions

Support driving first; walking/cycling/transit can be extensions.

Need map browsing, place search, nearby search, directions, and navigation.

Traffic should influence routes and ETA.

Map data changes much less frequently than traffic.

Need rerouting when user deviates or traffic changes materially.

Assume global coverage and hundreds of millions of users.

Street View and satellite imagery are optional follow-ups.

Strong openingI’ll split the design into map rendering, place/geospatial search, routing, and dynamic traffic/navigation. Static map and road data are heavily preprocessed and versioned. The online routing service searches a partitioned road graph using hierarchical speedups, while a separate streaming traffic pipeline continuously updates edge travel-time weights. Clients cache tiles and navigation state so temporary backend/network failures do not immediately stop guidance.



4. Functional Requirements

Area
	Requirement

Map
	Pan/zoom map, roads, labels, boundaries

Places
	Search address/POI and nearby places

Directions
	Route from A to B with alternatives

Navigation
	Turn-by-turn guidance and rerouting

Traffic
	Live congestion and incidents

ETA
	Current and predicted arrival time

Location
	User GPS updates / optional sharing

Updates
	Road closures, map corrections, new places

Extensions
	Transit, Street View, satellite, offline maps



5. Non-Functional Requirements

Property
	Target
	Design consequence

Map tile latency
	Very low
	CDN + immutable/versioned tiles

Route latency
	Sub-second to low seconds
	Preprocessed graph + hierarchy

Navigation availability
	High
	Client route cache + regional redundancy

Traffic freshness
	Seconds/minutes
	Streaming pipeline

Map freshness
	Hours/days acceptable for many changes
	Batch/incremental publishing

Scale
	Planetary graph + huge read QPS
	Partitioning and precomputation

Privacy
	Location is sensitive
	Minimize, protect, expire telemetry



6. Capacity Estimation

Dimension
	Illustrative assumption
	Implication

MAU
	1B
	Global serving footprint

DAU
	300M
	Heavy mobile traffic

Map interactions/day
	5B
	Tile CDN dominates reads

Route requests/day
	500M
	~6K average QPS, much higher peak

Navigation sessions/day
	100M
	Long-lived state and reroutes

Road graph
	100M+ nodes/edges scale class
	Cannot naïvely scan graph

Location probes
	Millions/sec possible
	Streaming aggregation required

Tile variants
	Many zoom levels/styles
	Object storage + CDN



7. Core APIs

API
	Purpose

GET /tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}?style=v
	Map tile

GET /places/search?q=...&lat=...&lng=...
	Place/address search

GET /places/nearby?lat=...&lng=...&radius=...
	Nearby POIs

POST /routes
	Compute route alternatives

POST /navigation/sessions
	Start navigation

POST /navigation/{id}/location
	Location update

GET /traffic/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}
	Traffic overlay

POST /map-feedback
	Road/place correction



8. Core Data Model

Entity
	Important fields

Place
	place_id, name, categories, lat/lng, address, geometry, metadata

RoadNode
	node_id, lat/lng, junction metadata

RoadEdge
	edge_id, from, to, distance, speed limit, restrictions, geometry

TurnRestriction
	incoming edge, outgoing edge, rule/time window

TrafficEdgeState
	edge_id, observed speed, confidence, timestamp

Incident
	geometry/edge IDs, type, severity, start/end

MapTile
	z/x/y, style/version, vector features

NavigationSession
	route, destination, progress, current matched edge

LocationProbe
	anonymous/session/device context, lat/lng, speed, heading, time



9. High-Level Architecture



Google Maps-style high-level architecture

10. Coordinate Systems and Geospatial Basics

Latitude/longitude identify positions on Earth but are awkward for direct rectangular indexing.

Use a projection such as Web Mercator for map tiles; routing still stores geographic coordinates/geometry.

Distance on Earth is not plain Euclidean over lat/lng for large distances.

Geohash/S2/H3-like hierarchical cells convert locations into spatial keys.

Hierarchical cells are useful for partitioning, nearby candidate discovery, aggregation, and traffic heatmaps.

Interview distinctionMap tiling, geospatial place search, and road routing are related but different problems. A tile grid is not a routing graph, and a geohash alone is not a shortest-path algorithm.



11. Map Tile Pyramid



Map tile pyramid across zoom levels

At zoom z, the world is divided into a 2^z by 2^z tile grid in common schemes.

Client requests only visible tiles plus a small prefetch margin.

Low zoom tiles contain generalized geometry; high zoom contains detailed roads/buildings/labels.

Tile URLs include map data/style version so they can be cached immutably.

Vector tiles are often preferable because client can render styles and labels flexibly.

12. Raster vs Vector Tiles

Aspect
	Raster
	Vector

Payload
	Pre-rendered image
	Encoded geometry/features

Client work
	Low
	Higher rendering work

Styling
	Fixed
	Dynamic

Retina/zoom
	More variants
	Scales well

Bandwidth
	Can be larger
	Often efficient

Caching
	Excellent
	Excellent with versioning



Recommended baselineUse versioned vector tiles for roads, labels, boundaries, and POIs; raster/satellite imagery remains image tiles. Serve both through CDN.



13. Map Data Build Pipeline

Ingest authoritative/public/provider road, boundary, address, and POI datasets.

Validate geometry and resolve conflicting updates.

Normalize entities into canonical map objects.

Build road topology and turn restrictions.

Generalize geometry by zoom level.

Generate vector tile features and search/geocoder documents.

Build routing graph partitions and preprocessing artifacts.

Publish a new immutable map version.

Roll out gradually; clients/CDN naturally migrate to new version.

14. Place Search and Geocoding

Place search maps text such as 'Connaught Place' or a street address to candidate geographic entities.

Text index stores normalized names, aliases, addresses, categories, tokens, language variants.

Geospatial index stores place cells/bounding geometry.

Query combines text relevance with proximity, popularity, category, locale, and open/availability signals.

Forward geocoding: text/address → coordinates/place.

Reverse geocoding: coordinates → nearest address/administrative hierarchy.

Ambiguous names require location context: 'Springfield' may match many cities.

15. Nearby Search

Convert user location to a hierarchical spatial cell.

Retrieve objects from the cell and neighboring cells covering requested radius.

Apply exact distance calculation after coarse cell filtering.

Filter by category/attributes.

Rank by distance plus relevance/popularity/quality.

Increase ring/cell coverage until enough candidates are found.

Dense cities need smaller cells or secondary partitioning to avoid hot buckets.

16. Spatial Index Choices

Index
	Strength
	Use

Geohash
	Simple string prefix hierarchy
	Basic partitioning/nearby

Quadtree
	Adaptive 2D subdivision
	Variable-density spatial data

R-tree
	Bounding boxes/geometries
	Spatial DB queries

S2/H3-like cells
	Hierarchical globe cells
	Global partitioning/aggregation



In an interview, choose one hierarchical cell system and explain candidate filtering plus exact distance. The exact brand of cell system is less important than the access pattern.

17. Road Graph Model



Road network as a weighted directed graph

Nodes represent intersections/shape points; directed edges represent traversable road segments.

Edge attributes include distance, road class, legal direction, toll, speed limit, access mode, turn cost, historical/live travel time.

Turn restrictions may require expanded state or explicit turn edges.

Route cost is often travel time, not physical distance.

Dynamic traffic modifies edge weights but topology changes less frequently.

18. Why Plain Dijkstra Is Not Enough

Dijkstra is correct for nonnegative edge weights, but exploring a huge fraction of a continental road graph for every request is too slow.

A* adds a heuristic such as straight-line lower-bound distance/time and explores fewer nodes.

Bidirectional search grows from source and destination.

Contraction Hierarchies preprocess shortcuts through less-important nodes.

Multi-Level Dijkstra / Customizable Route Planning partitions the graph into cells/levels and precomputes boundary shortcuts.

Landmark/ALT methods use precomputed lower bounds.

Production systems often combine hierarchy, partitioning, and dynamic-weight customization.

Interview answerStart with Dijkstra/A* for correctness, then explicitly explain the scale problem and introduce hierarchical preprocessing. That transition is usually more important than naming the fanciest algorithm.



19. A* Routing

Priority = cost_so_far + heuristic_to_destination.

Heuristic must not overestimate if optimality is required.

Straight-line distance divided by a generous maximum speed gives a lower-bound time heuristic.

A* is very useful locally, but long-distance routes still benefit from hierarchy/precomputed shortcuts.

Dynamic traffic changes edge weights, not the geographic heuristic.

20. Hierarchical Routing



Hierarchical route search

Search detailed local graph near source/destination.

Move quickly through a much smaller high-level graph for long-distance travel.

Precompute shortcuts/boundary distances for static topology.

Customize shortcut weights as traffic changes rather than rebuilding topology.

Partition artifacts by geographic region/cell for cache locality and deployment.

21. Route Request Flow

Geocode source/destination if needed.

Snap coordinates to candidate road edges/nodes.

Determine travel mode and constraints: avoid tolls/highways, vehicle restrictions, departure time.

Load relevant graph partitions/hierarchy.

Apply live/predicted edge travel-time weights.

Run hierarchical shortest-path search and obtain best route.

Generate 1–2 diverse alternatives if requested.

Expand shortcuts into actual road-edge sequence.

Generate maneuver instructions/polyline.

Return route, ETA, distance, traffic summary, and route version.

22. Route Alternatives

Naïvely asking for second shortest path may return nearly identical routes.

Penalize edges from best route or use K-shortest-path/diversity algorithms.

Require meaningful geometric/road overlap difference.

Rank alternatives by ETA, reliability, tolls, distance, user preferences.

Limit alternatives to a few; each extra route costs compute.

23. Traffic Data Sources

Source
	Signal

Anonymous GPS probes
	Observed speed and travel time

Navigation sessions
	High-quality route-aligned probes

Road sensors/providers
	Speed/flow/incident data

User reports
	Crashes, closures, hazards

Historical patterns
	Expected speed by time/day/season

Events/weather
	External features for prediction



24. Traffic Ingestion Pipeline



Live traffic streaming pipeline

25. Map Matching

Raw GPS points are noisy. Map matching infers which road edge the user actually traveled on.

Generate nearby candidate road segments for each GPS point.

Score candidates by distance, heading, speed, and road plausibility.

Use sequence continuity: adjacent observations should form a feasible path.

Hidden Markov Model/Viterbi-style matching is a common conceptual approach.

Low-confidence probes should not strongly affect traffic.

Map matching is essential before aggregating speed by road edge.

26. Traffic Aggregation

Group matched probes by road edge and short time window.

Estimate robust speed/travel time using weighted median/trimmed statistics rather than trusting every sample.

Track sample count and confidence.

Blend live observations with historical baseline when samples are sparse.

Decay stale live observations toward historical expectation.

Detect abrupt drops and spatially correlated slowdowns as incident signals.

Publish compact edge-weight updates to routing regions.

27. Historical and Predictive Traffic

Store typical edge travel time by day-of-week/time bucket/season.

For a route departing now, later edges are reached in the future; use predicted speed at expected arrival time, not only current speed.

Models can incorporate historical pattern, recent trend, events, weather, holidays, and neighboring edges.

Prediction uncertainty can affect route reliability ranking.

Fallback to historical speed when live data is missing.

28. ETA Calculation

ETA is the sum of expected travel times over route edges plus turn/intersection effects, but edge travel time depends on when the vehicle reaches each edge.

Start at departure timestamp.

For each route segment, query predicted travel time for its expected traversal time.

Accumulate segment time; this advances expected time for later segments.

Add turn/intersection penalties where modeled.

Apply learned calibration for systematic biases.

Return ETA plus optional confidence/range.

Important distinctionShortest distance, fastest route, and best ETA are different concepts. Routing optimizes a cost function; ETA estimates how long the chosen path will actually take.



29. Navigation Session Architecture

Client receives full route polyline, maneuvers, and enough local metadata to continue guidance briefly offline.

GPS updates are processed locally for immediate progress and optionally sent to backend.

Backend can map-match session progress and monitor material route/traffic changes.

Do not recompute the full route on every GPS sample.

Trigger reroute on off-route detection, closure, or meaningful ETA improvement.

Session state can be ephemeral; destination/history may be stored separately according to privacy/product settings.

30. Off-Route Detection and Rerouting

Client checks distance/heading relative to current route corridor.

Allow tolerance for GPS noise and parallel roads.

If off-route confidence persists across several samples, request reroute from current matched road position.

Traffic-triggered reroute should require a meaningful benefit to avoid route flapping.

Preserve destination and user constraints.

Rate-limit rerouting and compare new route against current remaining route.

31. Map and Traffic Caching

Layer
	Cached data
	Reason

Client
	Visible/nearby tiles, route, place details
	Offline tolerance and low latency

CDN
	Versioned map/satellite tiles
	Massive read offload

API cache
	Popular place queries/metadata
	Reduce search load

Routing node cache
	Hot graph partitions/shortcuts
	Fast route compute

Traffic cache
	Latest edge/cell state
	High read rate

Geocoder cache
	Popular address/place resolutions
	Repeated queries



32. Offline Maps

Download a bounded region's vector tiles, place subset, and routing graph package.

Version packages and support delta updates.

On-device routing uses local graph when network unavailable.

Live traffic and fresh closures may be missing; clearly degrade ETA/routing quality.

Storage budget requires region selection and geometry/detail compression.

Protect licensed/private datasets in offline packages.

33. Map Update Pipeline

Map corrections enter validation/reconciliation workflow.

Topology changes require rebuilding affected graph partitions and routing preprocessing.

POI/address changes update geocoder/search index independently when possible.

Tile pipeline regenerates only affected tiles across relevant zoom levels.

Publish new immutable versions and switch metadata pointers.

Urgent closures can be modeled as dynamic restrictions before full base-map rebuild.

34. Road Closures and Incidents

Represent closure as high-priority dynamic edge restriction/weight infinity.

Propagate to routing caches quickly.

Existing navigation sessions evaluate whether current route crosses affected edges.

Incident lifetime has start/end/verification state.

Do not wait for slow base-map publishing to handle urgent closure.

Merge reports from users/providers/sensors with confidence and moderation.

35. Partitioning the Road Graph

Partition geographically into cells/regions with boundary nodes.

Store local edges with partition; maintain cross-boundary connections.

Hierarchical routing precomputes boundary-to-boundary shortcuts.

Dense urban cells may require finer partitioning than rural areas.

Avoid route requests loading the entire planet graph.

Replicate neighboring boundary data to reduce cross-service chatter.

36. Cross-Region / Long-Distance Routes

Resolve source and destination local partitions.

Search source local graph to hierarchy/boundary.

Traverse high-level inter-region graph/highways.

Descend into destination partition.

Expand shortcut path into concrete road edges.

Apply dynamic traffic weights/customization throughout.

Fetch detailed geometry/instructions only for final chosen path.

37. Hotspots and Load Skew

City centers create heavy tile, place-search, and routing demand.

Popular POIs create hot metadata keys.

CDN absorbs static tile hotspots.

Replicate hot geospatial/search partitions and use read caches.

Routing partitions can be replicated and load-balanced independently.

Traffic ingestion hotspots need partitioning by cell/edge plus salting for very busy roads.

38. Location Privacy and Data Minimization

Raw precise location is highly sensitive; collect only what the feature requires.

Use short retention/aggregation for traffic probes where possible.

Separate identity from traffic telemetry and use coarse/anonymous identifiers where product allows.

Encrypt in transit/at rest and tightly restrict access.

Location sharing must be explicit and revocable.

Derived aggregate traffic should not expose individual trajectories.

Interview noteFor a maps design, privacy is architectural: traffic quality benefits from probes, but the system should not require retaining identifiable raw movement histories indefinitely.



39. Multi-Region Design

Tiles are globally distributed through CDN/object storage.

Place search and geocoding indexes are replicated to serving regions.

Routing graph partitions are replicated near expected traffic; route requests can be served regionally.

Traffic probes enter nearest region and stream into geographically partitioned aggregation.

Live edge-weight updates replicate to relevant routing regions.

Navigation sessions should survive regional control-plane failure by retaining route/client state.

Base map versions are immutable and globally published with controlled rollout.

40. Failure Scenarios

Failure
	Expected behavior

Tile origin unavailable
	CDN serves cached version; fail over origin

Place search shard down
	Replica serves; degrade optional ranking features

Routing partition unavailable
	Retry replica/alternate region

Traffic pipeline delayed
	Route using older live state blended with historical

GPS unavailable/tunnel
	Dead reckoning / route progress estimation temporarily

Client loses network
	Continue cached route; no fresh traffic/reroute

Map update partially built
	Keep previous map version active

Bad traffic spike
	Confidence/outlier filtering prevents immediate poisoning

Incident service down
	Routing continues without freshest incident layer

Navigation backend down
	Client retains current route and maneuvers



41. Consistency Model

Data
	Consistency
	Reason

Base map version
	Immutable/versioned
	Safe caching and rollback

Road topology publish
	Atomic per version/partition
	Avoid partial graph

Traffic weights
	Eventual, very fresh
	Streaming observations

POI/search index
	Eventual
	Derived

Urgent closure
	Fast dynamic propagation
	Safety/routing correctness

Navigation progress
	Best-effort/recent
	Client can guide locally

Location sharing
	Fresh with authorization checks
	User-facing state



42. Observability

Metric
	Why

Tile CDN hit rate/p95
	Map rendering

Route p50/p95/p99
	Core directions latency

Graph partitions touched/route
	Routing efficiency

A* nodes expanded / hierarchy usage
	Algorithm health

Traffic ingestion lag
	Freshness

Map-match confidence
	Probe quality

ETA absolute/percentage error
	Prediction quality

Reroute frequency
	Stability

Off-route false positives
	Navigation UX

Map publish age
	Data freshness

Closure propagation latency
	Safety



43. End-to-End Example: User Requests a Route

User searches 'Jaipur Airport'; place search resolves it to a place and coordinates.

Client sends source GPS, destination, driving mode, and preferences.

Routing service snaps both coordinates to plausible road edges.

Router loads source/destination local partitions and high-level shortcuts.

Traffic service supplies current/predicted edge weights.

Hierarchical search finds a few candidate routes.

Route service expands shortcut path, checks restrictions, and computes ETA.

Alternative route logic keeps only meaningfully different paths.

Instruction generator creates maneuvers and encoded polyline.

Client receives route and caches it.

During navigation, GPS is matched to route; client progresses maneuvers.

If a closure appears ahead or user leaves route, backend computes a new route from current matched edge.

44. End-to-End Example: Traffic Update

Thousands of devices send privacy-controlled location probes.

Stream pipeline validates timestamps/speeds and maps probes to road edges.

Windowed aggregator estimates speed/confidence per edge.

Live state compares observed speed with historical expectation.

Significant slowdown updates edge travel-time weight and may create incident candidate.

Routing caches/customized hierarchy receive new weights.

New route requests immediately account for congestion.

Existing navigation sessions are reevaluated only when change could materially improve route/ETA.

45. Final Production Architecture

Versioned vector/raster map tiles are generated offline and distributed via CDN.

Places and addresses are indexed by text plus hierarchical geospatial cells.

Road network is a directed weighted graph partitioned geographically and preprocessed into hierarchical shortcuts.

Routing starts with A*/shortest-path concepts but uses hierarchy/multi-level preprocessing for continental scale.

Traffic probes flow through map matching, validation, windowed edge aggregation, and predictive models.

Live/predicted traffic customizes road-edge/shortcut weights without rebuilding topology.

Navigation clients cache route/maneuvers and request reroutes only on meaningful deviation or conditions.

Urgent closures use a fast dynamic restriction layer; base map changes publish through immutable versions.

Multi-region replicas serve search/routing while CDN serves static map bytes.

Privacy controls minimize retention/exposure of raw precise location.

Final architecture in one sentencePrecompute and version the mostly static world—tiles, place indexes, road topology, and routing hierarchy—then continuously overlay dynamic traffic weights from privacy-controlled map-matched probes, allowing regional routing services to compute fast hierarchical shortest paths and clients to navigate reliably with cached route state.



46. Key Trade-offs

Decision
	Option A
	Option B
	Reasoned choice

Tiles
	Raster
	Vector
	Vector for dynamic styling; raster for imagery

Nearby index
	Flat lat/lng scan
	Hierarchical cells
	Cells + exact distance

Routing
	Plain Dijkstra
	Hierarchical/A*
	Hierarchy at global scale

Traffic
	Only live
	Live + historical
	Blend for coverage/prediction

Map updates
	Mutable in-place
	Versioned publish
	Versioned

Navigation
	Server every GPS point
	Client + server hybrid
	Hybrid

Closures
	Wait for map rebuild
	Dynamic overlay
	Dynamic fast path



47. Common Interview Mistakes

Saying 'use Dijkstra' and stopping there.

Using geohash as if it solves road routing.

Ignoring map tiles and CDN.

Recomputing routes on every GPS update.

Treating raw GPS as exact road position without map matching.

Using only current traffic for ETA of a long route.

Rebuilding the whole road graph for every traffic update.

Ignoring turn restrictions and one-way roads.

No urgent closure layer.

No client-side cached route/offline degradation.

Ignoring location privacy.

Not separating static map publishing from dynamic traffic.

48. 45-Minute Interview Flow

Time
	Coverage

0–5 min
	Requirements, modes, scale, freshness

5–10 min
	HLD and static/dynamic separation

10–15 min
	Tiles + geospatial place search

15–24 min
	Road graph + A* + hierarchical routing

24–31 min
	Traffic probes, map matching, aggregation

31–35 min
	ETA + navigation + rerouting

35–39 min
	Caching + partitioning + map updates

39–42 min
	Failures + multi-region + privacy

42–45 min
	Trade-offs and summary



Memorize this storyMap data → versioned vector tiles/search index/road graph → CDN and regional services. Route request → snap to roads → hierarchical search with traffic-weighted edges → ETA/instructions. GPS probes → map matching → edge speed aggregation → live/predictive traffic weights → reroute only when useful.



49. Interviewer Follow-Ups — Detailed Answers

Follow-up: Why can’t we just use Dijkstra for every route?

Detailed answer: Dijkstra gives the correct shortest path for nonnegative weights, but its search region can become enormous on a continental graph. A global road network contains tens or hundreds of millions of graph elements, and a route API must answer many requests concurrently. I would explain Dijkstra as the correctness baseline, then reduce search using A* and a hierarchical technique such as contraction hierarchies or multi-level partitioning. The route searches detailed streets only near the endpoints and uses precomputed high-level shortcuts for the long middle portion. This changes the online problem from exploring a large geographic area to exploring a much smaller relevant hierarchy.

Follow-up: How would you incorporate live traffic without rebuilding contraction hierarchies constantly?

Detailed answer: Separate topology preprocessing from dynamic weight customization. The road connectivity and shortcut structure change relatively slowly, while travel times change continuously. Precompute the hierarchy/shortcuts using topology and static attributes, then maintain shortcut weights derived from current edge weights. With customizable multi-level routing, traffic updates can recompute affected cell/boundary weights incrementally. If a particular hierarchy is difficult to update exactly, keep dynamic corrections at lower levels or use a hybrid A* around affected areas. The key is not rebuilding the entire graph for every speed sample.

Follow-up: How do you find nearby restaurants efficiently?

Detailed answer: Map the query location to a hierarchical spatial cell. Retrieve restaurant candidates from that cell and neighboring cells that cover the requested radius. The cell lookup is only a coarse filter: compute exact geographic distance for candidates afterward. Then apply category/open-now filters and rank by distance, text relevance, popularity, and quality. In dense areas, cells may be too large, so use finer cells or secondary partitioning. Continue expanding neighboring rings until enough candidates are collected or the radius is exhausted.

Follow-up: What is map matching and why is it necessary?

Detailed answer: Phone GPS is noisy and can place a car tens of meters away from its actual road, especially in cities, tunnels, or among tall buildings. Map matching converts a sequence of noisy coordinates into the most plausible road-edge sequence. For each point, generate nearby road candidates and score distance, heading, speed, and road type. Then use temporal continuity—often explained with an HMM/Viterbi-style model—to prefer a feasible sequence. Traffic aggregation and navigation progress should use matched edges rather than raw latitude/longitude.

Follow-up: How would you compute ETA for a one-hour trip?

Detailed answer: Do not sum every edge using the traffic speed observed at departure time. The user reaches later edges in the future. Starting from the departure timestamp, estimate the first edge travel time, advance the expected clock, then query the predicted travel time for the next edge at that future time. Continue along the route. Prediction can blend live speed, historical time-of-day/day-of-week patterns, recent trend, events, and weather. A final calibration model can correct systematic bias. This produces a time-dependent ETA.

Follow-up: How do you avoid rerouting the user constantly?

Detailed answer: Use hysteresis. A new route should replace the current route only when the user is confidently off-route, the current route becomes invalid, or the alternative provides a meaningful improvement beyond a threshold. Compare remaining ETA, reliability, tolls, and overlap. Require traffic changes to persist long enough to avoid reacting to noisy samples. Rate-limit reroutes and keep the current route if the difference is marginal. Otherwise navigation becomes unstable and frustrating.

Follow-up: How do map tiles scale?

Detailed answer: Pre-generate or incrementally generate versioned tiles for zoom levels. Store them in object storage and serve through a global CDN. The client requests only visible tiles plus a small prefetch ring and caches them locally. Because a tile URL contains the map/style version, published tiles are effectively immutable and can have long CDN TTLs. Vector tiles keep geometry compact and let the client style/render roads and labels; satellite imagery uses raster tiles.

Follow-up: How do you update one changed road without regenerating the world?

Detailed answer: Determine the affected geographic geometry. Rebuild only map tiles intersecting that geometry at relevant zoom levels, update the road-graph partition containing the edge and any impacted hierarchy boundary artifacts, and update search/geocoder data if addressability changed. Publish these artifacts under a new version. For an urgent closure, use the dynamic restriction layer immediately; the slower base-map rebuild can follow.

Follow-up: How do you model one-way streets and turn restrictions?

Detailed answer: Road edges are directed, so a one-way road simply has the permitted directed edge and not the prohibited reverse traversal. Turn restrictions are not captured by edge weights alone because legality can depend on the incoming edge. Model turn transitions explicitly or expand routing state to include the previous edge. Time-dependent restrictions—such as no turn during certain hours—are evaluated using traversal time.

Follow-up: How would you support transit?

Detailed answer: Transit is a different graph/time model. Stops and walking connections form nodes/edges, while trips follow schedules and service calendars. Use time-dependent routing algorithms and include transfers, walking, wait time, and real-time delay feeds. A multimodal route can connect walking → transit → walking. I would keep transit as a separate routing subsystem sharing place search, map rendering, and some navigation infrastructure.

Follow-up: How do you partition a global road graph?

Detailed answer: Use geographic cells/regions. Each partition owns internal road nodes/edges and identifies boundary nodes that connect to neighboring partitions. Hierarchical preprocessing computes intra-cell boundary shortcuts so long routes do not load every internal street. Dense cities can use smaller cells while rural areas use larger cells. Replicate boundary/neighbor metadata so route computation does not make excessive cross-service calls.

Follow-up: What if the traffic service is unavailable?

Detailed answer: Routing should not fail. Use the last known traffic snapshot if still reasonably fresh, then blend toward historical traffic profiles as data ages. If no dynamic data is available, route using historical/free-flow estimates. Mark internal confidence lower. Navigation remains functional, though ETA and congestion avoidance degrade. This is a good example of keeping dynamic traffic as an enhancement to a durable base road graph.

Follow-up: How do you detect traffic incidents from probes?

Detailed answer: Aggregate map-matched speeds by edge and short windows. Compare observed speed and volume against historical expectation and neighboring edges. A sharp persistent slowdown across connected edges can become an incident candidate. Combine this with explicit reports and provider feeds. Require confidence thresholds to prevent one faulty device from creating a false closure. Incident state should have lifecycle, severity, verification, and expiry.

Follow-up: How do you handle a GPS tunnel where location disappears?

Detailed answer: The client already has the route. It can estimate progress using last matched edge, speed/inertial signals if available, elapsed time, and route geometry. It should avoid aggressive rerouting while GPS confidence is low. When GPS returns, map-match the new point and reconcile progress. This is another reason navigation cannot depend on a server response for every location sample.

Follow-up: How would offline navigation work?

Detailed answer: Download a region package containing vector tiles, place/address subset, and compressed routing graph plus preprocessing artifacts. The device computes routes locally and caches maneuvers. Without network, live traffic, recent closures, and fresh POI data may be unavailable, so routing uses packaged/static or historical assumptions. When connectivity returns, apply delta updates and refresh dynamic restrictions.

Follow-up: What is the difference between geocoding and place search?

Detailed answer: Geocoding focuses on mapping an address or textual location representation to coordinates and vice versa. Place search is broader: businesses, landmarks, categories, aliases, popularity, and query intent. They can share indexes and entity IDs, but ranking and data sources differ. Nearby search additionally adds spatial radius/cell filtering.

Follow-up: How do you serve map data globally?

Detailed answer: Publish immutable map versions to object storage and CDN for tiles. Replicate place/geocoder indexes and road-graph partitions to regional serving clusters. Route users to nearby healthy regions. Dynamic traffic is streamed to the regions that need those edge weights. Because base artifacts are versioned, regions can roll forward independently and roll back safely.

Follow-up: How do you protect user location privacy while using it for traffic?

Detailed answer: Minimize collection and retention. For traffic, separate probe processing from account identity where possible, use short-lived identifiers, aggregate quickly to road-edge/window statistics, and discard raw precise points according to policy. Encrypt data, restrict access, and prevent aggregate outputs from exposing individual trajectories. Location sharing is a separate explicit user-facing authorization model.

Follow-up: How would you generate alternative routes?

Detailed answer: First compute the best path. To generate alternatives, use K-shortest/diverse-path techniques or temporarily penalize parts of the first route, then search again. Reject candidates that overlap too heavily or provide no meaningful choice. Rank the remaining few by ETA, reliability, tolls, distance, and user preferences. Do not return ten near-identical paths.

Follow-up: What is your failure strategy for navigation?

Detailed answer: The client stores the current route, maneuvers, geometry, and destination. If backend or network fails, it can continue guiding along that route. Tile cache keeps nearby map visible. If the user deviates while offline, local routing can help if an offline graph exists; otherwise guidance can resume after connectivity returns. Backend services are multi-region, and traffic/recommendation-like enhancements degrade before core route availability.

50. Additional Detailed Interview Q&A

1. Why separate static road topology from dynamic traffic weights?

Detailed answer: Their update frequencies are radically different. Road connectivity changes comparatively slowly, while speeds can change every minute. Keeping topology versioned and stable lets us heavily preprocess routing structure and cache graph partitions. Traffic becomes a small dynamic overlay of edge costs and restrictions. This reduces rebuild cost and lets the routing service continue operating even when the traffic stream is delayed.

2. What is the role of a geospatial cell in routing?

Detailed answer: It is mainly an organizational and lookup primitive: partition the planet, find nearby objects, aggregate traffic, and identify road-graph partitions. It does not itself compute the shortest path. The routing algorithm runs over the road graph; cell boundaries and precomputed shortcuts help it skip large internal regions efficiently.

3. How would you snap a route endpoint to the road graph?

Detailed answer: Search nearby road segments using the spatial index. Score candidates by distance, heading if available, accessibility for the requested mode, and whether the point can legally enter the road. A point near a highway overpass must not automatically snap to the highway if the user is on the street below. Keep several candidates and let routing feasibility help disambiguate.

4. Why are vector tiles useful on mobile?

Detailed answer: They transmit compact geometry and semantic features instead of a fully rendered bitmap. The client can style labels, support dark mode/language changes, render crisply across pixel densities, and rotate/tilt the map. The trade-off is more client CPU/GPU work and rendering complexity. Satellite imagery remains raster because the source is photographic.

5. How do you avoid tile seams and inconsistent labels?

Detailed answer: Tile generation uses shared geometry boundaries and deterministic clipping/simplification. Labels are often placed with awareness beyond a single tile or the client performs cross-tile label collision resolution. Version all neighboring tiles consistently so a client does not combine incompatible map generations for long periods.

6. How would you store road geometry efficiently?

Detailed answer: Routing only needs compact topology and attributes in the hot path. Store node coordinates using delta/compressed representations and edge geometry as encoded polylines or references. Detailed geometry can be separated from the core graph and hydrated only for the final path. This keeps routing partitions memory-efficient.

7. How do time-dependent turn restrictions affect routing?

Detailed answer: The legality/cost of a transition may depend on the arrival time. The routing state therefore evaluates the restriction at the expected traversal timestamp. For example, a turn may be prohibited during rush hour. This makes the graph time-dependent; preprocessing must preserve correctness or route around dynamic restrictions in a lower-level search.

8. What happens if live traffic says a road is extremely fast because of bad data?

Detailed answer: Use validation and confidence. Reject impossible speeds, compare against speed limits and historical distributions, require multiple independent samples where possible, and cap how aggressively a single window can alter weight. Low-sample edges blend strongly with historical baseline. This prevents one faulty probe from producing unrealistic shortcuts.

9. How do you estimate traffic on roads with no probes?

Detailed answer: Use historical profiles, road class/speed limit, neighboring-edge conditions, time-of-day, and model-based inference. The system should attach lower confidence. Routing can still operate with free-flow or historical weights; coverage improves as probes arrive.

10. How would you scale map matching to millions of probes per second?

Detailed answer: Partition the stream by spatial cell or candidate road region. Keep compact road geometry/indexes in memory on workers. Process short sequences per device/session with bounded state, emit matched edge observations, and expire state quickly. Autoscale by stream lag. Hot urban cells can be split/salted while preserving enough sequence affinity for matching.

11. Why not store every user GPS point forever for better models?

Detailed answer: It is expensive and creates unnecessary privacy risk. Traffic primarily needs aggregated edge/time observations, and model training can often use privacy-preserving sampled/aggregated data. Retain raw precise trajectories only when there is a justified product need and policy basis, with strict retention and access controls.

12. How do you choose when to refresh a route due to traffic?

Detailed answer: Estimate the remaining ETA on the current route using the newest traffic and compare it with a newly computed best route. Reroute only if improvement exceeds a threshold or a closure invalidates the path. Threshold can depend on trip length: saving one minute on a one-hour trip may not justify disruption, while a major incident does.

13. How do you keep route instructions stable after small traffic updates?

Detailed answer: Instructions are tied to the chosen road-edge path, not continuously regenerated from every weight change. As long as the path remains valid and no reroute threshold is met, the client keeps the same maneuvers. ETA may update independently. This separates 'time estimate changed' from 'path changed'.

14. How do you calculate distance between two lat/lng points?

Detailed answer: For small local calculations, projected coordinates or a haversine/great-circle approximation are common. For nearby search, use spatial cells for coarse filtering and exact geographic distance for final candidates. Do not compare raw degree differences as if one degree had a constant physical length everywhere.

15. How do you handle countries with different map rules and data quality?

Detailed answer: Keep source provenance, region-specific validation, address formats, languages, road restrictions, and legal requirements in the map-data pipeline. Serving APIs expose a common entity/graph model, but ingestion and ranking can be locale-specific. Versioning lets regions update independently while preserving global interfaces.

16. How would Street View fit?

Detailed answer: Street View is a separate imagery pipeline: capture panoramas, stitch/process them, geolocate along roads, blur sensitive content, store image pyramids, and serve through CDN. Map entities link road/place positions to panorama IDs. It shares geospatial indexing and CDN principles but is not part of the routing hot path.

17. How would satellite imagery fit?

Detailed answer: Ingest large georeferenced raster imagery, build multi-resolution tile pyramids, color-correct/stitch sources, and publish immutable raster tiles to CDN. Updates are batch-oriented and independent of road graph routing. The client overlays vector labels/roads when needed.

18. How do you prevent one dense city from overloading a routing shard?

Detailed answer: Replicate popular graph partitions across many routing workers and route requests using load-aware selection. Keep graph artifacts read-only/versioned so replication is cheap. For dynamic traffic, distribute compact weight updates to every replica. If a cell itself is too large, subdivide it while preserving hierarchy boundaries.

19. How do you roll out a new road graph safely?

Detailed answer: Build a complete new graph version and preprocessing artifacts offline. Validate connectivity, route regression tests, and sample ETAs. Load the version into a canary subset of routing workers, compare metrics, then increase traffic gradually. Keep the previous immutable version available for rollback. Never mutate the only live graph in place.

20. What is the final one-minute design summary?

Detailed answer: Static map data is ingested and published as immutable versions: vector/raster tiles for rendering, text+spatial indexes for places, and a partitioned directed road graph with hierarchical routing shortcuts. Tiles go through CDN. Route requests snap endpoints to roads and run a hierarchical A*/shortest-path search using live and predicted traffic weights. Traffic comes from privacy-controlled GPS/sensor streams, is map-matched to road edges, aggregated with confidence, and blended with historical patterns. Navigation clients cache route and maneuvers, send bounded progress updates, and reroute only for real deviation, closure, or meaningful ETA improvement. Regional replicas, versioned artifacts, dynamic closure overlays, and client-side fallback keep the system available.

51. Scenario-Based Deep-Dive Questions

A major stadium event ends and traffic changes in five minutes. What happens?

Probe volume rises around the stadium. Map-matching workers assign samples to outgoing road edges, and short-window aggregators detect speeds falling below historical expectations. Confidence rises quickly because many independent probes agree. Live weights propagate to routing replicas. New route requests avoid congested exits; existing sessions are reevaluated, but reroute hysteresis prevents unnecessary path changes. The predictive model also considers the event pattern for downstream edges.

A bridge closes suddenly. How do you remove it from routes immediately?

Create a dynamic closure restriction for the affected directed edges and publish it through a high-priority stream/cache invalidation path. Routing treats those edges as unavailable before the slower base-map update completes. Navigation sessions whose remaining path crosses the bridge are marked for reroute. Later, the map pipeline validates the closure and incorporates it into a new map/graph version if long-lived.

The user is on a parallel service road beside a highway. GPS is inaccurate. How do you avoid snapping incorrectly?

Generate both highway and service-road candidates. Distance alone is insufficient. Compare heading, speed, recent matched path, legal connectivity from the previous edge, and the sequence likelihood. The service road may be more consistent with previous points even if the highway is slightly closer geometrically. Maintain confidence and delay a hard switch until evidence is strong.

A region loses connectivity to the traffic stream. Can routing continue?

Yes. The routing graph and latest traffic snapshot are local. As live state ages, blend its influence down and rely more on historical traffic/free-flow. Route quality degrades gradually instead of failing. When the stream reconnects, apply newer edge versions/timestamps and discard stale updates.

A user requests a route from Delhi to Mumbai. Do we load every road in between?

No. The local detailed graph is searched near Delhi and Mumbai. The long middle portion uses a high-level highway/regional graph with precomputed shortcuts/boundary costs. Only partitions needed to expand the final route are hydrated for geometry and instructions. This is exactly why hierarchical routing is required.

52. Review Quiz with Answers

1. Why are map tiles versioned?

Answer: To make published tiles immutable/cacheable and allow atomic rollout/rollback.

2. What is the baseline graph representation?

Answer: Directed road nodes/edges with distance, restrictions, and travel-time cost.

3. Why does plain Dijkstra struggle?

Answer: It explores too much of a massive graph per request.

4. What is map matching?

Answer: Inferring the most likely road-edge sequence from noisy GPS observations.

5. How does live traffic reach routing?

Answer: Probe stream → map matching → window aggregation → edge weights → routing replicas.

6. Why blend historical traffic?

Answer: Live probes are sparse/noisy and future route edges need prediction.

7. How do you avoid reroute flapping?

Answer: Hysteresis, confidence, thresholds, and rate limits.

8. What is the role of hierarchical spatial cells?

Answer: Partitioning, nearby candidate lookup, aggregation, and graph organization.

9. How are urgent closures handled?

Answer: Dynamic restriction overlay before base-map rebuild.

10. Core architecture?

Answer: Versioned static map artifacts + CDN/search/routing hierarchy, overlaid with streaming traffic and client-assisted navigation.

53. 30-Second Final Interview Answer

30-second answerI would separate mostly static map data from highly dynamic traffic. The map pipeline publishes immutable vector/raster tiles, place/geocoder indexes, and a partitioned directed road graph with hierarchical routing shortcuts. Tiles are CDN-served. For directions, the service snaps endpoints to roads and uses hierarchical A*/shortest-path search rather than plain Dijkstra over the entire graph. GPS and sensor probes flow through map matching and windowed aggregation to produce live edge speeds, which are blended with historical/predicted traffic for routing and ETA. Navigation clients cache the route and maneuvers, progress locally, and request rerouting only on real deviation, closure, or meaningful time savings. Dynamic closure overlays, regional replicas, and offline/client fallback keep core navigation available.



54. Final Interview Checklist

Requirements and travel modes scoped.

Map tiles/vector-vs-raster/CDN covered.

Place search, geocoding, nearby search, and spatial index covered.

Road graph model including directed edges and turn restrictions covered.

Dijkstra/A* and need for hierarchical routing explained.

Graph partitioning and long-distance routing covered.

Traffic sources, streaming ingestion, map matching, aggregation, historical prediction covered.

Time-dependent ETA explained.

Navigation, off-route detection, reroute hysteresis, offline behavior covered.

Map updates, closures, immutable versions, and rollback covered.

Caching, hotspots, multi-region, failures, privacy, and observability covered.

20 detailed follow-ups, 20 detailed Q&As, and scenario questions included.
