notes.title: Redis Is NOT Just a Cache
notes.description: Redis Is NOT Just a Cache Redis = high-speed data infrastructure layer Redis can act as: Cache Database Queue Message broker Rate limiter Session store Distribu
notes.content:
Redis Is NOT Just a Cache

Redis = high-speed data infrastructure layer



Redis can act as:

Cache

Database

Queue

Message broker

Rate limiter

Session store

Distributed lock manager







Redis as Cache

Problem: Every request hits DB → slow response, high DB load, poor scalability.

Solution: Put Redis between App and DB.

Cache-Aside Pattern (most important):

App checks Redis.

Hit → return cached data.

Miss → fetch from DB → store in Redis → return.

Why Redis?

In-memory → very fast

TTL support → automatic expiration

Reduces DB load significantly

Example: SET product:101 "{json}" EX 300 → cache for 5 minutes.

Commonly cached: Products, recommendations, search results, home-page data.







Redis as a Database

Redis can also act as a primary database, not just a cache.

Why?

Persistence

Replication

Clustering

Extremely low latency

Good use cases:

Gaming / real-time state

Chat presence

Live dashboards

IoT / analytics

Example: HSET player:101 score 5000 level 12

Why not always Redis?

RAM is expensive

Limited complex querying

Not ideal for relational data

Not ideal for huge persistent datasets









Redis Persistence — RDB

Redis can persist in-memory data to disk so it can be restored after a restart.

RDB (Redis Database Snapshot):

Takes point-in-time snapshots of memory.

Saves them as dump.rdb.

On restart → Redis loads the snapshot back into memory.

Analogy: RDB = taking a photo of Redis memory periodically.

Advantages:

Compact

Fast recovery

Easy backups

Low runtime overhead

Disadvantage:

Possible data loss between snapshots. Example: 5-minute interval → crash after 4 minutes → last 4 minutes may be lost.

Best for: Backups, disaster recovery, caching, and workloads where some data loss is acceptable.



Configuration Example

In redis.conf

save 900 1

save 300 10

save 60 10000









Restart Flow

Redis starts

    ↓

Reads dump.rdb

    ↓

Restores memory





















Redis Persistence — AOF

AOF (Append Only File):

Logs every write operation to disk.

On restart → Redis replays the commands to rebuild the dataset.

File: appendonly.aof

Analogy:

RDB = photo of data

AOF = recording of operations

appendfsync Options

Mode
	Durability
	Performance

always
	Highest
	Slowest

everysec
	High
	Best balance / common choice

no
	Lowest
	Fastest

Advantages:

Better durability than RDB

Less data loss

Suitable for more critical data

Disadvantages:

Larger files

More disk I/O

AOF can be slower than RDB

AOF Rewrite: Compacts the log by replacing many operations with the current state. Example: INCR × 3 → SET counter 3

RDB + AOF

RDB → fast snapshots and recovery AOF → better durability and less data loss

Interview one-liner:

“AOF logs write operations and replays them during recovery. In production, I can combine AOF for durability with RDB for efficient backups and faster recovery.”



Example

Instead of:

INCR counter

INCR counter

INCR counter

Rewrite to:

SET counter 3

Smaller file.







Why Both?

RDB → fast backup/recovery

AOF → durability















Example 2— Queue System

Suppose Redis queue contains pending orders

Redis crashes.

Without persistence:

orders lost

AOF helps recover queue.

Example 3— Gaming Leaderboard

Suppose:

live rankings stored in Redis

Need:

restart recovery

RDB snapshots enough.

Minor loss acceptable.



Usually production systems use: Persistence + Replication

Replication

Redis master replicates data to replicas.

Benefits:

failover

high availability

disaster recovery





Interview Question

Why Is Redis Still Fast Despite Persistence?

Because:

persistence mostly asynchronous

main thread not heavily blocked

Redis uses background child processes



Background Save (BGSAVE)

Redis forks child process:

Parent → handles requests

Child → writes snapshot

Fork Mechanism

Redis uses:

copy-on-write

Efficient memory optimization during snapshot.



Important Persistence Commands



Important Real-World Tradeoff

Persistence improves:

durability

But adds:

disk IO

CPU usage

memory overhead

When NOT to Use Persistence

Pure cache systems sometimes disable persistence.

Example:

CDN cache

temporary recommendation cache

Why?

restart repopulates cache anyway

When Persistence Is Critical

Use persistence for:

queues

sessions

gaming data

financial counters

analytics

event streams

Redis Streams + Persistence

Redis Streams become very powerful because:

messages persist

consumers can replay events

This makes Redis closer to:

Kafka

RabbitMQ

in some architectures.





Redis as a QUEUE

Problem

Suppose:

user uploads image

image processing takes 10 sec

You CANNOT block request thread.

Solution

Use queue.

User uploads image

       ↓

Add job to Redis queue

       ↓

Worker processes later

Redis List-Based Queue

Producer: RPUSH jobs image_101

Consumer: LPOP jobs

Blocking Queue

Even better:

BLPOP jobs 0

Worker waits until job arrives.

HLD Example

Food Delivery

When order placed:

Order Service

   ↓

Redis Queue

   ↓

Delivery Assignment Worker

Benefits:

async processing

reliability

scalability

Queue Benefits

decoupling

async processing

retries

buffering traffic spikes

notes.title: Redis Is NOT Just a Cache · Redis as a MESSAGE BROKER
notes.description: Redis as a MESSAGE BROKER This means: services communicate through Redis. Redis Pub/Sub Publisher: PUBLISH news "new order" Subscriber: SUBSCRIBE news How It Wo
notes.content:
Redis as a MESSAGE BROKER

This means: services communicate through Redis.

Redis Pub/Sub

Publisher: PUBLISH news "new order"

Subscriber: SUBSCRIBE news

How It Works

Service A publishes event

         ↓

Redis channel

         ↓

All subscribers receive event

Example — Chat App

User sends message

     ↓

Chat Service publishes

     ↓

Connected users receive instantly

Real Use Cases

chat systems

notifications

live updates

multiplayer games

Pub/Sub is NOT durable

If subscriber offline:

message lost

Unlike Kafka/RabbitMQ.

Redis Streams (Modern Alternative)

Streams provide:

persistence

replay

consumer groups

Much more reliable.





Redis as a Session Store

Problem: If sessions are stored in app-server memory, a request routed to another server may not find the session.

Solution: Store sessions centrally in Redis.

User → Load Balancer → Any App Server → Redis

Example: SET session:abc123 "{user data}" EX 1800

→ Session automatically expires after 30 minutes.

Why Redis?

Fast

Shared across servers

TTL support

Ideal for temporary session data

Spring Boot: Spring Session + Redis can store application sessions in Redis.





Redis as a Distributed Lock Manager

Problem: Multiple servers may process the same operation → duplicate payment, double order, inventory issues.

Solution: Use Redis to allow only one server into the critical section.

SET lock:order123 uniqueId NX EX 10

NX → acquire only if lock doesn't exist

EX 10 → lock expires after 10 sec

Flow: Service A → acquires lock → processes order Service B → lock exists → cannot process

Why expiry? If Service A crashes, the lock automatically expires and avoids a permanent deadlock.

Advanced: Redlock is a Redis-based distributed locking approach involving multiple Redis nodes.







Redis as a Real-Time Analytics Engine

Redis is useful for fast counters, rankings, and live metrics.

Counters: INCR page:home:views

→ Atomically increments page views.

Trending / Rankings: Use Sorted Sets: ZADD trending 500 post101

→ Score determines the ranking.

Common use cases:

Page views

Active users

Trending posts/hashtags

Live metrics





Redis as a Leaderboard Engine

Use Sorted Sets (ZSET) when you need ranking + ordering.

Example: ZADD leaderboard 2000 kapil

→ Stores Kapil with a score of 2000.

Top 10 players: ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9

Why Redis?

Maintains sorted order

Fast ranking

Efficient top-N queries

Use cases:

Gaming

Coding contests

Fantasy apps

Real-time rankings



Summary:

“I’d use Redis Sorted Sets for leaderboards because they maintain scores in order and provide efficient ranking and top-N queries.”







Redis as a Feature Flag Store

Redis can store feature flags that applications can check at runtime.

Example: SET feature:new-ui true

Application checks the flag before enabling the feature.

Why Redis?

Changes take effect immediately

No redeployment required

Easy to enable/disable features

Use cases:

Gradual rollout (e.g., 5% users)

A/B testing

Instant feature rollback

Summary:

“I’d use Redis for feature flags when I need fast, centralized configuration changes without redeploying services.”







Redis as a Presence System

Redis can track real-time user presence such as online/offline and typing status.

Example: SET user:101:online true EX 60

→ Users are considered online for 60 seconds.

Heartbeat: Client periodically refreshes the TTL. If heartbeats stop, the key expires → user becomes offline.

Why Redis?

Very fast reads/writes

TTL automatically detects inactive users

Shared across multiple servers

Use cases:

Online/offline status

Typing indicators

Active devices

Interview one-liner:

“I’d use Redis with TTL-based heartbeats for presence, where the key expires automatically when a user stops sending heartbeats.”

notes.title: Redis Is NOT Just a Cache · Redis as GEOLOCATION ENGINE
notes.description: Redis as a Geolocation Engine Redis GEO is used for nearby-location searches. Example: Find available drivers within 5 km of a user. Why Redis? Stores latitude/
notes.content:
Redis as a Geolocation Engine

Redis GEO is used for nearby-location searches.

Example: Find available drivers within 5 km of a user.

Why Redis?

Stores latitude/longitude

Fast nearby/radius searches

Supports distance calculations

Useful for frequently changing locations

Internally: Redis GEO uses Sorted Sets + geospatial encoding (geohash) to index locations.

Example use cases:

Uber/Ola → nearby drivers

Food delivery → nearby restaurants

Store locator → nearby stores





Suppose:

thousands of drivers moving continuously

users requesting rides

need: Find nearest drivers within 5 km

Doing this in SQL repeatedly becomes expensive.

Redis GEO solves this efficiently.



Redis GEO Internally

Redis internally uses:

Sorted Set (ZSET)

       +

Geohashing



What is Geohashing?

Redis converts:

(latitude, longitude)

into a compact sortable representation called:

Geohash

Nearby locations produce similar geohashes.

This enables:

fast indexing

fast radius searches

















Redis GEO — Uber/Ola Example

Redis GEO is useful for real-time nearby-location searches, such as finding drivers within 5–10 km.

Add driver location: GEOADD drivers longitude latitude driverId

Find nearby drivers: GEOSEARCH drivers FROMLONLAT lon lat BYRADIUS 10 km

Other commands:

GEODIST → distance between two locations

GEOPOS → get coordinates

WITHDIST ASC → return distance and sort nearest first

HLD Flow

Driver App → Location Service → Redis GEO → Nearby Driver Search → Matching Service

Drivers periodically update their location. The ride service queries Redis for nearby available drivers.

Why Redis GEO?

In-memory → low latency

Efficient radius/proximity search

Handles frequent location updates

Avoids scanning all drivers

Scaling

Millions of drivers: shard by city/region/geohash prefix.

Stale drivers: use heartbeat + TTL/cleanup so inactive drivers aren't returned.

Internally: Redis GEO is implemented using a Sorted Set with geospatial encoding (geohash).





Spring Boot + Redis GEO Example

Add Dependency



<dependency>

   <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>

   <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-redis</artifactId>

</dependency>



Store Driver Location



@Autowired

private RedisTemplate<String, String> redisTemplate;



public void addDriver() {



   Point point = new Point(77.2300, 28.6100);



   redisTemplate.opsForGeo()

       .add("drivers", point, "driver:101");

}



Search Nearby Drivers



GeoResults<RedisGeoCommands.GeoLocation<String>> results =

   redisTemplate.opsForGeo().search(

       "drivers",

       GeoReference.fromCoordinate(77.2300, 28.6100),

       new Distance(10, Metrics.KILOMETERS)

   );







Production Design Example

Ride Matching System

User requests cab

      ↓

API Gateway

      ↓

Ride Service

      ↓

Redis GEO Search

      ↓

Nearest Drivers

      ↓

Notification Service

      ↓

Driver accepts ride



Why Redis GEO?

Very fast proximity searches

In-memory

Handles frequent location updates well

Limitations: Redis GEO is for nearby/radius searches, not advanced GIS. For complex spatial queries, consider PostGIS or Elasticsearch Geo.

Redis GEO vs Google Maps:

Redis GEO → stores and finds nearby locations

Google Maps → maps, routing, traffic, directions







Redis as EVENT STREAM PLATFORM

Using Redis Streams.

Supports

event sourcing

async microservices

consumer groups

replay

HLD Example

Order Service

   ↓

Redis Stream

   ↓

Inventory Service

Payment Service

Notification Service

notes.title: Redis — Important HLD Concepts
notes.description: Redis — Important HLD Concepts 1. Cache Invalidation Problem: DB is updated, but Redis still contains stale data. Solutions: Delete cache on DB update — most co
notes.content:
Redis — Important HLD Concepts

1. Cache Invalidation

Problem: DB is updated, but Redis still contains stale data.

Solutions:

Delete cache on DB update — most common with Cache-Aside

TTL — automatically expires stale data

Write-through — update DB + cache together

Interview point:

“The key challenge with caching is keeping cache and DB consistent.”



2. Redis Transactions

Redis supports: MULTI → commands → EXEC

But unlike SQL transactions:

No traditional rollback

Limited transaction semantics

Commands execute sequentially

Use when: Multiple Redis operations need to be executed together.



3. Pub/Sub vs Queue

Pub/Sub
	Queue

Real-time messaging
	Reliable processing

Message can be lost if subscriber is offline
	Message remains until consumed

Broadcasting
	Work distribution

Notifications, live updates
	Orders, background jobs

Interview point:

“Use Pub/Sub for real-time broadcasting; use Lists or Streams when reliable message processing is required.”



4. Redis Streams

Redis Streams provide persistent, ordered event streams.

Used for:

Event processing

Async microservices

Background processing

Consumer groups

Think of Streams as a lightweight Kafka-like event log.



5. Hot Keys

Problem: One extremely popular key receives millions of requests.

Example: celebrity:post:viral

→ One Redis node can become overloaded.

Solutions:

Local/in-process caching

Replicate popular data

Key sharding / key replication

Important HLD topic: Hot keys can create a single-node bottleneck even when the overall Redis cluster is healthy.



6. Cache Stampede

Problem: A popular cache entry expires → thousands of requests simultaneously hit the DB.

Cache expires

    ↓

1000s requests

    ↓

DB

    ↓

Overload

Solutions:

Mutex/distributed lock

Staggered/randomized TTL

Background cache refresh

Interview point:

“For popular keys, I’d prevent simultaneous cache misses using locking or proactive refresh.”



7. Sorted Sets (ZSET)

Sorted Sets maintain members with scores, making them ideal for ranking.

Important commands:

ZADD

ZRANGE

ZREVRANGE

ZSCORE

Use cases:

Leaderboards

Rankings

Trending content

Top searches

Example: ZADD leaderboard 2000 player101



Redis HLD Topics to Master

Cache-Aside + Cache Invalidation

TTL & Eviction

Cache Stampede

Hot Keys

Distributed Locks

Redis GEO

Sorted Sets

Pub/Sub vs Streams

Redis Persistence — RDB/AOF

Redis Cluster & Sharding

notes.description: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor: ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor is a concrete implementation of ScheduledExecutorService used to schedule t
notes.content:
ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor

ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor:



ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor is a concrete implementation of ScheduledExecutorService used to schedule tasks to run after a delay or periodically.

It extends:

ThreadPoolExecutor  and implements:

ScheduledExecutorService



Why do we need it?

It solves problems like:

Run a task after some delay

Run a task repeatedly (cron-like behavior)

Replace old Timer (which has limitations)





Key Features

Supports delayed execution

Supports periodic execution

Uses a thread pool (not single thread like Timer)

Handles exceptions better

Uses internal DelayQueue































public ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(int corePoolSize) {

   super(corePoolSize, Integer.MAX_VALUE,

         DEFAULT_KEEPALIVE_MILLIS, MILLISECONDS,

         new DelayedWorkQueue());

}







public ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(int corePoolSize,

                                  ThreadFactory threadFactory) {

   super(corePoolSize, Integer.MAX_VALUE,

         DEFAULT_KEEPALIVE_MILLIS, MILLISECONDS,

         new DelayedWorkQueue(), threadFactory);

}







public ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(int corePoolSize,

                                  RejectedExecutionHandler handler) {

   super(corePoolSize, Integer.MAX_VALUE,

         DEFAULT_KEEPALIVE_MILLIS, MILLISECONDS,

         new DelayedWorkQueue(), handler);

}







public ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(int corePoolSize,

                                  ThreadFactory threadFactory,

                                  RejectedExecutionHandler handler) {

   super(corePoolSize, Integer.MAX_VALUE,

         DEFAULT_KEEPALIVE_MILLIS, MILLISECONDS,

         new DelayedWorkQueue(), threadFactory, handler);

}





Important Methods

1. schedule() → Run once after delay



ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);

scheduler.schedule(() -> {

    System.out.println("Task executed after 3 seconds");

}, 3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);











2. scheduleAtFixedRate() → Fixed interval



scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {

   System.out.println("Running every 2 seconds");

}, 0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

Behavior:

Starts every 2 sec from start time

If task takes longer → next execution may overlap



3. scheduleWithFixedDelay() → Delay after completion



scheduler.scheduleWithFixedDelay(() -> {

   System.out.println("Running with delay");

}, 0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);







Behavior:

Waits 2 sec AFTER task finishes

No overlap → safer for long tasks 





FixedRate vs FixedDelay :



Feature
	scheduleAtFixedRate
	scheduleWithFixedDelay

Timing
	Based on start time
	Based on end time

Overlap
	Possible
	Not possible

Use case
	Monitoring, metrics
	Background jobs













Internal Working

Uses DelayQueue

Each task = ScheduledFutureTask

Tasks sorted by execution time

Worker threads pick tasks when delay expires

Flow:

Task → DelayQueue → Worker Thread → Execute







import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class SchedulerExample {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor scheduler =

                new ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(2);

        scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {

            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()

                    + " Running task " + System.currentTimeMillis());

        }, 0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

        try {

            Thread.sleep(10000);

        } catch (InterruptedException e) {}

        scheduler.shutdown();

    }

}





1. Why not use Timer?

Single thread → blocking issue

If one task fails → all stop



2. Difference between ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor and ThreadPoolExecutor?



Feature

Scheduling
	❌

Delay support
	❌

Queue

3. What happens if task throws exception?

 For periodic tasks:

Task stops executing further



4. Can tasks overlap?

scheduleAtFixedRate → YES

scheduleWithFixedDelay → NO



5. What is core pool size here?

Number of threads handling scheduled tasks

Fixed (no max pool like ThreadPoolExecutor)



When to Use in Real Systems

Health check scheduler

Polling APIs every few seconds

Cache refresh

Retry mechanisms

Heartbeat signals















Example : 







import java.util.concurrent.*;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {

        ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor scheduler =

                new ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor(2); // 2 threads

        scheduler.setRemoveOnCancelPolicy(true); // good practice

        scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {

            System.out.println("Running at: " + System.currentTimeMillis() +

                    " | Thread: " + Thread.currentThread().getName());

            try {

                Thread.sleep(2000); // simulate work

            } catch (InterruptedException e) {

                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();

            }

        }, 0, 3, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

        Thread.sleep(15000);

        System.out.println("Shutting down...");

        scheduler.shutdown();

    }

}

1. Core Parameters

ThreadPoolExecutor(

    int corePoolSize,

    int maximumPoolSize,

    long keepAliveTime,

    TimeUnit unit,

    BlockingQueue<Runnable> workQueue,

    ThreadFactory threadFactory,

    RejectedExecutionHandler handler

)

Meaning 

corePoolSize → min threads always alive

maximumPoolSize → max threads allowed

keepAliveTime → idle thread timeout

workQueue → where tasks wait

handler → rejection policy

The queue is shared by all worker threads in a ThreadPoolExecutor.

        ┌───────────────┐

        │   TASK QUEUE             │                ← shared

        └───────────────┘

          ↑   ↑   ↑   ↑

        T1   T2  T3  T4   ← worker threads





Execution Flow (Step-by-step)

When execute(task) is called:

If currentThreads < corePoolSize
 → create new thread

Else → put task in queue

If queue full & threads < maxPoolSize
 → create new thread

Else → reject task (via handler)



Worker Thread Concept

Each thread is a Worker

Worker:

runs tasks

fetches next task from queue

Uses runWorker() loop internally



Rejection Policies

Built-in:

AbortPolicy → throws exception

CallerRunsPolicy → runs in caller thread

DiscardPolicy → silently drops

DiscardOldestPolicy → removes oldest 





Queue Types Impact Behavior



Queue
	Behavior

LinkedBlockingQueue
	queue first, then scale

SynchronousQueue
	no queue → direct thread

ArrayBlockingQueue
	bounded queue



Internal Working



if (workers < corePoolSize)

    addWorker(task)

else if (queue.offer(task))

    // queued

else if (workers < maxPoolSize)

    addWorker(task)

else

    reject(task)

Why is newFixedThreadPool dangerous?

Uses unbounded queue

Can cause OOM (Out of memory risks)

Difference: core vs max threads?

Core → always alive

Max → burst handling

When threads die?

Only when:

idle > keepAliveTime

above above corePoolSize

or core timeout enabled

Why BlockingQueue?

Decouples producer & consumer

Controls load

notes.description: Hierarchy RADIUS: RADIUS: The RADIUS Protocol (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is a widely used networking protocol for authentication, authorizatio
notes.content:
Hierarchy











RADIUS:

RADIUS:



The RADIUS Protocol (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service) is a widely used networking protocol for authentication, authorization, and accounting (AAA). It is commonly used by ISPs, enterprise networks, and telecom systems to control access to network resources.



1. What is RADIUS?

RADIUS is a client-server protocol where:

Client : Network device (NAS: router, switch, access point)

Server : RADIUS server (validates users)

It works over UDP

Authentication → Port 1812

Accounting → Port 1813



2. Core Functions (AAA)

1. Authentication

Verifies who the user is

Username/password

Certificates

Tokens

2. Authorization

Determines what the user can access

VLAN assignment

IP allocation

Bandwidth limits

3. Accounting

Tracks user activity

Session start/stop

Data usage

Time duration



3. RADIUS Architecture

User : NAS (Router/Switch/AP) : RADIUS Server : Database

Flow:

User tries to connect (WiFi/VPN)

NAS sends request to RADIUS server

RADIUS validates credentials

Access Accept / Reject sent back

Accounting logs maintained



4. Packet Types

Authentication Packets

Access-Request : Sent by client

Access-Accept : Success

Access-Reject : Failure

Access-Challenge : Additional verification (OTP)

Accounting Packets

Accounting-Request

Accounting-Response



5. Key Features

Centralized authentication

Scalable for large networks

Supports multiple authentication methods (PAP, CHAP, EAP)

Encrypts only password (not full packet)



6. Example (WiFi Login)

User connects to enterprise WiFi

Access Point acts as NAS

Credentials sent to RADIUS server

Server validates (e.g., Active Directory)

User gets access if valid



7. Limitations

Uses UDP : unreliable transport

Only password is encrypted (rest is plaintext)

Less secure compared to modern protocols 





CORBA stands for:

Common Object Request Broker Architecture



CORBA is a standard defined by the Object Management Group that enables communication between distributed objects written in different programming languages and running on different machines.



Key Concept

Uses an ORB (Object Request Broker)

ORB acts like middleware that:

Finds the remote object

Sends request

Returns response



Tejas uses : JACORB

@Component

@Controller

Answer:

They are dependency aggregators.

Example:



spring-boot-starter-web

Tomcat

No logic, just dependency grouping



11. What is the DispatcherServlet lifecycle?

Answer:

Flow:

18. What are Application Listeners?

ApplicationReadyEvent

19. What is the difference between @Configuration vs @Component?





20. How does Spring Boot handle profiles?

Answer:



spring.profiles.active=dev

application-dev.properties





23. What is Lazy Initialization?

Answer:



spring.main.lazy-initialization=true

Beans created only when needed





3 Types of Web Application in Spring Boot



1. SERVLET (Default – Most Common)

Traditional blocking model

Based on:

Servlet API

Embedded servers: Tomcat, Jetty

Uses:

Spring MVC (@RestController, @Controller)

One thread per request





@RestController

   @GetMapping("/user")

       return "Hello";

   }

Example

Key Points

Easy to understand

Suitable for most CRUD apps

Blocking I/O (thread waits for DB/API response)



2. REACTIVE (WebFlux)

Non-blocking, async model

Based on:

Reactive Streams

Spring WebFlux

Mono, Flux

   return Mono.just("Hello");

}

Key Points

Handles high concurrency

Uses fewer threads

Best for:

Streaming

Real-time apps

High throughput systems



3. NONE (Non-Web Application)

No web server

Used for:

Dispatcher Servlet : is our first controller



































































DispatcherServlet in Spring Boot

The DispatcherServlet is the core component of Spring MVC. It acts as a Front Controller that handles all incoming HTTP requests and routes them to the correct handler (controller).



What it actually does

Think of it as a central traffic controller:

Receives every HTTP request

Decides which controller should handle it

Calls the controller method

Gets the response

Sends it back to the client



Request Flow (End-to-End)

Client

 → Filter

   → DispatcherServlet

     → Interceptor (preHandle)

       → Controller

     → Interceptor (postHandle)

   → Response



Internal Working (Step-by-Step)

1. Request comes in

Client sends request (/users)

2. DispatcherServlet receives it

Entry point of Spring MVC

3. Handler Mapping

Finds the correct controller using:

@RequestMapping

@GetMapping, etc.

👉 Uses: HandlerMapping



4. Handler Adapter

Invokes the controller method

👉 Uses: HandlerAdapter



5. Controller Execution



@GetMapping("/users")

   return userService.getAll();

}



6. View Resolver (if needed)

Converts response into:

JSON (REST)

HTML (MVC)

👉 Uses: ViewResolver



7. Response returned

Sent back to client 





What is Tomcat?

Apache Tomcat is an open-source web server and servlet container used to run Java web applications.



Tomcat is a server that runs your Spring Boot / Java backend application and handles HTTP requests.

What Tomcat actually does

Listens for HTTP requests (like http://localhost:8080)

Passes requests to your Java application

Executes servlets (like Spring’s DispatcherServlet)

Sends response back to client



Flow with Spring Boot

Client → Tomcat → DispatcherServlet → Controller → Response



Key Responsibilities

1. HTTP Server

Accepts requests from browser/Postman

2. Servlet Container

Runs Java servlets

Manages lifecycle (init, service, destroy)

3. Thread Management

Handles multiple users using thread pool



In Spring Boot

You usually don’t install Tomcat separately.

Spring Boot comes with embedded Tomcat:

spring-boot-starter-web



mvn spring-boot:run

It internally starts Apache Tomcat



Example

public class App {

   public static void main(String[] args) {

       SpringApplication.run(App.class, args);

   }

}

This automatically:

Starts Tomcat

Deploys your app

Opens port 8080

       return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(ex.getMessage());

   }

}









 







3 resolvers works in the same sequence from 1 to 3:

ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver

ResponseStatusExceptionResolver

DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver







The control comes to DefaultErrorAttributes, either from 1 or 2nd or 3rd resolver.











Another example:



















We are sending 400 (bad request), but still it is showing 500.

Why??









DefaultErrorAttribute:

is the default class used by Spring Boot to provide error details whenever an exception occurs.





We are not returning response entity means ,we are utilizing the exception resolver framework.



500 is default status code





We can create our own response entity, like below







If we don't return the response entity, then:



ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver will look for @ExceptionHandler annotation in our code.

and those methods can exist in BOTH:

controller class : @ControllerAdvice / @RestControllerAdvice







Q.) what ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver and DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver handles?

Ans.) 











Example 2 : 2 exceptionHandler (CustomException and Illegalargument exception)











Example 3 :  We can wrap multiple exceptions with same message and status code in single exceptionhandler











We can use response, ex in any order.













@ControllerAdvice is used for global handling of:

exceptions

model attributes

data binding

across multiple controllers.



Why We Use It

Without @ControllerAdvice: Same exception handling code repeated in every controller

With @ControllerAdvice: One centralized exception handler for all controllers













First priority is given to controller level than global level









Note: Custom exception implements runtime exception









Here CustomException is matched equally, so it will be called, if it was not there, then handleRuntimeexception will be called.





@RestControllerAdvice in Spring Boot

@RestControllerAdvice is used for global exception handling across all REST controllers.



Instead of writing try-catch blocks in every controller method, you can centralize exception handling in one place.

What is it?



@RestControllerAdvice

public class GlobalExceptionHandler {



}

It is a combination of:

@ControllerAdvice

@ResponseBody

So all methods return JSON automatically.













2. ResponseStatusExceptionResolver

Handles Uncaught exception annotated with @ResponseStatus annotation.



First it will go to first exception handler, check for @ExceptionHandler annotation, it will not find it, so now it will come to ResponseStatusExceptionResolver and check for @ResponseStatus

































In this case, ExceptionHandler is able to handle the exception, so it will not go to ResponseStatusExceptionResolver





Here, it is not going through the ExceptionHandlers, it is handled by Spring framework itself.



It only takes care of uncaught exception. 





















DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver 



DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver is a built-in Spring MVC exception resolver that handles Spring internal exceptions and converts them into proper HTTP status codes.

notes.content:
JPA + Transactions Interview Questions 



1. What is JPA? How is it different from Hibernate?

Answer:

JPA (Java Persistence API) is a specification.

Hibernate is a popular implementation of JPA.

👉 JPA defines:

Entity mapping

Persistence context

Query APIs (JPQL)

👉 Hibernate provides:

Actual ORM engine

Caching, lazy loading, dirty checking

Key Point:

JPA = Interface, Hibernate = Implementation





2. What is an Entity in JPA?

Answer:

An Entity is a Java class mapped to a database table.



@Entity



@Table(name = "users")



public class User {



   @Id



   private Long id;



}

Rules:

Must have @Entity

Must have primary key (@Id)

Should have no-arg constructor



   

🔥 2. ID Generation Strategies (VERY IMPORTANT)

Used with:



@Id



@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.X)



private Long id;



1. IDENTITY



@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)

👉 DB auto-increment

Example:

MySQL:



AUTO_INCREMENT

Pros:

Simple

DB handles ID

Cons:

No batching (important for performance)



2. SEQUENCE ⭐ (Best for performance)



@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE)

👉 Uses DB sequence

Example:



@SequenceGenerator(name="user_seq", sequenceName="user_seq")

Pros:

Supports batching

Better performance



3. TABLE (rarely used)



@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.TABLE)

👉 Uses separate table to store IDs

Cons:

Slow

Not recommended



4. AUTO



@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.AUTO)

👉 JPA decides:

MySQL → IDENTITY

PostgreSQL → SEQUENCE



 3. UUID as ID



@Id



@GeneratedValue



private UUID id;

When used:

Distributed systems

Microservices

Pros:

Unique globally

Cons:

Larger index → slower queries





3. What is Persistence Context?

Answer:

Persistence Context = First-level cache (Session)

Managed by EntityManager

Tracks all entities

Ensures identity guarantee

👉 Example:



User u1 = em.find(User.class, 1);



User u2 = em.find(User.class, 1);

👉 Both refer to same object

Important:

Prevents duplicate DB calls

Enables dirty checking





8. What is N+1 Problem?

Answer:

👉 Happens when:

1 query for parent

N queries for children

Example:



List<User> users = repo.findAll();



users.get(0).getOrders(); // triggers multiple queries

Solutions:

JOIN FETCH

@EntityGraph

Batch fetching





16. When does rollback happen?

Answer:

By default:

👉 Only on RuntimeException



@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)





















Using JDBC without Springboot:

If we have 2 db, we will have 2 persistence unit:



For each persistence unit, we need to create entity manager factory.







EntityManager : 

is the core JPA interface used to interact with the persistence context in Spring Boot / Hibernate.

It is responsible for:

Fetching entities

Updating entities

Managing transactions and cache (1st level cache)

Hibernate provides the implementation of jpa interface.

EntityManager consists the persistence context which consist the entity

Persistence context is placeholder for entities.

different functions

EntityManager and Persistence Context Relationship

What is ThreadLocal in Java?

ThreadLocal provides thread-local variables, meaning each thread gets its own separate copy of the variable.

notes.title: Messaging foundations
notes.description: Clarify Requirements Functional Requirements Producers publish messages to topics Consumers subscribe to topics Support: At-least-once delivery Ordering (per pa
notes.content:
Clarify Requirements

Functional Requirements

Producers publish messages to topics

Consumers subscribe to topics

Support:

At-least-once delivery

Ordering (per partition)

Horizontal scalability

Message retention

Replay capability

Consumer groups

Non-Functional Requirements

High throughput (millions msgs/sec)

Low latency (<10–50ms)

Durable storage

Fault tolerant

Multi-region capable

Observability (metrics, tracing)





















Message Queue vs Event streaming platforms:



Message queue:

Does not store the messages once consumed. (no retention)

Consumed only once.

Doesn’t maintain the order in which we send it.





Event Streaming platforms (Kafka) : 

Do all the above which





1. Core Philosophy

Feature
	Kafka
	ActiveMQ

Model
	Distributed log (pull-based)
	Traditional message broker (push-based)

Focus
	High throughput, event streaming
	Reliable messaging, enterprise integration



2. Architecture

Kafka

Distributed cluster

Topics → partitions → replicas

No central broker (distributed)

ActiveMQ

Broker-centric

Queue / Topic model

Typically centralized (can cluster)



4. Message Storage

Feature
	Kafka
	ActiveMQ

Storage
	Disk (append-only log)
	Memory + optional persistence

Retention
	Time/size based
	Until consumed

Replay capability
	Strong
	Limited





5. Performance

Feature
	Kafka
	ActiveMQ

Throughput
	Very high (millions/sec)
	Moderate

Latency
	Slightly higher
	Lower (real-time push)

Scaling
	Horizontal (partitions)
	Limited horizontal scaling



6. Ordering Guarantees

Feature
	Kafka
	ActiveMQ

Ordering
	Per partition
	Per queue

Global ordering
	Not guaranteed
	 Not guaranteed



7. Fault Tolerance

Feature
	Kafka
	ActiveMQ

Replication
	Built-in (ISR)
	Optional / weaker

Failure handling
	Automatic leader election
	Broker failover



8. Offset / Acknowledgement

Feature
	Kafka
	ActiveMQ

Tracking
	Consumer-managed offsets
	Broker-managed ACK

Control
	High flexibility
	Simpler





9. Use Cases

Kafka (Best for):

Event streaming

Log processing

Real-time analytics

Data pipelines



ActiveMQ (Best for):

Traditional messaging

Request-response

Transactional systems

JMS-based enterprise apps



10. Key Interview Differences 

Kafka:

Distributed log system

High throughput

Replay capability

Consumer-controlled offsets



ActiveMQ:

Traditional message broker

Push-based delivery

Strong JMS support

Simpler but less scalable









Messaging Models:



Point to point

Publish subscribe





Point to Point : a message is sent to the queue and consumed by one and only one consumer. There can be multiple consumers waiting to consume the message in the queue, but each message can be consumed by only a single consumer.

Once a message is consumed, it is removed from the queue. (no data retention )



Publish-Subscribe :

Topic: topics are the categories used to organise messages.(unique name across MQ).Messages are sent to and read from a specific topic.



We can use both models, publish subscriptions for implementing topics, and point to point for consumer groups. 



In Consumer groups: 

each message can be consumed by only one consumer in that group subscribe to that topic.









Partitions and Brokers : 



Now, what if data volume is too much to handle for a single server.



We can do Partition.



Partition is ordered, append only log.



Partitions are evenly distributed across servers in the message queue cluster.

These servers are called brokers.



“One broker = many topics (and partitions)”



Kafka Partition = Append-Only Log

Each partition is basically a sequential log file.

Example:

Topic: orders

Partition: P0

Internally stored like:

Offset | Message

----------------

0      | order1

1      | order2

2      | order3

3      | order4

Offsets are generated by Kafka broker when producer writes messages.

The producer does NOT create offsets.

Where Physically Stored?

On the broker disk.

Kafka stores partition data as log segment files.

Example path: /tmp/kafka-logs/orders-0/



Key rule

Topic → has multiple partitions (partition1, partition2)

Partition → belongs to exactly ONE topic

A partition is:

an ordered log of messages (FIFO)

tied to a single topic’s data stream

used for parallelism and scaling within that topic.

The position of a message in the partition is called an offset.





When a message is sent from the producer, it goes to any one of the partitions of that topic.



Each message has an optional message key, and all messages for the same key go to the same partition.

If message key is absent, it can go to any of the partition







How Partitions are created:

In Apache Kafka, partitions are not created dynamically by default — they are defined when the topic is created (or explicitly increased later).



1. Partition Creation at Topic Creation Time

When you create a topic, you specify:

Number of partitions

Replication factor

Example:

kafka-topics.sh --create \

  --topic orders \

  --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 \

  --partitions 3 \

  --replication-factor 2

This creates:

Topic: orders

3 partitions → orders-0, orders-1, orders-2

Important

Partitions are created:

At topic creation time

Or increased later using --alter

Kafka distributes partitions across brokers

Each partition has:

One leader

Multiple followers   in broker/s

Increasing partitions:

Does NOT rebalance old data

May affect ordering and key mapping





How Partitions used by Producer and Consumer:





When a topic has 5 partitions — how producer & consumer use them



Topic: orders

Partitions: P0, P1, P2, P3, P4





Q.) how kafka knows number of partitions for each topic

In Apache Kafka, the producer first fetches metadata from Kafka brokers.

That metadata contains:

topic names

number of partitions

partition leaders

replicas

ISR info

So producer already knows:

Topic: orders

Partitions:

   P0 -> Broker-1

   P1 -> Broker-3

   P2 -> Broker-2

before sending messages.



















1. How PRODUCER uses partitions

Producer decides which partition each message goes to



Case A: With key



partition = hash(key) % 5



userId=101 → P3  

userId=102 → P1





Same key → same partition

Maintains ordering per key



Ex - 		ProducerRecord<String, String>(

"Orders",

"user123", // key

"order created"

);



Case B: Without key

Round-robin:

Msg1 → P0 

Msg2 → P1 

Msg3 → P2 

Msg4 → P3 

Msg5 → P4 

Msg6 → P0 …



Load distributed evenly





Producer internally maintains a counter:

currentPartition++

And:

partition = counter % totalPartitions









Without key: Kafka does NOT guarantee ordering

2. How CONSUMER uses partitions

Consumers don’t pick partitions themselvesKafka assigns partitions via consumer group



consumer group : In Apache Kafka, a consumer group is a set of consumers working together to consume messages from a topic.



Producer

   ↓

Chooses partition (P0–P4)

   ↓

Message stored in that partition

   ↓

Consumer group

   ↓

Each partition assigned to one consumer

   ↓

Consumer reads sequentially from its partition







those consumers who subscribe to that topic, and may/may not be from same consumer group





Consumers subscribe to topics, but partition assignment and message sharing are controlled by the consumer group.





“Kafka combines queue and pub-sub models using consumer groups.”

notes.title: Consumer groups & coordination
notes.description: Now when it comes to Consumer, Consumers read from partitions A topic = > collection of partitions A consumer reads from specific partitions 2. Consumer Groups
notes.content:
Now when it comes to Consumer,

Consumers read from partitions 

A topic = > collection of partitions

A consumer reads from specific partitions

2. Consumer Groups 

Consumers are organized into consumer groups.

Each consumer group can have a different coordinator.



Topic: orders

Partitions: P0, P1, P2



Consumer Group A:

 C1 → P0

 C2 → P1

 C3 → P2

Rule:

One partition is consumed by only ONE consumer within a group

This avoids duplicate processing 



4. What if consumers < partitions?

Partitions: P0, P1, P2



Consumers:

 C1 → P0, P1

 C2 → P2

One consumer can handle multiple partitions



5. What if consumers > partitions?

Partitions: P0, P1



Consumers:

 C1 → P0

 C2 → P1

 C3 → idle

Extra consumers stay idle

Max parallelism = number of partitions



6. Offsets (how tracking works)

Each partition assigns sequential offsets to messages, but the consumer group maintains the read offset.

Partition P0: 

[offset 0] msg1

[offset 1] msg2

[offset 2] msg3

Consumer tracks: "I have read till offset 2"

Stored per:

consumer group

Partition

Where is the Read Offset Stored?

In Apache Kafka:

The read offset is stored in a special internal Kafka topic:  __consumer_offsets

This is:

A compacted topic

Distributed across brokers like any normal topic 

What Exactly Is Stored?

Offset is stored as a key-value record

Key: (group.id, topic, partition)

Value: offset = next message to read





7. Ordering guarantee

Ordering is guaranteed within a partition

Not across partitions 

Each consumer group can subscribe to multiple topics and maintain its own consuming offset.



New Consumers: 

1. How New Consumer Joins an Existing Group

Consumer 1:

props.put("group.id", "order-processors");

Consumer 2 (new instance):

props.put("group.id", "order-processors");  

Same group.id = same consumer group



2. Does Consumer “Know” Group Exists?

No lookup like:

“give me existing groups”

 Instead:

Consumer just sends JoinGroup(group.id)

Kafka decides:



Case 1: Group exists

Add consumer to group

Trigger rebalance



Case 2: Group does NOT exist

Create new group

Add consumer



 3. Internal Flow

Consumer starts with group.id

Sends: JoinGroup(order-processors)

Coordinator checks:

Group metadata

Either:

Join existing group 

Create new group 



Ex : 

//1. Add group id

Properties props = new Properties();

props.put("group.id", "order-processors");



// 2. Create Consumer

KafkaConsumer<String, String> consumer = new KafkaConsumer<>(props);



// 3. Subscribe to topic(s)

consumer.subscribe(Arrays.asList("orders"));



1. Group Coordinator (Consumers side)

Handles consumer groups only

What it manages

Consumer join (JoinGroup)

Consumer leave / crash

Partition assignment

Rebalancing

Who is it?

It is just one of the brokers

Kafka chooses a broker to act as Group Coordinator for a group

Triggered when:

Consumer added

Consumer removed

Consumer stops heartbeating





Consumer Group

   ↓

Group Coordinator (a broker)

   ↓

Assign partitions + manage rebalances



Note : Each consumer group can have a different coordinator.



2. Are Coordinators Separate Brokers?

Ans. )  No — there are NO special coordinator-only brokers

 Same brokers do EVERYTHING:

Store topic partitions

Serve producers/consumers

Act as group coordinators 

2. Cluster Controller (Brokers side)

Handles brokers and cluster state



What it manages

Broker join (new broker added)

Broker failure (node down)

Partition leader election

Metadata updates



Who is it?

 In modern Kafka:

Managed via KRaft (Kafka Raft mode)

One broker becomes Controller

(Older Kafka used ZooKeeper)



Triggered when:

Broker crashes

New broker added

Partition leader dies 



Mental model: 



Kafka Cluster

   ↓

Cluster Controller

   ↓

Manages brokers + partition leaders



Leader Election in Consumer Group:



During a rebalance, one consumer is elected as the Group Leader to decide partition assignment.



The FIRST consumer that successfully joins the group becomes the leader .



1. When Does a Leader Election Happen?

Leader election happens during:

New consumer joins

Consumer leaves / crashes

Topic subscription changes

All these trigger a rebalance



 Group Coordinator (broker-side)

Receives JoinGroup requests

Selects one consumer as leader



Flow : 

Step 1: Consumers Send JoinGroup

Step 2: Coordinator Collects All Members

Step 3: Leader Selection :



Kafka chooses:

The FIRST consumer that successfully joins the group



Step 4: Coordinator Responds

Coordinator sends JoinGroup response:

To Leader:

- full member list

- all subscriptions

- assignment responsibility

To Followers:

- wait for assignment





Step 5: Leader Computes Assignment

Leader:

Fetches metadata (topics → partitions)

Runs assignor:

Range

RoundRobin

Sticky

Creates mapping:

C1 → P0, P3

C2 → P1

C3 → P2





Step 6: SyncGroup Phase

Leader sends:

SyncGroupRequest(assignments)

Coordinator:

Stores assignment

Sends to all consumers





Step 7: Consumption Starts

Each consumer gets its partitions

Starts polling

 Consumer Group Leader vs Followers:

Exists inside a consumer group

Purpose:

Only for partition assignment during rebalance



Roles:



Role


	Responsibility



Leader Consumer


	Decides partition assignment

Follower Consumers


	Receive assignment





Key Points:

Temporary role (only during rebalance)

One of the consumers becomes leader

No data storage involved







Controller Broker :

There is only ONE active controller broker at any time in a Kafka cluster.

 1. Single Active Controller

In Apache Kafka:

At any moment, exactly one broker acts as the controller.

 What Does Controller Do?

Leader election for partitions

Detect broker failures

Maintain cluster metadata

Assign partition leaders 

 2. But All Brokers Are Eligible

 Important nuance:

Every broker can become controller

But only one is active at a time

 3. What If Controller Fails?

 Kafka automatically elects a new controller

Flow:

Current controller crashes

Remaining brokers detect failure

New controller is elected 

 4. ZooKeeper vs KRaft (Important)

🟡 Old (ZooKeeper):

Controller elected via ZooKeeper

🟢 New (KRaft mode):

Controller elected via Kafka’s own Raft quorum

 But rule remains same:

Only one active controller



 5. Why Only One?

Avoid conflicting decisions

Ensure consistent metadata

Prevent split-brain issues



 6. Is This a Bottleneck?

 Surprisingly, no:

Controller handles metadata only

Not actual data traffic

Data flow happens between brokers directly 



















How Controllers Are Elected in Kafka?

 1. Controller Election in ZooKeeper Mode (Old)



First broker to register itself as controller in ZooKeeper wins



Step-by-step:

1. Brokers start and connect to Apache ZooKeeper



2. Each broker tries to create a node:

/controller

 This is an ephemeral node



3. Race Condition

Only one broker succeeds

Others fail



4. Winner becomes Controller

Broker B1  creates /controller  becomes controller 

5. If Controller Dies

Ephemeral node gets deleted automatically

Other brokers retry

New controller elected

 2. Controller Election in KRaft Mode (Modern Kafka)

 No ZooKeeper — Kafka handles everything internally

Core Idea:

Controller is elected using Raft consensus algorithm

Step-by-step:

1. Dedicated Controller Quorum

Example:

Controllers: B1, B2, B3



2. Raft Election Happens

Brokers vote

One becomes leader of quorum



3. Leader = Active Controller

B2  wins election  becomes controller 



4. If Controller Fails

New election triggered

Another broker becomes controller







Raft consensus algorithm:

 What is Raft?

Raft is a consensus algorithm used to keep multiple nodes in sync and agree on a single source of truth.

🔹 3. Leader Election (Core Part)

Step 1: All Nodes Start as Followers

F1, F2, F3

Step 2: Timeout Happens

No heartbeat from leader 

One node becomes Candidate

Step 3: Election Starts

Candidate:

Increments term

Requests votes from others

Step 4: Voting

Each node votes once per term

Majority wins

F1 votes for C1 

F2 votes for C1 

Majority → C1 becomes Leader



Step 5: Leader Sends Heartbeats

Prevents new elections

Keeps followers alive 



Flow:

Client sends request to leader

Leader appends to its log

Leader sends to followers

Followers acknowledge

Majority → commit

notes.title: Replication, failures & recovery
notes.description: What if a partition crashes? First, important clarification: A partition itself doesn’t “crash” A broker (server) hosting that partition crashes Partition = rep
notes.content:
What if a partition crashes?

First, important clarification:

A partition itself doesn’t “crash”A broker (server) hosting that partition crashes



Partition = replicated log









How Kafka handles Broker Crash:



A broker can have MANY leaders (for different partitions).



In Apache Kafka:



Each partition has:

1 Leader

Multiple Followers (replicas)   (we keep in different brokers)



Example:



Partition P0:

  Leader   → Broker 1

  Follower → Broker 2

  Follower → Broker 3





Case: Broker with leader crashes:



Step 1: Failure detected

Broker stops sending heartbeats



Step 2: Cluster Controller reacts

Elects a new leader from followers



Before:

Leader → Broker 1



After crash:

Leader → Broker 2  



Step 3: Clients update metadata

Producers + consumers are informed:

"New leader for P0 is Broker 2"









Step 4: System continues

✔ Minimal downtime ✔ No data loss (if replication is configured correctly)

What about data safety?

Case 1: Safe (normal case)

Message replicated to followers ✔ No data loss

Case 2: Risky (edge case)

Leader crashes before replication completes ❗ Some recent messages may be lost

 Controlled via:

acks=all

min.insync.replicas

Consumer impact

Consumer temporarily fails to read

After leader election:

resumes from last offset

Producer impact

May get:

retry errors

Automatically retries after new leader is known 



Worst case scenario

All replicas of a partition crashPartition becomes unavailable





Kafka ensures availability through replication and leader-follower architecture, but guarantees depend on ISR and acknowledgment settings.



Leader Election in Partition (When broker goes down):



Each partition has one leader broker and multiple followers.

When the leader fails, Kafka elects a new leader from replicas.





First available replica in ISR (based on replica order)

1. Partition Structure

Example:

Partition P0:

Replicas = [B1, B2, B3]

Leader   = B1

ISR      = [B1, B2]



Replicas → all copies

ISR (In-Sync Replicas) → safe candidates

Leader → serves reads/writes



2. Who Performs Leader Election?

Controller Broker

Only one controller exists in cluster

Responsible for:

Detecting failures

Electing new leaders



3. Exact Flow (Step-by-Step)

Step 1: Leader Failure Detection

Broker (leader) crashes or becomes unreachable

Controller detects via:

Heartbeats

Metadata quorum (KRaft)

B1 (leader)



Step 2: Identify Affected Partitions

Controller finds:

Which partitions had leader = B1?

Example:

P0, P3, P7 affected

Step 3: Check ISR

For each partition:

P0:

Replicas = [B1, B2, B3]

ISR      = [B1, B2]

After failure:

ISR = [B2]



Step 4: Select New Leader (Deterministic)

Kafka chooses:

First available replica in ISR (based on replica order)

Replicas = [B1, B2, B3]

ISR = [B2]



New Leader = B2



Step 5: Update Metadata

Controller updates:

Leader = B2

ISR = [B2]

Stored in:

KRaft metadata log (modern Kafka)



Step 6: Notify Brokers

Controller sends LeaderAndIsr request:

B2 → becomes leader

Others → followers



Step 7: Clients Refresh Metadata

Producers/Consumers detect change

Fetch updated metadata

Redirect traffic to new leader

Important Rules (Interview Gold)

1. Leader is ALWAYS from ISR

Ensures:

No data loss

Consistency

2. Election is Deterministic

Based on:

ISR membership

Replica order

Not random Not load-based



5. Edge Case: ISR Empty

Clean Election (default)

No leader chosen

Partition unavailable

No data loss



Unclean Election

unclean.leader.election.enable=true

Choose out-of-sync replica

Possible data loss



6. KRaft vs ZooKeeper

ZooKeeper → old coordination

KRaft → internal Raft quorum

Election logic remains same



Controller + ISR + Order = Leader Election





Leader Election For Group Coordinator (one of the broker):



Leader Election for Group Coordinator is a bit tricky because it’s not a direct election like Raft or ISR.



“Kafka does not have a separate election mechanism for group coordinators. Instead, the coordinator for a consumer group is the broker that is the leader of the corresponding partition of the __consumer_offsets topic, determined by hashing the group.id. If that broker fails, a new partition leader is elected, which automatically becomes the new coordinator.”





Coordinator = Leader of offsets partition





🔹 1. How Coordinator is Determined

Add Consumer Group

group.id = order-processors

Step 1: Hash

hash(group.id) % num_partitions(__consumer_offsets)



Gives:  __consumer_offsets partition number

hash(group.id) → partition 1





Step 2: Find Leader of That Partition

__consumer_offsets-1 → Leader = B2

Final:

Coordinator = B2



🔹 2. Where “Election” Actually Happens

👉 Important:

There is NO direct election for coordinator

Instead:

Election happens here:

Partition leader election (ISR-based)



🔹 3. Failure Scenario (Real Flow)



🧩 Step 1: Coordinator Broker Fails

B2 (coordinator) ❌



🧩 Step 2: Partition Leader Election

For:

__consumer_offsets-5

Kafka elects new leader:

New Leader = B3



🧩 Step 3: New Coordinator

👉 Automatically:

Coordinator = B3



🧩 Step 4: Consumers React

Detect coordinator failure

Send FindCoordinator request

Rejoin group

👉 Rebalance triggered

🔥 Key Insights (Interview Gold)



🔹 1. No Separate Election Algorithm

❌ No Raft ❌ No voting

✅ Reuses:



🔹 2. Deterministic Mapping

Same group.id → same partition

Same partition → same coordinator



🔹 3. Load Distribution

__consumer_offsets has many partitions

Different groups → different coordinators

👉 Scales well





Partition leader election









Each consumer group has its own coordinator



Consumer Group
	Coordinator

order-processors
	B2

payment-service
	B1

analytics-group
	B3



🔹 2. Why Kafka Does This

✅ Scalability

Thousands of consumer groups

Load distributed across brokers

✅ No bottleneck

No single coordinator handling everything





🔹 3. How They Are Distributed

👉 Based on:

hash(group.id) → __consumer_offsets partition → leader broker

👉 That broker becomes coordinator









🔹 Core Idea

In Apache Kafka:

Group Coordinator is NOT elected separately 👉 It is derived from partition leadership of __consumer_offsets









__consumer_offsets 

. Special Property: Log Compaction

__consumer_offsets is a compacted topic



Only latest offset per key is kept

Old entries are removed

(order-processors, orders, P0) → offset 2  (order-processors, orders, P0) → offset 3  (order-processors, orders, P0) → offset 4



After compaction:

(order-processors, orders, P0) → offset 4



Group Coordinator Link 

👉 This topic is also used to:

Assign group coordinators

hash(group.id) → partition of __consumer_offsets

→ leader of that partition = coordinator





🔹 What is __consumer_offsets?

In Apache Kafka:

__consumer_offsets is a special internal Kafka topic used to store:

Consumer offsets

Consumer group metadata



🔹 1. Why Do We Need It?

Kafka needs to remember:

“Which message has a consumer group already processed?”



Example:

orders topic (Partition 0):

[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]



Consumer group: order-processors 

Last read offset = 3

This info is stored in: __consumer_offsets



🔹 2. What Exactly Is Stored?

Each record is key-value based



🔑 Key:

(group.id, topic, partition)



📦 Value:

offset = next message to read

metadata



Example:

Key:

(order-processors, orders, P0)



Value:

offset = 4

👉 Means:

Next message to read is offset 4



🔹 3. It Is a Normal Kafka Topic (Important)

Topic: __consumer_offsets

Partitions: ~50 (default)

Replicated: Yes

👉 Just like any topic:

Distributed across brokers

Has leaders and followers



🔹 4. How It Is Used (Flow)



🧩 Step 1: Consumer Reads Messages

Reads till offset 3



🧩 Step 2: Commit Offset

consumer.commitSync();



🧩 Step 3: Kafka Writes to Topic

__consumer_offsets



🧩 Step 4: On Restart

Consumer:

Fetch offset → resume from 4





Add/remove consumers:





Kafka’s Group Coordinator + metadata fetch determines all partitions for the subscribed topics.





Consumer joins a consumer group:

//order-processors is a group id

props.put("group.id", "order-processors");



Consumer subscribe to topic/topics:

consumer.subscribe(Arrays.asList("orders”,”payments")); 

// consumer can subscribe to multiple topics.



NOTE : 

2. Consumer sends JoinGroup request

Consumer does NOT directly know the Group Coordinator

It connects to any broker in the cluster

Consumer → Broker B1

2. Broker Finds the Group Coordinator

Kafka decides coordinator using:

hash(group.id) → __consumer_offsets partition → leader broker

So:

Each consumer group is handled by one specific broker

That broker = Group Coordinator



group.id = order-processors

hash → partition 5 of __consumer_offsets  

leader of partition 5 = Broker B3

So, Coordinator = B3



Note : Each consumer group can have a different coordinator.



In Kafka, A group coordinator is chosen per consumer group, not globally.

Broker Forwards JoinGroup Request

Now flow becomes:

Consumer → B1 → (forward) → Coordinator (B3)

 B1 is just a router here



What JoinGroup Request Contains:

It’s not just groupId, it includes:

JoinGroupRequest:

- group.id

- member.id (empty if new)

- session.timeout.ms

- subscribed topics

- assignment strategy (range/roundrobin/sticky)



JoinGroup(groupId, subscribedTopics)



Coordinator Handles the Request:

Coordinator does:

If new consumer:

Assigns member.id

If existing:

Validates membership

Then:

Adds consumer to group metadata



Broker receiving this forwards it to the Group Coordinator



Rebalance is triggered on consumer addition

Consumption is paused during rebalance



4. Leader election inside group

One consumer is chosen as Group Leader

Others are followers

 Leader’s job:

decide partition assignment 



5. Metadata Fetch

Coordinator provides leader with:

All consumers in group

All subscribed topics



Leader fetches metadata:

Topic → partitions mapping

Example:

orders → P0, P1, P2





6. Assignment strategy runs

  Leader uses assignor (range / round-robin / sticky):

Partitions: P0, P1, P2

Consumers: C1, C2





Leader decides:

C1 → P0, P1

C2 → P2



6. SyncGroup request

Leader sends assignment to coordinator

Coordinator distributes to all consumers



7. Consumers start consuming

Each consumer now knows:

"My partitions = P0, P1"

Then:

consumer.poll()





































Removed the Consumers:

Heartbeats

Consumer continuously sends:  Heartbeat()

If missed → consumer is considered dead

Session timeout

If no heartbeat within timeout:

consumer removed

rebalance triggered



Full lifecycle:

Start Consumer

   ↓

JoinGroup

   ↓

Coordinator assigns memberId

   ↓

Leader elected

   ↓

Partition assignment

   ↓

SyncGroup

   ↓

Start consuming

   ↓

Heartbeat loop



Kafka uses partition assignors:

Range Assignor (default simple one)

Round Robin Assignor

Sticky Assignor (important in real systems)



Assignor Behavior (Important)

1. RangeAssignor

Works topic by topic internally

But still ensures distribution across consumers

 Slight skew possible



2. RoundRobinAssignor

Treats all partitions as one list

Perfectly balanced



3. StickyAssignor (Most used)

Balances partitions

Minimizes movement during rebalance



1. Range Assignor (Topic-wise grouping)

Works topic by topic, then assigns ranges per consumer

Assignment:

orders:

C1 → P0

C2 → P1

payments:

C1 → P0

C2 → P1

Final:

C1 → orders-P0, payments-P0

C2 → orders-P1, payments-P1

 Insight:

Same index partitions grouped per consumer

Can cause imbalance if partitions uneven across topics



🔹 2. Round Robin Assignor (Global distribution)

 Treats all partitions as one flat list

Step:

orders-P0, orders-P1, payments-P0, payments-P1

Assignment:

C1 → orders-P0, payments-P0

C2 → orders-P1, payments-P1

(If more partitions → strict alternating)

 Insight:

Perfect balance

Ignores topic boundaries



🔹 3. Sticky Assignor (Production favorite)

 Goals:

Balance partitions

Minimize movement during rebalance



Initial Assignment (like round robin):

C1 → orders-P0, payments-P0

C2 → orders-P1, payments-P1

After Adding C3:

Instead of reshuffling everything:

C1 → orders-P0

C2 → orders-P1

C3 → payments-P0, payments-P1

 Moves minimum partitions











Producer Crash:



What happens when a Producer crashes?

A producer can crash:

Before sending message

While sending

After sending but before receiving ACK

Each case behaves differently.



Case-by-case breakdown

1. Producer crashes BEFORE sending message

 Message is never sent, Kafka never sees it

Result:

Message LOST

No recovery possible

2. Producer crashes AFTER sending but BEFORE ACK

Flow:

Producer sends message

Broker receives it

Producer crashes before ACK

Now producer doesn't know:

Was the message written? Or not?

Result:

Possible duplicate messages

 When producer restarts:

It retries sending (because no ACK received)





3. Producer crashes AFTER ACK received

 Message already confirmed by broker

Result:

No data loss

No duplicate (unless app retries wrongly)



How Kafka handles this internally

🔁 1. Retries (Producer Config)

retries = N

Producer automatically retries sending messages

Helps recover from temporary failures

BUT:  Can cause duplicates



2. Idempotent Producer 

enable.idempotence = true

Kafka assigns:

Producer ID (PID)

Sequence Number per partition

 Broker tracks:

Last sequence number

Result:

Duplicate messages are ignored

Guarantees Exactly-once per partition (no duplicates)



3. Acknowledgment Levels (acks)

acks = 0 | 1 | all

🔹 acks=0

No ACK

Fast but risky

Data loss possible



🔹 acks=1

Leader acknowledges

If leader crashes before replication:Data loss possible



🔹 acks=all (recommended)

Leader + ISR replicas confirm

Result:

Strong durability

No data loss (under normal conditions)



4. Replication (Kafka durability backbone)

Each partition has:

Leader

Followers (ISR)

 Message is safe only after replication

 5. Delivery Guarantees Summary





Guarantee
	Config Needed
	Behavior

At most once
	acks=0
	possible loss

At least once
	retries + acks=all
	duplicates possible

Exactly once
	idempotence + transactions
	no loss + no duplicates







Adding & Removing Brokers in Kafka

Brokers can be added or removed dynamically, but data must be rebalanced manually or semi-automatically.

1. Adding a Broker

Step 1: Start New Broker

Install Kafka

Configure:

broker.id=4

listeners=PLAINTEXT://localhost:9096

log.dirs=/kafka-logs-4

Start broker



Step 2: Broker Joins Cluster

Registers with controller

Becomes available for:

New partitions

Replica placement

Existing data is NOT automatically moved, we need rebalancing





Step 3: Rebalance Partitions

You must explicitly run:

kafka-reassign-partitions.sh

Moves partitions to new broker

Balances load

notes.title: Mockito
notes.description: Mockito Mocking helps achieve isolation by replacing real dependencies with fake (Mock) objects, so that our unit test do not use the real object. OrderService
notes.content:
Mockito





 

Mocking helps achieve isolation by replacing real dependencies with fake (Mock) objects, so that our unit test do not use the real object. 









OrderService "placeOrder(int amt)" invokes PaymentService "pay(int amt)" for placing the order. 



So, when we write Unit test cases for OrderService "placeOrder" method, we should not invoke PaymentService or any other class, we need to MOCK (fake object) them. 









So above, we mocked the call paymentService.pay(10). 



Mocking means: instead of invoking the real method, we tell the test framework, "when this method is called, just return the predefined value without executing the actual logic." 















What Mocking solves? 

Isolation: As discussed in above 2 scenarios itself. Mocking isolates the unit under test by replacing real dependencies withfake objects (Mock obj). 



Fast + no Flaky tests: 

a.No I/O calls,

b..No network calls.

c.No db access 



Tests become fast and stable. 



Controlled Output:

Mocking allow us to control the behavior and response of dependencies.

Enable testing of edge cases (like timeout) and failure scenarios easily. 



Reduced tight coupling: 

Without mocking, unit test depends on 

a.Database scheme 

b.Message broker 

c.External API etc..

Change in these system can cause unrelated unit tests to fail.



For ex: DB schema got changed -> results in failure of test cases which internally invokes DB. 







What's the difference between: Stubbing, Mocking and Spying 











Focus is only on input and output. 



Mocking: 

Stubbing is just one part of Mocking. 



Mocking provides more features like: 

Was a method called? 

How many time? 

With what arguments? 

In what order? 









Spying:







Need to be used carefully. There is a chance that we are trying to do stubbing but mistakenly also invoked real method. 







Safe implemenation, make use of : doReturn for stubbing, to avoid calling the real method. 









What? how come for When()…thenReturn() it is invoking the real method and why for doReturn().when() its notinvoking the real method?

notes.title: Mockito · Annotations:
notes.description: Annotations: Manually These classes are present in "Mockito core" library. So, we are using the Mockito manually: Creating the mock/spy manually. Stubbing manua
notes.content:
Annotations:









Manually









These classes are present in "Mockito core" library. 

So, we are using the Mockito manually: 

Creating the mock/spy manually. 

Stubbing manually 

Verifying manually 



all we need is "mockito-core" library: 





Junit Lifecycle and Manual Mock/Spy object creation: 























Not Safe, because: 

Test class instance is created only once and used by all test methods. 

So same mock object is used by all test methods and thus: 

Risk of leaking Stubs 

Interaction history (verify) 







2. Annotation Without Extension: 























These Mockito Annotations classes are present in "Mockito core" library. 





Cons of "Annotations without Extension": 



Boilerplate: In every class, we have to do: 



AutoCloseable closable;



@BeforeEach



closable = openMocks(this);



@AfterEach



closable.close();







Easy to forget close() 

Manually need to wire the mock creation with JUnit lifecycle. 

Need to make sure that its added it @BeforeEach and closed in @AfterEach. 

What if by mistake its added in @BeforeAll. 

So, manually need to do the wiring in JUnit lifecycle. 





Before we proceed to "Annotation with Extension" 



in Step3 I mentioned that "in real object member variables mock object is set" 







Step3: InjectMocks handling 

Create real object of the field annotated with @InjectMocks. 

And in real object member variables, set the mock objects, which are created in Step2. 



service = new OrderService(gateway, repo);

So, one question might come is: What are the different ways to set the member variables? And what are the Rules?

1. Constructor Injection (First Priority)

2. Setter Injection (Second Priority)

3. Field Injection (Last Priority)





















Lets try to cover all possible scenarios: 



Constructor Injection: 

Rules: 

Always pick the constructor with most parameter. 

Do not guess value for primitive data types. 

If Mock is not available for any constructor parameter object, use null (but do not create mock for that object). 

If not able to fill any parameters of picked constructor fallback to default constructor. 











Internally it will do: 



service = new OrderService(gateway, repo)

Found the Constructor which has all the Mock object Types. 







Use case #2: More than 1 Constructor present: able to resolve the dependencies 











Always pick the constructor with most parameter :

 Constructor picked : OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway, OrderRepository repo, SalesRepository salesRepo) 

PaymentGateway gateway = Mock is available 

OrderRepository repo = Mock is available 



If Mock is not available for any constructor parameter object, use null (but do not create mock for that object). 

SalesRepository salesRepo = No Mock object is available, so it will pass NULL. 



@InjectMock able to create OrderService object: 



service = new OrderService(gateway, repo, null)













Use case #3: More than 1 Constructor present: NOT able to resolve the dependencies 













Always pick the constructor with most parameter : Constructor picked : OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway, OrderRepository repo, int var) 

PaymentGateway gateway = Mock is available 

OrderRepository repo = Mock is available 



Do not guess value for primitive data types. 

int var , it is not able to resolved the parameter of the constructor picked. 



If not able to fill the parameters of picked constructor fallback to default constructor. 

Try to invoke: 



service = new OrderService();

But we don’t have default constructor in OrderService class, so it failed. 







Setter Injection: 

Rules: 

Always have default no-arg constructor present. why? because 1st priority is Constructor Injection but to move to Setter Injection, it should fail to resolve the parameters dependency of picked constructor and fallback to default constructor and then call setter methods on the newly object created. 



Setter method must follow the naming convention. 



setSalesRepo(SalesRepository salesRepo)

not: 



salesRepo(SalesRepository salesRepo)



addSalesRepo(SalesRepository salesRepo)



Setter method must exactly take 1 argument 



setAll(A a, B b)



Setter injection do not work for final fields. 





If Setter Injection is not possible for certain fields, then for those fields it try to do FIELD INJECTION through reflection (even private fields will get set but not final) 











Step1: Go for constructor Injection: 

Pick the constructor is most parameters: 



Constructor picked: 



OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway, OrderRepository repo, int var)



But 

It did not able to satisfy all the parameter of picked constructor (int var it do not able to guess the value) 



So, 

It fall back to Default no-arg constructor and able to find it. 





OrderService service = new OrderService();

Once object is created, now first Setter Injection ->then field injection is tried to initialize all the fields. 





Step2: Go for Setter Injection 

OrderService object has 3 fields :



private PaymentGateway gateway;



private OrderRepository repo;



private SalesRepository salesRepo;



It picks first field:



private PaymentGateway gateway;



Then it will try to look for its setter method:



setGateway(PaymentGateway gateway)



Setter method found:



Then it will check, do I have Mock object for this field type "PaymentGateway"



@Mock



PaymentGateway gate;

Yes it has, so it will invokes this setGateway method.

Now in OrderService object

gateway = Mock Gateway is set.



Now ,

OrderService object has 2 more fields which need to be set: 



private OrderRepository repo;



private SalesRepository salesRepo;

And for both the fields, it did not able to find the setter method.

so,



Step3: Go for field Injection for these fields



private OrderRepository repo = @Mock OrderRepository repo;



private SalesRepository salesRepo = @Mock SalesRepository salesRepo;

Even private fields are set.





1. Annotation With Extension: 

Its similar to "Annotation Without Extension" 

Only thing is: 

We don’t have to worry about openMock() 

Closing the resource 

Wiring into the Junit lifecycle. 

Its all managed by Extension. 











PaymentGateway.java 







OrderRepository.java 











1. MockitoExtension enable hooks in JUPITER code. 

Gets Lifecycle callbacks like: 

Before each Test 

After each test 













And this mockito-junit-jupiter also fetches "mockito-core" library, so we don’t specifically need to add mockito-core library: 



2. 

Before each Test method, it internally calls similar to: 

closable = MockitoAnnotations.openMocks(this); 

@Override 

public void beforeEach(final ExtensionContext context) { 

MockitoSession session =

Mockito.mockitoSession()

.initMocks(testInstances.toArray())

.strictness(actualStrictness)

.logger(new MockitoSessionLoggerAdapter(Plugins.getMockitoLogger()))

.startMocking();

. . .

}





3. 

After each Test method, it internally calls similar to: 

closable.close();

@Override

public void afterEach(ExtensionContext context) {

…

context.getStore(MOCKITO)

.remove(SESSION, MockitoSession.class)

.finishMocking(context.getExecutionException().orElse(null));

…

}





Construction, Setter and Field injection rules and process is same like Annotation without Extension.
